en: Śrīḥ! To Him who, through the differentiation of the three qualities (*guṇa*), has assumed the three forms— Cakradatta, Chapter 1.1.

Salutations to the three-eyed Lord, the master of the three worlds and the source of the three Vedas. (1) By Cakrapāṇi, renowned for his various medical treatises and effective formulations, this compendium is composed, containing both cryptic and explanatory statements. (2)
First, the physician should examine the disease; immediately after that, the medicine; and thereafter, he should perform the therapeutic procedure, preceded by knowledge.
In the case of acute fever (navajvara), one should avoid sleeping during the day, bathing, oil massage, food, and sexual intercourse.

One should avoid anger, exposure to strong winds, physical exercise, and astringent decoctions. In the case of fever, fasting alone is prescribed at the outset, except for fevers arising from wasting, wind-disorders, fear, anger, lust, grief, or exhaustion.

The dosha, located in the stomach (āmāśaya), destroys the digestive fire (agni) and obstructs the channels by means of undigested matter (sāma); therefore, it produces fever, and one should employ fasting (laṅghana). Fasting is the means for maturing the doshas and regulating the unstable digestive fire.
It destroys fever, stimulates digestion, and produces appetite, relish, and lightness. One should treat the patient with fasting that does not conflict with the vital breaths,
for health is the foundation of strength, and this sequence of treatment is intended for that purpose.

However, that [procedure] should be performed when one is afflicted by wind, hunger, thirst, dryness of the mouth, or vertigo; it should not be done for a child, an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or one who is weak.
It is appropriate when there is the discharge of flatus, urine, and feces, and when there is lightness of the body.
When there is purity of the heart, vomit, throat, and mouth; when exhaustion from the disease has passed;

when perspiration has arisen; when there is also a loss of appetite; when hunger and thirst arise together; and when the inner self is free from distress—then fasting (laṅghana) is to be prescribed. (10–11)
Fracture-like pain in the joints, aching of the limbs, cough, dryness of the mouth,
loss of appetite, anorexia, thirst, weakness of the ears and eyes, mental agitation,
frequent upward movement of wind (eructation), and darkness in the heart [are the premonitory symptoms]. || 12 ||
Excessive fasting leads to the loss of bodily heat and strength;
however, Vāgbhaṭa states that for one who has just eaten when fever arises from over-nutrition (santarpaṇa), emesis is recommended for those fit for emetic therapy.

Having recognized that the doshas— predominantly kapha, aggravated, located in the stomach (āmāśaya), and causing fever— are ready for ejection at the proper time, one should eliminate them by means of emetics in those fit for emesis.
Emesis is contraindicated for those whose doshas have not yet manifested and in the early stage of fever.
It causes heart disease, dyspnea, flatulence, and intense delusion.

In a fever born of Vāta and Kapha, one should give warm water to the thirsty patient; however, in a Pitta-born fever that has arisen suddenly, one should give water cooled and boiled with bitter herbs.
It is both an illuminant and a digestive, a destroyer of fever, a purifier of the channels, strengthening, a provider of relish and perspiration,
and auspicious. [This is prepared] with musta, parpaṭaka, uśīra, candana, udīcya, and nāgara.
One should give water that has been boiled and cooled to alleviate thirst and fever. The administration of primary medicinal substances is forbidden in the case of acute fever;
therefore, medicine used for the preparation of water, gruel, and so forth, is faultless.
When the six-fold preparation (ṣaḍaṅga) and other such formulations are applied to water that has been boiled and cooled, one should take one karṣa of it and prepare it in one prastha of water.
Half-boiled, it should be administered for drinking or in the preparation of gruels (peyā) and similar foods.
One who has undergone emesis or fasting should, at the appropriate time, be treated with gruels (yavāgū) prepared from their respective medicinal herbs, preceded by medicated scum (maṇḍa). Initially,
one should give parched grain porridge (lājapeyā), which is easy to digest, boiled with long pepper (pippalī) and ginger (nāgara).
One suffering from fever should drink a fever-alleviating gruel at the very beginning; one with hunger or weak digestion should drink it first.
In cases of pain in the sides, bladder, or head, one should drink a fever-alleviating gruel prepared with *śvadaṃṣṭrā* and *kaṇṭakārī*, made from red *śāli* rice.
When the digestive tract is obstructed and accompanied by nausea, the fever patient should drink boiled gruel (peyā) prepared with raisins,
long pepper root, chavya, citraka, and ginger; or with the light five-roots (pañcamūla), or with the heavy five-roots, or with both of these along with coriander.

The preparation of decoctions, soups, and gruels should be administered in sequence for [disorders of] wind-pitta, wind-kapha, the three doṣas combined, and pitta-kapha. A gruel made with *vyāghrī*, *duḥsparśā*, and *gokṣura* destroys the three doṣas.
One should cook half a *karṣa* of *kaṇā* and *śuṇṭhī*, or one *pala* of any paste-like substance,
having dissolved it with a *prastha* of water according to the proper method; this procedure for the six-fold preparation (*ṣaḍaṅga-paribhāṣā*) is generally accepted for preparations such as *peyā*.
One should say that gruel (yavāgū) is made from one-fourth the portion of rice that would normally be used for a meal.
Maṇḍa is without lumps (siktha), while peyā is endowed with lumps.
Yavāgū should have many lumps, whereas vilepī is thin and liquid.
Rice-gruel (anna) is prepared with five parts of water, while thick gruel (vilepī) is prepared with four parts.
Maṇḍa is prepared with fourteen parts, and barley-gruel (yavāgū) with six parts of water.
Just as rain falling upon a heap of dust saturates an excessive amount of mud, [so too does the water saturate the grain].
Likewise, when phlegm (kapha) has increased, or during the onset of disease, for those habituated to wine, in summer, when pitta and kapha predominate,
in cases of upward-moving hemorrhage (raktapitta), and in fever, gruel (yavāgū) that increases phlegm is harmful.
In that case, a satiating drink (tarpaṇa) should first be administered, prepared with parched grain flour (lāja-śaktu).
These parched grain flours, mixed with honey and sugar and combined with fruit juices that alleviate fever, should be stirred with a liquid to form the satiating drink.
Meat broth with rice is always beneficial for fever arising from fatigue, fasting, or wind; furthermore, mung-bean soup with rice should be given when it arises from phlegm.
That same preparation, combined with sugar, is beneficial for fever caused by cold-pitta.

Red rice and other such grains, as well as old *ṣaṣṭika* rice, are recommended along with barley gruel, boiled rice, and parched grain for those suffering from fever; these alleviate fever. However, a soup made of mung beans and *āmalaka* is beneficial when the fever is of a nature involving both wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*).
Soup made from small radishes is beneficial for disorders characterized by kapha and vāta;
soup made from neem and radishes is beneficial for disorders characterized by pitta and kapha.
[One may also use] mung beans, masūra lentils, chickpeas, horse gram, and pigeon peas.
At the time of eating, one should cause these to be given as soup to the fever patient:
the leaf of *paṭola*, eggplant (*vārtāka*), *kulaka*, *kāravellaka*, *karkoṭaka*, *parpaṭaka*, *gojihvā*, and young radish (*bālamūlaka*). (40–41)
One should cause the leaves of *guḍūcī* to be given as a vegetable to one suffering from fever;
the fever-patient should eat what is beneficial even if he has no appetite,
for by not eating at mealtime, he wastes away or even dies.
In cases of loss of relish for food, one should take the filaments of a citron with ghee and rock salt;
or, one should hold in the mouth a paste of emblic myrobalan, grapes, and sugar.
By constant use, or because of its sweet nature, even that which has become loathsome becomes wholesome.
One should again induce a sense of fondness through various imaginative methods;
at the end of the day, one should feed the patient—whether suffering from fever or recently recovered—a light meal.
At that time, due to the depletion of phlegm, the digestive fire becomes powerful and its heat is greatly increased.
During times of heavy meals, excessive secretions (abhiṣyanda), or when fever is present, one should never eat anything at all.
For such a person, unwholesome food is detrimental neither to life nor to comfort;
instead, fasting, sudation, time, gruel, and bitter tastes are the remedies. (46–47)
Purgatives for undigested humors [should be used] in acute fever;
the wise say that acute fever lasts for seven nights.
That which lasts twelve nights is moderate, and beyond that it is considered chronic.
One should administer a digestive (pācana) or pacifying (śamanīya) decoction to that fever patient after six days have passed, once they have been fed light food.
Beyond seven days, if the fever is not stagnant and still possesses *āma*, a digestive decoction should be used.
In the case of a disease without *āma*, one should administer pacifying (*śamana*) measures; in the case of a disease with *āma*, one should apply medicinal remedies.
Excessive salivation, nausea, impurity of the heart, and loss of appetite [occur]; along with lethargy, indolence, indigestion, a bad taste in the mouth, and heaviness of the limbs. (51)
Loss of appetite, excessive urination, stiffness, and a powerful fever are the symptoms of *āmajvara* (fever caused by undigested matter). One should not administer medicine in that state;
for medicine given during the presence of *āmadoṣa* causes the fever to flare up even more.

One should recognize that the morbid humor (doṣa) is ripe when the fever is mild, the body is light, and the impurities are mobile; at that time, the medicine for the fever should be administered. [The following are the ingredients:
ginger, devadāru, dhanyāka, and the two types of bṛhatī.

One should first administer a digestive medicine that removes fever to the one suffering from fever. A person who has drunk water, undergone fasting, is emaciated, has undigested food, has already eaten, or is thirsty should not take medicine— whether it be for purification or otherwise.
Medicine that possesses superior potency and is not deficient in its ingredients will undoubtedly and swiftly destroy that disease,
even when consumed by children, the elderly, young women, or those of delicate constitution.
It quickly leads to extreme exhaustion and a loss of strength.

(57) When the wind moves in its natural direction (anuloma), there is health, hunger, thirst, cheerfulness of mind, lightness, purity of the senses and eructations, and the appearance of the medicine as digested. (58)
Fatigue, burning sensations, prostration of the limbs, vertigo, fainting, headache, restlessness, and loss of strength—these are the symptoms when medicine remains undigested.
When there is a residue of medicine, food that is eaten or drink that is consumed likewise produces these effects, as does food taken while a residue of the previous meal still remains. || 59 ||
It brings about the subsiding of the disease, provokes other ailments,
and undergoes digestion quickly; it does not destroy strength,
is not obstructed, and does not repeatedly emerge from the mouth.

Furthermore, this very same medicine that was previously consumed and found effective should be administered to the elderly, children, the timid, and excellent women. There is no fixed rule regarding the dosage; one must consider the humors (doṣa), the digestive fire (agni), strength, and age.
Having examined the disease, the substance, and the patient's constitution, one should administer the proper dose.

One *pala* is the dose for a person of superior strength, three *akṣas* for one of medium strength, and half a *pala* for one of inferior strength; this applies to both the oily substances and the medicinal drugs used in decoction.
From one *karṣa* up to one *pala*, one should add sixteen times the amount of water;
from that point until one *kuḍava*, the water should be eight times the quantity.
For one *pala* of the substance to be boiled, one should prepare half a *prastha* of water and reduce it to one-fourth.
Thirty-two *māṣakas* constitute one *māṣa* according to Caraka; with those [māṣas], sixteen make a *pala*.
According to Suśruta, however, forty-eight [grains] make a *māṣaka*;
with twelve *dhānya-māṣas*, and with sixty-four of those, a *pala* is formed.

And this *pala*, which consists of five *rakti*-weights, is weighed as half a *pala* according to Caraka; for in the Caraka-saṃhitā, a *pala* is said to be that which is formed by sixty-four *māṣas* of ten *raktikas* each. (67)
Therefore, a pala consists of sixty-four māṣakas and ten raktikas;
this is approved by Caraka and employed by physicians in medical treatment.
A decoction of the five roots beginning with bilva (bilvādi-pañcamūla) should be used in fever caused by vāta.
A decoction of long pepper root (pippalīmūla), guduchi (guḍūcī), and ginger (viśvaja), or one made from kirātatikta, usira, amṛtā, uśīra, the two types of bṛhatī,
and gokṣura, along with sthirā, kalasī, and viśva, removes vāta-fever.
A decoction of rāsnā, vṛkṣādanī, dāru, sarala, and elavāluka,
combined with sugar and honey, cures fever caused by vāta.
It is held that the additive (prakṣepa) should be one-fourth the weight of the decoction, and in the case of medicated fats (sneha), it should be equal in weight to the paste (kalka).
I consider this to be a general definition; however, others have stated that even in the case of additions, one *karṣa* each of powder, paste,
and pills should always be taken with two *śukti*s of liquid, or drunk with four liquids.
The dosage for honey, ghee, and so forth in medicated oils and decoctions should be like that for powders.
Furthermore, this decoction consisting of the five roots beginning with Bilva, along with Guḍūcī and Āmalaka, is equal to Kustumburu in its efficacy for fever caused by Vāta.
A decoction made from pippalī, śārivā, drākṣā, śatapuṣpā, and hareṇu, taken with jaggery, destroys fever born of vāta.
Guḍūcī, śārivā, drākṣā, śatapuṣpā, and punarnavā [are likewise used].
This decoction with jaggery (guḍa) is a destroyer of vāta-fever.
Having boiled grapes, guḍūcī, kāśmarya, trāyamāṇā, and śārivā,
one should drink that decoction with jaggery to remove vāta-fever.
The juice of śatāvarī and guḍūcī, pressed out by a machine and mixed with an abundance of jaggery, immediately pacifies fever caused by vāyu. [79] Kaliṅga, kaṭphala, musta, pāṭhā, and tiktakarohiṇī—
When the fever has matured, drinking [the decoction] with sugar acts as a digestive (pācana) for Pitta-type fever;
when Pitta is present, a digestive preparation made from Tiktā, Abda, and Indrayava, taken with honey, is effective.
A preparation of Lodhra, Utpala, Amṛtā, Padma, and Śārivā, mixed with sugar, [is likewise used].
A decoction [of *guḍūcī*] or one derived from *parpaṭa* destroys fever caused by *pitta*.
A decoction of *paṭola* and *yavanī*, sweetened with honey,
subdues acute *pitta*-fever and, when drunk, destroys thirst and burning sensations.
One should drink water saturated with sugar, prepared from durālabhā, parpaṭaka, priyaṅgu, bhūnimba, vāsā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
[This is for one] afflicted by thirst, hemorrhagic fever (asrapitta), fever, and burning sensations.
|| 83 Trāyamāṇā, madhuka, pippalīmūla, kirātatiktaka, musta, and madhuka along with bibhītaka. || 84
This [mixture], when drunk with sugar, destroys fever caused by pitta.
Equal parts of raisins, licorice, neem, katukā, and rohiṇī should be boiled and kept overnight in dew; this [preparation] removes pitta-fever. 85
A single *parpaṭaka* is excellent for destroying fever caused by *pitta*; how much more so if it is combined with sandalwood, *udīcya*, and *nāgara*!
[This decoction] prepared with *viśva*, water, *parpaṭa*, *uśīra*, *ghana*, and sandalwood—
One should give very cold water, which cures thirst, vomiting, fever, and burning sensations (87).
A decoction of parpaṭa, amṛta, and dhātrī removes pitta-fever; likewise, a decoction of drākṣā and āragvadha, or alternatively, one of kāśmarī (88).
One should administer a decoction of grapes (*drākṣā*), chebulic myrobalan (*abhayā*), *parpaṭaka*, *abdatikta*, and the fruit of *sampāka* for [the treatment of] delirium,
fainting, vertigo, burning sensations, and emaciation.
In a fever arising from pitta accompanied by thirst, however,
Dhanyāka-water that has stood overnight, when drunk in the morning with sugar, quickly pacifies internal burning even if it has been deeply rooted for a long time. || 89-90 ||
For one afflicted by a fever of the Pitta type, one should employ cooling treatments;
with Vidārī, pomegranate, Lodhra, Dadhittha, and Bījapūraka,
one should apply an ointment to the head of the person suffering from thirst and burning sensations.

An application of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) fried in ghee and ground with sour liquids, or a plaster of it, removes burning sensations. Alternatively, one should lick [the affected area] with very cold pastes made from the leaves of the *palāśa* tree,
or with the froth produced from *badarī* sprouts, or from *ariṣṭaka*.
An application of paste made from kālīya, sandalwood, anantā, yaṣṭī,

badara, and kāñjika, mixed with ghee, should be applied to the head for the alleviation of thirst, burning sensations, and pain. [94] For one lying on his back, [the area of] the deep copper-colored...
Placing a vessel made of bell-metal or similar material at the navel,
a copious stream of water falling thereon quickly destroys the burning pain due to its great coolness. || 95 ||
Covering with cold sour gruel and cloth cures burning sensations;
in cases of dryness of the tongue, palate, throat, and kloma, one should apply the filaments of the mātuluṅga fruit mixed with honey and rock salt to the head. 96.

In fever caused by *kapha*, water boiled with the roots of *mātuluṅga*, *viśva* (ginger), *brāhmī*, and *granthika*, along with alkali, acts as a digestive (*pācana*); or alternatively, a preparation of *kaṇā* and other such drugs may be used.
[These include] *pippalī*, *pippalīmūla*, *cavya*, *citraka*, and *nāgara*.
Marica, elā, ajamoda, indrayava, pāṭhā, reṇuka, jīraka, bhārgī, the fruit of mahānimba, hiṅgu, rohiṇī, sarṣapa, viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, and mūrvā— this is the group that has been proclaimed. (98–99)
The Pippalyādi group subdues kapha and destroys coryza, anorexia, and vāta; it is digestive, alleviates abdominal tumors (gulma) and colic, and digests undigested matter (āma).
[One should take] Citraka, Nimba, Haridrā, Ativiṣā, and Vacā, which are pungent.

One should drink *kuṣṭha*, *indrayava*, *mūrvā*, and *paṭola* prepared with black pepper and honey for fever caused by phlegm (*ślaiṣmika-jvara*). [Likewise, one may take] *nimba*, *viśva*, *amṛtā*, *dāru*, *śaṭī*, *bhūnimba*, and *pauṣkara*. (101–102)
A decoction of *pippalī* and *bṛhatī* destroys fever caused by *kapha*;
likewise, a decoction of *sindhuvāra* leaves is a drying agent for fever born of *kapha*.
One should drink it when strength in the calves has diminished or when the ears are blocked.
The group consisting of āmalakī, abhayā, kṛṣṇā, and citraka breaks up all fevers and afflictions caused by phlegm; it is digestive and carminative. [The group] triphalā, paṭola, and vāsā...
In cases arising from phlegm (kapha), [one should use] chinnaruhā, atiktarohiṇī, and ṣaḍgranthā with honey;
or alternatively, a decoction of daśamūla and vāsaka. || 105 ||
A decoction of Musta, Vatsaka seeds, Triphalā, Kaṭurohiṇī, and Parūṣaka destroys fever caused by Kapha.
Kaṭphala, Pauṣkara, Śṛṅgī, and Kṛṣṇā, taken together with honey [are likewise effective].

This excellent electuary (leha) removes cough, dyspnea, and fever, and brings an end to phlegm. A karṣa measure of powder, paste, or pills—whichever is appropriate—should be licked with two shuktis of liquid, or drunk with four parts liquid. 107–108.
This linctus (avalehikā) is a destroyer of diseases of the supraclavicular region;
however, that which is taken before a meal is considered a remover of diseases of the infraclavicular region.
A combination of honey and Pippalī (Upakulyā) cures cough, dyspnea, and fever.
It destroys splenic disorders and hiccups, and is highly recommended for children;
it is beneficial when the doṣas are combined, acting as a digestive for those combined humors. [This is prepared] with viśvā, amṛtā, abda, bhūnimba, and the two pañcamūlis.
A decoction prepared [from these] quickly destroys fever arising from wind (vāta) and bile (pitta).
Water boiled with triphalā, śālmalī, rāsnā, rājavṛkṣa, and aparūṣaka swiftly removes fever arising from wind and bile.

Having decocted kirātatikta, amṛtā, drākṣā, āmalakī, and śaṭhī, one should drink that decoction with jaggery (guḍa) for disorders arising from pitta and vāta. [One may also use] a decoction prepared with nidigdhikā, balā, rāsnā, trāyamāṇā, and amṛtā.
A decoction made from *masūravidala* beans conquers fever caused by *vāta* and *pitta*.
*Guḍūcī*, *parpaṭa*, *musta*, *kirāta*, and *viśvabheṣaja*—this auspicious "Five-Fortunate" (*pañcabhadra*) formulation should be administered for fever caused by *vāta* and *pitta*. (114–115)
One should place madhuka, sārivā, grapes, madhuka, candana, utpala, kāśmarī, padmaka, lodhra, triphalā, padmakeśara, parūṣaka,
and lotus stalks in excellent water.
That [milk], mixed with honey, parched rice, and sugar,
when drunk and kept overnight, pacifies fever caused by wind and bile, as well as burning sensations, thirst, fainting, vomiting, and vertigo;
it also subdues internal hemorrhaging (rakta-pitta), just as the wind disperses clouds.
20. Paṭola, candana, mūrvā, tiktā, pāṭhā, and the group of drugs beginning with amṛtā remove pitta, kapha, anorexia, vomiting, fever, itching, and poison.
Guḍūcī, nimba, dhānyāka, padmaka, and the various types of candana [also have these properties].

This [decoction] destroys all fevers; however, the *guḍūcy-ādi* group is digestive and destroys nausea, anorexia, vomiting, thirst, and burning sensations. When phlegm (kapha) is predominant, one should use *kirātatiktaka*, ginger, *musta*, and *guḍūcī*.
In cases where pitta is predominant, one should drink [the decoction] with lotus stalks and water from the north-flowing river.
Kaṇṭakārī, amṛtā, bhārgī, nāgara, indrayava, āsaka, bhūnimba, candana, musta, paṭola, and kaṭurohiṇī [are used for this]. 121–122ab.

One should administer this decoction of *kāṣāya*; it removes fever caused by *pitta* and *kapha*, and cures burning sensations, thirst, loss of appetite, vomiting, cough, and pain in the heart and flanks.
The juice of *vāsā* along with its leaves and flowers, combined with honey and sugar, [is likewise effective].
It destroys fever born of phlegm and bile, as well as hemorrhagic fever (asṛkpitta) and jaundice (kāmalā).
This decoction, prepared from paṭola, picumarda, triphalā, madhuka, and balā, is effective for fever arising from the combination of bile and phlegm.
Guduchi, indrayava, arishta, patola, katurohini, nagara, candana, musta, and pippali combined with powder—
this is known as Amṛtāṣṭaka; it destroys fever caused by pitta and kapha.
It alleviates nausea, anorexia, vomiting, thirst, and burning sensations.
Paṭola, barley, dhanyāka, mudga, āmalaka, and candana alleviate thirst, vomiting, and burning sensations in fevers arising from pitta or from kapha-pitta.
One should drink this decoction of the five bitter herbs (*pañcatikta*) here, consisting of *kṣudra*, *amṛtā*, *nāgara*, *pauṣkara*, and *kirātatikta*.
It destroys all eight types of fever completely.
By drinking one akṣa measure of kaṭukā with sugar and warm water,
a person shall conquer fever arising from kapha and pitta.

A decoction of coriander (*dhānya*) and *paṭola* stimulates digestion, cuts through phlegm (*kapha*), harmonizes wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*), destroys fever, promotes digestion, and acts as a purgative.
In cases of fever caused by phlegm and wind, one should administer sudations prepared with dry substances.
By softening the channels, drawing [the humors] into the site of the digestive fire,
and destroying the stiffness caused by Vāta and Kapha, sudation dispels fever.
Indeed, sand-sudation involves pouring fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*) over a cloth heated in an iron pan and placed within the sand.
It pacifies diseases of wind and phlegm, as well as headaches, body aches, and the like.
(133) This triad of Musta, Nāgara, and Bhūnimba, each weighing three karṣas, pacifies phlegm, wind, and fever; it is digestive and destroys fever. (134)
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, and nāgara are known as the digestive-stimulating group (dīpanīya-varga), which removes diseases caused by kapha and vāta.
Water boiled with pippalīs is non-obstructive to the channels and stimulates digestion.

This decoction, prepared with *āragvadha*, *granthika*, *musta*, *tiktā*, and *harītakī*, destroys disorders of wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*), and cures splenic enlargement and fever. || 136 ||

This [decoction] made with *kṣudrā*, *amṛtā*, *nāgara*, and *puṣkarāhvaya* is beneficial for fever associated with *sāma*, *śūla*, *kapha*, and *vāta*, and it acts as a digestive stimulant (*dīpana*) and a digestive aid (*pācana*). || 137 || 26 ||

This decoction is prepared and is recommended for fevers arising from phlegm and wind, as well as those arising from the three doṣas, when accompanied by dyspnea, cough, anorexia, and pain in the flanks. || 138 ||

The decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī) mixed with long pepper (kaṇā) should be drunk in cases of Kapha-Vata disorders, indigestion, excessive sleepiness, pain in the flanks, dyspnea, and cough. Musta, parpaṭaka, ginger (śuṇṭhī), gudūcī, and duralabhā [should be used].
It removes disorders of phlegm and wind, as well as anorexia, vomiting, burning sensations, emaciation, and fever.

A decoction made from *dāru*, *parpaṭa*, *bhārgī*, *mustā*, *vacā*, *dhānyaka*, and *kaṭphala*, along with *abhayā*, *viśva*, and *bhūtika*, combined with *hiṅgu* and honey, [is similarly effective]. (140–141)
When drunk during a fever caused by *kapha* and *vāta*, it destroys hiccups, dyspnea, throat obstruction,
cough, emaciation, and excessive salivation, just as a thunderbolt destroys a tree.
[The dosage] for fats such as honey and ghee, as well as for decoctions, is like that for powders.
Honey, asafoetida, rock salt, and the group beginning with *jaraṇa* should each be one *śāṇa* in measure.
The filament of the *mātuluṅga* fruit, held in the mouth together with rock salt and black pepper— || 143 ||
It quickly destroys diseases of wind and phlegm, dryness of the mouth, numbness, and loss of appetite. (144) Fasting, sand-sweating, nasal medication, and likewise spitting [are also beneficial].
In a fever born of the three doṣas (tridoṣaja), linctus and collyrium should be administered first.
In a fever of combined morbidity (sannipāta-jvara), one should first eliminate the undigested matter (āma) and phlegm (kapha);
once the phlegm has been diminished, one should then pacify bile (pitta) and wind (vāta).
In cases of *sannipāta* (combined humors), one should practice fasting for three nights, five nights, or even ten nights, until health is observed.
That very capacity for endurance is the power of the *doṣas* themselves that enables fasting.
For no one who has diminished his humors (doṣas) can tolerate fasting and similar depletive therapies.
One should hold rock salt together with ginger juice and the three pungents (kaṭutrika) in the mouth up to the throat and spit it out again and again. (148–149)
By that [action], phlegm is drawn out from his heart, as well as from the sides, head, and throat; even when it is dried up, it is extracted, and lightness arises within him.
(150) There is pain in the joints, aching of the limbs, fainting, cough, and diseases of the throat.
Heaviness of the face and eyes, stupor, and nausea are pacified.
One should perform this once, twice, three, or four times, having observed the relative strength and weakness of the humors (doṣas).
Indeed, they declare this to be the supreme medicine for those afflicted by the combination of all three humors (sannipāta).
One should administer as a nasal drop (nasya) lukewarm juice of *mātuluṅga* or *ārdraka*, combined with the three salts (*trilavaṇa*), or any other sharp preparation prescribed for success;
by this, the phlegm is broken up, and once broken up, it is discharged.
Pain in the head, heart, throat, mouth, and sides is also pacified. 154.

Equal parts of madhūkasāra, rock salt (sindhūttha), vacā, black pepper (uṣaṇa), and long pepper (kaṇā) should be finely ground with water and used as a nasal drop (nasya) to restore consciousness. 155.
Saindhava salt, white pepper, mustard seeds, and kuṣṭha,
ground together with goat's urine and used as a nasal drop (nasya), ward off drowsiness. [Likewise,
a preparation] of śirīṣa seeds, cow’s urine, pippalī, black pepper, and saindhava salt [is effective].
An ointment for awakening [the senses] should be prepared with *rasāñjana*, realgar, and *vacā*. 157.
One should lick a fine powder of *kaṭphala*, *pauṣkara*, *śṛṅgī*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *yāsa*, and *kāravī*, together with honey. 158.
This electuary destroys even the most dreadful *sannipāta* (combined humoral disorder),
and it subdues hiccups, dyspnea, cough, and diseases of the throat.
It is used for the expulsion of phlegm moving upward and for procedures such as hot fomentation (*uṣṇasveda*).
In cases where honey is contraindicated due to heat, one should perform the treatment using the juices of fresh ginger.
Having taken one handful each of barley, jujube, horse-gram, mung-bean, radish, and sugar-cane pieces, one should boil them in eight times the amount of water.
This group known as *pañcamūla* (the five roots) removes wind, bile, and phlegm;
it is recommended for abdominal tumors (*gulma*), colic, dyspnea, cough, consumption, and fever.
The *pañcamūla-kirātādi* group should be employed in cases arising from all three *doṣas*.

When pitta is predominant, [it should be taken] with honey; when kapha is predominant, with long pepper (kaṇā). Bilva, syonāka, gambhārī, pāṭalā, and gaṇikārikā constitute this "great five roots" (mahat-pañcamūla), which is digestive and destroys kapha and vāta.
Śāliparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, the two types of bṛhatī, and gokṣura constitute the minor pañcamūla; it removes vāta and pitta and is aphrodisiac.
Both [the minor and major] together form the daśamūla, which cures fevers caused by the combination of all three doṣas (sannipāta).
Combined with powdered long pepper (pippalī), it is recommended for cough, dyspnea, drowsiness, and pain in the flanks; it destroys afflictions of the throat and heart,
or [is used] in chronic fever characterized by a predominance of vāta and kapha.

In cases arising from the three doṣas, the group of drugs beginning with kirātatikta mixed with daśamūla should be employed; or, for one seeking purification, it may be used unmixed with vivṛtā. || 167 ||
Daśamūlī, śaṭhī, śṛṅgī, pauṣkara, durālabhā, bhārgī, kuṭaja seeds, paṭola, and kaṭurohiṇī—
this is the eighteen-ingredient (aṣṭādaśāṅga) formulation, which removes fever caused by the combination of all three doṣas (sannipāta-jvara).

This decoction of bhūnimba, dāru, the ten roots (daśamūla), mahauṣadha, abda, tikta, indrabīja, dhanika, ibhakaṇā, and kaṣāya removes cough, cardiac oppression, pain in the flanks, dyspnea, hiccups, and vomiting. || 169 ||

Musta, parpaṭaka, uśīra, devadāru, and mahauṣadha quickly destroy every type of fever accompanied by trembling, delirium, coughing, loss of appetite, burning sensations, delusion, dyspnea, and so forth. || 170 || 36 || [Note: The numbering "170 36" appears to be a scribal or structural marker.]
Triphalā, dhanvayāsa, nīlī, kampillaka, trivṛt,
kirātatiktaka, pāṭhā, balā, kaṭukarohiṇī, madhuka, and pippalīmūla— this is called the group beginning with mustā (mustādi-gaṇa). 171–172.

This eighteen-fold formulation, thus described, is said by the wise to be beneficial for the pacification of *sannipāta* where *pitta* is predominant, as well as for stiffness of the neck (*manyāstambha*), oppression of the chest (*uroghāta*), and pain in the chest, flanks, and head. (173)
37. Śaṭhī, puṣkaramūla, vyāghrī, śṛṅgī, durālabhā, guḍūcī, nāgara, pāṭhā, kirāta, and kaṭurohiṇī—
this group beginning with śaṭhī destroys fevers caused by the simultaneous derangement of the three humors (sannipāta).
It is recommended for cough, cardiac oppression, pain in the flanks, dyspnea, and lassitude. (175) The two types of *bṛhatī*, *puṣkara*, *bhārgī*, *śaṭhī*, *śṛṅgī*, *durālabhā*,
the seeds of *vatsaka*, *paṭola*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*— (176)

The group beginning with *bṛhatī* is declared to remove fevers caused by the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta*), and it should be administered in all cases of cough and other such ailments, even when accompanied by complications. One should decoct nagara, daśamūla, and pippalī in water;
this should be administered in cases of sannipāta fever to those suffering from pain and distension in the heart and flanks,
and it will eliminate cough, dyspnea, weak digestion, and drowsiness.

A decoction made from the two groups of five roots (dvipañcamūlī), ṣaḍgranthā, viśvā, and the two types of gṛdhranakhī, is a supreme remedy for eliminating kapha and vāta, as well as for curing sannipāta. [Furthermore: kāravī, puṣkara, eraṇḍa, trāyantī, nāgara, and amṛtā...
The ten roots (daśamūlī), śaṭhī, śṛṅgī, yāsā, bhārgī, and punarnavā—these taken in equal parts, decocted with urine and drunk, cleanse the channels;
they quickly destroy even a severe, fully manifested fever of the abhinyāsa type. || 181–182 ||
A decoction made from *mātuluṅga*, *aśvabhida*, *bilva*, *vyāghrī*, *pāṭhā*, and *urubūka*,
enriched with salt and urine, cures *abhinyāsa*, abdominal distension (*ānāha*), and colic.
One should recognize that *abhinyāsa* accompanied by sleepiness as being caused by the depletion of the vital essence (*ojas*).
One afflicted by the obstruction of the throat, phlegm, dyspnea, hiccups,
or the state of near-death (saṃnyāsa) should drink the juice of *mātuluṅga* and fresh ginger with a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*),
along with *vyoṣa*, *abja*, *triphalā*, *tiktā*, *paṭola*, *ariṣṭa*, and *vāsaka*.

A decoction made from *sabhūnimbāmṛtāyāsa* (neem, guḍūcī, and kṛtavedhana) cures clear fever caused by the three doṣas. A decoction prepared with *trivṛt*, *viśālā*, *triphalā*, *kaṭukā*, and *āragvadha*, along with alkali (*kṣāra*), acts as a purgative and should be drunk to alleviate all fevers.
In a fever accompanied by the breaking out of perspiration, a powder made from fried horse gram (kulattha) should be administered.
One should rub a stiff tongue with rock salt, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and sour vetasa;
a dry or cracked tongue should be rubbed with grapes ground with honey.
In a fever caused by the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta), one should smear the mouth with ghee;
the root of *kākajaṅghā* placed upon the head induces sleep.
One should not nourish a patient suffering from sannipāta who is trembling and delirious.
Even when overcome by the burning heat of thirst, one should not give cool water;
at the end of a fever caused by the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta), a most terrible swelling arises at the base of the ear, and because of it, only a rare few are liberated.
One should first conquer that [condition] by bloodletting and the drinking of clarified butter (sarpiḥ),
using plasters (pradeha) that subdue kapha and pitta, as well as emetics and gargles (kavalagraha).
[The paste consists of] red ochre (gairika), sandy earth (pāṃśuka), ginger (śuṇṭhī), sweet flag (vacā), katuka, and sour gruel (kāñjika).
This is a highly effective medicinal paste for removing swelling from the ear in cases of *sannipāta* fever (193).
Equal parts of horse gram (*kulattha*), *kaṭphala*, ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), and *kāravī* should be applied as a warm compress repeatedly at the base of the ear (194).
One should drink a decoction of *nidigdhikā*, *nāgaraka*, and *amṛtā*, mixed with *pippalī*,
for chronic fever, loss of appetite, cough, and colic.

In cases of dyspnea, weak digestion, chest afflictions, and catarrh, this decoction of *chinnaruhā* (guḍūcī), combined with powdered *pippalī*, generally destroys upward-moving diseases; therefore, it is to be administered in the evening. || 195–196 ||
Prepared with the five roots (pañcamūlī), it destroys chronic fever and phlegm,
and cures cough, indigestion, loss of appetite, dyspnea, heart disease, anemia, and worms.
When the fever is chronic and the digestive fire is weakened, jaggery and long pepper (guḍapippalī) are recommended.
Kaliṅgaka, the leaf of paṭola, and kaṭukarohiṇī;
(198) paṭola, śārivā, musta, pāṭhā, and kaṭukarohiṇī;
nimba, paṭola, triphalā, mṛdvīkā, musta, and vatsaka. (199)
Kirātatikta, amṛtā, candana, viśvabheṣaja,
guḍūcī, āmalaka, and musta—
these five decoctions, completed in half-verses, quickly pacify the five types of fevers.
One afflicted by irregular fevers— whether continuous, quotidian, tertian, or quartan— should drink Triphalā mixed with plenty of jaggery;
or one may use the collyrium known as Dīrghapatraka-karṇa combined with Khadira.
On that day, betel leaves consumed in the morning destroy poison;
or one may take a decoction of *guḍūcī*, *mustā*, and *dhātrī* mixed with honey.
[Verse 203] 42. *Mustā*, *āmalaka*, and *guḍūcī*—
A decoction of Viśvauṣadha and Kaṇṭakārī, drunk with powdered Pippalī and honey, destroys irregular fever. || 204 ||
A decoction prepared with mahauṣadha, amṛtā, musta, candana, uśīra, and dhānyaka, combined with sugar and honey, destroys tertian fever (tṛtīyaka).
A decoction prepared with vāsā, dhātrī, uśīra, dāru, pathyā, and nāgara [also cures it].
A decoction of *sitā* (white sugar) mixed with honey cures quartan fever (*cāturthaka*).
The juice extracted from the leaves of *śephālī* taken with honey removes all fevers.
Cumin seeds combined with jaggery destroy irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*).
One who, afflicted by intermittent fever, eats the paste of garlic mixed with sesame oil daily, will properly conquer digestive weakness and destroy wind-related diseases. (207)
He too is soon liberated from fever and even from most terrible wind-related ailments;
one should consume garlic with ghee every morning.
Or one should drink increasing doses of long pepper (pippalī) while subsisting on milk and meat broth;
or one should drink six-pala of ghee, or drink myrobalan (pathyā) with honey; or likewise, milk, oil, ghee, vidārī root juice, sugarcane juice, and honey.
Having crushed these together, one should cause [the patient] to drink this, which destroys irregular fever (viṣamajvara):
long pepper, sugar, honey, ghee, and milk, according to one's strength.
Stirred with a churning-stick, it should be drunk as a destroyer of irregular fever.
When the urge for defecation arises, one should drink the dung of a cat with milk;
or, with the whey of curd or wine, one should take the dung of a bull along with rock salt, as well as *nīlinī*, *ajagandhā*, *trivṛtā*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*. (212–213)
When a fever approaches, one who has been prepared with oleation and sudation should drink wine with its dregs for the purpose of drinking, and eat peacocks for the purpose of eating; likewise,
one should employ partridges and peacocks in the case of intermittent fever.
One should drink well-prepared *peyā* (gruel) saturated with ghee, made with a thousand leaves of *amlōṭaja*, for three days; this cures quartan fever.
[Also, one may take] rock salt, long pepper, rice grains, and realgar.
Collyrium for the eyes ground with oil destroys intermittent fever (*viṣamajvara*).
Likewise, a nasal drop (*nasya*) consisting of equal parts of *vyāghrī* juice, asafoetida (*ahiṅgu*), and rock salt (*saindhava*) has the same effect.
[Furthermore,] that which is produced from *guggulu* and an owl's tail, firmly bound in black cloth...
This incense destroys quartan fever, just as the risen sun dispels darkness.
The juice of *śirīṣa* flowers combined with the two types of *rajanī* (turmeric),
when used as a nasal drop along with ghee, conquers quartan fever.
The juice produced from the leaves of the Agastya plant destroys quartan fever;
likewise, incense made of palankaṣā, nimba leaves, vacā, kuṣṭha, harītakī,
mustard seeds, and barley, mixed with ghee, is a destroyer of fever.

This "Unconquered" (Aparājita) incense, which cures all fevers, should be prepared with *puradhyāma*, *vacā*, *sarjani*, *nimba*, *arka*, *aguru*, and *dāru*. For one who is trembling, cat dung (*vaiḍāla*) should be added to the incense.
The root of *apāmārga*, tied to the waist with seven red threads on a Sunday, quickly destroys tertian fever (*tṛtīyaka-jvara*).
[Likewise,] *kākajaṅghā*, *balā*, *śyāmā*, *brahmadaṇḍā*, and *kṛtāñjali* [are effective].
Pṛśniparṇī, apāmārga, and likewise bhṛṅgaraja as the eighth—
having carefully uprooted the root of any one of these along with its flower,
and having wrapped it with a red thread, when bound [to the patient], it conquers the *aikāhika* fever.
The root of jayantī, when worn upon the head, removes all fevers; it overcomes common ailments and specifically conquers tertian and quartan fevers.
For in irregular fever (viṣamajvara), an external cause is generally the underlying factor.
On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, a childless ascetic died;
one should offer him water with sesame seeds, and the fever lasting for a single day will be released.
Holding an *aśvattha* leaf in his hand, he should perform the libation with this mantra.
By worshipping the god Soma together with his attendants, his mother-goddesses, and the Lord (Īśvara), one who is self-restrained is quickly liberated from chronic fever.
[One should likewise worship] Viṣṇu, the thousand-headed, the all-pervading Lord of the moving and unmoving.
By praising [the deity] with the Thousand Names, one dispels all fevers.
For those whose fevers are not pacified by astringents, forest decoctions, fasting, or light diets—because they are dry—clarified butter is the physician’s remedy for them. (230–231)

Even if ten days have passed, a wise physician, knowing that the patient has a predominance of *kapha* and has undergone emesis (*alaṅghita*), should not administer ghee; rather, he should treat him with palliative (*śamana*) measures.
Until lightness [of the body] is achieved, one should give food along with meat broth.
For the sake of meat, a wise physician should prescribe the flesh of the ena deer, the lāva bird, and others; however,
some physicians do not recommend chickens, peacocks, partridges, or cranes in cases of fever because of their heavy and hot nature.
If, due to fasting, the strength of the wind (vāyu) becomes excessive in fever, the physician who knows the variations of dosage and understands the proper time should administer these as well:
long pepper, sandalwood, nut-grass, ushira root, and katurohini.
Ghee prepared with kaliṅgaka, tāmalakī, śārivā, ativiṣā,
sthirā, drākṣā, āmalaka, bilva, trāyamāṇā,
and nidigdhikā immediately removes even chronic fever.
This Pippalyādi formulation subdues consumption, cough, headache, pain in the flanks, chlorosis, bodily fever, and irregular digestion;
in some tantras, it is prepared with milk.
In that very case where no mention of a paste (kalka) occurs in the context of the preparation of an oil or fat, a paste and a decoction (niryūha) are prescribed by the expert in fats;
it is solely on the strength of this statement that ghee is considered to be prepared with a paste. 239–240.
47. Where the proportions of water, oil, and medicinal herbs have not been specified, there the oil should be equal to the medicinal herbs, and the water four times the amount of the oil.
When no liquid is mentioned for a specific purpose, water is understood to be used in all such cases.
One should not remove ghee, oil, molasses, and the like from the fire on the same day;
for when they have stood overnight, they especially produce superior qualities.
When the oily paste, rolled between the fingers, becomes like a wick, [it is ready].
If no sound is heard when [the substance] is thrown into the fire, then one should indicate success;
likewise when the sound has ceased and the foam has subsided.
When there is perfection of smell, color, taste, and so forth, one should predict success.

Ghee (clarified butter) cooked with five *kolās* of each [of the aforementioned drugs] along with one *palika* of rock salt (*saindhava*), together with an equal quantity of milk, in the measure of one *prastha*, cures splenic enlargement, irregular fever, and abdominal tumors (*gulma*). Since no other liquid is specified here, milk alone is to be used as the fourfold liquid medium.
For when mixed with another liquid, milk becomes equal in consistency to oil.
Ghee prepared with the decoction of daśamūla, along with milk, the five spices (pañcakola),
and alkali, destroys all [ailments], including fever, cough, and weak digestion.

[This decoction cures] diseases of wind, bile, and phlegm, as well as splenic disorders and jaundice. Water should be four times the quantity of the drugs to be boiled; when reduced to one-fourth, it should be four times the quantity of the oil. The milk should be equal to the oil, and the paste (kalka) should be one-fourth the quantity of the oil.

In the preparation of an oily enema (sneha), if there are five or more liquid ingredients, they should be four times the quantity of the oil; however, if there are fewer than five, the liquids should be eight times the quantity of the oil.
In cases where there are four or fewer liquids, they say the liquids should be equal to the oil, or at least four times its amount.
Having boiled vāsā, guḍūcī, triphalā, trāyamāṇā, and yavāsaka, one should [prepare a medicated ghee] with that decoction and twice as much milk,
along with pippalī, māṃsī, mṛdvīkā, candana, utpala, and nāgara.
One should cook ghee with the paste of these [drugs] ground into a pulp; it removes chronic fever.
Oils prepared with the decoction and paste of guḍūcī, triphalā, vṛṣa, mṛdvīkā, and balā likewise destroy fever.
In cases of fever, gruels, decoctions, clarified butter, milk, and purgatives should be administered every six days, having observed the timing and the nature of the disease.
In chronic fever, when the phlegm has been diminished, milk is like nectar.

That very same [milk], if drunk while it is still fresh, kills a man like poison. By drinking milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī), one who is feverish is freed from cough, dyspnea, headache, pain in the flanks, and catarrh.
Eight parts of milk and four parts of water for every part of the medicinal substance—this is the rule for the preparation of milk decoctions; the milk should be reduced until only the milk remains.
[This preparation] is prepared with Trikaṇṭaka, Balā, Bilva, jaggery, and ginger.
Milk cures the obstruction of feces and urine, and removes swelling and fever.
One should boil vṛścīra, viśva, varṣābhū, payas, and water until only the milk remains; for that indeed destroys all fevers.

In fever, milk that is cold or lukewarm, combined with appropriate medicinal herbs, or prepared with the root of *eraṇḍa*, should be given; likewise, for those suffering from fever with abundant morbid humors (*doṣas*), the wise physician should administer it both upwards and downwards. (260)
One should administer a purificatory therapy at the proper time as prescribed in the Kalpa section.
Madana fruit, combined with either long pepper (pippalī), Indian berberry (kaliṅga), or licorice (madhuka), when drunk with warm water, acts as an emetic for the alleviation of fever.
A person suffering from fever should drink either āragvadha with milk or with the juice of grapes, or trivṛt or trāyamāṇā with milk.
For one who is emaciated by fever, neither emesis nor purgation is beneficial.
One may indeed remove his impurities with milk or with decoction enemas (nirūha). One should administer fever-alleviating decoction enemas along with oil enemas (anuvāsana),
as well as those which will be described in the Siddhisthāna for when the doshas have reached the colon (pakvāśaya).
In cases of heaviness, headache, and impaired functioning of the sense organs due to chronic fever, one should administer head-purgatives (śīrṣavirecana) that stimulate the appetite,
as well as oil massages, medicinal pastes, unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), and similar treatments.
The physician should administer [medicines] prepared with cold or hot substances after differentiation in the case of chronic fever (jīrṇajvara).
By these means, the fever that has moved to the external channels is quickly pacified;
the limbs attain comfort, and strength and complexion increase.
Oil prepared with *suvarcikā*, *nāgara*, *kuṣṭha*, *mūrvā*, *lākṣā*, *niśā*, *lohitayaṣṭikā*,
and six times the amount of buttermilk (*takra*) is used for fever.
From massage with it, coldness and burning sensations are dispelled.
(269) In this case, buttermilk made from curd with its whey is desired; the cooking of oil is also like that of ghee, though the foam in oil is greater. (270)

One should cook one *prastha* of oil with one *āḍhaka* of fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*) and the following ingredients: *mūrvā*, lac, the two types of *haridrā*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *indravāruṇī*, *bṛhatī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *kuṣṭha*, *rāsnā*, *māṃsī*, and *śatāvarī*. (271)
The oil known as Aṅgāraka liberates one from all fevers.
One should cook oil with the pastes of lac, turmeric, and mañjiṣṭhā, along with six times the amount of sour gruel (āranāla); this removes burning sensations and cold-fevers.
Half a *kuḍava* of barley powder and half a *pala* of *mañjiṣṭhā*,
cooked with one *prastha* of oil in a hundred times as much *kāñjika*,
conquers fever, burning sensations of great intensity, and the shivering of the limbs. (274)

Oil prepared with *sarja* and sour gruel (*kāñjika*), rubbed with cold water and applied as an ointment, immediately removes fever and burning sensations, and alleviates the burning of *vātāsra*. The oils known as *Candanādya* and *Agurvādya* have been proclaimed by Caraka. (275–276)
Likewise, Nārāyaṇa oil is supreme for removing chronic fever;
by drinking ghee or by its application as an ointment, fever resulting from injury shall not occur. For those with chest wounds or ulcers, it serves as the treatment for those wounds and sores.

A wise person should conquer fevers caused by medicinal herbs, perfumes, or poison by means of anti-poisonous remedies, decoctions, and likewise by preparations made from all types of fragrant substances; furthermore,
one should conquer fevers arising from malevolent magic (abhicāra) or curses through fire oblations (homa) and other such rites.
Through acts of charity, auspicious rites, and hospitality, one overcomes the effects of portents and planetary afflictions;
through anger, one overcomes bile-born ailments; and through desired objects as well as virtuous speech, one attains consolation and the pacification of wind-born disorders. (280)
And by means of gladdening things, the fevers of desire, anger, and fear are pacified.
From desire, the fever of anger goes to its destruction; from anger, that which arises from desire perishes;
and from both of these, the fever arising from fear and grief is destroyed.

One should overcome mental afflictions arising from possession by spirits through the binding, entering, and striking prescribed in the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā), and one should pacify the mind with soothing measures.
Furthermore, one should avoid excessive physical exertion, sexual intercourse, bathing, and long walks.
One who has been freed from fever should not engage in activity until he has regained his strength;
[the signs of recovery are] a light body, the departure of fatigue, delusion, and heat, as well as the proper digestion of food, ease, excellence of the sense organs, and freedom from pain.
Perspiration, sneezing, a mind returning to its natural state, a desire for food, and itching on the head are the signs of the subsiding of fever.
(285) Adhikāra 2.
In cases of fever with diarrhea (jvarātisāra), a regimen beginning with thin gruel (peyā) is beneficial for one who has undergone fasting (laṅghita).
A person suffering from fever and diarrhea should drink either sour or boiled gruel prepared with *pṛśniparṇī*,
*balā*, *bilva*, ginger (*nāgara*), blue lotus (*utpala*), and coriander (*dhānyaka*).
Pāṭhā, indrayava, bhūnimba, musta, parpaṭaka,
and amṛtā— these, along with mahauṣadha, conquer diarrhea accompanied by fever.
[2] Nāgara, ativiṣā, musta, bhūnimba, amṛta, and vatsaka— [3]

A decoction made from *hrīvera*, *ativiṣā*, *musta*, *bilva*, *dhānyaka*, and *nāgara* removes all fevers and destroys all types of diarrhea. One should drink this, which cures the obstruction of mucus, alleviates colic, and digests undigested toxins (*āma*).
It cures diarrhea accompanied by blood, whether with fever or without fever.
[This is prepared] with guḍūcī, ativiṣā, dhānyaka, śuṇṭhī, bilva, abda, bālaka, pāṭhā, bhūnimba, kuṭaja, candana, uśīra, and padmaka.
This decoction should be drunk cold for the alleviation of fever and diarrhea; it destroys nausea, anorexia, vomiting, thirst, and burning sensations.
[It consists of] uśīra, bālaka, musta, dhanyāka, and viśvabheṣaja.
Samaṅgā, dhātakī, lodhra, and bilva are digestive stimulants and carminatives;
they destroy anorexia, slimy stools, constipation, and excessive pain, as well as dysentery with blood, whether accompanied by fever or free from it.
A decoction prepared with the five roots (pañcamūlī), balā, bilva, guḍūcī, musta, nāgara, pāṭhā, bhūnimba, hrīvera, and the bark and fruits of kuṭaja,
destroys all types of diarrhea, as well as fever, morbid humors, and vomiting.
It destroys severe asthma accompanied by the complication of colic, as well as cough.
Kaliṅga, ativiṣā, śuṇṭhī, kirātatiktaka, water,
and yavāsaka undoubtedly destroy fever, diarrhea, and burning heat.
Vatsaka, kaṭphala, dāru, rohiṇī, gajapippalī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, pippalī, dhānya, bilva, pāṭhā, and yavānikā—
both of these successful formulations (siddhiyoga) have been declared in half a verse each.
[This decoction] specifically pacifies fever and diarrhea, and alleviates burning sensations and cutting pains.
Water boiled with ginger, amṛtā, bhūnimba, bilva, vālaka,
vatsaka, mustā, ativiṣā, and uśīra removes fever and diarrhea.

A decoction made from musta, bilva, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, bhūnimba, and vatsaka, combined with honey, overcomes severe fever and diarrhea. [16] A decoction made from ghanajala, pāṭhā, ativiṣā, pathyā, utpala, dhānya, rohiṇī, and viśva...
Water prepared with indrayava conquers fever accompanied by diarrhea.
[17] Kaliṅga, bilva, jambu, āmra, kapittha, rasanjana, lac, the two types of haridrā, hrīvera, kaṭphala, and śukranāsikā— [18]
Having ground lodhra, mocarasa, conch-shell, dhātakī, and the sprouts of the vaṭa tree with rice-water, one should drink pills the size of an akṣa fruit,
dried in the shade, for the swift pacification of fever and diarrhea.
These also clarify the blood and destroy colic and diarrhea.
One should drink blue lotus, pomegranate bark, and lotus filaments with rice-water; this destroys fever and diarrhea. (20–21)
Take equal parts of the three pungents (vyoṣa), seeds of vatsaka, nimba, bhūnimba, mārkava,
citraka, rohiṇī, pāṭhā, dārvī, and ativiṣā;
grind all these into a fine powder and add an equal amount of vatsaka bark.

Having combined all these together, one should drink them with rice-water; or one may lick this with honey. It is a digestive and astringent medicine that alleviates thirst and loss of appetite, and destroys fever and diarrhea.
It destroys jaundice, disorders of the duodenum, abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, urinary disorders, anemia, and edema. One should drink one akṣa measure of Viśva with a decoction of Daśamūla.
In cases of fever, diarrhea, swelling, and disorders of the *grahaṇī*,
*viḍaṅga*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *dāru*, *pāṭhā*, *kaliṅgaka*,
combined with *marīca*, destroy swelling and diarrhea. (26–27)
With *kirāta*, *abda*, *amṛtā*, *viśvacandana*, *udīcya*, and *vatsaka*,
there is alleviation of swelling and diarrhea, and especially the destruction of fever. [Likewise] with *kirāta*, *abda*, *amṛtā*, *udīcya*, *musta*, *candana*, and *dhānyaka*.
It pacifies swelling, diarrhea, thirst, and burning sensations, and destroys fever.
(29) Chapter 3:
Since there is no treatment for diarrhea that disregards the sequence of undigested (*āma*) and digested (*pakva*) stages, [this chapter follows that order].
Therefore, in all cases of diarrhea, the characteristics of undigested (āma) and digested (pakva) stool should be known:
undigested stool sinks in water due to its heaviness, whereas digested stool floats,
except when there is excessive liquidity, compactness, coldness, or corruption by phlegm (śleṣman).
Feces that are foul-smelling, accompanied by flatulence, constipation, pain, and excessive vomiting indicate the presence of undigested matter (āmadoṣa).
Conversely, when free from such matter, the stool sinks [in water].
In the case of undigested matter, fasting is recommended at first, followed by digestive treatments.
And at the conclusion of fasting, one should engage in physical exercise and eat light food.
There is no other medicine in this world that, by means of a single fast, pacifies the aggravated accumulation of the humors in a strong person and also brings them to maturation.

To one who is thirsty, water boiled with *hrīvera* and *śṛṅgavera*, or with *mustā* and *parpaṭaka*, or even water boiled with *mustā* and *udīcya*, should be given. At the time of eating, when he is emaciated by hunger, one should feed him light foods.
A gruel prepared with medicinal herbs, parched grain flour, and roasted grain flour are beneficial for those suffering from diarrhea.
A scum-like liquid strained through cloth and lentil soup should also be drunk.
A thick ball of food is heavy, while the same food becomes light when it is very coarse or otherwise reversed in its preparation.
A linctus made of groats would digest quickly due to its softness.
[The ingredients are: *śāliparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *bṛhatī*, *kaṇṭakārikā*, *balā*, *aśvadaṃṣṭrā*, *bilva*, *pāṭhā*, *nāgara*, and *dhānyaka*.
This is beneficial when combined with food for all those suffering from diarrhea.
Gruels prepared with śāliparṇī, balā, bilva, and pṛśniparṇī,
and soured with pomegranate, are beneficial for those suffering from diarrhea caused by pitta and kapha.
While consuming gruel, one should indeed employ condiments;
for gruels prepared with vegetables, meat, or fruits, as well as those that are sour, are difficult to digest. Alternatively, it may be prepared with the five grains or with all types of grain.
Food should be prescribed by the physician for those suffering from diarrhea caused by vāta and kapha.
Water boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī) is for vāta-pitta, while water boiled with the five spices (pañcakola) is for kapha; this water cures thirst, burning sensations, and diarrhea.

One should consume food proven effective by these two methods of preparation for one whose accumulated *doṣas* have been intensified by undigested food (*vidagdha-āhāra*). These [doṣas] lead to diarrhea; therefore, one should cause them to be expelled further.
However, one should not administer a digestive concentrate (saṃgrahaṇa) to someone suffering from diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātisāra).
For the morbid humors (doṣas), when bound up at the outset, produce many diseases: edema, anemia, splenic enlargement, leprosy, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargements, and fever.

In cases of *daṇḍaka*, *alasa*, abdominal distension, as well as *grahaṇī* and hemorrhoids, for one suffering from depleted tissues and strength with excessive morbid humors (*doṣa*) and profuse discharge,
even undigested matter (*āma*) should be checked with astringents; for if it is treated with digestive stimulants (*pācana*), death may occur.
One who suffers from diarrhea that is either scanty or obstructed, or accompanied by pain,
should be purged with lukewarm pastes of *abhayā* and *pippalī*. [One should also administer] *dhānyaka*, *nāgara*, *musta*, *vālaka*, and *bilva*.

This "Quadruple Grains" (dhānyacatuṣka) group destroys colic and constipation, acts as a digestive, and stimulates the digestive fire; however, when used in cases of Pitta, it should be prepared without ginger (śuṇṭhī).
Furthermore, [the following group consists of] long pepper (pippalī), ginger (nāgara), coriander (dhānya), bishop’s weed (bhūtika), chebulic myrobalan (abhayā), and sweet flag (vacā).
Hrīvera, bhadramustā, bilva, nāgara,
dhānyaka, pṛśniparṇī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, samaṅgā, and kaṇṭakārikā—
these three combinations for those suffering from atisāra are prescribed in half-verse units. || 22–23 ||
These names— Pramathyā— are proclaimed in sequence for Kapha-Pitta, Vāta, and for use as a digestive and stimulant formulation;
they consist of Tryūṣaṇa, Ativiṣā, Hiṅgu, Balā, Sauvarcala, and Abhayā.
Having drunk this with warm water, one may destroy severe acute diarrhea (āmātīsāra).
Alternatively, [one may take] long pepper root, the two types of long pepper, leadwort, black salt, sweet flag, the three pungents, asafoetida, atis-root, and chebulic myrobalan.
One suffering from diarrhea caused by phlegm (kapha) should drink the powder of the *haridrādi* or *vacādi* groups with warm water; likewise,
a wise person should administer the *pippalyādi* group in cases of undigested matter (*āma*), along with sugar-candy soups or gruels.

This well-cooked sugar-curd soup (khaṇḍayūṣa) is prepared with buttermilk (takra), wood-apple (kapittha), sorrel (cāṅgerī), black pepper (marica), cumin (ajājī), and leadwort (citrika). This other variety is the kāmbalika,
which consists of sour curd (dadhyamla) combined with salt, oil, sesame seeds, and lentils.
Alternatively, a decoction of *nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, and *mustā*, or *dhānyaka* and *nāgara*, destroys thirst, diarrhea, and colic; it is digestive, appetizing, and light.
[Likewise,] *pāṭhā*, seeds of *vatsaka*, *harītakī*, and *mahauṣadha* [are similarly beneficial].

This dysentery, accompanied by pain, arises from the stomach and consists of phlegm combined with bile; it certainly binds the feces. One should boil either *mustā* or twenty *bhadrakāhvaya* fruits in milk [and administer it]. || 31-32 ||

That milk, when drunk while still containing its residual water, cures diarrhea with pain caused by undigested matter (āma). However, when chronic diarrhea has become ripe and the *grahaṇī* is moistened by the [excessive] discharge, then the treatment for constipation (*saṃgrāhika*) should be performed immediately.

The five roots (*pañcamūlī*), *balā*, *viśva* (ginger), *dhānyaka* (coriander), blue lotus (*utpala*), and *bilva* should be given with buttermilk (*takra*) or with any one of the other [liquids] for one suffering from diarrhea caused by wind (*vāta*). [Likewise,] *kañcaṭa*, *jambū*, pomegranate (*dāḍima*), *śṛṅgāṭaka*, leaves, *bilva*, and *hrīvera* [should be used]. 34–35.
Even the swift-flowing Gaṅgā, together with its clouds and serpents, a physician might arrest by making a very firm embankment with ground āmalaka fruits;
he should quickly fill the navel region with the fresh juice of ginger.
One should suppress the terrible dysentery that is like the rush of a river.
One should drink kirātatiktaka, musta, vatsaka,
and rasāñjana with honey to destroy bile-induced dysentery and alleviate pain.
One who subsists on a liquid diet and drinks water boiled with one *pala* of *vatsaka* seeds will quickly conquer abdominal disease accompanied by *pitta*.
[Likewise, one may use] *madhuka*, *kaṭphala*, *lodhra*, and the rind of the pomegranate fruit.
In cases of Pitta-type diarrhea, one should administer [the powder] mixed with honey along with rice-water.
Kuṭaja, ativiṣā, musta, haridrā, and the two parṇinīs,
taken with honey and sugar, are recommended for those suffering from diarrhea caused by Pitta and Kapha.
Having boiled the bark and fruit of *kuṭaja* with *musta*, one should drink the water;
combined with sugar and honey, it quickly conquers diarrhea.
A decoction of *bilva* and mango stones, drunk with honey and sugar, [achieves the same].
It destroys vomiting and diarrhea, just as the sacrificial fire consumes the oblation.
A decoction of *paṭola*, barley, and *dhanyāka*, when well-cooled and mixed with sugar and honey, should be drunk; it is a destroyer of vomiting and diarrhea.

One should administer Priyaṅgu, Añjana, and Musta with honey and rice-water according to the patient's strength; this destroys thirst, diarrhea, and vomiting. Kaliṅgaka, Vacā, Musta, Dāru, and Ativiṣā should be taken in equal parts.
One suffering from diseases of pitta and vāta should drink the paste (kalka) with rice-water.
One should drink a decoction (kaṣāya) of kuṭaja, dāḍima, musta, dhātakī, bilva, bālaka, lodhra, candana, and pāṭhā, mixed with honey.
The group known as Kuṭajādigaṇa is recommended for cases of fever with colic, blood in the stool, and slimy discharges; it is the destroyer of all types of diarrhea.
[It consists of] samaṅgā, ativiṣā, musta, viśva, hrīvera, and dhātakī.
A decoction of *kuṭaja* bark, its fruit, and *vilva* cures all types of diarrhea.
The fresh juice extracted from the leaves of *hijjala* should be drunk with honey,
or else a decoction of *kuṭaja* bark conquers diarrhea caused by undigested matter (*āmātisāra*).
Having ground the young shoots of the banyan tree finely with rice-water, one should drink it mixed with buttermilk; this cures the pain of diarrhea.
Drinking half a karṣa of aṅkoṭha root ground with rice-water also removes [diarrhea].
This paste, drunk from the tender leaves of the *vavola* tree, cures all types of most terrible diarrhea and diseases of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*).
A decoction made from the bark of the *kuṭaja* tree, thickened and well-cooled, likewise removes diarrhea.
Lohita combined with ativiṣā acts as a cure for all types of diarrhea;
in this case, they say that the powder of ativiṣā should be added as one-eighth part of the decoction,
but it is our opinion that it should be added as a quarter part of the linctus.
The roots of *sadārvī*, *aṅkoṭa*, and *pāṭhā*, the bark of *kuṭaja*,
the resin of *śālmalī* and *śāla*, and *dhātakī*, *lodhra*, and pomegranate—
having ground these in equal parts (*akṣa*) and made them into boluses with rice-water, [one should administer them]. || 56–57 ||
Having risen in the morning, a person afflicted by severe diarrhea should drink each of these individually mixed with honey; this preparation known as Aṅkoṭavaṭaka destroys all types of dysentery.
A gruel prepared with half milk and half goat’s urine, along with *hrīvera*, blue lotus, ginger, and *pṛśniparṇī*, cures bloody diarrhea. [Likewise,
a gruel prepared with] *rasāñjana*, *ativiṣā*, the fruit of *kuṭaja*, and its bark [is effective].
One should drink dhātakī and ginger with rice-water mixed with honey;
this expels severe blood-dysentery,
kindles the weak digestive fire, and also alleviates colic pain.
Viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, musta, devadāru, pāṭhā, and kaliṅgaka,
combined with marica, destroy swelling and diarrhea.
[62] Vatsaka, ativiṣā, and bilva— these, along with [the aforementioned], [are effective].
A decoction prepared with northern musta is beneficial in cases of diarrhea that is accompanied by undigested matter (āma), colic, and blood, even when it has been chronic. || 63 ||
A decoction of the barks of *dāḍima* and *vatsaka*, drunk with honey,
immediately conquers even difficult-to-cure diarrhea accompanied by blood. One should eat *bilva* with jaggery (*guḍa*) to destroy bloody diarrhea.
It destroys colic caused by undigested matter (āma-śūla) and constipation, and it eradicates diseases of the abdomen.
Equal parts of bilva, usira, dhātakī, pāṭhā, śuṇṭhī, and mocarasa, when drunk with jaggery and buttermilk, stop even difficult-to-conquer diarrhea (atīsāra). 65–66.
The barks of śallakī, badarī, jambu, priyāla, āmra, and arjuna,
drunk separately with milk and enriched with honey, destroy [excessive] blood. Then, one should crush the tender shoots of jambu, āmra, and āmalakī.
Having collected their fresh juice, one should mix it with goat’s milk;
this, when drunk combined with honey, destroys bloody diarrhea.
Bilva fruit prepared with goat’s milk, combined with sugar and *mocarasa*, [should be taken].
Rice-leaf (*taṇḍulīya*) combined with *kaliṅga* powder, drunk with the water of the month of Jyeṣṭha along with sugar and honey, destroys bloody diarrhea.
Having drunk the paste of *śatāvarī* with milk, one who eats only milk will be victorious [over the disease].
A person suffering from bloody diarrhea should drink ghee prepared with that [mixture].
One pala of *kuṭaja* should be taken and boiled in water reduced to one-eighth;
in the same manner, it should be cooked again, combined with pomegranate juice.
One should prepare this decoction until it has the appearance of lymph;
a patient suffering from bloody diarrhea should drink half a karṣa of it with buttermilk.
Even one who is destined to die will certainly not fall within the reach of death.
When the quantity of water is not specified, it should be equal to the decoction; since [the rule] is that the portions are equal.
A paste of black sesame seeds combined with a portion of sugar, when drunk with goat's milk, immediately stops bleeding.
In cases of burning or suppuration of the anus, physicians recommend sprinkling with the decoction of *paṭola* and *madhuka*,
or even with goat’s milk.
In the case of prolapse of the rectum (*gudabhraṃśa*), the treatment prescribed for that condition should be performed.
One should treat diarrhea that is painless, well-formed, accompanied by a burning sensation, long-standing, and characterized by various colors with *puṭapāka* preparations.
[The preparation should consist of] thick, ungnawed *kuṭaja* bark that has been softened.
Having taken it and crushed it excessively at that very moment,
he sprinkled it with water and rice from the hollows of *jambū* and *palāśa* leaves, bound it with *kuśa* grass, and smeared thick mud over the outside. || 78 ||
Having well-steamed this [mixture] and pressed it to extract the juice, one should administer it mixed with honey to a patient suffering from diarrhea;
this formulation is honored by Kṛṣṇātreya and Pūjita.
In the removal of all types of diarrhea, the king [of medicines] himself is the sovereign.
Due to the heaviness of its own juice, one should drink a *puṭapāka* dose;
this is the cooking of a *puṭapāka*, characterized by an outward reddish color.

One should wrap a ball of bark from the *dīrghavṛnta* tree with the leaves of *kāśmarī*, coat it well with clay, and roast it thoroughly over charcoal embers. Once cooked, one should remove it, squeeze it, and carefully extract the juice.
One should drink it cooled and mixed with honey for abdominal disease.
One hundred palas of crushed *kuṭaja* root should be boiled in one *āḍhaka* of water;
when the decoction is reduced to one-fourth, it should be strained and cooked again into a linctus.
Having added two palas of the powder of sauvarcala, yavakṣāra, biḍa, saindhava, pippalī, dhātakī, indrayava, and ajājī,
one should lick it in a quantity the size of a jujube fruit, combined with honey and boiled [in water].
It conquers diarrhea with both mature and immature stools, various colors, and pain;
it overcomes the difficult-to-cure disease of the digestive tract (grahaṇī) as well as dysentery (pravāhikā). [Take] one tulā of fresh girimallikā.
Having crushed and cooked it, one should extract the juice; once that is well-strained, one should grind together with *śālmalī* [the ingredients] finely, measuring one *pala* each.
Having added pāṭhā, samaṅgā, ativiṣā, musta, bilva, and the flowers of dhātakī, one should boil them further until—
The paste for the ladle and the expressed juice should be drunk by one who knows the proper time, either with water,
or with rice-gruel (maṇḍa), or even with goat's milk.
It destroys all severe diarrhea—
whether black, white, red, or yellow—
as well as various disorders of the digestive tract and blood.
This "Eightfold Kutaja" formulation necessarily destroys colic, hemorrhoids accompanied by blood, and even menstrual disorders that are otherwise incurable. (89)
For ten *tulās* of medicinal substance, one *droṇa* of water is prescribed; for one *droṇa* of water, one *tulā* of substance is considered the standard measure.
[The ingredients are: the seeds of *vatsaka*, the excellent bark of *dārvī*, *pippalī*, *śṛṅgavera*, *lākṣā*, and *kaṭukarohiṇī*.
Ghee prepared with these six [drugs] should be drunk after consuming thin gruel;
it quickly conquers even severe diarrhea caused by the three doṣas.
[Ghee] cooked with the milky trees [and] urasā...
Ghee prepared with the pastes of those [drugs] and milk, combined with half a part of sugar-candy and a quarter part of honey,
pacifies even severe bloody diarrhea. || 92 ||
When digested, goat's milk is like nectar, especially in cases of diarrhea;
it should be administered prepared with medicinal herbs or boiled in water.
[One may also give] young wood-apple, jaggery, oil, long pepper, and ginger.
When Vata is obstructed, accompanied by pain and dysentery, one should lick a paste of Pippali or that derived from Marica with milk;
this destroys even long-standing dysentery within three days. (94–95)

A paste of young *bilva* fruits mixed with an equal amount of sesame paste, along with the essence of curd, sour gruel, and plenty of fat, should be taken as a confection (*khaṇḍa*) to destroy dysentery (*pravāhikā*).
For diarrhea (*pravāhaṇa*), one should lick a mixture of *bilva*, black pepper, jaggery, and *lodhra* combined with oil.
One afflicted by flatulence should eat with curd that is mixed with whey and honey,
or even with well-heated, slightly bitter, boiled water.
One whose digestive fire is blazing yet who passes stool without fecal matter (niṣpurīṣa) and who has diarrhea with frothy excrement, should drink cooled milk saturated with honey,
along with treacle, ginger, curd, oil, milk, and ghee.
One should abandon a patient suffering from diarrhea upon observing swelling, pain, fever, thirst, dyspnea, cough, anorexia, vomiting, fainting, and hiccup; likewise,
a man who has excessive urination and passes broken stools does not survive.
One suffering from diarrhea should avoid bathing, oil massage, immersion baths, heavy or unctuous foods, excessive eating, physical exercise, and exposure to the heat of fire. (100) Chapter 4.

One should treat a disorder of the *grahaṇī* based on the principles of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*); one should digest its undigested matter (*āma*) according to the procedure prescribed for diarrhea (*atīsāra*).
When the *rasa* (plasma) is accompanied by *āma* and has permeated the body, fasting and digestive treatments (*pācana*) are required.

To this person whose internal disposition has been purified, one should give light food such as peya (gruel) prepared with the five pungent fruits (*pañcakola*) and other ingredients, and furthermore, digestive stimulants (*dīpaka-yoga*). [For example:
a preparation of wood-apple (*kapittha*), *bilva*, *cāṅgerī*, buttermilk, and pomegranate.
A digestive gruel made with the five roots (pañcamūla) is beneficial for *grahaṇī* associated with *vāta*.

For those suffering from *grahaṇī* disorders, buttermilk is wholesome because it stimulates digestion (*dīpana*), is constipating due to its lightness, and— owing to its sweet post-digestive effect (*madhura-pākitva*)— does not provoke *pitta*.
Because it is astringent, hot, and expansive, and because of its dryness, it is beneficial for kapha; yet, because it is sweet, sour, and thick, fresh [mudga] is non-burning and beneficial for vāta.
[One should take] ginger, musta, ativiṣā, and guḍūcī...
One should drink [this] boiled with water in equal parts when there is weak digestion, constant vomiting,
and in cases of chronic diarrhea associated with undigested matter (āmānubandha).
One should administer dhanyāka, ativiṣā, udīcya, yavānī, musta, nāgara, balā, dviparṇī, and bilva as a digestive stimulant (dīpana) and carminative (pācana).
Citraka, pippalīmūla, the two alkalis (kṣāra), and the salts [should also be used].
One should powder together vyoṣa, hiṅgu, ajamodā, and cavya.
A pill made from these with the juice of mātuluṅga or sour pomegranate digests undigested matter (āma) and quickly kindles the digestive fire.
One should add here five types of salt— sauvarcala, saindhava, viḍa, audbhida, and likewise sāmudra— in equal proportions.
[Add] a paste of the tender fruit of the śrīphala.
Mixed with powdered *nāgara* (ginger) and combined with jaggery, when consumed while subsisting on buttermilk, it conquers even the most violent disease of *grahaṇī*. || 11 ||
Jambul, pomegranate, śṛṅgāṭa, pāṭhā, and the tender leaves of kañcaṭa, along with ripe and aged bilva fruit, sugar, and ginger—
this [preparation] destroys all types of diarrhea and even the most difficult-to-overcome grahaṇī disorder.
A decoction of *nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, and *musta* serves as a digestive for undigested matter (*āma*).
For *vātagrahaṇī*, however, one should use the powder known as *hiṅgu-aṣṭaka* and medicated ghees. [One should also take] *nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, *musta*, *dhātakī*, and *rasāñjana*.
One should drink an equal quantity of the powder of vatsaka-bark, madana-fruit, bilva, pāṭhā, and kaṭurohiṇī, along with honey and rice-water,
in cases of pitta-type grahaṇī disorder and when blood is passed in the stool. (15)

This powder, beginning with ginger (nāgara), honored by Kṛṣṇātreya, conquers hemorrhoids, pain in the rectum, and dysentery. The preparation of rice-water should be done according to the measure used for a cold decoction (śītakaṣāya).

Some authorities prescribe the soaking of rice with water possessing eight qualities. One should grind together equal parts of bhūnimba, kaṭukā, vyōṣa, mustaka, and indrayava; sixteen parts of citraka and vatsaka bark should also be powdered.

When drunk with cooled water and jaggery, it cures disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), abdominal tumors (gulma), jaundice, fever, anemia, urinary disorders, loss of appetite, and diarrhea. Through the addition of jaggery, the water becomes "jaggery-water" (guḍāmbu), endowed with the color and taste of jaggery.
When the *grahaṇī* is afflicted by *śleṣman*, one should, after the patient has been properly vomited,
increase the digestive fire with pungent, sour, salty, alkaline, and sharp substances.
[One should also administer] long pepper with its roots, the two types of alkali, and the five salts.
Having prepared equal parts of mātuluṅga, abhayā, rāsnā, śaṭhī, marica, and nāgara, one should drink that powder in the morning with warm water;
it increases strength, complexion, and digestive fire in cases of grahaṇī-doṣa caused by kapha.
