Ghee prepared with these very same medicinal herbs should be drunk when Vāta is predominant. One should burn two palas each of *bhallātaka*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and the three salts as "inner-smoke" (*antardhūma*) using the fire of cow-dung.
This alkaline preparation should be drunk with clarified butter, or added to food;
it cures heart disease, anemia, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), abdominal tumors, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and colic.
In cases of grahaṇī caused by all [three] doshas, however, the general treatment is prescribed.
A powder made from black pepper, ginger, and the bark of *kuṭaja*, each increasing in double proportion,
when mixed with jaggery and drunk after churning [the mixture], [cures fever].
This is renowned as a remedy that removes disorders of the *grahaṇī*.
[27] With *pāṭhā*, *bilva*, *citraka*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *jambū*, pomegranate, *dhātakī*, *kaṭukā*, *ativiṣā*, *musta*, *dārvī*, *bhūnimba*, and *vatsaka*— [28]
One suffering from vomiting, fever, diarrhea, and colic should drink a powder made from all these ingredients along with *kauṭaja* (indrayava), mixed with honey and rice-water.
This overcomes thirst, burning sensations, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, anorexia, and weak digestion.
With equal parts of yavānī, pippalīmūla, caturjātaka, and nāgara; with marica, agni, jala, jīraka, dhānya, and sauvarcala;
and with vṛkṣāmla, dhātakī, kṛṣṇā, bilva, dāḍima, and tinduka—[these should be combined].

A powder prepared with three parts of *triguṇa*, six parts of *ṣaḍguṇasita*, and eight parts of *kapittha* overcomes diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), consumption, abdominal tumors, diseases of the throat,
cough, dyspnea, anorexia, and hiccups; this is known as the "Eightfold Kapittha" formulation.
Seven karṣas of tugākṣīrī and two karṣas each of the four spices (cāturjāta);
one pala each of yavānī, dhānyaka, ajājī, granthi, and vyoṣa; and eight palas of pomegranate [juice] and sugar—all combined together. || 33–34 ||
This *Dāḍimāṣṭaka* powder possesses qualities similar to the *Kapitthāṣṭaka*.
[Take] four palas from the stem of the *sudhā* plant, three palas from the three salts, one *kuḍava* of eggplant (*vārtāku*), eight palas of *arka*, and two palas of *citraka*. (35)
These pills, burnt in the juice of *vārtāku* and taken after meals,
quickly digest whatever has been eaten. They are beneficial for cough, dyspnea, and hemorrhoids, and they are also effective in destroying cholera, catarrh, and heart disease.
Having cooked one pala of jaggery and eight palas of ghee with a paste of tryūṣaṇa and triphalā measuring the size of a bilva fruit, a person with weak digestion should drink an appropriate dose.
One should cook ghee with a decoction of masūra and a paste of bilva as an internal ingredient.
It destroys all diseases of the abdomen, as well as *grahaṇī*, anemia (*pāṇḍu*), and jaundice (*kāmalā*).
However, a decoction made solely from rice and parts of animals, even if left overnight, is harmful to the bodily humors (*doṣala*).
[This decoction] is boiled in water from the ten roots (*daśamūla*) with the addition of the inner substance of ginger (*viśvauṣadha*).
Ghee cures swelling and the disease of malabsorption (grahaṇī).
Ghee prepared with a paste of ginger promotes the downward movement of flatus and destroys malabsorption, anemia, splenic enlargement, cough, and fever.
Clarified butter (haviḥ) boiled with the decoction and paste of *citraka* cures disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*),

and it alleviates abdominal tumors (*gulma*), edema (*śotha*), abdominal enlargement (*udara*), splenic disorders (*plīha*), colic (*śūla*), and hemorrhoids (*arśas*), while acting as a digestive stimulant (*pradīpana*). [Verse 42] Bilva, *agni*, *cavya*, fresh ginger (*ārdraka*), and *śṛṅgavera*— [Verse 43]
Clarified butter prepared with a decoction and a paste,
along with goat's milk, is an excellent elixir (ariṣṭa) for curing disorders of the digestive tract, as well as swelling, weak digestion, and loss of appetite.

Clarified butter (sarpis) cooked with the expressed juice of cāṅgerī and with the pastes (kalka) of these— nāgara, pippalīmūla, citraka, hastipippalī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, pippalī, dhānya, bilva, pāṭhā, and yavānikā— [is effective].

This ghee, prepared with the four products of the cow and with curd, alleviates phlegm and wind; it dispels hemorrhoids, disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), dysuria, dysentery, pain from prolapse of the rectum, and flatulence. (45–46)
Black pepper, long pepper root, ginger, long pepper, marking nut, bishop’s weed, embelia, and elephant pepper;
asafoetida, black salt, biḍa salt, rock salt, and barberry.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with half-*pala* portions each of sea salt, alkali from barley (*yavakṣāra*), *citraka*, and *vacā*,
using a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūlī*) and twice as much milk. (48–49)
This prepared [preparation] is beneficial for those with weak digestion; it destroys disorders of the *grahaṇī*, relieves constipation, undigested matter (*āma*), debility, and splenic enlargement.
It also cures cough, dyspnea, consumption, hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano.
It destroys diseases born of phlegm (kapha), those born of wind (vāta), and those arising from worms;
it quickly annihilates all of them, just as dry wood is consumed by fire.
[One should take] sauvarcala salt, pañcakola, rock salt (saindhava), hapuṣā, and vacā. || 51-52 ||
Having made a paste of half a *pala* each of *ajamodā*, barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), cumin (*jīraka*), *audbhida* salt, black cumin (*kṛṣṇājājī*), and *bhūtīka*,
[one should add] the juice of ginger, sour gruel (*cukra*), milk, whey, and sour *kāñjika*.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla).
It should be administered by the wise either together with a meal or without food,
for the treatment of worms, splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, indigestion, fever, skin diseases, and dysentery.
It destroys diseases of wind (vāta), disorders of phlegm (kapha), colic, loss of appetite, jaundice, consumption, cough, debility, and disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī).
This preparation, named Mahā-ṣatpalaka, is like the thunderbolt of Indra to a tree.

16–18. Molasses, honey, and sour gruel (kāñjika) should be placed in a clean vessel and left for three nights upon a heap of grain; that fermented liquid is called *śukta*. Here, salt, molasses, honey, *āranāla*, and *mastu* [are used] in sequence. 57–58.
One *prastha* of rice-water,
three *prasthas* of water from the husks, half a *prastha* of sour gruel (*amla*), and one *pala* of fermented radish (*amlamūlaka*).
Eight *guḍa* (pulses) of sugar,
two *māṇika* of purified ginger,
and two *pala* each of rock salt and cumin.
Having placed two palas each of black pepper and long pepper along with a pair of haritaki fruits into a sturdy,
oily vessel, it should be buried in a heap of grain such as barley.
One should keep it for three days in summer, four days at the end of the rainy season,
and during the onset of flowers in the monsoon.
After eight days from this [point], when it has reached sixty-six [days], one should drain this and powder it,
combined with one pala of the four aromatics (cāturjāta).
That which is both sweet and sour destroys various diseases produced by the disorders of wind (vāta), phlegm (kapha), and blood (āmadoṣa).
Having destroyed dyspnea, chronic fever, anemia, wind-disorders, abdominal tumors, colic, and abdominal enlargements, it kindles the digestive fire.
(61) One pala each of yamānī, āmalaka, pathyā, and marica [should be taken].
One should grind five *pala* portions of salts together into a powder.
A person should drink the *takrāriṣṭa* produced therein from bell-metal;
it is a digestive stimulant that removes swelling, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, worms, urinary disorders, and abdominal enlargements.
One should give one *āḍhaka* each of vāṭya, barley-flour, and separately,
medium-sized radishes.
One should give sixty-four prepared portions;
having washed them in a vessel of one *droṇa* of water, one should place this, combined with the collection of medicinal herbs, into a well-washed jar.
The two types of alkali, *tumburu*, *vastagandhā*,
*dhanīyaka*, *biḍa* salt, *saindhava* salt, *sauvarcala* salt, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and *śirāṭikā*. || 65 ||
One should add two palas of cavya and these other ingredients, each measuring one pala; having crushed them into small pieces, one should place them in a jar. || 66 ||
Kṛṣṇā, ajājī, upakuñcikā, asurī, and kāravī— this [mixture],
when applied for a fortnight, bestows strength, complexion, and a firm body.
It promotes youth and bestows great strength.
Because it was first prepared with the thought, "Whom shall I revive?
those who know the truth call it *kāñjika*.
It digests food during the period of digestion; therefore, they call it *āyāma*. It also cures ascites, abdominal tumors, and splenic enlargement.
It cures heart disease, flatulence, loss of appetite, weak digestion, colic localized in the abdomen,
hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano. (69)
When consumed by men in various ways, it quickly destroys all wind-related diseases (vātāmaya) for people;
[this is prepared] with three prasthas of āmalakī juice.
To one *śuddha* of clarified butter, having added half a *tulā* of jaggery,
along with the powders of *granthika*, *jīra*, *cavya*, *vyoṣa*, *ibhakaṣṇā*, *hapuṣā*, and *ajamoda*. || 71 ||
Having added one *pala* each of viḍaṅga, sindhu (rock salt), triphalā, yavānī, pāṭhā, agni (citraka), and dhānya, and eight *palas* of powdered trivṛt—
One should cook eight *vaṣṭu* measures of oil according to the prescribed method.
One should consume that [preparation] in the measure of an *akṣa* fruit, combined with the three aromatics (*trisugandhi*), acting as one pleases.
By this, all disorders of the *grahaṇī*, along with asthma, cough, hoarseness of voice, and swelling,
as well as chronic sluggishness of the digestive fire, are pacified. || 73 ||
This confection known as Kalyāṇaka is prescribed as the cause for the increase of virility in men and for the destruction of barrenness and disease in women. (74)
Physicians slightly fry *trivṛt* in oil;
here, because of the similarity to the [mental] state mentioned [in the previous verse], one *pala* each of the three aromatics (*trisugandha*) is used.
[Then there is] well-steamed *kūṣmāṇḍaka* gourd, grown [wild], with its seeds and skin removed.
One should slowly cook one hundred palas of these [ingredients] in one prastha of ghee in a copper vessel:
pippalī, pippalīmūla, citraka, hastipippalī, dhānyaka, viḍaṅga, yamānī, and marica. (76–77)
One pala each of triphalā, ajamodā, kaliṅga, ajājī, and saindhava, eight palas of trivṛt,
eight palas of oil, and fifty palas of jaggery. || 78 ||
When it is combined with three *prasthas* of *āmalaka* juice and a coating of *dārvī* has been applied,
one should then remove it; according to one's capacity, one should prepare lumps of jaggery weighing one *karṣa* or half a *karṣa*.
Employed according to this very method, one shall forcibly conquer these: chronic diarrhea (grahaṇī), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), hemorrhoids (arśas),
fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara), fever, flatulence, heart disease, abdominal tumors (gulma), abdominal enlargements (udara), and choleraic dysentery (viṣūcikā).
It dispels jaundice, anemia, and the twenty types of urinary disorders (prameha);
it also removes gout, erysipelas, ringworm, skin diseases, and halimaka, as well as all aggravated disorders of phlegm, bile, and wind.
For those men who are emaciated by disease, emaciated by old age, or exhausted by women, this [preparation] is aphrodisiac, strengthening, and indeed a restorer of youth.
Known as Guḍakalyāṇaka, it is the supreme means for barren women to conceive.
The pill known as Kṣudhāvatī, which is to be administered in cases of amlapitta, is described there [in that context].
For its purification, mercury and sulphur, in equal proportions, should be ground together until they attain the appearance of collyrium (kajjala) in a sturdy vessel. || 85-86 ||
Then, having liquefied [the substance] in an iron vessel over a fire of *bādara* wood,
one should gradually form it into the shape of a *parpaṭikā* by pouring it onto a plantain leaf placed upon cow dung; this yields two *rakti*s of it.
The application [of the medicine] lasts for up to twelve *raktikās* for half a watch (*prahara*).
Beyond that, there is the consumption of much betel nut (*pūga*) during the day; furthermore, on the third [day], meat, clarified butter, and milk are prescribed here.
One should avoid burning substances, women, the root of the *arambhā* plant, and mustard oil;
having abandoned small fish, aquatic creatures, and birds, one should drink milk while remaining awake.
This [remedy] destroys malabsorption (*grahaṇī*), consumption (*kṣaya*), leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), emaciation (*śoṣa*), and indigestion (*ajīrṇa*).
This is known as Rasaparpaṭikā, as formulated by Cakrapāṇi.
Having ground one māṣa each of mercury and sulphur in a vessel, they should be placed [therein]; then, on top of that, two māṣas of Taṇḍulīya, crushed with the fingernails, should be added.
Then, having covered the [opening] with Nepalese copper or similar metal and made it well-sealed,
one should fill the entire vessel above with dust;
then fire should be applied beneath the vessel as far as the tube for the deceased.
One *raktikā* of copper filings, one *raktikā* of the powder of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*),
and one *raktikā* of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), along with *viḍaṅga*— these should be mixed with honey and clarified butter and licked on the first day. || 94-95 ||
The increase of one *rakti* per day should be maintained steadily for the three [substances] beginning with copper; however, when a distinction is intended regarding the addition of *viḍaṅga*,
then one should add two more *raktis* of *viḍaṅga*.
For twelve days there is an increase in the dose, after which this process of reduction follows.
This Tāmrayoga always conquers grahaṇī, sour bile (amlapitta), consumption, and colic; it increases strength, complexion, and the digestive fire.
Chapter 5:

The means for the treatment of diseases characterized by foul-smelling discharges (durnāman) are proclaimed to be fourfold; among them, the first is described as being treatable by medicine, alkaline therapy, surgery, and cauterization. 1.

Whatever after-drink (anupāna) or medicinal substance conduces to the downward movement of vāyu and increases the strength of agni, that should be used constantly by those suffering from hemorrhoids. For dry hemorrhoids, sharp treatments such as medicinal pastes (pralepa) and the like are prescribed.
Upon observing blood in those suffering from discharges, treatment for blood and bile disorders should be administered.
(3) An ointment of snuhī milk mixed with turmeric destroys hemorrhoids when applied as a paste;
by rubbing with the powder of kośātakī, those arising in the anus fall away. (4)
The milky sap of *arka*, the milky sap of *sudhā*, the tender leaves of bitter *tumbī*,
*karañja*, and the root of *bastamūla* constitute an excellent ointment for hemorrhoids. A suppository made from the fruit of *guḍaghosā* applied to the anus destroys hemorrhoids.
An ointment made from the paste of *jyotsnikā* root is beneficial for bleeding hemorrhoids (6).
A pill consisting of three parts of *tumbī* seeds and one part of *saudbhida* salt, ground with *kāñjī*,
destroys hemorrhoids when applied to the anus by one who eats buffalo curd (7).
An alkaline preparation made from the roots of *apāmārga* combined with *haritāla* applied as an ointment certainly destroys hemorrhoids occurring on the penis.
Likewise, the powder of *pathyā* and *kośātakī* from the region of *mahārodhi* [is effective].
By applying a paste of *kapha*-alleviating substances, one undoubtedly destroys hemorrhoids located on the penis and the rectum.
One should treat hemorrhoids accompanied by diarrhea caused by *vāta* with the same regimen used for *vātātisāra*,
and those with hard stools repeatedly with the procedure prescribed for *udāvarta*.
In cases of obstructed stool, buttermilk combined with *yamānī* and *viḍa* salt is beneficial;
indeed, there is no medicine superior to buttermilk for hemorrhoids caused by *vāta* and *śleṣman*. It should be administered according to the specific dosha, either with fat or without fat.
Hemorrhoids do not grow again when struck by buttermilk (takra).
Having ground the root of *citraka*, one should smear it upon a jar;
one should drink the buttermilk or curd produced therein, which destroys hemorrhoids. (12–13)
Abhayā taken with jaggery pacifies pitta and kapha, removes itching, scratching, and pain, and quickly destroys hemorrhoids when administered.
Abhayā mixed with jaggery and long pepper (pippalī), and fried in ghee, [achieves the same].
Or one may consume the *trivṛt* mixed with *danti*, which acts as a purgative;
or one may consume the combination of sesame and *aruṣkara*, which increases the digestive fire,
removes skin diseases and hair, and is the most excellent destroyer of hemorrhoids.
Three parts each of *tila*, *bhallātaka*, *pathyā*, and jaggery, taken in equal proportions,
destroy hemorrhoids, cough, and dyspnea, and remove splenic disorders, anemia, and fever. Alternatively, one should administer *harītakī* with jaggery that has been soaked overnight in cow’s urine.
Or one should cause him to drink buttermilk mixed with the five pungent spices (pañcakolaka).
Having cooked a bulb from the śūraṇa plant smeared with clay in the fire according to the puṭapāka method, he should eat it with oil and salt for the cessation of hemorrhoids.
Whoever eats a steamed eggplant fruit that has been fried in ghee after being boiled in alkaline water from the *ghoṣā* plant,
and who drinks buttermilk— surely he attains [longevity]. 20.
In that very moment, the hemorrhoids of men— whether acquired later in life or even congenital— are destroyed within seven nights.
If one first eats a handful of black sesame seeds followed by cold water,
hemorrhoids are destroyed, and it bestows firmness to the teeth and nourishment to the body.
[22] (4) [The same applies to] the roots of dantī and citraka, and of both the five-roots groups (pañcamūla).
Having crushed the portions consisting of one-pala parts, one should boil them in a droṇa of water;
one should add three palas of the leaves of triphalā to it,
along with a tulā of jaggery, and let that sit for half a month in a vessel smeared with ghee.

One should drink this daily in small quantities; it liberates one from hemorrhoids, destroys malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) and anemia (pāṇḍuroga), facilitates the downward movement of flatus and feces, stimulates digestion, and overcomes anorexia.
This is known as Dantya-riṣṭa.
The preparation of *ariṣṭa* and other elixirs should be made in a vessel smeared with *dhātakī* and *lodhra*.
He who eats a magnificent bolus (*modaka*) made of *nāgara*, *aruṣkara*, and *vṛddhadāruka* mixed with jaggery [attains long life].
It instantly makes a child who has been afflicted by every kind of disease caused by evil names (durnāma) grow into an adult.
In the powder (cūrṇa), the amount of jaggery (guḍa) should be known to be equal [to the other ingredients]; in the sweetmeat (modaka), it should be double.
Three palas of ginger, a fourth part of black pepper,
half a kuḍava of long pepper, one pala of cavya,
one pala of tālīśapatra, and half a pala of keśara. || 28–29 ||
Two palas of pippalī root, half a karṣa of patra, one karṣa of fine elā, and one karṣa each of tvak and mṛṇāla—
these should be made into a powder together with thirty palas of jaggery. || 30 ||
The pill is the size of a dice and is known as "Prāṇadā" (Life-giving).
It should be taken first, and afterwards, according to one's strength,
one should drink wine, meat broth, soup, milk, or water.
It destroys all types of cataracts— those congenital, those caused by external substances, those arising from wind, bile, or phlegm, and those produced by the combination of the humors—
as well as alcoholism, dysuria, diseases of the wind, and throat obstructions. (33)
In cases of irregular fever (viṣamajvara), weak digestion, and likewise in jaundice (pāṇḍuroga);
for those suffering from worms and heart disease, as well as those afflicted by abdominal tumors (gulma) and colic, and those overcome by asthma and cough— this [mixture] is like nectar.
In cases of diarrhea caused by pitta or bile, *abhayā* should be substituted for *śuṇṭhī*.

For those suffering from *amlapitta*, weak digestion, or hemorrhoids, one should administer this powder after adding sugar four times the weight of the powder, and it should be used as a life-saving remedy. || 36 ||
A decoction as an after-drink (anupāna) should be administered in diseases arising from phlegm (śleṣman):
one pala for a phlegmatic condition, two palas for a wind-born (vātaja) condition, and three palas for a bile-born (pittaja) condition.
[The powder consists of] five palas of harītakī (pathyā), one pala of cumin (ajājī), and one pala of black pepper (marica). 37–38.
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, and nāgara, each increasing by one pala in sequence, along with two palas of yavakṣāra;
eight palas of bhallātaka, and the bulbous root (kanda) is considered to be double that amount. (39)
Having prepared these *vaṭakas* (boluses) in a quantity equal to an *akṣa*, with double the amount of jaggery,
one should eat them in the morning and drink buttermilk or water afterwards.
This stimulates a sluggish digestive fire and cures *grahaṇī* and anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*).

Kāṅkāyana declared to his disciples that for those afflicted by hemorrhoids, the physician's victory—consisting of viḍaṅga pith, āmalaka, and iron—is the best treatment, even without the use of surgical instruments, caustics, or fire.
(42) 7. [Of] the essence of viḍaṅga, āmalaka, and iron...
One pala each of trivṛt and three palas of jaggery, combined with six and twelve parts respectively,
should be made into thirty pills over the course of a month. || 43 ||
It is said that this Samānibhadra was created by the eminent Yakṣa Nivāraṇa for the sake of the Śākya monk;
indeed, it is the destroyer of cough, consumption, and leprosy.
For those suffering from fistula-in-ano, splenic enlargement, ascites, or hemorrhoids,
one who indulges in activities, food, and recreation as desired will, by means of this [remedy], become young again even if old. (44–45)

Take one part each of black pepper, great medicinal root (mahauṣadha), *citraka*, and *śūraṇa*; each subsequent ingredient is double the amount of the preceding one, and the portion of jaggery (*guḍa*) is equal to the total weight of all these ingredients combined.
This celebrated *modaka* should be consumed;
it kindles the digestive fire and uproots diseases such as colic and abdominal tumors.
It completely eliminates elephantiasis and quickly destroys hemorrhoids as well.
Therein, there are sixteen parts of *śūraṇa* (mountain ginger) and eight parts of *mahauṣadha* (ginger).
Add half a part of black pepper, and then half of that again.
The parts of triphalā, kaṇā, roots, tālīśa, aruṣkara, and krimighna are equal to the part of mahauṣadha; tālamūlī is one-eighth of a part.
A portion equal to that of śūraṇa should be given of vṛddhadāraka as well;
having ground all these together with bhṛṅgarāja and a part of marica,
this modaka, combined with double the amount of jaggery, should be consumed by those possessing great wealth.
It would cause calamity to others who lack the food that is beneficial for gurus and *vṛṣya* (aphrodisiac).
By this "King of Formulas" (*yogarāja*), Bhasmaka was previously produced in Agastya, and likewise in Bhīma and Māruti; by means of it, those two became great eaters. 51–52.
Not only does the great-virulent śūraṇa root cause an increase in digestive fire, strength, and intellect;
even without the use of surgical instruments, caustics, or fire, it overcomes hemorrhoids (arśas),
as well as swelling, elephantiasis (ślīpada), and disorders of the grahaṇī arising from phlegm and wind.
It destroys wrinkles and graying hair, bestows intelligence, and virility.

It always destroys hiccup, dyspnea, cough, pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman), urinary disorders (prameha), and even severe splenic enlargement; this is indeed a rejuvenative elixir (rasāyana) for men.
Sixteen parts of powdered śūraṇa,
half as much of citraka, and one part each of mahauṣadha, abda, and marica.
A bolus made with jaggery is for the conquest of *durnāman* (consumption).
In the bolus, the jaggery acts like a *modaka*, causing it to attain the state of a solid mass.
[The ingredients] are *vyoṣa*, *agni* (citraka), *aruṣkara*, *viḍaṅga*, sesame, and *abhayā*.
This powder, taken daily with jaggery,
overcomes hemorrhoids, skin diseases, poison, swelling, constipation, weakness of the digestive fire, worms, and anemia. (58)
One should consume this powder made from ginger, long pepper, black pepper, *nāgadalatvak*, and cardamom— increased in quantity progressively from the last upward—
and mixed with an equal amount of sugar, for the cure of hemorrhoids and weak digestion.
In cases of cough, loss of appetite, dyspnea, and diseases of the throat and heart,
[one should administer] the best salts, *vahni*, *kaliṅga*, barley,
*cirabilva*, and *mahāpicumarda*.
Drink [this] for seven days, churned and stirred, if you wish to crush the growths of the anus;
[take] triphalā, the five salts, kuṣṭha, and kaṭukarohiṇī.
Devadāru, viḍaṅga, and the fruits of picumarda;
balā, atibalā, the two types of haridrā, and suvarcalā—having gathered these ingredients together with the juice of the bark of karañja. || 61–62 ||
Having ground it and made it into pills the size of a jujube stone, the wise man should take them one by one for each respective disease;
when drunk with warm water, it rekindles a diminished digestive fire.
It cures hemorrhoids when taken with *takra* (buttermilk), and one should expel abdominal tumors (*gulma*) with sour [liquids].
An insect bite is treated with water, while skin diseases are cured with *khadira* decoction.
Dysuria is treated with water, and heart disease with [the same] combined with oil.
Combined with the juice of *indrāsana*, it is known to destroy all fevers;
when mixed with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, it is remembered as an immediate remover of colic.
When mixed with the juice of *kapittha* and *tinduka*, however—
It destroys all poisons when administered through the consumption of food and drink.
Combined with the juice of cow dung, it cures all forms of leprosy;
when combined with a decoction of *śyāmā*, it destroys abdominal dropsy.
It generates a desire for food; when eaten on top of a meal, it cures all eye diseases when ground with honey. By the mere act of licking it, it immediately destroys vaginal discharges in women.
In legal disputes, gambling, battle, hunting, and similar activities, a man who has smeared himself with this [ointment] shall quickly attain victory. [The ointment consists of:
the three triads (triphalā), vacā, hiṅgu, pāṭhā, alkali, and the two types of niśā (turmeric and black turmeric).
Cavya, tikta, kaliṅga, agni, śatāhvā, and the salts; || 71 || granthi, bilva, and ajamodā—this group is considered to consist of twenty-eight [substances].
One should have these made into a fine powder in equal parts. || 72 ||
Then, a man should drink *viḍālapadaka* with warm water; furthermore, he should always lick it combined with castor oil.
Thus, it destroys cough, as well as swelling, hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano.
Heartache, pain in the flanks, wind-tumors (vātagulma), as well as abdominal diseases (udara),

hiccups, asthma, urinary disorders (prameha), jaundice, anemia (pāṇḍuroga), ailments arising from undigested matter (āmānvaya), upward movement of gases (udāvarta), hernia (antravṛddhi), and worms in the rectum; || 74–75 ||
Furthermore, there are other disorders of the *grahaṇī* which I have described for those afflicted by severe fever and those whose minds are possessed by spirits;
as well as that which increases progeny for women who are childless.
This powder named Vijaya was honored by Kṛṣṇātreya.
Trivṛt, tejovatī, dantī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, citraka, śaṭī, gavākṣī, musta, viśvāhva, viḍaṅga, and harītakī—[these are the ingredients]. 78.
These should be measured in palas: eight palas of aruṣkara, six palas of vṛddhadāru, and sixteen palas of śūraṇa.
These are to be boiled in two droṇas of water until reduced to one-fourth.
That strained juice should again be boiled with three times as much jaggery;
one should cook that linctus until it reaches the consistency for coating a ladle. Then, having removed it from the fire, one should add these powders.
One should take two-pala portions each of trivṛt, tejovatī, kanda, and citraka;
likewise, six-pala portions of elā, tvak, marica, and gajāhvā.
Having thus added thirty-two palas [in total], one should set the powder aside.
Then one should employ it in the proper measure; once digested, the patient should subsist on milk and meat broth.
It conquers the five types of gulma, urinary disorders (prameha), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), chlorosis (halīmaka), all forms of hemorrhoids (arśāṃsi), as well as all abdominal enlargements (udarāṇi).
It kindles a weak digestive fire (grahaṇī), removes consumption (yakṣman), and likewise treats chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), catarrh (pratiśyāya), and Āḍhyavāta; indeed,
this auspicious electuary (leha) is the best remedy for all diseases.
And this "Enemy of Leucoderma" (Durnāmāri) has been seen to be effective when applied a thousand times over;
those who employ it remain free from disease for a hundred years.
It generates longevity and destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
This is the best of elixirs, the supreme producer of intelligence; this "Glorious Bahuśāla" jaggery is celebrated as the enemy of hemorrhoids.
When thrown into a vessel filled with water, if the jaggery does not float, [it is of the highest quality].
When it is thrown [into the fire], it remains motionless; when dropped, it does not break apart.
When it becomes like a coating on a ladle, or as light as cotton wool—this is declared to be the proper cooking for all substances such as molasses and the like. || 89-90 ||
When it has reached maturity, the jujube fruit (guḍa) makes a pleasant sound when cracked, feels pleasant to the touch,
yields juice when pressed, and possesses fragrance, color, and flavor.
[One should] boil two thousand bhallātaka fruits in one droṇa of water.
When that liquid has been reduced to one-quarter, the physician should add a *tulā* of jaggery;
then, having cut up five hundred *bhallātaka* fruits, he should cause them to be added right there.
Once this is prepared, [he should add] *triphalā*, *vyoṣa*, *yamānī*, *mustā*, and rock salt.
A person, rising in the morning and considering their digestive fire, should take one *karṣa* measure each of cinnamon bark, cardamom, cinnamon leaves, and *keśara*, and eat it. This cures leprosy,
hemorrhoids, jaundice, urinary disorders, malabsorption syndrome, abdominal tumors, and anemia.
This *guḍabhallātaka* indeed destroys splenic enlargement, cough, worms, diseases of the anus, and hemorrhoids; it is the best remedy for those suffering from hemorrhoids.
(95) Daśamūlī, amṛtā, bhārgī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, citraka, and śaṭhī— [these are used together]. (18)
A wise person should boil one thousand *bhallātaka* fruits with *palāśa* in a *droṇa* of water until a quarter remains;
into that decoction,
having added one *tulā* of jaggery, one should remove it once it has become a thick consistency like a linctus.
One should administer one *kuḍava* each of honey, long pepper oil, and castor oil, as well as one *kuḍava* each of cinnamon, cardamom, and black pepper;
this cures hemorrhoids, cough, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), anemia, and edema.
It is known that jaggery and *bhallātaka* destroy the exhaustion caused by fire (fever).
[One should take] *cavya*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *pāṭhā*, alkali (*kṣāra*), *kustumburu*, *yamānī*, the root of *pippalī*, and both *biḍa* and *saindhava* salts. (100)
One should cook ghee by grinding together *citraka*, *bilva*, and *abhayā*, along with four times the amount of curd, for the purpose of restoring the downward movement of flatus (*vāta*).
This cures dysentery (*pravāhikā*), prolapse of the rectum (*gudabhraṃśa*), difficult urination (*mūtrakṛcchra*), and excessive discharge (*parisrava*).
This ghee also cures pain in the rectum and the groins.

For one who drinks this clarified butter prepared with the three pungents (vyoṣa) as the internal ingredient in three times the amount of alkaline water from the ash of the palāśa tree, the hemorrhoids undoubtedly fall away.

One *prastha* of ghee, with one *pala* each of the five pungent spices (*pañcakola*) containing salt, cooked in three parts water and an equal amount of milk, cures fever, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, and cough. One should cook [the paste] in four *droṇas* of water with *kaṇṭakārī*, *amṛtā*, and *śata*.
In that regard, ghee prepared with agni, triphalā, vyoṣa, pūtika bark,
kaliṅgaka, kāśmarya, and viḍaṅga is a cure for hemorrhoids and urinary disorders;
it is named Siṃhyamṛta and was spoken by the Knower of Reality.
Having ground pippalī, madhuka, bilva, śatāhvā, madana, vacā,
kuṣṭha, śaṭhī, puṣkara, citraka, and devadāru,
one should cook oil combined with twice the amount of milk.
This is the best non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana) for those suffering from hemorrhoids and obstructed flatus;
it cures prolapse of the rectum, colic, dysuria, dysentery,
weakness of the waist, thighs, and back, and distension of the groin.

One should overcome the discharge of mucus, swelling in the anus, suppression of flatus and feces, and the excessive manifestation of the humors by means of an unctuous enema (anuvāsana). In the case of hemorrhoidal growths (raktārśas), the physician should initially ignore the bleeding blood.
When the malignant blood has been suppressed, however, there arise colic, constipation, and diseases of the blood;
[these are treated by] a gruel (peyā) prepared with parched grain (lāja), sour sorrel (cukrikā), plantain (kadala), saffron (kesara), and blue lotus (utpala).
It stops hemorrhaging;
likewise, it does so with *balā* and *pṛśniparṇī*.
Alternatively, a decoction of *śakra* with *viśva*, or else the tender fruits of *bilva*, [achieve the same].

In the same way, an application of jyotsnikā root should be employed by those suffering from bleeding hemorrhoids; likewise, one should practice the consumption of fresh butter with sesame seeds, or the consumption of saffron,
fresh butter, and sugar.
By the habitual consumption of the cream of curd churned with water, hemorrhoids that involve the flow of blood are pacified.
[This is achieved] with *samaṅgā*, blue lotus, *mocāhvā*, *tirīṭa*, sesame, and sandalwood.
Goat's milk should be administered to cure hemorrhaging from the anus.
One hundred palas of *kuṭaja* bark should be boiled in one droṇa of water; when reduced to one-eighth, the decoction should be removed from the heat.
Furthermore, one should cook the strained decoction until it reaches the consistency of a linctus (leha),
adding bhallātaka, viḍaṅga, the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā),
as well as rasāñjana, citraka, and the fruits of kuṭaja. (117)
One pala each of vacā, ativiṣā, and bilva—
having powdered these and thirty palas of jaggery— one should store them together;
then one should add one kuḍava of honey and likewise one kuḍava of ghee.
This electuary pacifies hemorrhoidal diseases arising from blood,
as well as those caused by vāta, pitta, kapha, and the combination of all three (sānnipātika). It also destroys all diseases born of hemorrhoids (durnāma).
It cures acid dyspepsia (amlapitta), diarrhea, anemia (pāṇḍuroga), anorexia, weakness of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-mārdava), emaciation, edema, and jaundice (kāmalā).
As an after-drink (anupāna), one should administer ghee, honey, buttermilk, water, or milk.
A linctus made from *kuṭaja* is prescribed for the destruction of worms and hair.
One hundred palas of fresh *kuṭaja* bark should be boiled with rainwater.
As long as that substance remains unsweetened, its own juice (svarasa) should then be extracted. [123] The juice of *mocā* and *samaṅgā*...
And one part each of phalinī and the other three [drugs] should be taken, and an equal amount of vatsaka seeds, powdered, should be added to this. || 124 ||
Once purified and boiled down until thickened, it should be taken while still liquid enough to coat the back of a ladle; it is to be administered in the appropriate dose at the proper time.
This medicinal preparation, which conquers hemorrhaging, should be drunk with goat’s milk or with rice-scum (maṇḍa),
according to the strength of one's digestive fire.
Having digested the medicine, one should eat śāli rice with milk or a decoction [of herbs]. This cures diarrhea caused by hemorrhoids.
This medicinal preparation (rasakriyā) quickly destroys colic with blood-tinged pain and even severe hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta), as it acts on both parts of the body.
Ghee prepared with the paste of kuṭaja fruit, bark, and filaments, along with nīlotpala, lodhra, and dhātakī, should be administered.
In the case of blood-piles (raktārśas) treated with a probe (śūla),
the physician [should take] avākpuṣpī, balā, dārvī, pṛśniparṇī, trikaṇṭaka, nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, and śaṅkha, each measured at two palas. (128–129)
This decoction should be ground with jīvantī, kaṭurohiṇī, pippalī, pippalīmūla, marica, devadāru,
kaliṅga, śālmalī flowers, vīrā, candana, and añjana.
Kaṭphala, citraka, musta, priyaṅgu, and ativiṣā;
the filaments of the lotus and water-lily, samaṅgā, along with nidigdhikā, viśva, mocarasa, and pāṭhā—each of these ingredients should be one karṣa in weight. (131–132)
One should prepare a decoction by boiling four *prasthas* [of the herbs] down to one *prastha*;
a *prastha* should be understood as thirty-two *palas*. Two *prasthas* of the fresh juice of *suniṣaṇṇaka* and *cāṅgerī* [should also be used]. || 133 ||
One should cook one prastha of ghee with all these aforementioned ingredients.
This is used for dysentery, diarrhea, disorders of the three doṣas, hemorrhage, tenesmus, prolapse of the rectum, and various types of slimy discharges.

This ghee, which increases strength, complexion, and digestive fire, should be administered according to the prescribed rules for frequent episodes of flatulence, swelling, colic, anal diseases, intestinal obstruction, deep-seated wind disorders, weak digestion, and loss of appetite. (136)
Either among various kinds of food and drink, or [food] that is exclusively wholesome,
on an auspicious day and under an auspicious lunar mansion, having first performed the rites of purification, one should collect *kālamuṣkaka* wood, burn it, and gather the ashes. (137–138)
Taking one *āḍhaka* of this, the physician should boil it in a *droṇa* of water;
when reduced to one-fourth, he should strain it through a cloth and boil it again after adding one *kuḍava* of conch-shell powder. || 139 ||
Gradually, over a mild fire, it should be cooked until its body becomes thick and solid.
Then, [one should add] sarjikā and yavaśūka, along with śuṇṭhī, marica, pippalī, vacā, ativiṣā, as well as hiṅgu and citraka.
Having added eight *māṣaka* measures of these powders separately and stirred them with a ladle, one should place them in an iron vessel.
This caustic, equal to fire, has been proclaimed by Kāśyapa and others.
A person of great intelligence should boil one *āḍhaka* of the ashes of *kālakamukaka* in six times that amount of water in a sturdy iron vessel.
Having repeatedly crushed pieces of conch-shell navel in a mortar with a pestle and burnt them in fire,
one should cast the purified residue into [the vessel].
If this caustic from castor seeds burns even better than a hundred words,
then when three-quarters of it has mostly evaporated, its clarity, smoothness, and redness [remain].
When it has fully formed, it should be drained; the alkaline water is then desired to be collected.
It is thoroughly mixed with a fourth, an eighth, or a sixteenth part [of the ingredients].
The alkaline water (kṣārodaka) and the conch-shell-like (śaṅkhaka) [alkaline] are prescribed in sequence as medium and superior;
the cooking of the alkali is said to be neither too thick nor too thin.
This alkaline preparation, prescribed for conditions such as *durnāmaka* (hemorrhoids), is used for rubbing over the affected area.

However, that which is intended for internal consumption in cases such as abdominal tumors (*gulma*) should be strained twenty-one times in six parts of water; some authorities say in four parts of water. || 146–147 ||
A thread that has been repeatedly soaked in the powder of *rajanī* and the milky sap of *snuhī*,
when tied very tightly, pierces hemorrhoids and fistula-in-ano.
One should apply it first to the right side, then the left, and subsequently to those located on the back and the front, in due order.
Having lubricated [the area] with the five-fold oil (pañcatikta), one should cauterize it with alkali or fire.
Hemorrhoidal growths caused by Vāta and Kapha should be treated with alkali; those caused by blood and Pitta should be treated with fire.
One should cut off large growths that have small roots and then cauterize them, provided the patient is strong.
Likewise, having cut away the *carmakīla* (skin tag), one should cauterize it with either [of the two methods];
a color resembling that of a ripe *jambu* fruit is praised as the result of cauterization with alkali (*kṣāra*).
Having scraped the hemorrhoid with the leaves of *gojī* and *śephālikā*, one should apply an ointment.
Having sealed the opening of the apparatus, one should leave it for a hundred days with an alkaline solution.
Then, having removed it, one should examine it; if it resembles a ripe jambū fruit, that is excellent, otherwise one should apply the ointment again.
That [wound], soaked in cold water and clarified butter, should be smeared with a paste of *yaṣṭīmadhu*.
It should not be depressed, should resemble the color of a palmyra fruit, and should have blood remaining when cauterized by fire.
Having extinguished the pain produced by the fire with honey and clarified butter, [one should proceed].

Once it has been properly cauterized, the physician should apply a plaster consisting of *tugākṣīrī*, *plakṣa*, *candana*, and *gairika*, combined with *amṛta* and *sarpiṣ*. Then, he should have the patient sit for a moment in a vessel filled with water.
In cases of obstruction of urine and feces, an alkaline preparation should be drunk with warm water;
for burning sensations arising from the bladder and other regions, an application of ghee washed a hundred times [with water] should be used.
One who understands the nature of digestion should consume fresh grain, black gram, buttermilk, and similar foods to promote it.
For the sake of purifying the qualities [of the body], one should drink an excellent decoction together with guggulu.
When that has been digested, wholesome food such as śāli rice and mung beans, along with bitter substances, clarified butter, and rock salt, should be consumed.
Once all the wounds have healed, the physician, having applied an alkaline preparation (kṣāra), should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana).
One should consume the digestive stimulant and carminative *pippalyādi* oil. [To prepare it:
one should boil eight *palas* each of *trivṛt*, *citraka*, *nirguṇḍī*, *snuhī*, *muṇḍitikā*, and *jaṭā* in one *droṇa* of water. (160)
Three palas of viḍaṅga, three karṣas each of the three pungents (vyoṣa),
five palas of triphalā, and one pala of śilājatu— whether it has been processed with divine herbs or with vaikaṅkata wood— one should place [these ingredients together].
Twelve *pala*s of powdered gold and iron should be given,
combined with twenty-four *pala*s of honey and sugar; once it has become solid and well-cooled, one should administer it after it has been removed from the heat.
This is known as Agnimukha, the supreme destroyer of diseases;
it quickly equalizes the digestive fire, making it as powerful as the fire of universal destruction (Kālāgni).
Even mountains are consumed by the ingestion of this for embodied beings.
Ghee, along with strengthening foods and drinks, milk, and meat broth, is beneficial;
it removes hemorrhoids, anemia, edema, skin diseases, and splenic enlargement, as well as premature graying of hair, āma-vāta, and diseases of the rectum. (166)
There is no disease that this [remedy] does not destroy in an instant.
One should avoid foods beginning with the letter 'ka', such as *karīra* (cassia fistula) and sour gruel (*kāñjika*); otherwise, iron dross and indigestible matter will flow from the body.
Citraka, triphalā, musta, granthika, cavikā, amṛtā,
hastipippalī, apāmārga, daṇḍotpala, and kuṭheraka—
one should boil four-pala portions of each of these in one droṇa of water.
Having cut two thousand *bhallātaka* fruits, one should cause them to be placed right there.
With that [decoction] reduced to one-fourth, the physician should cook half a *tulā* of refined iron (*tīkṣṇaloha*) and two *kuḍava*s of ghee in an iron vessel. || 170–171 ||

One should prepare one *pala* each of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *vahni*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *biḍa* salt, *audbhida* salt, black salt (*sauvarcala*), and *viḍaṅga*. Likewise, one *kuḍava* each of *vṛddhadāru* and *tālamūlī* [should be taken].
Having made a powder of eight palas of śūraṇa, one should add it [to the preparation]. When it has been cooked and cooled, two kuḍavas of honey should be added;
then, at the time of the morning meal, one should eat it according to one's strength.
It quickly dispels hemorrhoids, disorders of the digestive tract, anemia, loss of appetite, worms, abdominal tumors, urinary stones, urinary disorders, and colic;
it promotes the increase of semen and destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
This is the most excellent elixir (rasāyana), supreme in removing all diseases.
One part of mercury (rasa) should be combined with equal parts of viḍaṅga, marica, and abhraka;
these should be ground repeatedly in the juice of gaṅgāpālaṅka.
A quantity of blood [in the stool] destroys hemorrhoids and excessively stimulates the digestive fire.

One should avoid suppressing natural urges, sexual intercourse, riding on the back of animals, sitting in a squatting posture, and foods that aggravate the respective doshas, for these are detrimental to those suffering from hemorrhoids. (178)
Chapter 6: 1.
One should provide protection when [the digestive fire] is deficient; suppress the wind (vāta) when it is irregular;
counteract bile (pitta) when it is sharp; and purify phlegm (śleṣman) when it is dull. 1.
This powder, consisting of equal parts of the three pungents (trikaṭuka), ajamodā, rock salt (saindhava), and the two types of cumin (jīraka),
with one-eighth part of asafoetida (hiṅgu) added,
should be taken at the first meal with ghee in the measure of one kuḍava.
It generates the digestive fire and destroys diseases of the wind (vāta).
This great medicinal powder of *samaya*, *vaśūka*, and others, when licked with ghee at the time of sunrise, [produces these effects].
A single great medicine, consisting of warm water mixed with sugar, immediately quells hunger.
One should drink warm rice-scum (annamaṇḍa) combined with asafoetida and sauvarcala salt.
Even a weak fire, when combined with everything, may blaze up though it was uneven;
it awakens hunger, cleanses the bladder, bestows vitality, and increases the blood.
Manda (the scum of boiled rice) indeed possesses eight qualities: it removes fever, destroys phlegm and bile, and subdues wind.
One should drink the bark of the Udumbara tree combined with cow's milk.
Or one should drink milk-rice (pāyasa) prepared with these two for the pacification of excessive digestive fire.
Whatever medicine is heavy, nourishing, and productive of phlegm—all that is beneficial for excessive digestive fire; having consumed it, one should sleep during the day.
One should provide him with food again and again even if it has not been digested, so that, having obtained fuel within, he does not collapse.
[One should administer] the six pungents (ṣaḍūṣaṇa) with a decoction of viśvā, abhayā, and guḍūcī.
When phlegm is excessive and the digestive fire is weak, one should drink [the decoction] perfumed with cinnamon leaves;
this is called the "five-spices" (pañcakola) along with black pepper, known as the "six pungents" (ṣaḍūṣaṇa).
Harītakī, when consumed with ginger or with jaggery, [is beneficial].

Or even salt from the Indus region, taken continuously, kindles the digestive fire. Indeed, he whose fire has been extinguished who drinks a powder of rock salt, pathyā, and magadhodbhava, along with fire (citraka), with warm water, [is restored].
In this world, even excellent fresh food, when eaten with meat and ghee, is reduced to ashes in an instant. [The remedy is:
Sindhūttha, hiṅgu, triphalā, and yamānī—
One should prepare small boluses with equal parts of the three pungents (vyoṣa) and jaggery;
by consuming them,
even one with weak digestion can eat a large quantity until satisfied.
Viḍaṅga, bhallātaka, citraka, amṛtā, and nāgara, taken with equal parts of jaggery and ghee,
destroy those men whose digestive fire is weak.
They become like fires equal to the submarine fire (vāḍava).
[One may take] ginger with jaggery, or long pepper (upakulyā), or myrobalan (pathyā) as the third, or pomegranate.
One should always consume salted fresh ginger at the beginning of a meal when there is indigestion, anal diseases,
and constipation; it is wholesome, pleasing to the heart, and stimulates the digestive fire.

A confection (*khaṇḍa*) made with *kapittha*, *bilva*, *cāṅgerī*, black pepper (*marica*), cumin (*ajājī*), and *citraka* removes phlegm and wind, is constipating, and acts as a digestive stimulant and carminative. [Likewise, a preparation] of long pepper (*pippalī*), ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), *devadāru*, and *citraka* [is similarly beneficial]. (15–16)
The physician should prepare a decoction with cavikā, bilva pulp, ajamodā, harītakī, mahauṣadha, yamānī, dhānyaka, marica,
as well as jīraka and hiṅgu, along with sour gruel (kāñjika).
This sour gruel named Śārdūlaka bestows digestive fire and strength.
When fried with Siddhārtha oil, it dispels ten diseases:
cough, asthma, diarrhea, anemia, and jaundice.

Undigested matter (āma), abdominal tumors with colic (gulma-śūla), painful wind-tumors (vāta-gulma), hemorrhoids, and swelling— these are treated by administering [medicines] after eating and drinking,
according to suitability, using the method for preparing milk-decoctions (kṣīra-pāka-vidhāna) as a model for preparing sour gruel (kāñjika).
Let there be one part of asafoetida, and vacā should be double that amount.
Pippalī should be threefold, and ginger fourfold;
yamānikā should be fivefold, and harītakī sixfold.
Citraka should be sevenfold and Kuṣṭha eightfold;
this powder, which removes Vāta, should be drunk immediately with clear wine (prasannā),
or with curd, whey, liquor, or lukewarm water.
It cures chronic constipation, indigestion, splenic enlargement, and abdominal diseases; it relieves those whose limbs are wasting away or who have consumed poison;
it removes hemorrhoids, stimulates the digestive fire, destroys phlegm, and eliminates abdominal tumors.
This powder, named Agnimukha, quickly destroys cough and dyspnea, as well as consumption; it is never countered by anything. [In its preparation:
mercury is half a part, and equal amounts of viḍaṅga, marica, and abhraka are added.
Having kneaded it with rice-water, one should make a pill the size of a *guñjā* seed.
This should be consumed alone with rice-water as the after-drink; it kindles the digestive fire.
In this application, a diet of water and rice is desired for suitability.
Two types of alkali, *citraka*, *pāṭhā*, the salts of *karañja*, small cardamom, cinnamon leaf, *bhārgī*, *krimighna* (vidanga), asafoetida, *pauṣkara* root,
*śaṭhī*, *dārvī*, *trivṛt*, *musta*, *vacā*, and likewise *indrayava*.
Dhātrī, jīraka, vṛkṣāmla, śreyasī, and upakuñcikā;
amlavetasa, amlikā, yamānī, and suradāru; along with abhayā, ativiṣā, śyāmā, havuṣā, and āragvadha—these should be taken in equal parts. || 30-31 ||
One should prepare fine powders of equal parts of sesame, muṣkara, śigru, kokilākṣa, and palāśa, along with their ashes and iron filings, all heated and sprinkled with cow's urine. || 32 ||
One should also saturate it for three days with the juice of *mātuluṅga*,
for three days with fermented gruel (*śukta*), and for three days with the fresh juice of ginger.
This powder produces an extremely powerful digestive fire and possesses a brilliance equal to a blazing flame.
When administered according to the prescribed method, it quickly destroys diseases, as well as indigestion, abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic disorders, hemorrhoids,
abdominal enlargements, hernias, prostate enlargement (aṣṭhīlā), and gout (vātaśoṇita). || 35 ||
It drives away formidable diseases and kindles the extinguished digestive fire.
Having placed rice accompanied by all kinds of condiments in a fine vessel,
one should cause [the patient] to consume a portion of this powder the size of a cat's paw.
From the mere milking of the cow, all that becomes liquefied and warm.

[The ingredients are: long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), coriander (dhanyāka), black cumin (kṛṣṇajīraka), rock salt (saindhava), biḍa salt, cinnamon leaf (patra), tālīśa, and saffron (keśara).
Of these [five spices], take two-pala portions each; likewise, five palas of *sauvarcala* salt; one pala each of black pepper, cumin, and ginger; half a pala each of cinnamon and cardamom;
and two *kuḍavas* of sea salt.
One *kuḍava* of pomegranate and two *palas* of *amlavetasa*,
finely ground into a powder, rich in fragrance and like nectar—
this is the salt named Bhāskara, created by Bhāskara. (41)
For the benefit of the world, this [preparation] removes diseases caused by wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman).

It destroys wind-induced abdominal tumors (vātagulma) and whatever pains caused by wind (vātaśūla) there may be, when buttermilk is combined with whey, wine, *sīdhu* liquor, *śukta*, and sour gruel (*kāñjika*). (42–43)
For one who eats the meat of wild animals and various broths, the digestive fire becomes quickly capable of digesting even if it was previously weak.
[It cures] hemorrhoids, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, leprosy, and fistula-in-ano.
It cures heart disease, disorders of undigested food (āmadoṣa), and various ailments located in the abdomen;
it also removes splenic enlargement, urinary stones, asthma, cough, abdominal worms,
and especially various diseases such as gravel (śarkarā) and the like.
It destroys various types of jaundice, just as a thunderbolt [destroys all things].
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, citraka, hastipippalī,
hiṅgu, cavya, ajamodā, and the five salts— these are the ingredients.
One should add two types of alkali and hapuṣā, each measuring half a pala (48).
One should cook one prastha of fresh ginger juice with one prastha of ghee, along with curd, sour gruel, and vinegar, each equal in measure to the quantity of oil (sneha) (49).

This is known as Agnighṛta; it is highly praised for those with weak digestion, is the best destroyer of hemorrhoids, and likewise removes abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, cysts, goiters, cough, phlegm, fat, and disorders of vāyu.
(50) It also cures glandular swellings, tumors, scrofula, and disorders of kapha, fat, and wind.
It destroys disorders of the *grahaṇī*, as well as swelling and fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇḍara). Whatever diseases are located in the bladder and whatever are situated in the abdomen,
it quickly destroys them all, just as the risen sun destroys darkness.

Ghee prepared with twelve *palas* of the five pungent spices (*pañcakola*), four times as much whey (*mastu*), and the alkalis (*kṣāra*) will destroy weak digestive fire and *kapha*-type abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
One should boil five hundred *bhallātaka* fruits in one *droṇa* of water.
One should remove the decoction when one-eighth remains;
then, taking one *prastha* of ghee, one should cause these ingredients to be added:
the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), leadwort (*citraka*), and elephant pepper (*hastipippalī*). || 54–55 ||

One should add half a *pala* each of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *cavya*, *ajamodā*, the five salts, the two alkalis (*kṣāra*), and *hapuṣā*; likewise, one should add curd, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), and vinegar (*śukta*) in quantities equal to the measure of the oily substances (*sneha*).
The fresh juice of ginger and likewise the juice of *saubhāñjana*—
having combined all of these together, one should cook them slowly over a mild fire.
This is called *agnighṛta*, and it is highly recommended for those with weak digestive fire.
It is the best destroyer of hemorrhoids (arśas), restores the downward movement of obstructed flatus (mūḍhavāta),

and is effective in cases of abdominal tumors arising from kapha and vāta (gulma), elephantiasis (ślīpada), ascites (dakodara), edema (śotha), anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya), cough (kāsa), malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and dyspnea (śvāsa). || 59 ||

He quickly destroys these, just as the risen sun destroys darkness. (60) The two *pañcamūlas*, *triphalā*, *arkamūla*, *śatāvarī*, *dantī*, *citraka*, *āsphītā*, *rāsnā*, *pāṭhā*, *sudhā*, and *śaṭhī*. (61)
Having separately burnt ten-pala portions [of each substance] and collected the ashes,
one should strain those ashes through a water-droṇa twenty-one times.
One should then cook that liquid over fire until only a fourth part remains.
Then, having added a *tulā* of jaggery, one should cook it over a gentle fire.
Once the jaggery is known to be properly prepared, one should add these powders: *vṛścikālī*, the two types of *kākolī*, and *yavakṣāra*.
These five parts, each consisting of five *kalās*, and five *palas* separately of *harītakī*, *trikaṭuka*, *sarjikā*, *citraka*, and *vacā*—
one should add two *palas* each of *hiṅgu* and *amlavetasa* therein. (65)
Having made a pill the size of an *akṣa* fruit, one should eat it according to one's strength.
This [medicine] digests indigestion; once digested, it also kindles the digestive fire.
Whatever is eaten shall be digested, and it removes jaundice.

It quickly subdues splenic disorders, hemorrhoids, swelling, phlegmatic cough, and anorexia; it also cures weak digestion, irregular digestion, skin diseases, urinary disorders, and abdominal tumors when phlegm is located in the throat and chest.
This is known as Kṣāraguḍa; one should employ it for those afflicted by disease.
For nasal diseases, Citrakaharītakī should be prepared;
excluding the juice of Dhātrī, that which is prescribed here is Citraguḍa, which kindles the digestive fire.
Emesis induced with vacā and salt water is recommended for one suffering from āma.
Indeed, food that has been partially digested (vidagdha) in a person quickly reaches full digestion through cold water.
For that [cold water] indeed destroys his bile by its coolness and, due to its moist nature, leads it downward.
But for one whose food is burned immediately after eating—
He whose heart, chest, and throat are burning will indeed find relief by licking *abhayā* combined with grapes, sugar, and honey. || 72 ||
Harītakī prepared with fermented rice-water (dhānyāmla),
combined with long pepper, rock salt, and asafoetida,
along with charcoal and smoke, overcomes even severe indigestion.
Having conquered it immediately, one should produce hunger.
In the case of *viṣṭabdha*, sweating is beneficial, as is the drinking of salt water;
when there is a residual taste [of food], one should sleep during the day, undergo fasting, and avoid wind.
Those exhausted by physical exertion, sexual indulgence, travel, or riding vehicles;
those suffering from diarrhea;
and those afflicted by colic, dyspnea, or thirst.
Infants afflicted by hiccups and wind, those emaciated and depleted of phlegm, the elderly overcome by intoxication, and those suffering from indigestion of nutritional fluids.
Likewise, those who have remained awake at night and have fasted should be allowed to sleep freely during the day.
A wise person should indeed smear the abdomen with asafoetida, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and rock salt.
One should practice sleeping during the day; it destroys all types of indigestion.
A wise person should administer water prepared with coriander and ginger;
it pacifies the indigestion of undigested matter (āma), stimulates the digestive fire, and cleanses the bladder.
The physician, having ascertained the movement of the humors (doṣas), should administer a powder of Sauvarcala salt combined with Pathyā and Pippalī, along with buttermilk or warm water,
for the four types of indigestion (ajīrṇa), weak digestive fire (mandānala), and loss of appetite (aruci).
It quickly subdues flatulence, vāta-gulma, and colic. For a strong person who has been oleated, if there is a suspicion of indigestion at the time of eating—
One who eats wholesome food should first, without hesitation, consume *abhayā* with *śuṇṭhī*, and then eat his meal.
One with weak digestion may take a small amount of raw [food] along with *abhayā*, jaggery, and *nāgara*.
Having eaten, one should consume food with buttermilk combined with the six pungent spices;
once it is known that the person suffering from cholera has been made to vomit, purged, or has undergone proper fasting therapy.
One should properly treat one afflicted by hunger with peyas and other foods that stimulate digestion and promote maturation.
[One should also apply] a paste of kuṣṭha and saindhava salt combined with sour gruel and oil.
A lukewarm massage with *viṣūcī* [oil] relieves the pain of *khallī*. A decoction made from *karañja*, *nimba*, *śikharī*, *guḍūcī*, *arjaka*,
and *vatsaka*, when drunk, destroys severe *viṣūcikā* caused by food poisoning.
Having obtained vyoṣa, the fruit of karañja, haridrā,
and the root of mātuluṅgī, these should be dried in the shade and made into pills.
One may destroy *viṣūcī* by means of collyrium for the eyes made from jaggery, the essence of *puṣpa*,
long pepper, rice, *girikarṇikā*, and turmeric. || 85 ||
A pill made of *añjana* combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭu*) dissolves *viṣūcikā*; likewise, [a preparation] of cinnamon bark, *patra*, *rāsnā*, *aguru*, *śigru*, and *kuṣṭha*— 86.
An ointment made from ground rāmlā, vacā, and śatāhvā destroys cholera (viṣūcikā);
likewise, oil cooked with these same ingredients serves the same purpose.
In cases of thirst without distress, water infused with cloves or nutmeg is recommended, or cold water boiled with *bhadraghana*.
When dysentery has become excessively aggravated, the application of heat to the palms of the hands is praised as a remedy.
For one suffering from alasaka, emesis should first be induced with warm salt water.
Then, sudation, medicinal suppositories, and fasting should be employed; this sequence increases the digestive fire.
Furthermore, if the abdomen is painful and distended, one should apply a plaster made of sour substances ground into a paste.
A warm powder made from *dāru*, Himalayan ginger, *kuṣṭha*, *śatāhvā*, asafoetida, and rock salt, along with *yava* flour and alkali, taken with buttermilk,
destroys pain in the abdomen.
One may apply fomentation using *vaṭa* leaves filled with much warm air, or by other means such as the heat of the palms;
however, even if suffering from intense pain, one who has indigestion (*ajīrṇin*) should not drink medicine that cures colic (*śūla*).
Fire covered by the *doṣas* is not capable of digesting [them]; it destroys the flood of *doṣas*. (92) Adhikāra 7: 1.
*Pārasī-yamānikā* (Greek Aparājitā).
Taken in the morning with aged water and preceded by jaggery, it quickly expels the multitude of worms residing in the digestive tract.
One should drink the juice extracted from *pāribhadra* and *arkapatra*, mixed with honey;
or likewise the juice of *kebuka*, or the juice of *pattūra*.
One should lick the powder of *viḍaṅga*, which destroys worms, with honey. (2)
A decoction of mustā, ākhuparṇī, phala, and dāruśigru, combined with kṛṣṇā and the bark of krimiśatru,
[destroys] even long-standing [parasites] by both routes.
It destroys worms and diseases born of worms.
(3) Having eaten a cake made from ground *ākhu-parṇī* leaves and flour, one should afterwards drink *sauvīraka*; this is a supreme destroyer of worms. (4)
One should drink the fresh juice of *palāśa* seeds mixed with honey,
or one should drink the paste of those seeds with buttermilk to destroy worms;
or otherwise, one should employ the *surasā* group of drugs in every way.

One should drink vidanga, saindhava salt, kṣāra, kāmpillaka, and harītakī ground together with buttermilk for the eradication of all worms. [6] [One should also take them] with vidanga, pippalīmūla, śigru, and marica. [7]
Barley gruel prepared with buttermilk and suvarcikā salt destroys worms.
Bimbī-ghee, when drunk, kills worms located in the stomach and the intestines.
Likewise, triphalā, trivṛtā, dantī, vacā, and kāmpillaka [are used for this purpose].
Clarified butter prepared with these [drugs] in cow's urine is effective for destroying worms.
One should prepare three *prasthas* of *triphalā*, one *prastha* of *viḍaṅga*, and two *palas* of *daśamūla*, procuring them as available.
When one *droṇa* of water has been reduced to one-quarter, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with it, adding rock salt; that *pala* [of the resulting preparation] destroys worms.
This *viḍaṅga*-ghṛta should be licked together with sugar.
It drives away all worms, just as a released thunderbolt [drives away] the Asuras.
A paste made from the leaves of the Dhattūra plant combined with Rasendra,
or even one made from betel leaves, is a destroyer of lice.
Sesame oil prepared with viḍaṅga, sulphur, and realgar, along with fragrant water,
brings about total destruction [of worms] from birth.
A louse is accompanied by nits. 15.
Chapter 8.
Having examined a patient suffering from anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya), one should treat him accordingly.

Once the patient has been purified through both upper and lower channels and has been treated with unctuous substances using ghee, one should administer preparations consisting of powdered *harītakī* mixed with abundant honey and ghee. || 1 ||
One should drink ghee processed with turmeric and the three myrobalans, or likewise oil,
or one should drink preparations made from purgative substances.
And one should administer purgative formulations with ghee.
Now, the procedure for wind-born [fever] is oleaginous; for that born of bile, it is bitter and cold;
for that born of phlegm, it should be pungent, dry, and hot; and for that caused by a combination of humors, the treatment should be mixed accordingly.
In cases of Pitta-type jaundice, one should drink half a pala of Trivṛt powder mixed with two parts sugar.
However, for Kaphaja-pāṇḍu, one should take decomposed Harītakī combined with cow’s urine;
or alternatively, ginger and iron powder, or Pippalī and Pathyā, or Aśmajatuka.
Or one suffering from phlegm and jaundice should drink guggulu with cow's urine. Alternatively,
for the purpose of pacifying jaundice, a person should drink iron powder that has been processed in cow's urine for seven nights along with milk.
A bolus made from the powder of all these along with honey and mixed with buttermilk is recommended even in cases of advanced anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya). || 8 ||
Iron rust that has been heated and repeatedly purified with cow urine should be combined with honey and ghee, and this powder should be administered with food.
It stimulates the appetite, generates digestive fire, and removes swelling and the disease of jaundice.

Equal parts of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the three myrobalans (triphalā), musta, viḍaṅga, and citraka, along with nine parts of freshly prepared iron powder— this powder should be consumed with honey and ghee;
it cures anemia, heart disease, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, and jaundice.
Three parts of triphalā, three parts of trikaṭuka, one part of citraka root, and likewise of viḍaṅga;
fifty parts of asmanjana and the same amount of silver ash.
Eight parts of purified honey, eight parts of iron powder,
and eight parts of white sugar— all this, finely ground into a smooth powder, should be saturated with honey and placed in a beautiful iron vessel.

Then one should eat a dose equal in size to an udumbara fruit; by this daily practice, once it has been digested by the digestive fire, one may eat as desired, with the exception of horse gram (kulattha), black nightshade (kākamācī), and pigeons.
This yoga, known as Yogarāja, is like nectar;
it is the most excellent elixir (rasāyana), supreme in removing all diseases,
[including] anemia, poison, cough, consumption, and irregular fever.

It specifically destroys skin diseases, chronic fever, urinary disorders, dyspnea, hiccup, anorexia, epilepsy, jaundice, and hemorrhoids. Viśālā, kaṭukā, musta, kuṣṭha, dāru, and kaliṅgaka— [these are the ingredients].
Two *karṣas* each of *dvipicu*, *mūrvā*, and half a *karṣa* of *ghanapriyā*—
having drunk this powder with pleasant water, one should then lick it with honey.
This cures anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*), fever, burning sensations, cough, asthma, and loss of appetite.
It conquers gulma, constipation, āmavāta, and bitter bile (tiktapitta).
Milk boiled in an iron vessel should be drunk for seven days while following a wholesome diet;
one suffering from jaundice, consumption, or affliction by disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī) should drink it.

One should administer auspicious *pañcagavya* or even the "great bitter" (*mahātiktaka*) for the purpose of oleation to a patient suffering from jaundice and anemia. For one afflicted by jaundice who has undergone oleation, one should first employ a purgative.
Thereafter, a pacifying treatment should be administered by a knowledgeable physician:
the juice of triphalā, or of guḍūcī, or of dārvī, or of nimba. (24)
When consumed in the morning combined with honey, it removes jaundice; for one suffering from excessive desire, the juice of *droṇapuṣpī* is prescribed as a collyrium.
Alternatively, one may prepare a powder of *niśā*, *gairika*, and *dhātrī*.
Either the root of *karkoṭa* as a nasal medication (*nasya*) or the fruit of *jālinī* should be used for inhalation.
For those suffering from jaundice (*kāmalā*), *tribhaṇḍī* with sugar is beneficial, as is *gavākṣī* and ginger with jaggery.
One suffering from jaundice (kāmalā) or anemia (pāṇḍuroga) should lick a paste of dārvī, triphalā, vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, and iron powder, combined with honey and ghee.
Iron powder, harītakī, and haridrā in equal parts should likewise be taken with honey and ghee.
One suffering from jaundice (kāmalā) should lick powdered *bhayā* with jaggery and honey.
Or, by licking a mixture of *dhātrī*, iron powder, *vyoṣa*, *niśā*, honey, ghee, and sugar, one quickly overcomes even severe jaundice.
Having burnt iron dross with wood from axle-trees and quenched it eight times in cow’s urine, one should reduce it to powder; when licked with honey, it acts over a long period.
It destroys the disease known as kumbha-pāṇḍu.
One should employ the entire therapeutic regimen for pāṇḍuroga (anemia/jaundice) in cases of halīmaka;
furthermore, whatever treatment is prescribed for kāmalā should also be administered by the best of physicians.
One should cook iron powder in eight times its quantity of cow’s urine together with equal parts of viḍaṅga, musta, triphalā, devadāru, and the six pungents (ṣaḍūṣaṇa).
Having made pills of one akṣa each from these, one should consume them day after day.
One afflicted by jaundice and anemia attains comfort after a long time.
[34] Trikaṭu, triphalā, musta, viḍaṅga, cavya, citraka, the bark of dārvī, the mineral mākṣika, granthika, and devadāru; [35]
Having separately powdered two-pala portions of each of these,
one should cook them in eight times the amount of urine until they become like pure collyrium; then, one should add double the amount of powder of *maṇḍūra* (iron rust) to that.

One should make pills (vaṭakas) equal in size to an udumbara fruit; these should be consumed with buttermilk starting from the digestive fire [in the morning], and once they are digested, a meal that is wholesome to the patient should be taken. Indeed, these maṇḍūra-pills are life-givers for those suffering from jaundice (pāṇḍu-roga).
It pacifies skin diseases, chronic jaundice, edema, stiffness of the thighs, disorders of phlegm, hemorrhoids, jaundice, urinary disorders, and splenic enlargement.
Maṇḍūra (iron rust) is recommended to be taken after being repeatedly washed in urine.
One should cause eight times the amount of urine to be taken along with powdered maṇḍūra.
[Then take] punarnavā, trivṛt, śuṇṭhī, pippalī, marica, viḍaṅga, devadāru, citraka, and that which is called puṣkara.
Take equal parts of triphalā, the two types of haridrā, dantī, cavikā, the fruit of kuṭaja, tiktā, pippalīmūla, and mustaka; then add double that amount of maṇḍūra. || 42 ||
Having boiled [the powder] in eight times its quantity of cow urine, one should store it in a greasy vessel.
It cures anemia, edema, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, colic, hemorrhoids, worms, and abdominal tumors.
[One should take] the five-kola group (pañcakola), black pepper, devadāru, and the three fruits (triphalā). 44.
Take three-pala portions each of viḍaṅga and musta; when these powders have been prepared, add double that amount of maṇḍūra.
Having cooked this in eight times the quantity of urine until it has become thick, one should remove it from the fire.
Then, one should drink pills the size of a *akṣa* fruit with buttermilk while subsisting on buttermilk alone.
This conquers jaundice, weak digestion,
loss of appetite, hemorrhoids, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, or even stiffness of the thighs.
This [preparation] named Maṇḍūravajra destroys worms, splenic disorders, abdominal enlargements, and diseases caused by artificial poisons; it is a destroyer of the entire host of maladies.
[48] 11. Having squeezed two thousand *dhātrī* fruits, the physician [should extract] the juice.

One afflicted by jaundice should drink a preparation containing one-eighth part honey, half a kuḍava of powdered long pepper (pippalī), and mixed with half a tula of sugar; this should be cooked and kept in a smooth jar. Once digested, he should eat wholesome and moderate food. || 49-50 ||
This Arishta destroys jaundice, anemia, heart disease, gout, irregular fevers, cough, hiccups, anorexia, and dyspnea. One Prastha of aged ghee prepared with half a Prastha of grapes [is effective].
It removes jaundice, abdominal tumors, anemia, fever, and great swelling.
(52) Buffalo ghee prepared with turmeric, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), neem (*nimba*), *balā*, and licorice (*madhuka*), along with milk, is an excellent remedy for jaundice. (53)

One *prastha* of ghee, with four times as much milk, should be prepared by boiling it with one *akṣa* each of mūrvā, tiktā, niśā, yāsa, kṛṣṇā, candana, parpaṭa, trāyantī, vatsaka, bhūnimba, paṭola, ambuda, and dāru.
It cures paleness, fever, eruptive boils, swelling, hemorrhoids, and internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta).
[55] Trikaṭu, bilva, the two types of turmeric, triphalā, the two types of punarnavā, mustā, iron filings, pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, and devadāru; [56]
Ghee cooked with vṛścikālī, bhārgī, and milk pacifies all disorders caused by the consumption of clay. (57) Section 9.
That which is not excessive at the beginning should be administered even to a strong person or one who has eaten,
for it causes heart disease, anemia, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, fever, and so forth.
[This applies] to one whose humors have moved upward and to one suffering from *lohitapitta* (hemorrhagic disease) at the outset.
For one whose strength, flesh, and digestive fire are not diminished, fasting (apatarpaṇa) should be administered.

When [the disorder] moves upward, nourishing therapy (tarpaṇa) should first be performed, followed by purgation; when it moves downward, a liquid gruel (peyā) and emesis should first be given according to the patient's strength.
One should administer a satiation therapy (tarpaṇa) with ghee, honey, and parched grain flour;
when drunk at the proper time, it removes upward-moving hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta).
[One should also drink] water prepared with dates, grapes, madhūka, and parūṣaka.
Boiled and cooled, it should be administered with sugar for the purpose of satiation.
A bolus (modaka) made of trivṛtā, triphalā, śyāmā, pippalī, sugar, and honey cures fever caused by the combination of all three doṣas (sannipāta), as well as upward-moving hemorrhage (raktapitta).

When the downward movement [of the doshas] has first occurred, gruel prepared with śāliparṇī and other herbs should be given; for vomiting, a churned drink (mantha) mixed with madana fruit, honey, and sugar is prescribed.
[The grains to be used are: śāli, ṣaṣṭika, nīvāra, koradūṣa, and praśātikā.

Śyāmāka and priyaṅgu are the foods for those suffering from raktapitta. Masūra, mudga, caṇaka, and the fruits of the samudga and āḍhakī, prepared as soups or broths, are recommended for those with raktapitta.
Vegetables such as *paṭola*, the tips of *vetra*, *taṇḍulīya*, and others are beneficial,
as is the meat of the common quail (*lāvaka*), pigeon, rabbit, antelope, deer, and similar animals.
One should also administer water boiled with ginger and the six medicinal herbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

One should treat with stabilizing (stambhana) therapies a patient who is emaciated in flesh and strength, a child, an elderly person, or one afflicted by wasting (śoṣa), provided they cannot be subjected to emesis or purgation. One should administer the juice of vṛṣa leaves, squeezed out and mixed with honey and sugar.
By drinking this, even the most severe raktapitta is pacified;
having dissolved priyaṅgu, mṛttikā, añjana, and lodhra in a decoction of āṭarūṣaka, one should drink it with honey to alleviate raktapitta. || 13 ||
Having drunk the decoction of vāsā, utpala, mṛd, priyaṅgu, lodhra, añjana, and the filaments of ambhoruha, combined with sugar and honey, they destroy [the disease].
To quickly suppress the aggravated impulse of pitta and blood,
one should drink the fresh juice of vāsaka mixed with honey and powdered tālīsa.

A decoction of *āṭarūṣaka*, *mṛdvīkā*, and *pathyā*, mixed with sugar, removes disorders of *kapha*, *vāta*, and *pitta*, as well as *tamaka-śvāsa* (asthma), hoarseness of voice, and *rakta-pitta* (hemorrhagic conditions). || 15 ||
Rich with honey, it cures cough, asthma, and hemorrhaging (rakta-pitta).
While Vāsā exists, and while there is hope for life, why should one suffering from hemorrhaging, consumption, or cough despair? (16–17)
The juice produced from the fruit of the *phalgu* tree, taken with honey, quickly destroys the blood; likewise does a decoction of the root of *madayantī*, mixed with honey and sugar. (18)
Atasī flowers, samaṅgā,
pāṭhā, and the bark of the aru tree, when drunk with water, pacify raktapitta.
If he eats with mung bean soup,
