and if the blood-bile (raktapitta) does not subside when the kapha has been conquered by various astringent formulations and the digestive fire is kindled, then milk should be used for that condition where vata is predominant.
One should regularly consume goat's milk or cow's milk boiled in five times its quantity of water, mixed with sugar and honey; or one may take milk boiled with the *pañcamūla* (the five roots),
along with a small portion of grapes, the *parṇinīs*, or *madhuka*.
Milk prepared with *śvadaṃṣṭrā* and *śatāvarī* cures hemorrhaging. 22.
*Pakva-udumbara*, *kāśmarya*, *pathyā*, *kharjūra*, and *gostana*, when licked individually with honey, destroy *raktapitta*. 23.
Mustā, śākhoṭa,
tvak, and two drops of rasa, doubled with ghee; this paste of bhūnimba is directed upward.
It brings about the alleviation of bile-blood disorders, dyspnea, and cough. By licking the powder of the flowers of *khadira*, *priyaṅgu*, *kovidāra*, and *śālmali* with honey, one attains health.
Abhayā combined with honey is considered digestive and appetizing;
it destroys phlegm and blood-bile (raktapitta), and cures colic and diarrhea.
Pathyā, when saturated seven times in the fresh juice of vāsaka, [performs these same functions].
Or, black iron (kṛṣṇā) licked with honey quickly conquers raktapitta.
In the process of impregnation (bhāvanā), a liquid should be added that thoroughly effects moistening.
Half an akṣa each of cardamom, cinnamon leaves, and cinnamon bark, as well as half a pala of long pepper (pippalī).

The physician should grind one pala each of sugar, licorice, dates, and raisins, mix them with honey, and form them into pills. Then, one should consume one pill, the size of an akṣa, every single day.
Cough, dyspnea, fever, hiccup, vomiting, fainting, intoxication, vertigo, spitting of blood, thirst, pain in the flanks,
loss of appetite, swelling, splenic disorders, excessive vāta, hoarseness of voice, and wasting from chest injury. || 31 ||
This pill is nourishing, aphrodisiac, and destroys *raktapitta*.
In cases of breath smelling of iron and eructations smelling of blood,
one should eat one *śāṇa* measure of *pṛthvīkā* with double the amount of sugar.
Nosebleed [is treated by] āmalaka fruit ground with oil and fried in ghee,
which acts like a dam against the force of water.
One should apply a plaster on the head;
when [the discharge] flows from the nose, water mixed with sugar should be administered, or milk through the nostrils.
One should drink grape juice with milk and ghee, or sugarcane juice with sugar, which is beneficial;
or a nasal drop (nasya) made from the juice of pomegranate flowers or from dūrvā grass may be used.
A preparation made from mango seeds or onions conquers bleeding from the nose.
However, when there is excessive discharge from the penis, an urethral enema (uttara-basti) should be administered; alternatively, one may drink milk boiled with the five roots known as *tṛṇa*.

One should cook the king of ghees (*sarpirāja*) over a mild fire with one *karṣa* each of these: dūrvā grass, the filaments of the blue lotus (*utpala*), mañjiṣṭhā, elavāluka, sugar, cold usīra, musta, candana, and padmaka.
Having added rice-water and goat's milk in a fourfold quantity, one should administer it as a drink if blood is being vomited; as a nasal drop if it has reached the nose;
and if it flows from both ears, one should fill the ears with it.
If the blood flows from the eyes, one should fill the eyes with it;
if it issues from the penis or the anus, one should employ it in enema treatments (basti);
and if it issues from the pores of the skin, one should apply it as an ointment (abhyaṅga). || 41 ||
Having ground śatāvarī, dāḍima, tintiḍīka, kākolī, medā, madhuka, vidārī,
and the root of bījapūraka;
The wise physician should cook ghee with four times the amount of milk;
that ghee destroys cough, fever, distension, constipation, colic, and internal hemorrhaging (rakta-pitta).

Two *prastha*s of the juice of the roots of *śatāvarī* are prescribed, along with an equal amount of milk; one should cook these in one *prastha* of ghee with *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *medā*, and likewise *mahāmedā*. (44)
The physician should drain the prepared mixture consisting of kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, mṛdvīkā, madhuka, mudgaparṇī, māṣaparṇī, vidārī, and red sandalwood, combined with sugar and honey. || 45-46 ||
This supreme aphrodisiac (vājīkaraṇa) should be administered in cases of disorders of blood and bile (raktapitta), diseases of wind and blood (vātarakta), and in those with diminished semen.
It also cures burning sensations in the shoulders and head, as well as fever arising from bile (pitta).
This *śatāvarī* ghee quickly destroys these diseases— pain in the genitals, burning sensations, and bilious dysuria— just as the wind scatters torn clouds;
it increases strength, complexion, and digestive fire.

By the force of the statement, "The paste is remembered as one-fourth part of the fat; likewise honey and sugar [are added] to the paste," it should be added to the fat so that it constitutes one-fourth.
50. [One should take] vāsā along with its branches, leaves, and roots.
Having prepared a decoction and given its paste along with flowers, one should cook ghee; when taken with honey, that quickly destroys [excessive] blood.
Because of the abundance of the paste from śaṇa, kovidāra, vṛṣa, and kakubha, the flower-paste amounts to four palas per prastha.
There are one hundred palas of aśvagandhā and half that amount of gokṣura.
Śatāvarī, vidārī, śāliparṇī, and likewise balā;
the sprouts of the aśvattha tree, lotus seeds, punarnavā, the fruit of the kāśmarī, and similarly the seeds of the māṣa bean. || 53–54 ||
One should boil ten *pala* portions each of [the following] separately in four *droṇas* of water;
when one-fourth remains, one should remove the decoction.
[The ingredients are: *mṛdvīkā*, *padmaka*, *kuṣṭha*, *pippalī*, and red sandalwood (*raktacandana*). || 55 ||
Vālaka, nāgapuṣpa, and likewise the fruit of ātmaguptā;
blue lotus, the two types of śārivā, and especially the group of life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs—each in the measure of one karṣa, along with two palas of sugar. || 56–57 ||
One should cause one āḍhaka of the juice of *pauṇḍraka* sugarcane to be added there,
and cook it with four times as much milk to produce one prastha of ghee. This cures *raktapitta*, wasting due to chest injury (*kṣatakṣīṇa*), jaundice, and gout (*vātaśoṇita*).
It destroys jaundice, as well as swelling, discoloration of the complexion, loss of voice, anorexia, dysuria, and pain in the flanks;
this should be administered to kings who frequent large harems.
For women who are childless, for those whose bodies are weak, for the impotent, for those with scant semen, for the aged, and for those with diminished virility—
this is the best strength-giver, heart-tonic, aphrodisiac, drinkable elixir (rasāyana).
It produces vigor and splendor, increases longevity and vital breath,
and enhances the semen of a man whose senses are weak;
he becomes freed from all diseases, like a tree sprinkled with water.

Known as Kāmadeva, it is recommended for all diseases. One should cook seven *prasthas* of clarified butter together with the juices of *śatāvarī*, *payas*, grapes, *vidārī*, sugarcane, and *āmalaka*. (64)
One should drink this, combined with one-quarter part sugar, to cure *raktapitta* (hemoptysis/blood-bile).
It is strengthening, energizing, aphrodisiac, and a destroyer of hunger, heart disease, chest wounds, Pitta-type colic, vaginal wind, and menorrhagia.
One hundred palas of well-steamed *kūṣmāṇḍaka* (pumpkin gourd), with the seeds removed, should be cooked slowly in one *prastha* of heated clarified butter in a sturdy copper vessel.
When the cooking reaches a consistency resembling honey, one should then add one hundred pieces of sugar-candy.

Two palas each of long pepper (pippalī) and ginger (śṛṅgavera), and two palas of cumin (jīraka); half a pala each of cinnamon (tvak), cardamom (elā), cinnamon leaves (patra), black pepper (marica), and coriander (dhānyaka)—
one should place these into it ground into powder, and stir them repeatedly with a ladle.
Once cooked, one should place it in a vessel after adding honey and half as much ghee; a patient suffering from raktapitta, chest wounds, or consumption,
and afflicted by cough, dyspnea, fainting, vomiting, thirst, and fever, should consume it according to their digestive strength.

This proven *kūṣmāṇḍaka-rasāyana*, prepared by the two Aśvins, is aphrodisiac, rejuvenating, and restores strength, complexion, and clarity; it heals chest wounds, is nourishing, and awakens the voice. (71–72)
A vessel should be provided for cooking with kūṣmāṇḍaka juice according to the measurement of the pieces of āmalaka, until as much essence as possible has been extracted;
here too, the cooking is done with a seal, [using the fruit] peeled and de-seeded.
One *prastha* of *kūṣmāṇḍa* (pumpkin gourd), weighing fifty *palas*, should be boiled in clarified butter;

one hundred *palas* of sugar-candy should be taken and cooked in an *āḍhaka* of *vāsā* decoction, along with one *karṣa* each of *mustā*, *dhātrī*, auspicious *bhārgī*, and the three aromatics (*trisugandha*).
One should administer one pala each of ativiṣā, viśvadhanyāka, and marica, along with one kuḍava of pippalī and one māna of honey;
this cures cough, dyspnea, consumption, hiccups, internal hemorrhaging, and halīmaka.
It cures heart disease, acid dyspepsia (amlapitta), and chronic catarrh.
Taking one *tulā* of *vāsā*, the physician should boil it in eight times its quantity of water; when reduced to one-fourth, he should cook one *āḍhaka* [of ghee] with that decoction.
One hundred palas of powdered abhayā and one hundred palas of pure sugar, two palas of pippalī powder,
and one kuḍava (or one pala) of well-ground caturjāta, [should be added] once the [mixture] has been cooked and cooled, along with honey.

One suffering from *rakta-pitta*, wasting due to chest wounds (*kṣata-kṣayī*), afflicted by cough and asthma, or tormented by consumption (*yakṣman*), should eat [this] after throwing it [into the mixture] and stirring it. [The ingredients are:
*śatāvarī*, *chinnaruhā*, *vṛṣa*, *muṇḍitikā*, and *balā*. 80.15.
One should boil five palas each of tālamūlī, gāyatrī, the bark of triphalā, bhārgī,
and puṣkaramūla separately in one droṇa of water until only one-eighth remains. || 81-82 ||
Twelve *pala*s of powdered *rukmaloha* (golden iron), even if treated with divine herbs or honey,
should be administered; sixteen *pala*s of clarified butter, equal in quantity to the sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*), should be given by the wise.
One should cook it in a copper vessel like a preparation of jaggery (guḍapāka) according to one's desire.

Half a prastha of honey should be added, along with auspicious mineral pitch (aśmajatuka), cinnamon (tvac), vṛddhadāraka (śṛṅgī), viḍaṅga, black pepper (kṛṣṇā), ginger (śuṇṭhī), and cumin (ajājī)— one pala each of these.

Having added the powder of triphalā, dhānyaka, patra, two parts each of marica and keśara, and having stirred it well, one should store it in a greased vessel. Then, one should administer it at the appropriate time in the measure of a cat's paw-print (biḍālapadaka).
One should consume beef broth with milk as an after-drink, as well as meat broth and milk;
these are heavy, aphrodisiac, and nourishing after-drinks that are unctuous and strengthening,
[and they cure] blood-bile disorders, consumption, cough, and especially colic in the digestive tract.
It destroys vātarakta, prameha, śītapitta, vomiting, fatigue,
swelling, anemia, skin diseases, as well as splenic enlargement,
constipation, hemorrhaging, and acid dyspepsia (amlapitta). || 89 ||
It is beneficial for the eyes, nourishing, aphrodisiac, auspicious, and increases affection;
it bestows health and progeny, is excellent, and increases desire, digestive fire, and strength.
It is proclaimed that the first among these, the *khaṇḍaka* (sugar-candy), brings about prosperity and lightness.
One should employ the meat of the goat, the pigeon, the partridge, the francolin, the hare, the kuraṅga deer, and the black antelope.
One should also provide the drinking of coconut milk and the consumption of suniṣaṇṇaka and vāstuka greens.
Dried radish, cumin, patola, the fruit of bṛhatī, the fruit of vārtāka,
ripe mango, dates, sweet pomegranate, and whatever meat originates from marshy regions— all these begin with the letter 'ka'. (93–94)
One who prepares [the medicine] must especially avoid [impurities] such as *khaṇḍaka*;
here too, processes such as *puṭana* (encapsulation) are desired, just as in the case of other metals.
Furthermore, whatever medicine has been prescribed for bile-fever (*pittajvara*), both externally and internally, [should be applied].
That which is beneficial for *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) and beneficial for those who are emaciated or suffering from chest wounds [is recommended].
96. Chapter 10. Rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wheat, barley, green gram (*mudga*), and others are auspicious.
Alcoholic drinks and the meat of wild birds and animals are recommended for those who are drying up.
For those who are withering away and have wasted flesh, one who knows the proper procedures should provide meat prepared according to the rules;
specifically, he should give the meat of carnivorous animals, as it is particularly nourishing.

For those with a predominance of the doshas, emesis along with purgation is recommended; for those who have undergone oleation and sudation, one should employ unctuous therapy that does not cause depletion. Once the gastrointestinal tract is purified, one should apply procedures that are nourishing and digestive-stimulant.
The strength of men depends on semen, and life indeed depends on the impurities; therefore, one should diligently preserve both the impurities and the semen of a patient suffering from consumption.
[One should give] pippalī, barley, kulattha, and ginger. (5)
One should drink aged meat broth prepared with pomegranate and *āmalaka*; by this, six disorders, such as chronic catarrh (*pīnasa*) and others, are eliminated.
In this context, the quantity of the substance, water, and flour used in the broth follows the rules of the culinary science (*sūdaśāstra*).
There should be twelve palas of meat for one prastha of thick broth, but six palas for thin broth.
One should prepare a meat ball (vaṭaka) with the meat, and drink water boiled with coriander, long pepper, ginger, and the ten roots (daśamūlī) when the broth is very clear.
For the alleviation of pain in the sides, fever, dyspnea, catarrh, and other ailments,
*aśvagandhā*, *amṛtā*, *abhīru*, the ten roots (*daśamūlī*), *balā*, *vṛṣā*, *puṣkara*, and *ativiṣā* destroy consumption for those who subsist on milk and meat broth.
A decoction prepared with the ten roots (daśamūla), balā, rāsnā, puṣkara, suradāru, and nāgara should be drunk for [relief of] pain in the flanks, shoulders, and head. || 10 ||
To pacify coughs caused by dryness and other ailments, one should add the powdered bark of *kakubha*, *nāgabalā*, and the seeds of *vānarī* to water while it is being boiled with milk.
Cooked [meat] combined with ghee, honey,
and sugar cures consumption and other ailments,
as does the meat of the pigeon, the peacock, the sheep, and the deer, each taken separately. 12.

Meat powder drunk with goat’s milk is a supreme remedy for consumption (yakṣman); likewise, the root of gajabalā, licked with honey and the essence of flowers, brings about the complete destruction of wasting disease (kṣaya). (13)
Having drunk the *vāyasajaṅghā* plant with milk alone,
or having licked a preparation of black grapes and sugar mixed with honey and oil, destroys consumption (*kṣaya*). 14.
One suffering from consumption should lick a paste made of *vāsā*, *aśvagandhā*, and *kṛṣṇā* (long pepper) combined with honey and ghee;
or, while subsisting on milk, one who licks fresh butter mixed with sugar and honey attains incomparable nourishment.
(15) If [the patient] consumes ghee and honey in equal proportions, he likewise gains great strength.
Sugar, *tugākṣīrī*, long pepper, and *bahulā* bark—
starting from the last and doubling each subsequent ingredient— one should form a linctus with honey and ghee;
having powdered this, one should consume it, for it removes dyspnea, cough, and consumption.
For one suffering from a stiff tongue, loss of appetite, weak digestion,
pain in the flanks, burning sensations in the hands, feet, and shoulders, as well as fever, blood disorders, and upward-moving hemorrhages, [one should use] cloves, kakkola, ushira, and sandalwood.
Equal parts of natam, blue lotus, and jīraka;
along with truṭi, kṛṣṇā, aguru, bhṛṅga, keśara, kaṇā, viśvā, nalada, and ambuda. || 19 ||
Equal parts of snake-gourd, nutmeg, and bamboo-seed, finely ground into a smooth powder along with white sugar,
provide nourishment and kindle the digestive fire.
It bestows strength, is most aphrodisiac, and alleviates the three doṣas;
it cures constriction of the chest, asthma, throat obstruction, cough, hiccup, anorexia, consumption, and chronic rhinitis.
It destroys dysentery with tenacious stools, fistula-in-ano, tumors, urinary disorders, and abdominal tumors accompanied by fever. Tālīśapatra, marica, nāgara, and auspicious pippalī—
With each subsequent ingredient increasing by one part, two and a half parts of cinnamon and two and a half parts of cardamom should be added;
to this, white sugar eight times the amount of long pepper should be given.
This powder is an excellent digestive stimulant that cures asthma, cough, and loss of appetite.
This [preparation] removes heart disease, anemia, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, splenic enlargement, emaciation, and fever;
it destroys vomiting, diarrhea, and colic, and it facilitates the downward movement of obstructed wind (*mūḍhavāta*).
One should prepare pills by cooking this powder with sugar candy (*sitopāla*).
For pills are considered lighter than powders due to their contact with fire; some prescribe them for the Pitta-type [fever], using *vaṃśalocanā* along with *śṛṅgī*,
*arjuna*, and *aśvagandhā*.
Nāgabalā, puṣkara, abhayā, and chinnaruhā, combined with tālīsa and other [ingredients], form a linctus with honey and ghee that destroys consumption (yakṣman). || 26 ||
Madhu, tāpya, viḍaṅga, ashmaja, tuttha, loha, ghee, and abhayā,
when consumed by one who eats wholesome food, destroy even the most virulent form of yakṣman (consumption).
Likewise, vyoṣa, śatāvarī, the three fruits (triphalā), and the two types of balā [are effective].
This yoga, combined with iron powder, removes all diseases.
It destroys chest wounds as well as diseases of the throat, and it cures the most violent pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman), stiffness of the arms, and facial paralysis.
Take seven karṣas of pure mercury and grind it with the fresh juice of jayā and ārdraka on a stone slab in a mortar until it becomes a solid mass; then,
one should further process it by saturating it with the juices of jalakarṇī and kākamācī.
One pala of *saugandhika* root, processed with the fresh juice of *bhṛṅga*,
powdered and combined with mercury, should be triturated in two palas of goat’s milk until it forms a thick mass, which is then made into pills the size of a soaked pea.
Having first worshipped Śiva and satisfied the twice-born,
one who has digested his food should eat only a single meal, subsisting on milk, meat, and broth;
[this cures] all forms of consumption, cough, hemoptysis, and loss of appetite.
It cures even that acid dyspepsia (amlapitta) which has been abandoned by hundreds of physicians.
[One should take] cardamom, ajamoda, āmalaka, abhayā, akṣa, gāyatrī, nimba, aśana, and śālasāra.
Having boiled viḍaṅga, bhallātaka, citraka, the three pungents (kaṭutrika), ambhoda,
and surāṣṭrikā in water, one should cook ghee with that [decoction].
When this has been thoroughly prepared and poured out,
one should add thirty palas of white sugar and six palas of tugākṣīrī to it. || 36 ||
One should add twice as much honey to a prastha of ghee, then place it in a churner and stir it; thereafter,
one should lick it, one pala at a time, every morning.
Afterwards, one may drink milk without restraint.
For this is supremely conducive to wisdom, purifying, beneficial for the eyes, and likewise most conducive to longevity.
It quickly dispels consumption, colic, anemia, and fistula;
furthermore, nothing at all is to be avoided here.
And this elixir (rasāyana), when practiced,
consists of balā, vidārī, the small five roots (hrasvā pañcamūlī), and punarnavā;
along with one handful each of the leaf-buds (śuṅgā) from each of the five milk-exuding trees (kṣīravṛkṣa).
In a decoction of these [drugs] consisting of two parts of milk and one part of Vidārī and Ajakarṇa,
one should cook one Āḍhaka of ghee with one Akṣa-measure of the pastes of the Jīvanīya [herbs]. When it has been strained and cooled, one should add thirty-two Palas of sugar.
One *kuḍava* each of the powders of wheat, long pepper, bamboo-manna, and water-chestnut, combined with honey, should all be thoroughly stirred with a churning-stick until thickened;
having then formed them into balls of ghee-jaggery (*sarpirguḍa*), one should wrap them in birch bark.
Having eaten those *palika* measures, one should drink milk and wine as an after-drink (*anupāna*) in cases of phlegm,

consumption, cough, wasting from chest injury, exhaustion from women, carrying loads, or emaciation, as well as in cases of hemoptysis, fever, chronic catarrh, and pain localized in the chest. (43–44)
These are recommended for pain in the sides or head, and for disorders of the voice or complexion.

For these thirteen pala-measures of the drugs, water should be boiled down, fearing that the quantity of the substance might be too small; [the water should be] eight times the weight of the drugs. Vidārī and āja-rasa (goat's milk) should each be equal in measure to the decoction.
Some authorities, however, have stated that the decoction of the aforementioned drugs should be equal in quantity to the clarified butter. Bilva, agnimantha, syonāka, kāśmarya, pāṭalī, balā,
the four types of parṇī, pippalī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and the two types of bṛhatī— [these are the ingredients].
Śṛṅgī, tāmalakī, drākṣā, jīvantī, puṣkara, aguru, abhayā,
amṛtā, ṛddhi, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, śaṭhī, musta, punarnavā, medā, sūkṣmailā, utpala, and candana. || 48 ||
One pala each of vidārī, vṛṣamūla, kākolī, and kākanāsikā,
along with five śata (five hundred) of āmalaka fruits, should be placed together and boiled in one droṇa of water. || 49–50 ||
Then, having recognized that these medicinal herbs have lost their potency,
the physician should remove that juice and that *āmalaka* fruit, de-seed it, and fry it in twelve *palas* of oil and clarified butter, adding half a *tulā* [of sugar].
One should properly prepare one *ṣaṭpala* of purified sugar-candy (*matsyaṇḍikā*) like a linctus (*leha*).
Once it has been prepared and cooled, one should add six *palas* of honey, four *palas* of *tugākṣīrī*, and likewise two *palas* of long pepper (*pippalī*). (52–53)
One should add one *pala* each of cinnamon-bark (*tvak*), cardamom (*elā*), cinnamon-leaves (*patra*), and *keśara*.
This is called *cyavanaprāśa*, declared as a supreme rejuvenative (*rasāyana*). It specifically removes cough and asthma, and is thus prescribed.
It promotes the growth of the limbs for those who are emaciated, wounded, aged, or young;
it removes loss of voice, diseases of the chest, heart disease, gout, thirst, and disorders of the urine and semen.
One should administer its dose to one who would otherwise be unable to eat;
by its use, Cyavana, though very old, became young again.
It bestows intelligence, memory, luster, and freedom from disease.
Excellence of the body, strength of the senses, supreme delight in women, increase of the digestive fire, clarity of complexion, and the downward movement of the wind (vāta). 58.
By the application of this elixir,
even an old man, through entering the medicinal chamber (kuṭī-praveśa), shall cast off the form produced by old age and regain his former appearance.
It possesses the appearance of those in the bloom of youth.
(59) When white sugar-candy is obtained, one should gently roast the *dhātrī* fruit;
generally, when the substance is cooked in water consisting of four parts, it becomes devoid of its original flavor. (60)
Jīvantī, madhuka, grapes, and the fruits of kuṭaja;
śaṭhī, puṣkaramūla, vyāghrī, gokṣuraka, and balā; nīlotpala, tāmalakī, trāyamāṇā, and durālabhā.
Having ground pippalī in equal measure, the physician should cook it with ghee.
This foremost ghee dispels the elevenfold manifestation of the host of diseases that has arisen from the Lord of Disease (Rogeśa).
Clarified butter prepared with long pepper and jaggery, combined with goat’s milk,
is for the purpose of increasing the digestive fire in those suffering from wasting and cough.
One should boil one *tulā* each of licorice, *balā*, *guḍūcī*, and the minor *pañcamūla*.
When one-eighth part of water remains in the winnowing basket,
one should cook ghee in that vessel with three parts of the juice of *dhātrī* and *vidārī*, along with a *maṇa* of milk and well-ground *jīvanīya* herbs; this is the *pārāśara* ghee.
When practiced regularly, it uproots consumption (rājayakṣman) along with its army.
Taking one *tulā* of goat meat, one should prepare it in salt water;
when reduced to one-quarter, one should cook one *prastha* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) with that very decoction.
And having properly prepared [the oil] with one pala each of the pastes of ṛddhi, vṛddhi, the two types of medā, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, kākolī, and kṣīrakākolī,
one should remove it from the heat once it is well-cooked and administer it when it has cooled. || 68–69 ||
One should add eight palas of sugar and one kuḍava of honey;
by drinking one pala each every morning, it destroys even invincible consumption (yakṣman),
as well as wasting from chest wounds (kṣatakṣaya), cough, pain in the flanks, and loss of appetite.
It destroys hoarseness of voice, chest disease, and even most severe asthma.
Having boiled one hundred palas of goat meat in two droṇas of water...
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with water that is eight parts [of the ghee] and well-prepared, along with the paste (*kalka*) of the *jīvanīya* [drugs]. (72)
This meat-ghee, taken in the measure of one *kuḍava*, destroys bile and wind; when consumed combined with meat-broth, it also cures diseases born from those [humors]. (73)
Violent cough and asthma, consumption, terrible pain in the sides and heart, and wasting due to the exhaustion of travel.
And it pacifies yet another [disease].
Ghee prepared with goat dung juice, urine, milk, and curd [is likewise effective].
One should boil [the drugs] in a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) along with alkali;
this is supreme for removing consumption (yakṣman) and for the pacification of cough and dyspnea.
75.17. One should cook [the drugs] in a decoction of the two pentads of roots (dvipañcamūla).
Having properly added one *prastha* of meat broth and a paste of *balā* as the internal ingredient (*garbha*) to two *prasthas* of milk, one should prepare it together with one *prastha* of ghee.
It is prescribed as a remedy for consumption arising from all types of trauma, as well as for colic, chest wounds, wasting diseases, and coughing.
[One should cook] one *tulā* of *nāgabalā* in a remaining eighteenth part of a *droṇa* of water.
One should prepare ghee and milk in equal proportions with a decoction of *teja* [iron];
[adding] half a *pala* each of *atibalā*, *balā*, *yaṣṭi*, *punarnavā*,
*prapauṇḍarīka*, *kāśmarya*, *priyāla*, and *kapikacchu*.
This ghee prepared with *aśvagandhā*, *asitābhīru*, the two types of *medā*, the three types of *trikaṇṭaka*, lotus stalks, *viṣa*, *śālūka*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and *kaśeruka*,
along with *nāgabalā*, cures *raktapitta*, chest wounds, and consumption.
It destroys burning sensations, vertigo, and thirst, and is supremely conducive to strength and nourishment (80).
It is strengthening, vitalizing, life-prolonging, and a destroyer of wrinkles and graying hair; by using it for six months, even an old man becomes like a youth (81).

Having drunk ghee prepared with the fresh juices of *nirguṇḍī*— including its roots, fruits, and leaves— one who is emaciated by consumption (*kṣaya*) shines like a god, freed from disease. [One should take] *balā*, *aśvadaṃṣṭrā*, *bṛhatī*, *kalasī*, *dhāvanī*, and *sthirā*...
Having prepared a decoction of nimba, parpaṭaka, musta, trāyamāṇā, and durālabhā,
one should add tāmalakī, śaṭhī, drākṣā, puṣkaramūla, medā, and āmalakas as a paste.
Ghee prepared with that [decoction] of ghee and milk is a supreme remedy for fever;
it pacifies wasting and cough, and removes pain in the head and the sides of the chest.
(85) This is stated following the *vāsādyaghṛta* mentioned by Caraka.
In this context, they say that one should add either ghee or decoction, each twice the quantity of milk separately.
One should also add sandalwood water, nakha, vāpya, yaṣṭī, śaileya, padmaka, mañjiṣṭhā, sarala, dāru, śaṭī, elā, pūti, and keśara.

Patra, oil, murā, māṃsī, kakkola, vanitāmbuda, the two types of haridrā, śārivā, tiktā, lavaṅga, aguru, kuṅkuma, tvak, reṇu, and nalikā— with these [ingredients], oil and four times as much whey (mastu) [are combined]. || 88 ||
Prepared with lac juice, it is a destroyer of planetary afflictions and a producer of strength and complexion (89).
It destroys epilepsy, fever, insanity, malevolent spells, and misfortune; it promotes longevity and nourishment, and is an excellent means of subjugation (90).
Goat meat, goat milk, goat ghee with sugar,
and lying on a bed made of goat-skins in the midst of goats destroy consumption (yakṣman).
[One should also take] chest-hair, *akṣata*, and lac mixed with honey and milk.
One should drink it immediately; once digested, one should eat food with sugar and milk.
For the purpose of healing a wound, one who has been wounded should drink milk boiled with *ikṣvālikā*, lotus root, lotus filaments, and sandalwood, mixed with honey. (92–93)

Balā, aśvagandhā, śrīparṇī, bahuputrī, and punarnavā, when practiced daily with milk, destroy *kṣatakṣaya* (wasting disease caused by chest injury). Ghee [prepared with] balā, nāgabalā, arjuna, and water—
This proven preparation, containing a quarter-part of the paste of yaṣṭīmadhu,
pacifies severe heart disease, pain, wounds, internal hemorrhaging, cough, and disorders of wind and blood. || 95 ||
Chapter 11:
Vāstūka, vāyasī vegetables, radish, suniṣaṇṇaka, oils and other fats, various foods, milk, sugarcane juice, and molasses. || 1 ||
Curd, sour gruel, sour fruits, and clear wine are recommended for coughs caused by Vata, as are substances that are sweet, sour, and salty.
One should consume rice, barley, wheat, and ṣaṣṭika rice along with the meat of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals.
One should feed him wholesome meals with the juices of black gram (*māṣa*) and *ātma-guptā*, or with soups (*yūṣa*).
A decoction prepared from the five roots (*pañcamūlī*), combined with the powder of long pepper (*pippalī*),
constantly dispels vāta-type cough for one who eats food with meat broth.
This "Unconquered" (Aparājita) electuary, containing *śṛṅgī*, *śaṭhī*, *kaṇā*, *bhārgī*, jaggery, *vārida* (musta), and *yāsaka*, along with oil, destroys coughs caused by Vāta.
The powders of *viśva*, *dusparśa*, *śṛṅgī*, *drākṣā*, *śaṭhī*, and sugar [are used for this].
By licking [this] with oil, one conquers even a severe cough arising from wind (vāta).
A linctus made of bhārgī, drākṣā, śaṭhī, śṛṅgī, pippalī, and viśvabheṣaja,
combined with jaggery and oil, is beneficial for those suffering from coughs caused by wind.

In cases of pitta-type cough with thin phlegm, the physician should administer *trivṛt* combined with sweet substances; in cases of thick phlegm, it should be given for the purpose of purgation combined with bitter substances. Śyāmāka, *yava*, and *kodrava* grains should be taken with sweet meat broths of wild animals.
Soups made from mung beans and other pulses, along with bitter vegetables, are beneficial when taken in moderation.
Water boiled with balā, bṛhatī, vāsā,
and grapes should be drunk, combined with sugar and honey, to alleviate pitta-type cough.
One should drink milk boiled with the decoction of the five roots beginning with *śara*, as well as *pippalī* and *drākṣā*, mixed with honey and sugar. [Likewise,
one may take it] with *kākolī*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, the two types of *medā*, *vṛṣa*, and *nāgara*.
In cases of cough caused by pitta, one should also prepare meat juices, milk, and vegetable soups.
Indeed, this mixture of grapes, āmalaka, and dates, combined with long pepper (pippalī) and black pepper (marica), should be licked with honey and ghee to alleviate pitta-type cough.
Dates, long pepper, grapes, sugar, and parched rice in equal parts, taken as a linctus with honey and ghee, is an excellent remedy for pitta-type cough.
Śaṭhī, hrīvera, bṛhatī, sugar, and viśvabheṣaja— [these, combined with honey and ghee, are likewise effective]. 14.65–66ab.
Having ground [the seeds] and strained the juice, one should drink it with ghee; this cures bile-induced cough.
Powdered lotus seeds taken with honey cure bile-induced cough.
A patient suffering from phlegm-induced cough who is strong should first be treated with emesis.
One should treat the patient with barley-based foods that are pungent, dry, and hot, as well as with substances that subdue *kapha*.
One should eat light foods with soups made from long pepper and alkaline substances, or from horse gram (*kulattha*), or radish, or with meat broths seasoned with pungent spices. (16–17)
One should drink a decoction prepared with pauṣkara, kaṭphala, bhārgī, viśva, and pippalī in cases of an excess of kapha, cough, dyspnea, and cardiac oppression. [Alternatively,
one may take] the fresh juice of śṛṅgavera combined with honey.
One should administer this, which destroys dyspnea and cough, and removes catarrh and phlegm,
along with green gram, *āmalaka*, barley, pomegranate, *karkandhu*, radish, and ginger.
A soup made from ginger, long pepper, and horse gram is "nine-limbed" (navāṅga) and destroys diseases caused by phlegm;
it is effective for pain in the flanks, fever, asthma, and cough arising from phlegm.
One should drink water boiled with the ten roots (daśamūlī) mixed with powdered long pepper (pippalī).
[21] Kaṭphala, kattṛṇa, bhārgī, musta, coriander (dhānya), vacā, abhayā, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, pārpaṭaka, śuṇṭhī, and surāhvā, boiled together in water— [22]
Honey mixed with asafoetida should be drunk in cases of cough caused by vāta and kapha,
as well as in throat diseases, consumption, colic, asthma, hiccups, and fever.
A decoction prepared from kaṇṭakārī combined with black pepper cures all types of cough.

A *bibhītaka* fruit, smeared with ghee and wrapped in cow dung, should be steamed over a fire; held firmly in the mouth, it certainly cures cough. The fresh juice of *vāsaka*, mixed with honey, should be drunk by one who eats wholesome food.
In cough caused by pitta and kapha, and especially in raktapitta (hemoptysis), [one should use] pippalī, madhuka, drākṣā, lākṣā, śṛṅgī, and śatāvarī;
with these, tugākṣīrī should be double the amount, sugar four times the amount of all [the other ingredients]. || 26 ||
One should lick that with honey and ghee for the cessation of cough caused by chest injury (kṣata).
Pippalī, padmaka, lākṣā, and the well-cooked fruit of bṛhatī,
combined with ghee and honey, form a linctus that destroys cough and dyspnea.
A pill should be prepared from equal parts of the powder of *harītakī*, *nāgara*, and *musta* mixed with jaggery; held in the mouth, it wards off [diseases].
[It cures] increased and severe dyspnea and cough. 29–30:
One *karṣa*, half a *karṣa*, one *upala* (two *palas*), and half a *karṣa* each of long pepper (*pippalī*) together with black pepper (*marica*), pomegranate, jaggery, and *yāvaśūka*. 30.
This medicine is beneficial even for those coughs which are incurable by all medicinal herbs, abandoned by all physicians, and even for those who vomit pus—
consisting of cloves, nutmeg, and long pepper.
Having divided these into portions mixed with honey, one should give half a pala of black pepper and four palas of ginger.
This powder, equal to sugar, will forcibly and swiftly destroy these diseases by its power:
cough, fever, anorexia, urinary disorders, and abdominal tumors.
It cures dyspnea, weak digestion, and disorders of the *grahaṇī*.
(33) Harītakī, *kaṇā*, ginger, and black pepper combined with jaggery are declared to be a cough-destroying bolus (*modaka*) that eliminates thirst and loss of appetite. (34)
With tālīśa, vahnidīpyaka,
cavikā, śuṇṭhī, amlavetasa, and vyoṣa in equal parts, combined with an equal amount of the three aromatics (trisugandhi)—
A pill should be prepared with jaggery for [the treatment of] cough,
dyspnea, anorexia, catarrh, and obstructions of the heart, throat, and speech.
In cases arising from *grahaṇī* and hemorrhoids,
there is a pill named *vyoṣāntikā*. Here, because of the requirement for refinement, three parts of the fragrant substances (*trisugandha*) should be taken as four *māṣa*s.
One should inhale the medicinal smoke made from realgar, orpiment, licorice, spikenard, nut-grass, and ingudi for three days;
thereafter, one should drink milk mixed with jaggery. This cures coughs arising from individual doshas, from combinations of two doshas, or from all three doshas combined.
Even with hundreds of applications, one may achieve what has not been previously cured:
a leaf smeared with realgar (manaḥśilā) and dried in the heat of the sun, when taken as a medicinal smoke with milk, destroys even severe coughs. (39)
Equal parts of *arka* and *challī* stones, with half that amount of the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*) powdered together,
should be cast into fire; the knower of yoga should drink the resulting smoke,
and thereafter chew betel or drink milk or water.
The five types of coughs are quickly pacified; of this there is no doubt.
(41) Vārtākī bark, having been quickly impregnated with black pepper, realgar, and the milk of *arka*, should be dried.
By inhaling smoke prepared according to the prescribed rite,
coughs are pacified.
One should cook ghee with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī) and a paste of bhārgī.
A decoction of *dakṣa* (cock) and partridge, or that which is supreme for curing wind-dysentery (*vātakāsa*), [is prepared as follows]:

one *prastha* of ghee should be cooked with one *āḍhaka* of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and one *akṣa* each of the following: *puṣkaramūla*, *śaṭhī*, *bilva*, *surasā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*). (43–44)
In cases of cough where vāta and kapha predominate, and in all types of dyspnea characterized by kapha and vāta, this should be administered as a drink with gruel.
[In the case of] ten roots (daśamūlī), one prastha of clarified butter should be added to four prasthas of the decoction.
Well-prepared with the five pungent spices (pañcakola) and alkaline substances,
this paste effectively cures cough, pain in the heart and flanks, and eliminates hiccups and dyspnea; the best of physicians prescribe a paste weighing exactly six palas for this preparation.
A *prastha* of ghee prepared with thirty *pala*s each of the juices of *kaṇṭakārī* and *guḍūcī* cures vāta-type cough and stimulates the digestive fire.
Ghee cooked with the paste of *rāsnā*, *balā*, *vyoṣa*, and *śvadaṃṣṭrā* [achieves the same].
Ghee prepared with the juice of *kaṇṭakārī* destroys the five types of cough.
One *prastha* of ghee should be cooked with one *āḍhaka* of the juice from the leaves, roots, and branches of *kaṇṭakārī*, along with *balā*, *vyoṣa*, *viḍaṅga*, *śaṭhī*, and *citraka*.
With sauvarcala salt, yavakṣāra, bilva, āmalaka, and puṣkara;
with vṛścīra, bṛhatī, pathyā, yamānī, pomegranate, and ṛddhi;
and with drākṣā, punarnavā, cavya, dhanvayāsa, and amlavetasa. || 51 ||
One should cook [this] with śṛṅgī, tāmalakī, bhārgī, rāsnā,
and gokṣuraka; this Kaṇṭakārī-ghṛta, prepared with these pastes, is recommended for all types of coughs as well as hiccup and dyspnea, and it destroys diseases caused by phlegm.
One should prepare rāsnā, daśamūlī, and śatāvarī in one droṇa of water,
along with one pala each of the three [drugs], three mānikās of kulattha, badara, and yava,
and half a tulā of goat meat; then, with that entire remaining [decoction]...
One *āḍhaka* of ghee, with an equal amount of milk, boiled with one *pala* each of the ten *jīvanīya* drugs as a paste— this should be administered for nasal drops, internal potions,
and oil enemas in various wind diseases (*vātaroga*), after careful consideration of the specific condition.
It overcomes cough, wasting, dyspnea, pain in the flanks, anorexia, diseases of the entire body or of a single limb, as well as splenic disorders and upward-moving wind (ūrdhvānila).
[The drugs are: Jīvaka, Ṛṣabhaka, the two Medās, the two Kākolīs, and the two Śūrpaparṇikas.
Jīvantī and madhuka constitute the ten-fold group known as jīvaka.
[One should take] the ten roots (daśamūlī), svayaṃguptā, śaṅkhapuṣpī, śaṭhī, balā, hastipippalī, apāmārga, pippalīmūla, and citraka.
One should boil two palas each of bhārgī and puṣkaramūla, one āḍhaka of barley, and one hundred harītakīs in five āḍhakas of water.
When the barley is softened, that decoction should be strained, as should those one hundred harītakīs.
Having added one *tulā* of processed jaggery and one *kuḍava* each of ghee and oil,

along with the powder of long pepper (*pippalī*), one should consume it once it has cooled; then, having added honey, one should regularly eat two *abhayā* fruits from this rejuvenative (*rasāyana*) preparation.

It destroys wrinkles and graying hair, increases strength, vitality, and the elimination of waste, and cures the five types of cough, consumption, dyspnea, hiccups, and irregular fevers. Likewise, it overcomes malabsorption syndrome, hemorrhoids, heart disease, anorexia, and chronic rhinitis.
This auspicious and excellent elixir was prescribed by Agastya. One *tulā* of *kaṇṭakārī*, including its roots, flowers, leaves, and thorns, should be immersed in one *droṇa* of water.
One should place one hundred *harītakī* fruits there, and having cooked them until only a quarter remains,
one should add one hundred pieces of jaggery (*guḍa*) to this [mixture] over the fire.
Then, having removed it once it has cooled, one should add the three pungents (kaṭutrika) in the measure of two palas and six palas of flower-juice to it. || 66 ||

One pala of the four ingredients should be cast [into the preparation] according to the digestive fire; when administered according to the prescribed method, this electuary cures disorders arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha.
It destroys coughs caused by two doṣas as well as those caused by all three;
it also cures that which arises from wasting (kṣaya), that born of chest injury (kṣataja), along with chronic catarrh (sapīnasa), dyspnea (śvāsa), and chest wounds (uraḥkṣata).
This potent elixir (rasāyana), taught by Bhṛgu for the eleven forms of the fierce consumption disease (yakṣman), shall indeed be effective.
(68) Chapter 12.

For one afflicted by hiccups and dyspnea, sudation is first desired after anointing with oil, using unctuous preparations combined with salts to gently facilitate the downward movement of vāta. Purification (śodhana) via the upper and lower routes is prescribed when the patient is strong; for those who are weak, palliative therapy (śamana) is considered appropriate.
Colamajjā, añjana, parched grain, tiktā, kāñcana, gairika;
kṛṣṇā, dhātrī, sugar, śuṇṭhī, kāśīsa, curd, and the name [of the plant];
the fruit and flower of pāṭalī, kṛṣṇa, dates, and mustaka.
These six linctuses, prepared with honey, cure hiccup when taken as electuaries.
Madhuka combined with honey, Pippalī mixed with sugar,
and Nāgara combined with jaggery— these three types of nasal drops (nāvana) also cure hiccup.
Fly excrement mixed with breast milk should be used as a nasal drop (nasya) along with water from lac;
or, for one overcome by hiccups, breast milk mixed with sandalwood should be administered,
or one should drink the juice of citron combined with honey and sauvarcala salt.
For one suffering from hiccup, goat's milk prepared with *nāgara* (ginger) is beneficial; likewise,
a powder of *kṛṣṇā*, *āmalaka*, and *śuṇṭhī* combined with honey and sugar should be administered repeatedly to ward off hiccup and dyspnea.

One suffering from hiccup or dyspnea should drink bhārgī with viśvā along with warm water; or ginger with sugar and bhārgī combined with sauvarcala salt. [Or] śṛṅgī, the three pungents (kaṭutrika), the three fruits (phalātraya), and kaṇṭakārī—

One should drink the powder of bhārgī, sapuṣkarajaṭā, and the five salts with non-cold water in cases of hiccup, dyspnea, upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), cough, anorexia, and chronic catarrh. || 9 ||
One should drink either a paste of *abhayā* and *nāgara*, or a paste of *pauṣkara*, *yavaśūka*, and *marica*, with warm water.
For one suffering from dyspnea and hiccup,
this decoction prepared with *amṛtā*, *nāgara*, *phañjī*, *vyāghrī*, and *parṇāśa* serves to pacify them. || 10 ||
Yellow [powder] mixed with powdered kaṇā quickly conquers cough and dyspnea.
A decoction of daśamūlī, however, when sprinkled with puṣkara powder [achieves the same].
It pacifies dyspnea and cough and destroys pain in the flanks and the heart.
Water boiled with *kulattha*, ginger, *vyāghrī*, and *vāsā*, when drunk together with *puṣkaramūla*, eradicates hiccup and dyspnea.
Having mixed jaggery with bitter oil, one should lick them in equal proportions;
by practicing this for three weeks, one shall conquer asthma from its very root.
[14] Of śṛṅgī, mahauṣadha, kaṇā, ghana, and puṣkara...

A powder composed of *śaṭhī*, black pepper, and sugar, drunk with the decoction of *amṛtā*, *vṛṣa*, and the five roots (*pañcamūlī*), shall pacify even the most severe and violent asthma within three days. (15)
By licking a paste of turmeric, black pepper, grapes, jaggery, rāsnā, pippalī, and śaṭhī mixed with oil, one may overcome even life-threatening dyspneas (śvāsa) and powerful hiccups (hikkā). 16.
It removes even violent hiccups.
Powdered peacock-tail ash mixed with pippalī powder, when licked with honey, quickly destroys even severe dyspnea. (17)
One karṣa of the powder of *kaliphalaka*,
licked while thoroughly mixed with honey,
removes dyspnea before long.
And also *prabalā* and *uddhaṃsikā*.

[One should prepare] one *prastha* of ghee with twice as much milk and four times as much water, along with *hiṃsrā*, *viḍaṅga*, *pūtīka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), and *citraka*. || 19 ||
One should cook it with kola-measures; for this indeed dispels cough, dyspnea, hemorrhoids, anorexia, abdominal tumors, diarrhea, as well as wasting.
Tejovatī, abhayā, kuṣṭha, pippalī, and kaṭurohiṇī—
Bhūtīka, the root of the lotus (pauṣkara), palāśa, citraka, śaṭhī, sauvarcala, tāmalakī, rock salt (saindhava), the paste of bilva,
tālīśapatra, jīvantī, and vacā— these, each measured in the quantity of one akṣa. || 21–22 ||
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with four times as much water and *hiṅgupāda* (asafoetida) as an ingredient;
by drinking this according to one's strength, a person shall conquer hiccup and asthma,
as well as swelling, wind-disorders, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), and pains in the heart and flanks.
Having taken five hundred *bhārgī* plants and another ten *mūlī* roots,
as well as one hundred *harītakī* fruits, one should boil them in four times the amount of water. When that decoction is reduced to one-fourth and strained through a cloth, [one should proceed].
Having stirred the purified scale and then added the *guḍa* (molasses) and *abhayā*,
one should cook it again over a gentle fire until it reaches the consistency of a linctus (*lehavat*).
When it has cooled, one should add six *pala*s of honey to it.
One pala each of the three pungents (trikaṭu) and the three aromatics (trisugandha),
and two karṣas of yavakṣāra, should be powdered and then added.
One should consume one abhayā fruit and lick half a pala of the linctus.

It destroys most severe dyspnea as well as the five types of cough; indeed, it bestows clarity of voice and complexion and stimulates the digestive fire. When the measurement is given in terms of weight (palas), doubling is not intended here.
Since there are one hundred *harītakī* fruits here, one *prastha* of water [is required]; [one should take] one *āḍhaka* of water.
Having taken one hundred each of *kulattha*, *daśamūla*, and likewise *dvija-yaṣṭikā*, one should boil them in a *droṇa* of water.
When only a quarter part remains, one should add half a *tulā* of jaggery;
once it has cooled and is cooked, one should add eight *palas* of honey,
six *palas* of *tugākṣīrī*, and two *palas* of *pippalī*.
One should consume that, combined with the three fragrant substances (trisugandhika), according to the strength of one's digestive fire.
It destroys asthma, cough, fever, hiccup, and likewise the tamaka type of asthma.
Regarding the measurement of a *droṇa*, it should be understood here as three *droṇas* for every hundred [units].
In the case of vāta, oil with salt is desired; in pitta, ghee with honey; and in kapha, honey with alkali and pungent substances—a *kuḍava* measure is recommended. (1)
When [phlegm] is located in the throat, the palate, the tongue, and the roots of the teeth,
phlegm is extracted by that [method], and his voice becomes clear. In the first case, lukewarm water should be drunk after consuming rice with ghee and jaggery.
In cases arising from pitta, one should diligently drink ghee with milk, rice, and water.
For a wise person suffering from hoarseness caused by kapha, one should drink a decoction of pippalī, pippalīmūla, marica, and viśvabheṣaja with urine.

In cases of hoarseness caused by fat (medas), the procedure prescribed for phlegm (kapha) is desired; however, in cases born of wasting (kṣaya) or those caused by all three doṣas (sarvaja), one should perform the treatment after first informing the patient of the prognosis.
[The recipe includes] cavya, sour vetasa, the three pungents (kaṭutrika), and tamarind (tintiḍīka).

A powder made from equal parts of tālīsa, jīraka, tugākṣīrī, and dahanā, combined with the three aromatics (trisugandhi) and softened with jaggery, is recommended for disorders of the voice, chronic catarrh, phlegm, and loss of appetite.
In cases of hoarseness of voice, one should hold in the mouth either khadira wood smeared with oil,

or myrobalan (pathyā) combined with long pepper (pippalī), or with ginger (nāgara). Alternatively, one may take ajamodā, turmeric (niśā), āmalakī (dhātrī), alkali, and citraka (vahni), having ground them into a fine powder.
Having licked [this] mixed with honey and clarified butter, one dispels hoarseness of voice.
A powder of *kalitaru* fruit, *sindhuka*, and *kaṇā*, when licked with buttermilk, removes [the same].
For hoarseness of voice, one should drink the powder of *āmalaka* with cow's milk;
or else, the paste of *badarī* leaves fried in ghee and mixed with rock salt.
One should administer this electuary in cases of impairment of voice and cough.
He whose voice is impaired by speaking loudly should drink boiled milk mixed with sugar and honey, along with [medicinal] drugs of the sweet group.
Ghee cooked with the fresh juice of *vyāghrī*, along with *rāsnā*, *vāṭyāla*, *gokṣura*, and *vyoṣa*, cures impairment of the voice.
It cures the five types of cough.
(12) Having taken dry substances, in the absence of fresh juices, they should be cooked in eight times the quantity of water and the decoction should be taken when reduced to one-fourth. (13)
Clarified butter with long pepper, along with the juices of *bhṛṅgarāja*, *amṛtā* (guduchi), *vāsaka*, and the ten roots (*daśamūla*), and *kāsamarda*.
It is proven that honey conquers hoarseness of voice and cough.
14. Adhikāra 14.
In cases of wind (vāta), one should induce emesis; in bile (pitta), purgation; and in phlegm (kapha), emesis.

One should perform actions that are pleasing to the heart and provide mental delight when [the disease] arises from mental distress. In the case of vomiting caused by wind (vāta), one should duly drink a powder with water infused with *vacā*, or with oil, warm water, or wine, whichever is appropriate.
In cases of Pitta-type vomiting, emesis induced by a mixture of *kṛṣṇā*, *viḍaṅga*, barley ash, *hareṇu*, *bhārgī*, *rāsnā*, *elā*, asafoetida, rock salt, and ginger, combined with jaggery,
water, and sweet substances, is recommended.
A linctus made of rock salt, sugar, honey, and ghee is desired; however, for one who has vomited due to a kaphaja disorder, neem water should be drunk,
or water from the *rājadruma* tree mixed with honey and abundant *dīpyaka*.
Or else, one should employ that same powder which was prescribed for the wind-born (vātaja) type; likewise, one should treat all [types] with that which is effective against all.
[The powder consists of: kuṣṭha, sauvarcala salt, ajājī, sugar, marica, and biḍa salt.
Dhātrī, elā, padmaka, uśīra, pippalī, candana, utpala, lodhra,
tejovatī, pathyā, tryūṣaṇa, yavāgraja, the exudation of fresh dāḍima, ajājī, and sugar— [these constitute the formulation].

These four formulations, each containing a *kuḍava* measure and combined with oil and honey, destroy the four types of anorexia—those caused by vāta and the other [doṣas] individually, as well as those caused by all of them together.
(7) [The ingredients are: tvak, musta, elā, dhānya, musta, and āmalaka.
Cinnamon bark, *dārvī*, *yamānī*, *pippalī*, and *tejavatī*—
these five, including *yamānī* and *tintiḍīka*, are declared in the quarters of these verses to be cleansers of the mouth and destroyers of all loss of appetite.
Tamarind with jaggery-water, combined with cinnamon, cardamom, and black pepper,
taken in a dose of one kuḍava, is recommended for diseases characterized by a lack of desire for food.
[Also beneficial are] kāravī, cumin, black pepper, grapes, vṛkṣāmla, and pomegranate.
Sauvarcala salt, jaggery, and honey destroy all forms of loss of appetite.
The three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), and the two types of turmeric,
when powdered and mixed with barley-ash, [act as a remedy].
One should administer honeyed preparations for the purpose of holding them in the mouth,
as well as other medicinal substances that are bitter and pungent.
The juice of pomegranate combined with powdered feces and honey [is also used].
Even an incurable loss of appetite can be cured by holding this mixture in the mouth.
One should prepare one karṣa each of yamānī, tamarind, ginger, amlavetasa, pomegranate, and sour jujube.
One should grind together half a karṣa each of dhānyaka, sauvarcala salt, ajājī, and varāṅga, along with one hundred pippalīs, two hundred maricas,
and four palas of sugar.
This powder cleanses the tongue, is beneficial for the heart, and stimulates the appetite for food (16).

It alleviates pain in the cardiac region and colic in the flanks, destroys constipation and abdominal distension, removes cough and dyspnea, is astringent, and cures disorders of the digestive tract and hemorrhoids (17).
Eighteen fruits of *śigru*, ten *marica* peppers, twenty *pippalī* peppers,
one *pala* of fresh ginger, and one *pala* of jaggery.
Three *prasthas* of *māranāla* from the tree [are taken],
combined with this *viḍalavana* (black salt),
stirred with a whisk, fragrant and rich in scent.
That which destroys a thousand consonants is to be known as the *kalahaṃsaka* [mudrā]. 19.
Chapter 15.
Since all types of vomiting are considered to arise from the agitation of the stomach (āmāśaya), one should therefore first employ fasting (laṅghana),
with the exception of that caused by Vāta.
Purification (saṃśodhana) or the removal of phlegm and bile [is also beneficial].
Milk mixed with water, when drunk, destroys vomiting arising from emesis;
one should drink ghee with rock salt to ward off vomiting caused by wind (vāta).
Or one should drink a soup of mung beans and āmalaka with ghee and rock salt, or a gruel prepared with the five roots mixed with honey;
this is for the purpose of restoring downward movement in cases of the pitta-type [fever].
Trivṛt should be administered with the juices of grapes, vidārī, and sugarcane;
however, when pitta has increased excessively and is located in the seat of kapha, one should conquer it by means of sweet substances directed upwards.
When the patient has been purified, one should administer a churned drink (mantha) or a thin gruel (peyā) mixed with honey, sugar, and parched grain, or even with the juice of mung beans.
Or [one may eat] śāli rice with the juices of wild animals. 5.
Having mixed āmalaka juice with an akṣa-measure of sandalwood and combined it with honey, one should drink it; by that, vomiting is averted. 6.
A paste of *candana*, *mṛṇāla*, *bālaka*, *nāgara*, and *vṛṣa*,
drunk with rice-water and honey, overcomes vomiting.
A decoction of fried green gram (*mudga*), along with parched grain (*lāja*), honey, and sugar [is also effective].
This remedy, which destroys vomiting, diarrhea, thirst, burning sensations, and fever, has been proclaimed.
One should lick the powder of *harītakī* mixed with honey; once the morbid humors have been expelled through the lower tract, vomiting will quickly cease.
One should drink a decoction prepared from guḍūcī, triphalā, ariṣṭa, and paṭola, mixed with honey; this quickly destroys vomiting caused by pitta and acidity.
A decoction of parpaṭaka, when drunk with honey, is a destroyer of vomiting. (10–11)
In a case characterized by kapha, emesis is recommended using *piṇḍītaka* fruits combined with long pepper (*pippalī*), mustard, neem water, and rock salt.
In a case of vomiting, [one should administer this] for the purpose of cleansing the seat of phlegm (kaphāmāśaya).
(12) A powder of viḍaṅga, triphalā, and viśva mixed with honey overcomes vomiting born of phlegm; or else, [a powder] of viḍaṅga, plava, and śuṇṭhī [does so]. (13)
One may take the powder of *badara* with *jāmbava*, or *karkaṭaka-śṛṅgī* combined with *mustā*,
or *durālabhā* mixed with honey.

One should lick [this] for the purpose of suppressing phlegm and vomiting; or else, a satiation (tarpaṇa) with honey is a remedy for all three [doshas]. A decoction (kaṣāya) prepared according to rule from guḍūcī is known as "the cold" (himasaṃjñita).
In all three cases, it may be wholesome when combined with honey.
That decoction which emerges from water that has been heated with medicinal substances and then left overnight is declared to be "cold" (śīta).

In the preparation of cold water (*śītakaṣāya*) and hot infusion (*phāṇṭa*), one pala of medicinal drug is soaked in six or four palas of water; in the preparation known as decoction (*rasa*), two palas [of drug] are used.
A decoction of *śrīphala* or *guḍūcī*, combined with honey, [is recommended].
In cases of the three types of vomiting, a cold decoction of *mūrvā* with rice-water should be drunk;
or, one who drinks small amounts repeatedly of water boiled with the tender leaves of *jambu*, *āmra*, *gavedhuka*, *dhānya*, *sevya*, and *hrībera* mixed with honey [is cured].

Vomiting is pacified by licking a preparation of the three fragrant substances (trisugandhi) mixed with honey; likewise, durālabhā taken with honey destroys it. The juice of jātī fruit combined with kapittha, pippalī, and marica [also serves this purpose].
This linctus, combined with honey, pacifies even severe vomiting.
Having ground one pala each of āmalaka fruit, grapes, and sugar, and adding one pala of honey and one kuḍava of water [to this], [one should prepare the linctus]. 21–22.

When strained through a cloth and drunk, [this mixture] of cardamom, cloves, nāgakeśara, the marrow of kola, parched rice, priyaṅgu, ushira, sandalwood, and long pepper destroys vomiting born of the three doṣas.
Having licked these powders combined with honey and white sugar,
one overcomes vomiting born of phlegm, wind, and bile.
[23] The marrow of *kola* and *āmalaka*, along with honey, feces, sugar, and honey— [23] (continued).
A linctus made from black rice grains quickly suppresses vomiting.
Having burnt dry bark of the *aśvattha* tree and extinguished it in water, that water, by the mere act of drinking, conquers even difficult-to-overcome vomiting.

Guḍūcī combined with sandalwood, properly ground with milk and stirred with that same liquid, should be drunk to destroy vomiting of blood.
