Three electuaries—consisting of honey, *abhayā*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), and coriander; and *pathyā*, *amṛtā*, black pepper, honey, and long pepper—are for the alleviation of all types of vomiting and loss of appetite. (27)
One should cook one *prastha* of clarified butter with the paste and decoction of *padmaka*, *amṛta*, *nimba*, *dhānya*, and *candana*.
This is a supreme remedy for preventing vomiting, alleviating thirst and loss of appetite, and removing burning fever. (28)
Chapter 16:
When thirst arises from wind (vāta), curd with jaggery is recommended,
as well as nourishing and cooling juices, and especially the juice of *guḍūcī*.

Regarding the five groups of five-limbed [medicinal plants] that have been described: a person should drink water prepared with those in the first group while it is pleasantly warm, in a small quantity.
One should never suppress thirst;
water boiled with pitta-alleviating substances, or even milk, destroys [the fever] arising from pitta. 3.

For thirst caused by pitta, one should drink water mixed with *kāśmarya* sugar, sandalwood, *uśīra*, *padmaka*, grapes, and *madhuka*. For thirst born of pitta, however, the juice of ripe *udumbara* fruit [is recommended].
Likewise, the decoction or cold infusion of that [same group], or water prepared with the śārivādi group,
or milk-ghee processed with the jīvanīya group, should be used for thirst born of vāta and pitta.
Similarly, water combined with grapes, sandalwood, dates, ushira, and honey,
along with śārivā and the rest, and the five roots of grass (tṛṇapañcamūla).
Likewise, one should prepare astringent decoctions from sweet groups such as the blue lotus (*utpala*) and others, or similarly from *madhūka* flowers and other such substances.
Oil prepared with bilva, āṭarūṣaka, dhātakī, pañcakola, and darbha overcomes vomiting born of kapha;
moreover, emesis is beneficial in this condition.
With heated water infused with nimba blossoms;
along with cumin, fresh ginger,
and sauvarcala salt, all soaked in half-water.
Heart-pleasing and fragrant liquors, when drunk, immediately allay thirst and,
by warding off pain arising from wounds, [bring relief].
One may conquer [the disease] arising from wasting by drinking juices and blood; milk-water, meat-broth, or honey-water will destroy it. || 10 ||
By consuming heavy food and speaking aloud, one may overcome all thirst except that caused by consumption (kṣaya);
likewise, cooled water mixed with parched grain flour, honey, and crushed jaggery [is effective]. || 11 ||
A person afflicted by thirst should drink [the decoction] combined with *kāśmarya* sugar.
Here, milk quickly pacifies the thirst of men who are excessively dry and weak.
Or goat's meat fried in ghee,
when cold, has a sweet taste that is pleasing to the heart;
or one may drink a decoction of mango and jambu mixed with honey.
It dispels all vomiting and likewise draws away thirst.
One should drink the shoots of the *vaṭa* tree, sugar, *lodhra*, pomegranate, and *madhuka* with rice-water; this prevents vomiting and thirst. (14–15)
For one who regularly uses these as nasal drops (nasya) or drinks them—namely, goat's milk, sugarcane juice, milk, liquorice, honey, and blue water-lily—the most severe thirst is surely pacified.
[16] [Thirst is also relieved] by milk, sugarcane juice, and wine; or by honey, rum, and molasses-water. [17]
A gargle with *vṛkṣāmla* and other sour fruits prevents dryness of the palate;
in cases of dryness of the palate, one should drink clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) or even the scum of clarified butter (*ghṛtamaṇḍa*).
Those who are severely exhausted by fainting, vomiting, thirst, burning sensations, women, or wine [should also be treated thus].
In cases of internal hemorrhage (raktapitta) and alcoholism (madātyaya), one should drink cold water.
Fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) destroys bad taste in the mouth, impurities, and foul odors; that same liquid, when drunk without salt, is an excellent remedy for dryness of the mouth.
Holding a mouthful of honey in the mouth produces clarity in the oral cavity, heals wounds in the mouth, and pacifies burning sensations and thirst.
(21) The juice of *kola*, pomegranate, *vṛkṣāmla*, *cukrīkā*, and *cukrikā* [is likewise beneficial].
An application of the five sour fruits (pañcāmlaka) to the face immediately subdues thirst.
Or, one who is thirsty should be made to drink water mixed with sugar up to the throat, or even be made to vomit; by that means, the thirst is pacified.
A firm pill made from the sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree, liquorice, honey, *lāja* (parched rice), and blue lotus, when placed in the mouth, quickly subdues thirst.
Cold rice of red *śāli* variety mixed with honey [is likewise beneficial].
One should feed him with that; by this, vomiting and thirst arising from long-standing illness shall be pacified.

(25) A patient afflicted by a chronic disease who is emaciated and tormented by thirst will, if he does not obtain water when asking for it, very quickly meet his death or suffer from a long-term illness. (26)
One who is thirsty falls into delusion; through delusion, one gives up one's life.
Therefore, in all circumstances, water is never prohibited anywhere.
(17) Adhikāra 17
Jewels cooled by a single immersion, cooling ointments with their fragrant oils, the breeze from fans, and scented drinks— these are the remedies.
In all types of fainting, these are prohibited;
however, sweet juices and the meat-broths of wild animals, along with pomegranate, are always effective in this category.
Likewise, barley, red śāli rice, satīna, and mung beans are recommended for cases of fainting.
One should administer decoctions that destroy fever according to the specific humor involved.
In fainting caused by blood, cold treatments are beneficial. In fainting caused by alcohol, one should vomit the alcohol and enjoy sleep as comfortably as possible.
In fainting caused by poison, one should administer anti-poisonous medicines.
Kola, majjā, uśīra, and keśara, when drunk with cold water, overcome fainting; or, when licked with honey, they conquer thirst.
[Likewise,] that which arises from mahauṣadha, amṛtā, kṣudrā, pauṣkara, and granthika [is effective].
One should drink a decoction mixed with *kaṇā* (Piper longum) in cases of fainting and intoxication.
For the destruction of dizziness, one should drink milk prepared with the roots of *śatāvarī*, *balā*, and *drākṣā*, along with sugar; or else, the seeds of *vāṭyālaka*.
One should drink a decoction of durālabhā with ghee for the alleviation of vertigo;
or the administration of triphalā, or even the administration of milk, or the elixirs (rasāyana), or the kumbha-sarpis ghee is recommended. 8.
Triphalā taken with honey at night, followed by jaggery and fresh ginger in the morning while eating wholesome food, destroys [diseases] within seven days.
[One should treat] fainting, cough, jaundice, and insanity [with these remedies]. Eye-salves, nasal drops, medicinal smokes, insufflations,
pricking with needles, cauterization, and squeezing between the nails are recommended.
Plucking out the hair of the head and body, biting with the teeth, and rubbing against her when she is protected— these are beneficial for her confinement.
(11) Chapter 18.
Mantha, prepared with dates, raisins, *vṛkṣāmla*, *amlīka*, pomegranates, *parūṣaka*, and *āmalaka*, cures disorders caused by wine.
One pala of the ground substance should be added to four palas of cold water.
One should thoroughly rub [the powder] in an earthen vessel and drink two palas of it; or else,
one may take it mixed with sesame and mung beans, or combined with pomegranate and āmalaka,
or with the juice of grapes, āmalaka, dates, and parūṣaka.
One should prepare various kinds of refreshing drinks, broths, and meat juices.

For one who has consumed aged liquor, a small amount of wine mixed with sauvarcala salt, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and water should be given; this cures the complications arising from the excessive drinking of wind-increasing (vāta) liquors.

Mudga soup mixed with sugar, or the meat broth of peafowl seasoned with salt, should be employed; furthermore, all cooling therapies are to be applied in cases of *pitta*-dominant *pānātyaya*. In *pānātyaya* arising from *kapha*, one should administer fasting according to the patient's strength.

One should drink wine, composed and with a focused mind, combined with digestive-stimulating (dīpanīya) medicinal herbs. In cases of alcoholism caused by all [three] doshas, this entire treatment should be employed; through these combined measures, the disorder of intoxication (madātyaya) attains pacification.
If, however, one does not administer milk following the sequence of wine,
then once the *kapha* has been diminished by fasting and other such measures, and weakness and lightness have arisen;
[one should then use] milk, which possesses qualities equal to *ojas* and is the opposite of wine.
One should gradually consume milk preparations or wine in very small quantities.
Furthermore, ghee prepared with a decoction of *punarnavā* and a paste of *yaṣṭīmadhu*, when drunk, bestows nourishment upon one whose vital energy has been destroyed by the drinking of liquor.
Five parts of sauvarcala salt, ajāji, vṛkṣāmla, and amlavetasa, with half a part each of cinnamon, cardamom, and black pepper, combined with one part of sugar—
this eight-ingredient salt (lavaṇāṣṭaka) is highly beneficial and an excellent stimulant for the digestive fire.
In cases of alcoholism (madātyaya) where kapha predominates, one should administer a purifier of the channels.
A powder consisting of chavya, sauvarcala salt, hiṅgu, pūraka, viśva, and dīpyaka should be given with wine; it removes the afflictions of pānātyaya.
One who is bathed in water, whose limbs are anointed with sandalwood paste,
who wears a garland, and who drinks liquor accompanied by meat as a side-dish along with devotion, shall certainly not suffer from diseases.
It subdues the mind and does not lead to intoxication.
That beverage made from grapes, wood-apple fruits, and pomegranates,
enriched with honey and sugar, removes the confusion caused by drinking.
One should drink ghee prepared with a decoction of *pathyā* or with the juice of *dhātrī*, or even *kalyāṇaka* ghee, to remove intoxication and fainting;
it also cures vomiting, fainting, diarrhea, and intoxication caused by betel nut.
Cold water, when drunk to satiety, immediately pacifies it.
Furthermore, the intoxication from betel nut is alleviated by smelling wild cow dung, by drinking water, or by eating salt;
likewise, the pain from the powder is relieved by gargling with sugar.
Inhaling a small amount of the powder of conch-shell dust removes intoxication;
the juice of the *kūṣmāṇḍaka* gourd mixed with jaggery pacifies intoxication caused by *madana* and *kodrava*;
and *dhustūra* milk taken with sugar, when used as a drink, likewise cures it. (19)
An intelligent person should lick [the paste] smeared with ghee purified a hundred times, mixed with barley flour, or with kola and āmalaka, or even with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla). 19.1.
One should cover all his limbs with a garment moistened with fresh *āraṇāla* (lotus stalks),
and then anoint him with *lāmajja*, sour gruel (*śukta*), and sandalwood paste.
He should be fanned by a palm-leaf fan from which drops of sandalwood water are dripping.
One afflicted by the heat of burning should sleep upon a bed made of lotus petals and plantain leaves.
For the purpose of quelling thirst and burning sensations, cold water is recommended for sprinkling, immersion baths, and the use of fans.
One should alleviate internal burning sensations with well-cooled milk, decoctions of milk-yielding trees mixed with sandalwood, and other such cooling substances;
as well as with [milk] prepared from kuśa grass and the like, śālaparṇī, and the jīvakādi group.
Oil or ghee [is] a destroyer of burning sensations and a subduer of Vāta and Pitta.
(6) A plaster consisting of phalinī, lodhra, sevya, ambu, hemapatra, kuṭannaṭa, combined with the juice of kālīyaka, is recommended for burning sensations. (7)
A man afflicted by burning heat should immerse himself in a wooden tub filled with water mixed with the powder of *hrībera*, lotus buds, *uśīra*, and sandalwood. (8) Adhikāra 20.
In insanity caused by Vata, the administration of oleation followed by purgation is first prescribed;
in that caused by Pitta or Kapha, emesis is primary, followed by the sequence beginning with enemas (basti).
Whatever else is to be taught in the treatment of epilepsy (apasmāra) [is also applicable here].
In cases of insanity (unmāda), that same treatment should be applied because the doshas and the affected tissues (dūṣyas) are common [to both conditions].
2. The fresh juices of brāhmī, kūṣmāṇḍī, ṣaḍgranthā, and śaṅkhapuṣpikā—
These [medicines], mixed with honey and kuṣṭha, are seen to cure insanity when taken separately.
Water boiled with the ten roots (daśamūla), combined with ghee or meat broth, [is also effective].
Or [one may take] old ghee mixed with powdered white mustard seeds, or pure old ghee alone.
Ghee that has stood for ten years becomes "of pungent scent" (ugragandha); beyond that, it is called "very old" (prapurāṇa), resembling the color of lac juice and cool in nature.
Furthermore, milk-rice (pāyasa) prepared with white *unmatta* from the northern direction and combined with jaggery and ghee destroys all types of insanity born of the humors (*doṣa*).
In cases of insanity, the juice of the *tāla* tree branch should be drunk either mixed with honey or pure.
Mustard oil is recommended for use as a nasal drop and for anointing.
Raw *caṭakī* (a type of lizard) that has drunk milk destroys insanity;
it should be bound, smeared with mustard oil, and placed face-up in the sun.
Siddhārthaka, hiṅgu, vacā, karañja, and devadāru; mañjiṣṭhā, triphalā, śvetā, the bark of kaṭabhī, and the three pungents (kaṭutrika)—
these in equal parts, along with priyaṅgu, śirīṣa, and the two types of rajanī.
This medicine, ground with goat's urine, serves as a drink, an eye-salve,
an errhine, an ointment, as well as for bathing and anointing; it destroys epilepsy, poison, and insanity, and removes misfortune and fever.
It destroys fear of living beings and is praised at the king's gate;
likewise, ghee prepared with this [formula], or with cow's urine, serves that same purpose.
[The ingredients are] the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), asafoetida, salt, *vacā*, and *kaṭukarohiṇī*.

The seeds of *śirīṣa* and *naktamāla*, along with white mustard seeds, ground with cow’s urine, form a medicinal wick (*varti*) suitable for eye-salve (*añjana*). This cures quartan fever, epilepsy, and insanity. (13–14)
For one who is pure but has fallen away from proper conduct, strong nasal drops, eye ointments, flogging, and the stimulation of the mind, intellect, memory, and sensory perception are beneficial.
Likewise, threats, intimidation, gifts, consolation, cheering, and instilling fear are also helpful.
Surprise, arising from forgetfulness, leads the mind toward its natural state.
One should bring to rest those [disturbances] born of desire, grief, fear, anger, joy, envy, and greed by means of their very opposites.
But for one whose mind is afflicted by the loss of a beloved object, one should conquer that [affliction] through the acquisition of something similar, as well as through consolation and tranquility.
(18) Anointing the body, massage, medicinal smoking, and the drinking of clarified butter [are also beneficial]. (5)
One should employ that which awakens the mind, intellect, memory, and perception;
one may also give the great *kalyāṇaka* or the mental *ghṛta*, as well as *nārāyaṇa-taila* and *mahānārāyaṇa-taila*. || 19–20 ||
Viśālā, triphalā, kauntī, devadāru,
elavāluka, sthirā, nata, the two types of rajanī, the two types of śārivā, priyaṅgu, nīlotpala, elā, mañjiṣṭhā, dantī, dāḍima, and keśara. || 21 ||
Tālīśapatra, bṛhatī, fresh jasmine flowers,
viḍaṅga, pṛśniparṇī, kuṣṭha, candana, and padmaka—
using these twenty-eight paste ingredients, each weighing one akṣa.
Having added four times as much water, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee;
it is effective for epilepsy, fever, cough, consumption, weak digestion, wasting, gout, catarrh,
and tertian or quartan fevers.

In cases of vomiting, hemorrhoids, dysuria, and those afflicted by erysipelas (visarpa), as well as in itching, jaundice, insanity, irregular urinary disorders, and poisoning; and for those whose minds are possessed by spirits, those with stammering speech, and those lacking semen—[this [remedy] is indicated]. || 25–26 ||

This medicated ghee is recommended for women and those who are barren; it bestows fortune, longevity, and strength. It destroys misfortune, sin, and demons, and wards off all malevolent planetary influences. This auspicious ghee is also excellent for rites intended to ensure the birth of a male child.
This is the *kṣīrakalyāṇaka* (milk-excellence) preparation, consisting of two parts water and four parts milk.
Having boiled twenty-one [herbs] beginning with *sthira* in water,
one should cook ghee in that decoction along with four times the amount of milk from a cow that has recently calved (*gṛṣṭi*).

With equal parts of the pastes of vīrā, dvimāṣā, kākolī, svayaṃguptā, ṛṣabhaka, ṛddhi, and medā, that is the Great Kalyāṇaka [Ghṛta]; it is especially nourishing and is the supreme remedy for the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta). || 30 ||
With two-pala portions each of the decoction ingredients consisting of the five roots (pañcamūla), *avakāśmarī*, *rāsnā*, *eraṇḍa*, *trivṛt*, *balā*, *mūrvā*, and *śatāvarī*,
along with one part of the *kalyāṇaka* formula, this ghee is known as *caitasa*.
The pacification of all mental disturbances is considered supreme.
Here, one prastha of ghee should be cooked with a decoction of four droṇas of water;
the paste (kalka) prescribed for Kalyāṇaka should be prepared here as a fourfold quantity.
Jaṭilā, pūtanā, keśī, cāraṭī, markaṭī, vacā,
trāyamāṇā, jayā, vīrā, coraka, kaṭurohiṇī, vayasthā, śūkarī, chatrā, sāticchatrā, and palaṅkaṣā. || 34 ||
Mahāparuṣadantā, Vayasthā, the two types of Nākulī,
Kaṭumbharā, Vṛścikālī, and Sthirā— ghee prepared with these destroys quartan fever, insanity, possession by grahas, and epilepsy. || 35–36 ||
This ghee, named Mahāpaiśācika, is like nectar; it produces intelligence, intellect, and memory, and promotes the growth of the bodies of children.
[It is prepared] with two palas each of asafoetida, sauvarcala salt, and the three pungents (vyoṣa), along with one āḍhaka of ghee.
Oil prepared with four times the amount of cow’s urine is a destroyer of madness. One should boil half a *tulā* of fresh garlic, dehusked,
along with half that amount of *daśamūlī*, in two *āḍhakas* of water.
When one-quarter remains, one should add a *prastha* of ghee and the juice of garlic, along with the juices of jujube (*kola*), radish (*mūlaka*), *vṛkṣāmla*, citron (*mātuluṅga*), and ginger;
and half as much of pomegranate juice, wine (*surā*), whey (*mastu*), and sour gruel (*kāñjika*). || 40 ||
One should prepare [this] with triphalā, dāru, salt, vyoṣa, and dīpyaka;
with half-pala portions each of yamānī, cavya, hiṅgu, and amlavetasa.
This, once cooked, should be drunk as it removes colic, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and abdominal enlargement.
It removes jaundice, anemia, splenic disorders, gynecological ailments, worms, fever,

and other diseases of wind and phlegm, as well as insanity. For exogenous [fevers], the prescribed treatment consists of drinking clarified butter and the like, along with mantras and other such measures.

A physician, remaining pure, should conquer adventitious insanity according to the prescribed rules by means of worship, offerings of oblations, sacrifices, burnt offerings, mantras, collyrium, and other such remedies. [44] He should administer a compound made of black pepper, long pepper, rock salt, honey, and cow-bile. [45]
An ointment arising from all [these] elements destroys great insanity;
and a pill-ointment (guḍikāñjana) prepared with dārvī and honey under the Puṣya asterism [is likewise effective].
Alternatively, black pepper and meat, kept in a jar, serve as an ointment when combined with bile.
For one who perceives a transformation [of consciousness] and whose memory has been destroyed by the afflictions and malevolent spirits, [the following remedy is prescribed]: 47.
Incense made from nimba leaves, vacā, asafoetida, snake slough, and mustard seeds destroys possession by ḍākinīs and others, and eradicates the insanity caused by bhūtas. 48.
Cotton seeds, peacock feathers, bṛhatī, discarded flower offerings, piṇḍītaka, cinnamon, vāṃsī, the excrement of a cat, chaff, and vacā—
An incense is prepared from equal parts of human hair, snake slough, cow horn, elephant tusk, asafoetida, and black pepper.
It is traditionally taught as a destroyer of afflictions by Skanda, insanity, piśācas, rākṣasas, and spirits, as well as fever.
This [remedy] for destroying brahmarākṣasas consists of the juice of ripe indrī fruit mixed with urine.
A nasal medication (nasya) made from white mustard, *jyeṣṭhā* water, and clarified butter, along with ghee, removes [the influence of] spirits.
A wise person should avoid sharp treatments such as collyrium and anything cruel for one who is insane due to the influence of gods, sages, ancestors, or gandharvas.
Chapter 21:
One should generally treat vātika epilepsy with enemas, paittika with purgatives, and ślaiṣmika with emetics. 1.
Listen now to the yogas that bring about pacification for the sake of liberation from epilepsy, for one who is thoroughly purified and properly consoled on all sides: realgar,
*tārkṣya* (emerald), and the excrement of a pigeon.
Collyrium [prepared from these] cures epilepsy and especially insanity.
For epilepsy and insanity, nasal drops and collyrium should be prepared from liquorice, asafoetida, vacā, vakra, śirīṣa, and garlic, along with goat’s urine.
Dog’s bile extracted under the Puṣya asterism is an ointment that destroys epilepsy;
that same substance mixed with clarified butter is considered an excellent fumigation.
[5] It is also prepared from the [bile or parts] of a mongoose, owl, cat, vulture, insect, snake, and crow.
The physician should cause fumigation to be performed with their beaks, feathers, and excrement.
Having ground kāyasthā, autumnal mudga beans, musta, uśīra, and barley, along with the three pungents (vyoṣa), in goat's urine, he should prepare a medicinal wick (varti).
In cases of epilepsy, insanity, snakebite,
affliction by poison, ingestion of poison, or death by drowning, these [herbs] are like nectar.
They also [counteract] the effects of *rākṣasīs*, leprosy, *pūtanās*, *keśīs*, and *corakas*.
An ointment made from substances ground with urine, or even a sprinkling with urine itself;
likewise, a plaster made from burnt *jatuka*, cow dung, or goat hair; or a plaster of *siddhārtha* and *śigru* prepared with urine—these remove epilepsy.
One who eats rice with milk and consumes the powder of *vacā* with honey will certainly conquer even a most terrible epilepsy that has arisen long ago.
Ink is made by burning the noose from the neck of a hanging man.
Taken with cold water, it destroys even violent epilepsy (12).
Garlic oil prepared with milk, or śatāvarī,
or the juice of brahmī taken with honey, is a remedy for all types of epilepsy (13).
Having roasted a goat’s horn until it is sapless and made it into a powder,
one who eats that preparation with sour substances casts away epilepsy.
For one who has trembling of the heart, pain in the eyes, perspiration, and coldness of the hands and other limbs—

One should administer for him water decocted with the ten roots (daśamūlī) and the Kalyāṇa-ghṛta. Ghee prepared with equal parts of cow dung juice, sour curd, milk, and urine, when perfected, destroys quartan fever, insanity, possession by spirits, and epilepsy.
The two groups of five roots (pañcamūla), triphalā, the two types of rañjanī, the bark of kuṭaja, saptaparṇa, apāmārga, nīlinī,
kaṭurohiṇī, sampāka, the root of phalgu, and puṣkaramūla together with durālabhā. || 17 ||
Having boiled two palas [of each] in one droṇa of water until reduced to one-fourth,
[one should add] bhārgī, pāṭhā, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), trivṛtā, nicula, śreyasī, māḍakī, mūrvā, dantī, bhūnimba, and citraka. || 18–19 ||

One should grind two parts each of the two *śārivās*, *rauhiṣa*, *bhūtika*, and *madayantikā*— each in the measure of one *akṣa*— and cook them with one *prastha* of clarified butter along with equal quantities of cow-dung juice,
sour curd, milk, and urine.
That which is known as the "five products of the cow" (pañcagavya) is great and like unto nectar.
It is [efficacious] in cases of epilepsy, fever, cough, swelling, abdominal enlargements, tumors, hemorrhoids, anemia, jaundice, and chlorosis.
It destroys misfortune, evil spirits, and demons, and it eradicates quartan fever.
7. Śaṇa, trivṛt, eraṇḍa, daśamūlī, śatāvarī, 23. rāsnā, māgadhikā, and śigru—these should be boiled, with two palas each.
Vidarī, madhuka, the two types of medā, the two types of kākolī, and sugar; with these,
along with kharjūra, mṛdvīkā, abhīru, yuñjāta, and gokṣura— this excellent ghee should be cooked using the ingredients of the Caitasa-ghṛta.
Known as Mahācaitasasaṃjñā, it destroys all forms of epilepsy, overcomes chronic poisoning, insanity, catarrh, and tertian and quartan fevers;
it conquers evil and misfortune, and wards off all planetary influences.
It indeed removes cough and dyspnea, and it purifies the semen and menses.

Herein, the procedure for the measure of ghee and the method of decoction is considered to be the same as that previously mentioned; and the paste (kalka) is one-fourth [the weight of the ghee], along with the substances specified for the aforementioned paste.
When the *yuñjānaka* fruit is not available, the top of a palmyra palm (*tālamastaka*) is prescribed.
One should cook ghee with eighteen times its quantity of *kūṣmāṇḍaka* juice and a paste of *yaṣṭīmadhu*;
drinking that destroys epilepsy.
With *brahmī* juice, along with *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *śaṅkhapuṣpī*,
[this] ancient [preparation] is purifying and removes insanity, possession by spirits, and epilepsy. With *palaṅkaṣā*, *vacā*, *pathyā*, *vṛścikālī*, *arka*, and mustard seeds...
With *jaṭilā*, *pūtanā*, *keśī*, *lāṅgalī*, *hiṅgu*, *coraka*, garlic, *atirasā*, *citrā*, *kuṣṭha*, and the excrement of carnivorous birds,
[one should cook] with four times as much goat's urine as available. || 32 ||
Oil prepared with these is effective for massage and destroys epilepsy.
An oil made from mustard seeds, cooked with four times the amount of goat urine, may be used for massage; furthermore, cow dung and urine may be used for drinking and as an unguent.

For those suffering from disorders of vāta, one should treat all such patients with foods that are sweet, sour, salty, and unctuous, as well as with oil massages, oleation enemas, and similar therapies. 1.22.1
Specifically, when the wind (vāta) is located in the abdomen, a person should drink alkaline preparation (kṣāra);

when it is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), the treatment for one who has undergone purification (śuddha) should be applied according to the nature of the disorder. When the wind is located in the stomach, emesis should be induced, followed by the sequential administration of therapies.
This formulation of six *dharaṇas* should be administered with pleasant water for seven nights.
Citraka, indrayava, pāṭhā, kaṭukā, ativiṣā, and abhayā constitute the formulation of six *dharaṇas*, known as the pacifier of great diseases.
A tenth part of a pala is a dharaṇa;
this is the system of Suśruta,
according to which five guñjās constitute one māṣa.
It should be administered daily with a suitable enema nozzle.
When Vāta has reached the colon (pakvāśaya), unctuous purgation is beneficial,
as are cleansing enemas and soothing enemas enriched with salt.
One should burn the latex of *snuhī*, salt, and *vārtāku* along with oil inside a covered jar using cow dung;
that resulting oil and salt are supreme for destroying Vāta. Furthermore, when [Vāta] has entered the bladder, a procedure for purifying the bladder should be performed.
When [the vāta] has reached the skin, flesh, blood, and vessels, one should perform bloodletting.
A wise physician should also employ oleation, poultices, thermal cautery (agnikarma), bandaging, and massage when the vāta has reached the ligaments, joints, and bones.
When [the fever] resides in the skin, one should employ sudation, oil massage, immersion baths, and pleasant food;
when it resides in the blood, cold poultices, purgation, and bloodletting are indicated.
When it resides in the muscle and fat, non-unctuous enemas and pacifying treatments are prescribed. (10)
One should conquer [the disease] reaching the bones and marrow with external and internal unctuous substances (snehas).
When the semen is located there, exhilaration, food, and drink that increase strength and semen are beneficial;
however, seeing that the semen has its passage obstructed, one should administer a purgative.
When the fetus is dried up by wind, or when children are becoming emaciated,
milk boiled with sugar, madhuka, and kāśmarya is beneficial for their restoration.
When the wind has reached the head, one should employ treatments that alleviate wind-related diseases of the head.
Having opened the mouth wide and pressed the jaw with the two thumbs, one should raise it with the two index fingers;
this elevation of the chin is beneficial.
In cases of facial paralysis (ardita), a person should eat a ball of black gram mixed with fresh butter.

Having eaten with milk, meat broth, and the juice of *daśamūlī*, one should drink the juice of *daśamūlī* while being devoted to oleation, massage, head-poultices (*śirobasti*), internal administration, and nasal drops.
He shall conquer facial paralysis (*ardita*) by drinking clarified butter after each meal.
A decoction prepared from the five roots (pañcamūlī) or the ten roots (daśamūlī),
as well as dry sudation (rukṣasveda) and nasal medication (nasya), are recommended for stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha).
In cases of speech impairment or disorders of the vessels (dhamanī) caused by Vāta, holding oil gargles (snehagaṇḍūṣa) is advised.
4. Turmeric, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, long pepper, ginger, cumin, *ajamodā*, licorice, and rock salt—
these should be taken in equal parts and made into a fine powder.
A person should stir that powder with clarified butter and consume it every day;
within twenty-one nights, that person will become a possessor of the power of hearing (śrutidhara),
possessing a voice like the rumbling of clouds or a kettledrum and the sound of a cuckoo in rut.

The Kalyāṇaka electuary overcomes dullness, stammering, and muteness; it likewise conquers Vāta located in the three trunks (trika-skandha) as well as that which has reached the neck (manyā). Emesis and nasal medication (nasya), when administered skillfully, destroy [the disease].
A decoction of māṣa, balā, śukaśimbī, kattṛṇa, rāsnā, śvagaṇḍhā, and urubūka, when used as a nasal drop or drunk, [is effective].
Slightly warm and combined with asafoetida and salt,
it removes hemiplegia, stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), and pain in the ears and nose.
One certainly conquers even invincible and agonizing vāta within seven days by drinking a decoction of daśamūla,
balā, and māṣa, mixed with oil and clarified butter.
Having eaten in the evening, one should drink at night [a decoction] for Viśvācī and Apabāhuka;
or else, one should drink the fresh juice of Balā, Pāribhadra, or Ātmaguptā.
He who administers nasal drops with meat broth will have arms as strong as a diamond within a month.
One should drink [a decoction] boiled with black gram (*māṣa*), *ātmaguptā*, castor seed (*eraṇḍa*), and *vāṭyālaka*.
Combined with asafoetida and rock salt, it prevents hemiplegia (pakṣāghāta). In cases of wasting of the arms, one should drink ghee after eating the Mahākalyāṇaka formulation.
When vāta is aggravated in the heart, milk from a cow that has calved for the first time (aṃśumatī) is beneficial.
Harītakī, vacā, rāsnā, rock salt (saindhava), and amlavetasa,
combined with an appropriate measure of ghee, destroy apatantraka. One pala, half a pala, and one pala of well-minced garlic [should be used].

Having powdered equal parts of asafoetida, cumin, rock salt, black salt, and the three pungents (śuṇṭhī, marica, pippalī), each measuring one māṣaka, and having sprinkled these over [the preparation] and stirred it well,
one should consume it according to one's digestive fire in the morning, followed by a decoction of castor root as an after-drink.
One *māṣa* should be consumed daily and continuously;
it quickly destroys wind-diseases (*vātaroga*), including facial paralysis (*ardita*) and convulsions (*sāpatantraka*), as well as diseases affecting a single limb or the entire body. (32)
It cures stiffness of the thighs, sciatica, and especially worms in the abdomen;
it destroys diseases of the waist and back, and particularly the abdominal enlargement (udara).
Sour curd, taken before a meal along with vacha and pungent spices, destroys these ailments.
Other treatments for vāta diseases, such as the regimen for apatānaka, are also beneficial;
one should treat a person with kubja using vāta-alleviating drugs and daśamūla. However, if the condition has progressed excessively, one should avoid treating it with fats or meat soups.
In cases of *tūnī* and *pratitūnī*, one should drink the powder of the *pippalyādi* group with lukewarm water;

or, in cases of flatulence (*ādhmāna*), one should take a fatty substance with salt and ghee, or alkali and asafoetida. Fasting, fomentation with the heat of the palms, and medicinal suppositories (*phalavarti*) are also recommended.
In this condition, one should employ digestive stimulants (dīpana), carminatives (pācana), and purificatory enemas (basti).
In the case of flatulence (pratyādhmāna), however, emesis, fasting (laṅghana), and digestive stimulants are likewise indicated.
For both pratyaṣṭhīlā and aṣṭhīlikā, the treatment is similar to that for internal abscesses (antarvidradhi) and abdominal tumors (gulma).

One should drink the decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī), balā, rāsnā, guḍūcī, and viśvabheṣaja with castor oil for cases of sciatica (gṛdhrasī), lameness, and paraplegia. A decoction prepared from the leaves of śephālikā, cooked over a gentle fire, [is also beneficial].

Merely by drinking it, one may eliminate the incurable disease of sciatica (gṛdhrasī); a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla) combined with castor oil and trivṛt-ghee, or simply trivṛt itself, removes the pain of sciatica and abdominal tumors (gulma). || 41 ||
Or one should drink oil, ghee, or the juice of fresh ginger and citron, along with sour gruel and jaggery,
for pain in the waist, thighs, back, sacrum, and abdominal tumors.
Castor oil is prescribed for the removal of sciatica (gṛdhrasī).
Alternatively, a person should drink castor oil with cow's urine for one month; this application removes sciatica and stiffness of the thighs.
Long pepper that has been finely powdered, when drunk with cow urine and castor oil,
destroys sciatica (gṛdhrasī) arising from phlegm and wind that has persisted for a long time. A man who eats food prepared and cooked with castor oil [obtains similar benefits].
One afflicted by sciatica (gṛdhrasī) attains the former state [of health] by consuming eggplant (vārtāka).
Alternatively, castor seeds ground with milk and ginger,
or cooked rice (pāyasa) prepared with the fruit of the *rubu* plant, when consumed, cures the pain in the waist caused by sciatica.
One should take one pala of rāsnā and five karṣas of guggulu,
form them into pills with clarified butter, and consume them to cure sciatica (gṛdhrasī). A man afflicted by sciatica should first be properly purified through digestive and cleansing therapies.
Having recognized a person whose internal fire is inflamed, one should treat them with enemas (basti).
One should not perform the procedure of enema at the outset until the upper tract has been purified; for in that case, the unctuous substance is useless, like an oblation poured into ashes.
When intense oleation and sudation have been applied to the calf of one afflicted by *gṛdhrasī*,
and it has been thoroughly massaged with the feet, one should carefully draw down the *gṛdhrasī* through a narrow channel into the little toe.
Having recognized the elevated knot situated in the deep vein (kaṇḍarā),
one should quickly incise it with a surgical instrument, extract that [growth] which resembles a coral sprout, cauterize it with fire, and then apply a paste of yaṣṭyāhvā and sandalwood.
One should lance the vein four finger-breadths below the *indravasti*;
if it does not subside, one should cauterize the little toe of the foot.
He who drinks the fresh root of *tagara* ground with buttermilk [is cured].
One afflicted by wind-diseases of the groin is liberated from them in an instant;
one should drink either a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūlī*) or water boiled with ginger (*nāgara*).
In all cases of pain in the waist, [one should apply] oil derived from *eraṇḍa*.
In cases of Viśvācī, lameness, and paraplegia, as well as burning and tingling sensations in the feet, deformities of the "jackal's head" (kroṣṭuśīrṣa), and the disorder known as Vātakaṇṭaka,
one should pierce the veins as previously described; this treatment removes wind-related diseases.
One should drink guggulu, kroṣṭuśīrṣa, or vṛddhadāraka with a decoction of guḍūcī and triphalā, or with milk, or with castor oil,
in cases of vātakaṇṭaka; one should also perform bloodletting repeatedly.
Or one should drink castor oil, or indeed cauterize [the area] with pure substances.
In the case of a callus (khallī), there should be fomentation, massage, and poulticing with unctuous, sour, and salty substances.
Furthermore, a powder made from Triphalā and Pippalī, each weighing one Pala, should be applied.
One should soak [the ingredients] in water decocted from the ten roots (daśamūla), adding half a pala each of cinnamon-bark (tvak) and cardamom (elā).
Then, having added five palas of guggulu and formed them into boluses (vaṭaka),
this [remedy], through the regular consumption of meat broth, [cures] wind-diseases (vātaroga), especially [those caused by] vāta.
It destroys those residing in the joints, bones, and marrow, just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree.
(61) One should boil the substance to be processed until it is equal [in weight] to the liquid; the decoction should be one-eighth part of that.
It should be soaked while moist for a day; this procedure of soaking is to be performed for seven days. (62)
14. Aśvagandhā, hapuṣā, guḍūcī, śatāvarī, gokṣura, vṛddhadāraka, rāsnā, śatāhvā, aśaṭhī, and yamānī.
And with equal parts of these, along with *nāgara*, a powder should be made; in this [mixture], *kauśika* (white honey) should be added in an amount equal [to the powder],
and likewise, clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) should be given in half that portion.
Then, having taken a dose of about half an akṣa, one should take it as an after-drink with wine, vegetable soups,
liquor, or lukewarm water.
In cases of stiffness in the waist, sciatica, or pain in the arms, back, jaw, knees, or both feet, one should use either milk or meat broth.
When the wind resides in the joints,
has entered the bones, reached the marrow, or is located in the tendons, one should conquer the skin diseases (kuṣṭha) associated with vāta and kapha.

Those who know the truth declare that there are thirteen [types of] heart-seizing disorders caused by wind, as well as those arising from defects of the womb; these also apply to cases of fractured bones, piercing wounds, and lameness caused by wind.

Having first conquered the *varaka* (flatulence), it is beneficial for wind (*vāta*) when the wind is not obstructed by food; in that case, scraping (*ullekha*) is indicated, as it is digestive, carminative, and light.
However, in the case of numbness due to wind (*supti-vāta*), the physician should repeatedly perform bloodletting (*asṛṅmokṣa*).
One should also apply a plaster made from the smoke of a salt-house treated with oil.
There should be the drinking of ghee, oil, fat, and marrow, as well as massages, enemas,
oleaginous sudations, and staying in a windless place with warm coverings.
Flavors, milks, and foods that are sweet, sour, and salty—
whatever is nourishing is all recommended for those suffering from wind diseases.
Soup made with *paṭola* and *pālaka* is aphrodisiac, alleviates wind, and is light.
Soup prepared with vāṭyālaka is supremely destructive of wind (vāta).
[One may prepare it] in the decoction of balā, pañcamūla, or daśamūla, using separately the meat of goat, head of a sheep, aquatic animals, marsh-dwellers, carnivores, or birds. || 72-73 ||
Having prepared unctuous juices seasoned with sour curd and the three pungents (vyoṣa),
one should feed the person afflicted by wind diseases with those juices made distinctly salty.
Milk boiled with the two pañcamūlis and balā is beneficial for wind disorders.
Bājigandhā, the three types of balā, daśamūlī, mahauṣadha,
the two types of gṛdhranakhī, and rāsnā constitute the group that destroys vāta.
(75) 16 Kola, kulattha, devadāru, and rāsnā—
A poultice consisting of black gram, linseed, sesame seeds, costus, sweet flag, the two types of dill, barley flour, sour liquids,
and hot substances is for those suffering from diseases of Vata. || 76 ||
Veśavāra made from marshy meat, applied warm as a poultice, destroys Vāta.
Flesh without bones, ground, steamed, and mixed with jaggery, ghee, long pepper (kṛṣṇā), and black pepper (marica), is known as veśavāra. (17–77)
The *kākolyādi* group, combined with all sour substances,
along with meat from marshy animals that has been well-steamed and mixed with all types of fats, made lukewarm and clearly salty, is proclaimed as *sālvaṇa*. (78–79)
Therefore, one should always administer an enema for those suffering from wind disorders (vāta),
using the Bhadradārvādi group which subdues wind, or the Kākolyādi group according to Suśruta. In this case,
the medicine should be equal in quantity to the meat, and its sourness should be adjusted by the amount of sour liquid used.

A poultice (paṭṭī) should be used for the purpose of fomentation, and sour liquids such as kāñjika are desired. Here, the "four unctuous substances" (catuḥsneha) should be used in such a quantity that thorough fomentation occurs;
they may be used in their entirety, in half-doses, or according to availability. || 81-82 ||
The instruction "one should employ" applies everywhere in the case of collective actions.
83. Ghee cooked with a decoction and paste of *aśvagandhā*, with four times the amount of milk, destroys wind (vāta), acts as an aphrodisiac, and increases muscle mass.
Ghee cooked with a decoction of daśamūla, one pala each of the jīvanīya drugs, and milk, provides nourishment and relieves afflictions caused by vāta. In this preparation,
the decoction should be three times the amount of the ghee (one prastha), and the milk should be equal in quantity to the ghee.

One should boil a goat, stripped of its skin and deprived of its horns, hooves, and so forth, along with the two groups of five roots (pañcamūlī), in one droṇa of water. When reduced to one-fourth, one should cook one prastha of ghee with that decoction.
This preparation, known as Chāgalādyam, consists of the Jīvanīya group of drugs along with Kaṭyāhva, milk, and Śatāvarī; it cures all disorders of Vāta,
as well as facial paralysis (ardita), earache, deafness, muteness, and nasal speech.

This clarified butter is recommended for those who are dull-witted, stammering, or lame, as well as for those with clubfoot, gout, or hunchback; it is also praised in cases of facial paralysis and hernia.
According to the scriptural injunction regarding the weight of ingredients, there should be one *droṇa* of goat meat and one *tulā* of the ten roots (*daśamūla*).
Half a *tulā* each of the two types of *yaṣṭyāhva* (liquorice) should be added according to the twofold instruction.
Elā, murā, śarala, śailaja, dāru, kauntī, caṇḍā, śaṭī, nalada, campaka, and *hemapuṣpa* [are also to be added].
Sthauṇeya, gandharasa, pūtidala, mṛṇāla, śrīvāsa, kunduru, nakha, ambu, varāṅga, kuṣṭha, kālīyaka,
jalada, karkaṭa, and candana— śrī— [91]

Having processed castor oil with saffron and safflower, along with *mṛkkā*, *turuṣka*, and *laghulāmbha*, combined with a decoction of *balā* and milk, and mixed with curd; [this is the result of the *rjāti*].

One should cook it together [with these]; they declare this to be beneficial for wind-related disorders (*vātāmaya*), as it promotes strength, complexion, and the body's form. Oil cooked with the decoction and paste of *balā*, combined with milk, [is likewise effective].
Prepared in this manner with śirīṣa, it cures all disorders of vāta. Likewise,
[one may prepare it] with a decoction of balā roots, a decoction of daśamūla,
a decoction of barley, jujube, and horse gram, or with milk.

Take eight parts each of the eight auspicious substances and one part of oil; having added the sweet group of drugs together with rock salt, as well as aguru, resin of the sarja tree, sarala, and devadāru, one should cook them together.
Mañjiṣṭhā, candana, kuṣṭha, elā, and kālānuśārivā;
|| 96 || māṃsī, śaileyaka, patra, tagara, śārivā, vacā, śatāvarī, aśvagandhā, śatapuṣpā, and punarnavā. || 97 ||
Having properly prepared this, one should place it in a pitcher made of gold, silver, or even clay, and store it well-protected.
This is known by the name Balā-taila; it cures all disorders of the wind (vāta).
One should cause the woman who has recently given birth to take an iron dose according to her strength.

And for a woman desiring conception, or a man whose semen is depleted, or one with diminished *vāta*, or one struck in a vital organ (*marman*), or wounded, or even one who has been crushed; [for all these, this should be administered].
And when one is overcome by broken strength and exhaustion, one should employ this in every way;
it dispels all disorders such as *ākṣepaka* and other diseases of Vāta,
as well as hiccups, cough, *adhimantha*, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and difficult-to-cure asthma.
By using this for six months, one eliminates intestinal hernia (antravṛddhi); the man becomes possessed of fresh bodily constituents and attains stable youth.
Indeed, this should be performed by kings and those men who hold royal office.
Those men who are happy, delicate, and strong [should take this].
Bilva, agnimantha, śyonāka, pāṭalā, pāribhadraka, prasāraṇī, aśvagandhā, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā. || 104 ||
One should boil ten *pala* portions each of *balā*, *atibalā*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and *punarnavā* in four *droṇas* of water;
having strained it when reduced to one-fourth, one should add one *prastha* of oil.
Śatapuṣpā, devadāru, māṃsī, śaileyaka, and vacā; || 106 || candana, tagara, kuṣṭha, and the four types of elāparṇī;
rāsnā, turagagandhā, saindhava, and punarnavā. || 107 ||
Having ground two-pala portions of these [ingredients], one should add them [to the oil] and provide an equal amount of śatāvarī juice; furthermore,
having added either goat’s or cow’s milk four times the quantity [of the oil].
It is highly recommended for drinking, enemas, massage, and even as food.
Whether it be a horse broken by wind, an elephant, or a human being, one who is lame or crawls on a wooden board is cured by this oil. (109–110)
In cases where there are winds in the lower parts of the body or those located in the middle of the head;
in toothache, lockjaw, stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), or throat obstruction (galagraha);
when one limb withers away, or when one's gait is unsteady—[these are signs of approaching death]. || 111 ||
Those men whose senses are decayed, whose semen is lost, and who are emaciated by fever;
those who are deaf, whose tongues are stammering, and who are dull-witted; and that woman who has few offspring, or who does not conceive—[for these, this rite is prescribed]. (112–113)
For those whose testicles are afflicted by wind (vāta) and who suffer from severe enlargement of the intestines (antravṛddhi), this excellent oil is prescribed; it is known by the name Nārāyaṇa.
In the absence of *tagara*, *natam* should be used here, or alternatively, *śīyalichopaḍa*.
25. Śatāvarī, aṃśumatī, pṛśniparṇī, śaṭī, varā, the roots of eraṇḍa, the two types of bṛhatī,
pūtika, the roots of gavedhuka, and likewise sahacara.
One should boil ten-pala portions of these [drugs] in one droṇa of water; when reduced to one-fourth and strained, one should add this internal essence (garbha),
namely punarnavā, vacā, dāru, śatāhvā, candana, and agaru.
One should grind together half-pala quantities each of śaileya, tagara, kuṣṭha, elā, māṃsī, sthitā, balā, aśvagandhā, saindhava salt, and rāsnā;
then one should add two prasthas each of cow’s milk and goat’s milk. || 118 ||
One should cook one prastha of the juice of śatāvarī with one prastha of oil.
Listen now to the potency of this prepared oil for horses, elephants, and likewise for men who have suffered fractures from wind (vāta).
This oil should be administered as a remedy for all wind disorders;
by drinking it, a man will certainly become long-lived and firm. A female mule may even conceive a fetus, so what need be said of a human woman?
It destroys heartache and pain in the sides, as well as hemicrania (ardhāvabhedaka), scrofula (apacī), cervical adenitis (gaṇḍamālā), gout (vātarakta), lockjaw (hanugraha),
jaundice (kāmalā), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), and even urinary calculi (aśmarī). || 122–123 ||
This supreme remedy, known as Nārāyaṇa, which brings an end to wind-diseases, was proclaimed by the Blessed Viṣṇu.
Having boiled one hundred palas of Aśvagandhā in one droṇa of water until one-eighth remains, [one should proceed].

Having strained [the decoction], one should cook the oil, adding four times as much milk and a paste made of lotus stalks (mṛṇāla), lotus roots (śālūka), lotus fibers (bisa), lotus filaments (kiñjalka),
mālatī flowers, hrībera, madhuka, śārivā, and the stamens of the lotus (padmakeśara). || 125–126 ||
Medā, punarnavā, drākṣā, mañjiṣṭhā, the two types of bṛhatī,
elā, elavāluka, triphalā, musta, candana, and padmaka— [a decoction] prepared with these cures vāta residing in the blood, as well as raktapitta and asṛgdara. || 127 ||
It destroys [diseases], bestows nourishment and strength, and increases the flesh of those who are emaciated.
It cures disorders of the semen and the female reproductive tract, removes dryness of the nose, and by means of drinking, massage, and oil enemas, it makes even eunuchs virile.
One should cook oil with an equal quantity of the fresh juice of *mūlaka* (radish), milk, curd, and sour gruel (*kāñjika*), along with a paste of *balā*, *citraka*, rock salt (*saindhava*),
long pepper (*pippalī*), *ativiṣā*, *rāsnā*, *cavikā*, agallochum (*aguru*), and *citraka*.
Oil prepared with bhallātaka, vacā, kuṣṭha, śvadaṃṣṭrā, viśvabheṣaja, puṣkaramūla,
śaṭhī, bilva, śatāhvā, nata, and devadāru, when drunk,
destroys even the most violent intoxications caused by vāta.
He who, afflicted by diseases of wind (vāta), drinks oil cooked with the paste and fresh juice of garlic,
his wind-related ailments will indeed perish quickly.
Like vast texts that have been poorly grasped.
133.29 That which has been cooked with a great abundance of the juices of *ketakī*, *nāgabalā*, and *atibalā*.
Oil prepared with a non-trivial amount of water from parched grain (tuṣodaka) destroys wind located in the bones;
because of the word "non-trivial" (analpa), it is understood that the decoction and the parched-grain water are used in equal measure.
Even an oil that is free from paste may be prepared with only a liquid medium.
[Take] two palas of rock salt, five of ginger, two each of pippalīmūla and citraka, twenty bhallātaka seeds, and two āḍhakas [of oil]. (135–136)
One should cook one prastha of oil with these [herbs] along with Āraṇālā; this bestows offspring and cures sciatica, elephantiasis, hemorrhoids, pain, and all disorders of Vāta.
(137) For contracted limbs, oil prepared with Māṣa and Saindhava salt should be used for massage.
When the poison has reached the head and arms, nasal medication (nasya) and a drink to be taken after a meal should be administered;
in this case, a decoction prepared from black gram (māṣa), rock salt (saindhava),
and a paste (kalka) of thirty-two māṣas each of ātmaguptā, ativiṣā, and urubūka [should be used].
Oil prepared with well-ground rāsnā, śatāhvā, and salts, along with four parts of a decoction of māṣa and balā, destroys pakṣavāta. || 139 ||
Having added thirty-three māṣas to one prastha [of the herbs], one should cook them properly in one āḍhaka of water.
When the liquid is reduced to one-fourth, one should add four times as much milk,
one prastha of sesame oil, and a paste (kalka) measuring one akṣa.
The eight vitalizing drugs (jīvanīya), along with śatapuṣpā,
rock salt, rāsnā, ātmaguptā, madhuka, balā, vyoṣa, and trikaṇṭaka,
[are used] for hemiplegia, facial paralysis, and severe earache caused by vāta.
It is recommended for dullness of hearing, lack of hearing, and cataracts born of the three doṣas;
it is also praised for hand-tremors, head-tremors, facial paralysis,
avabāhuka, kalāyakhaja, and for use as a drink, anointment, or enema.
This *māṣa*-oil is excellent for removing diseases of the regions above the clavicle.
[It is prepared] with the decoctions of *māṣa*, *atasī*, *yava*, *kuraṇṭaka*, *kaṇṭakārī*, *gokaṇṭa*, *tuṇṭuka*, *jaṭā*, and *kapikacchu*.
With a decoction of cotton seeds, hemp seeds, horse gram, jujube, and kola, as well as with the broth of goat meat, along with ginger, long pepper, and *śatapuṣpā*— 145.
This oil known as Māṣākhya, cooked with the roots of Sairaṇḍa, Sapunarnavā, Saraṇī, Rāsnā, Balā, Amṛtalatā, and Kaṭuka, cures avabāhuka (sciatica). || 146 ||
Hemiplegia (ardhāṅgaśoṣa), apatānaka, āḍhyavāta,
ākṣepaka accompanied by tremors of the arms and shaking of the head—
[these are treated] by means of nasal therapy, enema procedures, and affusion.
It destroys all pains of the waist, hips, and knees.

[One should take it] separately in a decoction of black gram (māṣa), in a decoction of balā, in a decoction of rāsnā, in a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), and in a decoction derived from goat meat, along with barley, jujube (kola), and horse gram (kulattha). || 147–148 ||
Having added one *prastha* of oil and four times as much milk (*caturguṇa*),

the physician should cook it with *rāsnā*, *ātmaguptā*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *śatāhvā*, castor root (*eraṇḍa*), *mustaka*, the *jīvanīya* drugs, *balā*, and the three acrids (*tryūṣaṇa*), each weighing one *akṣa*. (149)
In cases of trembling of the hands, trembling of the head, wasting of the arms, and avabāhuka;
in deafness, earache, and severe ringing in the ears; in facial paralysis, ardita, kubja, gṛdhrasī, and apatānaka—[this [remedy] is effective]. (150–151)
One should employ this excellent Māṣa oil for enemas, massages, internal drinks, and nasal drops; it removes diseases of the regions above the clavicle.
Here, six measures of decoction (kvātha) have been mentioned using their case endings.

Having added half an *āḍhaka* of *māṣa* beans and half a *tulā* of the ten roots (*daśamūla*), one should boil thirty *palas* of goat meat in one *droṇa* of water. When the decoction has been strained, cooled, and reduced to one-fourth its original volume: || 153–154 ||
One should provide one *prastha* of sesame oil and four times as much milk,
along with *ātmaguptā*, *urubūka*, *śatāhvā*, the three salts (*lavaṇatraya*), the *jīvanīya* group of drugs, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *cavya*, *citraka*, and *kaṭphala*. (155)

One should prepare [the oil] over a gentle fire with a paste consisting of equal parts (one akṣa each) of trikaṭu, pippalīmūla, rāsnā, madhuka, saindhava, devadāru, amṛtā, kuṣṭha, vājigandhā, vacā, and śaṭī. || 156–157 ||
In cases of wind afflicted by hemiplegia, deafness, lockjaw, tinnitus, headache, and tridoshaja blindness;
and in cases of dizziness of the hands, feet, head, and neck, as well as sluggish gait. || 158 ||

This oil is praised for use in the treatment of *kalāya*, *khañja*, *pāṅgulya*, *gṛdhra*, *āmavāta*, and *bāhuka*; it is recommended for drinking, enemas, massage, nasal administration, and filling the ears or eyes, as it removes all diseases caused by Vāta. (159–160)
Having boiled the *dvipañcamūla* (the two groups of five roots) with sixteen times as much oil,

one should cook an *āḍhaka* measure of black gram (*māṣa*) in that decoction; then, having added four times as much of that liquid along with an equal amount of milk, one should cook one *prastha* of oil.
And for the sake of the paste, the wise physician should add these medicinal substances:
aśvagandhā, śaṭī, dāru, balā, rāsnā, prasāraṇī, kuṣṭha, parūṣaka, bhārgī, the two types of vidārī, and punarnavā. (162–163)
Having collected mātuluṅga fruit, cumin, asafoetida, śatapuṣpikā, śatāvarī, gokṣuraka, the root of pippalī, citraka,
the entire jīvanīya group, and rock salt; || 164 ||
Knowing this great Māṣa oil to be well-prepared and perfected,
one should employ it for enemas, massages, internal drinks, and nasal drops in cases of hemiplegia, lockjaw, facial paralysis, and apatantraka. (165–166)
Likewise, [it is used] for avabāhuka and viśvacī, for those who are lame or club-footed, for stiffness of the jaw and neck,
for vātika adhimantha, for the loss of semen, and for ringing in the ears and severe earache.
One should prescribe this medicine for the pacification of *kalāya-khañja*.

Having boiled one *āḍhaka* of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) in a *droṇa* of water until it is reduced to a quarter, the decoction should be four times the amount of oil; this same procedure applies when using a decoction of black gram (*māṣa*). || 168-169 ||
One should boil the bones of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals in water; then,
one should cook that fat again with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) along with jīvaka,
ṛṣabhaka, āsphotā, vidārī, and kapikacchu.

With a paste of wind-alleviating and life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs, [this oil] should be prepared with two parts of milk. Once it is cooked, through nasal drops (nāvana), massage (abhyaṅga), oral intake, and unctuous enemas (anuvāsana),
it quickly dispels the Vāta located in the head, the flanks, the bones, and the abdominal cavity.
For those whose marrow has been wasted away and whose semen and vital energy (ojas) have diminished,
this [preparation], which bestows strength and nourishment, shall be like nectar for them. One prastha of triphalā and two kuḍavas of kulattha [beans] [should be taken].

Five palas each of *kṛṣṇagandhā* and *āḍhakī*, two palas each of *rāsnā* and *citraka*, and one pala each of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) should be boiled in one droṇa of water until reduced to one-fourth;
[the resulting liquid] should be measured separately in one prastha each. || 174–175 ||
Wine, sugar-cane juice, curd, sour gruel, fermented rice-water,
the juice of *kola*, pomegranate, and *vṛkṣāmla*, oil, ghee, fat, marrow, milk, and six *pala* measures of the *jīvanīya* (life-promoting) drugs. 176.
Having added a paste, one should properly cook this great unctuous substance (mahāsneha).

One should administer this massage in cases of Vāta located in the vessels, marrow, or bones; in diseases affecting the whole body or a single limb; and in cases of tremors, convulsions, and pain. || 177-178 ||
One hundred *prasāraṇī* plants, crushed and boiled in one *āḍhaka* of pure water, should be reduced to one-quarter.

To this, one should add an equal amount of oil, curd, and sour gruel (*kāñjika*), along with double the quantity of milk and two-pala portions of the following paste ingredients: [The list of paste ingredients follows: ... Thus it is prepared. (179)
Citraka, pippalīmūla, madhuka, saindhava, vacā,
śatapuṣpā, devadāru, rāsnā, vāraṇapippalī, the roots of prasāraṇī, māṃsī, and bhallātaka. (180–181)

One should cook the oil over a mild fire; it conquers diseases caused by Vāta and Kapha and dispels the eighty Vāta disorders occurring in men and women, including hunchback, stiffness, lameness, sciatica, club-foot, and facial paralysis. (182)
It also cures stiffness of the jaw, back, head, and neck.
[One should take] one *tulā* each of *prasāraṇī*, *aśvagandhā*, and *daśamūla*, separately, into a *droṇa* of water, until one-fourth remains. (184)

One āḍhaka of oil, four parts of milk, an equal amount of curd, and two parts of kāñjika, along with two palas each of granthika, kṣāra, prasāraṇī, akṣa, and saindhava; and one pala each of mañjiṣṭhā, agni, yaṣṭyāhva, and the jīvanīya group [of herbs]. || 185 ||
Having added five palas of ginger and thirty bhallātaka fruits, one should cook [the mixture] according to the method for enemas (basti) and so forth;
this destroys wind (vāta) located in the joints, channels, and bones, and serves to increase virility, enthusiasm, memory, wisdom, strength, complexion, and digestive fire. || 186–187 ||
One should add three hundred *akṣas* of black salt (*sauvarcala*) here. Having boiled the *prasāraṇī* plant along with its roots and leaves during the autumn season,
one hundred [palas] should be taken from the *sahacara*, and likewise one hundred from the *śatāvarī*.

The physician should cook one āḍhaka of oil with four times as much water and the juices of balā, ātmaguptā, aśvagandhā, and ketakī— one hundred palas of each— along with one āḍhaka each of curd-whey (mastu),
meat broth, sour gruel (cukra), and milk. || 189–190 ||
One should cook it with one āḍhaka of curd over a gentle fire; the dosage of these substances to be administered is half a pala each. [The ingredients are:
tagara, madana, kuṣṭha, keśara, mustaka, and tvak.

Rāsnā, rock salt (saindhava), long pepper (pippalī), spikenard (māṃsī), mañjiṣṭhā, liquorice (yaṣṭikā), as well as medā, mahāmedā, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, dill (śatapuṣpā), vyāghranakha, dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), and devadāru. || 192–193 ||
Having ground together kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, vacā, and bhallātaka, one should prepare prasāraṇī; once cooked,
it should be strained and stored while neither overcooked nor undercooked.
Listen as I declare where and where it should be bestowed:
upon those who are hunchbacked, those who are lame, and likewise those who are dwarfish;
for whomsoever a single limb withers, and those whose bones and joints are broken. (195–196)
This is the supreme aphrodisiac for those with vitiated wind-blood (vāta-śoṇita), those whose minds are afflicted by wind, and those whose semen is exhausted due to women;
it should be administered as an enema, for drinking, as an external massage, and even as nasal drops.
When applied, it quickly pacifies various diseases born of Vāta.
And from *chinnā* one *tulā*,
from *rubuka* one *tulā*, from *rāsnā* and *śirīṣa* one *tulā*, and from *devāhvā* along with *ketaka* one hundred *ghaṭas*.
Having boiled one-sixteenth part of water,
one should add a jar of oil, two jars of dregs-water,
and an āḍhaka of whey. || 199 ||
Then, having added one āḍhaka each of fermented gruel, goat’s milk, sugarcane juice, and cow’s milk, along with *pṛkkā*,
*karkaṭa*, *jīvaka*, and the rest, as well as *vikāsā*—
With *kākolikā*, *kacchurā*,
small cardamom, camphor, *kunda*, *sarala*, saffron, spikenard, and *nakha*.
With *kālīya*, *utpala*, *padmaka*, *nīlāhvaya*, *niśā*, *kakkolaka*, and *granthika*;
with *cāmpeya*, *abhaya*, *coca*, *pūga*, and *kaṭukā*— 200.
With nutmeg,
costus, storax, deodar, sandalwood, sweet flag, bitumen, and rock salt;

With *tailābhya*, *udakaṭaṃbhara*, *aṅghrinālikā*, *vṛścīra*, *kaccoraka*, musk (*kastūrī*), *daśamūla*, and *ketaka*— Please note that this is a fragmentary line from a Sanskrit medical or pharmacological text (likely a *yoga* or compound formula). With *dhyāmā*, *aśvagandhā*, and water;
with the fruits of *kauntī*, *tārkṣaja*, and *śallakī*, and with *laghu*, *śyāmā*, *śatāhvā*, and *maya*.
One should cook a large quantity with bhallātaka, triphalā, lotus filaments (abjakesara), mahāśyāmā, and cloves (lavaṅga),
together with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and another portion of triphalā.
One should destroy that wind by means of warm food, fire, and the procedures of drinking, anointing, enemas, and nasal drops. || 202 ||
It pacifies those arising from phlegm and those from bile, whether they have spread through the entire body, half the body, or specific parts, including the joints, bones, and marrow.
It nourishes various types of bodily constituents (dhātus), makes them firm, and bestows fresh youth upon men.
It bestows great strength even upon the aged and grants conception to barren women; by drinking this oil, even an old woman may give birth to a son. (203)
By this [water], trees that have withered when watered produce fruit;
they become glossy and firm.
Men, cattle, horses, and elephants whose limbs are broken become very firm again.
[There are] three hundred varieties of *prasāraṇī* with roots, leaves, and branches.
One hundred parts of śatāvarī, likewise one hundred of aśvagandhā;
one hundred of ketakī, one hundred of daśamūla, one hundred of vāṭyālaka, and one hundred of sahacara. || 205–206 ||
Having added one hundred droṇas of water until only one-hundredth part remains,
then with that decoction, twice the amount of decoction, very clear āraṇālaka, and one āḍhaka of whey; || 207 ||
One should place one *droṇa* of oil, combined with an *āḍhaka* each of milk, *śukta*, sugarcane juice, and the meat-broth of a goat, into a sturdy vessel. Hereafter,
I shall describe those substances which are to be ground into a paste.
Bhallātaka, nata, śuṇṭhī, pippalī, citraka, śaṭhī, vacā, pr̥kkā, prasāraṇī, and the root of pippalī;
likewise devadāru, śatāhvā, sūkṣmailā, tvac, and vālaka.
Saffron, lac-dye, manjiṣṭhā, turuṣka, nakhi, and agaru;
camphor, kunduru, niśā, lavaṅga, dhyāmaka, and candana; kakkola, nalikā, musta, kālīya, utpala, and patrakam. || 211–212 ||
Śaṭī, hareṇu, śaileya, śrīvāsa along with ketakī,
triphalā, kacchurā, bhīru, saralā, padmakeśara, priyaṅgu, uśīra, nalada, the group beginning with jīvaka, and punarnavā. (213)
Having taken three-pala portions each of the ten roots (daśamūla), aśvagandhā, nāgapuṣpa, rasāñjana,
the fruits of kaṭuka, jāti, and pūga, and the resin of śallakī, one should cook them slowly over a mild fire. || 214–215 ||
This *prasāraṇī* is prepared by cooking it in a wide and very sturdy vessel;
its application for those afflicted by disease is prescribed here as being of six kinds.
Through massage, it destroys [the disorder] located in the skin, and likewise, through drinking, that which is located in the internal organs.
Likewise, [a medicine] that has gone upward from food situated in the subtle channels acts as a nasal therapy (nasya);

when it reaches the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), it is an enema (vasti) or a decoction enema (nirūha). This is indeed like nectar for colts and young horses throughout their entire bodies. || 217–218 ||
This very same [remedy] applies to humans, elephants, and even cattle;
likewise, great trees that have withered are drenched with this oil,
whereupon they sprout again and become laden with branches and fruit.
Even an old man becomes young again by this oil.
A woman who does not conceive also gives birth after drinking it; and a man who is childless likewise obtains a son after drinking it.
It shall quickly destroy the eighty diseases born of wind, those of bile, those of phlegm, and even those arising from the combination of the humors (sannipāta).
By this, a great rite for ensuring male offspring has been performed for those with impaired vision, such as Andhaka.
Having also offered an oblation to Viṣṇu, one should employ this oil.
Half a *tulā* of *rāsnā* and *kilima* is added to the decoction;
however, if *bhallātaka* cannot be tolerated, red sandalwood (*raktacandana*) is used in its place.

Cinnamon leaf, *patramadhukī*, kuṣṭha, campaka, and red ochre (*gairika*), along with *granthi*, *uśīra*, and *maruvaka*, are added in abundance. Camphor is not given; instead, the preparation of scented water is performed with pearl-shells (*śukti*). || 225 ||
The purification of substances and the method of cooking are similar to those for *prasāraṇī*.
[Take] three hundred parts of *prasāraṇī* and two parts each of *pītasahācara*, *aśvagandhā*, *eraṇḍa*, *balā*, *varī*, *rāsnā*, and *punarnavā*. 226–227.
One *tulā* each of *ketakī*, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *pṛthaktvak*, and *pāribhadraka*; likewise, half a *tulā* from *kilima*;
half a *tulā* from *śirīṣa*; and twenty-five [palas] of *lākṣā*.
One should likewise prepare all these, including the *lodhra* leaves, together in one place;
when there are five hundred and twenty-five *āḍhaka*s of water,
one should leave behind two *droṇa*s [of the decoction], along with twenty-six *āḍhaka*s of sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
One should take ten separate prasthas each of milk and curd, one āḍhaka of sugarcane juice, and likewise three tulās of goat meat; then,
having cooked these with forty-five prasthas of water, one should dry the mixture.
And from seventeen *prasthas* of decoction, specifically of *mañjiṣṭhā*,
one should prepare [the oil] using these liquids measured at one *kuḍava* each and one *āḍhaka* total; this should be combined with one *droṇa* of well-purified sesame oil and one *prastha*.
One *droṇa* of *kāñjika* (fermented rice water) is prescribed here along with *śukta*;
the initial cooking is performed with these liquids, using a paste (*kalka*) consisting of *bhallātaka*,
*kaṇā* (long pepper), *nāgara* (ginger), and *marica* (black pepper), each measured at six *palas*.
If the bhallātaka is not available, red sandalwood (raktacandana) is prescribed.
Pathyā, akṣa, dhātrī, sarala, śatāhvā, karkaṭī, vacā, corapuṣpī, śaṭī, musta, the two kinds of padma, and utpala [are also used]. || 235–236 ||
Pippalīmūla, mañjiṣṭhā, aśvagandhā, punarnavā,
the combined daśamūla, cakramarda, rasāñjana, gandhatṛṇa, haridrā, and likewise the group of jīvanīya [drugs]. || 237 ||
The first decoction is prepared with three-pala portions of each of these:
devapuṣpī, bolapatra, the resin of śallakī, śailaja, priyaṅgu, uśīra, madhurī, māṃsī, dāru, balā, and acala. (238–239)
Śrīvāsa, nālikā, khoṭi, sūkṣmailā, kunduru, murā,
the three types of nakha, tvak, patrī, apāmārga, pūti, campaka, madana, reṇukā, pṛkkā, and maruva— one pala each of these. || 240 ||
A second cooking with fragrant water is prescribed for each [ingredient] individually.
As for the fragrant water, there should be twenty-five palas each of cinnamon-bark (*tvak*), *patrī*, *patra*, *uśīra*, *mustaka*, and the root of *balā*. (241–242)
In this process for preparing perfumed water (gandhāmbu), one should take half a bhāga of kuṣṭha and twenty-five prasthas of water; it should be boiled until half remains.
A third boiling is desired using both perfumed water and sandalwood water.
In this case, the paste consists of keśara, kuṣṭha, tvak, kālīyaka, kuṅkuma,
bhadraśrī, granthiparṇa, latākastūrikā, as well as lavaṅga, aguru, kakkola, jātīkoṣa, and phala. (244–245)
Cardamom, cloves, and *chalvī* should each be taken in a measure of three *pala*s;
one *pala* and a half of musk (*kastūrī*) and one *pala* of camphor (*candra*) are also taken.
Furthermore, for the purpose of infusion (*vedha*), camphor and sandalwood (*mada*) should again be added in those same measures. || 246 ||
This is proclaimed as the Mahāprasāraṇī, fit for royal consumption;
it possesses the qualities of all *prasāraṇīs* due to its supreme strength.
In this preparation, the method is as follows: one *prastha* of fermented gruel (*śukti*) and five *āḍhakas* [of other ingredients]. || 247–248 ||
One *kuḍava* of *kāñjika*, one *prastha* of curd, eight *palas* of cleaned fresh sour radish, and likewise sixteen *palas* of [fresh ginger];
and separately, *kaṇā*, cumin, rock salt, turmeric, and black pepper.
Two palas [of the ingredients] are placed in a prepared vessel and left in clarified butter for eight days;
when it has been perfected as *śukta*, it should be removed and taken out, at which time three karṣas each of the four spices (*caturjāta*) should be added.
The washing of perfumes with water from the five sprouts is likewise their purification; the refinement and the specific distinction herein shall now be described.
[These consist of] the fruits of the mango, the rose-apple, the wood-apple, the citron, and the bilva.
In all perfuming rituals, one should use leaves and the five sprouts.
Having soaked the fingernail in these— either with the liquid of *caṇḍī*-cow dung or with tamarind juice— if these are unavailable, one should use an earthen vessel instead.
Having extracted it again, washed it, and roasted it,
one should sprinkle it with water infused with jaggery and *pathyā* (harītakī); in this way, it is purified— of this there is no doubt.
