46. Having boiled [the ingredients] in cow urine and in *ālambuṣaka* water, and then again in the water of the five-leaved tree (*pañcadala*), one should subject them to steam-bath (*bāṣpasveda*) with fragrant water. || 256 ||
A cloth stained with pungent perfumes is indeed purified in this way, as is a garment especially so;
likewise, a mustaka root that has been slightly crushed and kept for three days in fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika),
then steamed in water from the five young shoots (pañcapallava) and dried in the sun.
One should roast it while being sprinkled with jaggery-water, and then grind it into powder.
It becomes pure when processed with goat’s urine and *śobhāñjana* juice; likewise, stone (calamine) purified by boiling in sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and roasted with *apathyā*, jaggery, and water.
One should sprinkle it thus again with various flowers and perfume it; having smeared it with the alkaline juice of apāmārga, snuhī, and other plants as available,
one should thoroughly foment it with steam and remove any putridity along with the body hair.
One should cook it in a swing-oven (dolāpakva) and then cook it again in water infused with the sprouts of the *pañcaka* plant.
Then, having pressed it like a wicked man oppresses a virtuous person, one should bring it to a state free of oiliness.
Furthermore, one should repeatedly saturate it with the juices of goat's flesh and *śobhāñjana*.

One should cook it at the root of a *śigru* tree within a cup formed by the petals of a *ketakī* flower; thus purified, it becomes equal to musk. *Turuṣka* should be processed with honey, and *kāśmīra* with clarified butter.
The wise [should treat] iron with blood, and granthiparṇaka with cow's urine;
madhurī with honey-water, and patra with rice-water.
When slightly caustic and fragrant, it burns yet does not turn to ash.
Yellow, possessing the fragrance of the *ketaka* flower, light, and unctuous—such is the best of musk;
they say that the unripe is superior in quality to the ripe camphor.
Even among those, that which is not small and resembles crystal is the most excellent.
The best sandalwood is ripe, possessed of its bark, unctuous, and green in luster;
it is like a deer's horn, and when broken even slightly, no fragments fall from it. It may be red or yellow. (267–268)
A stone shaped like a glass-stick (kācatuṇḍa), glossy and heavy, is the best type of guru;
likewise, that which is produced from śāli rice, having few glossy filaments, red in color, round, and fleshy, is also excellent.
Murā that is yellow is declared the best; māṃsī has the appearance of reddish-brown matted hair.
Reṇukā that has the shape of a mung bean is praised; likewise, a thick substance produced in marshy regions is commended. A nutmeg (*jātīphala*) that is fragrant, oily, and heavy is recommended.
Small cardamom (*elā*) with fine fruits is excellent, as is *priyaṅgu* that is dark and pale.
Nail-wood, horse-hoof wood, and elephant-ear wood are also recommended here;
for these and others, freshness is the most excellent quality.
[47] *Jiṅgī*, *coraka*, *devadāru*, and *sarala*—
With vyāghrī, vacā, celaka,
tvak, patra, along with gandhapattraka, śaṭī, pathyā, akṣa, dhātrī, and ghana;
By these refined and purified [substances],
measured by the number designated as "two palas," and contained within one *prastha* of oil, it becomes stable.
One should cook the *gāndhika* [ointment] with pastes of two *pala* each of *māṃsī*, *mura*, *adama*, *campaka*, *sundarī* bark, *granthi*, *ambu*, *ruṅ*, *marubaka*, and *pṛkkā*.
Having taken one *pala* each of *śrīvāsa*, *kunduru*, *nakhī*, *nalikā*, and *āmiṣī*, one should cook them again with *elā*,
*lavaṅga*, *calacandana*, *jātī*, and *pūtī*.
When cooked with half-palas each of kakkolaka, aguru-latā, and ghusṛṇa,
combined with musk and nutmeg, and possessing pure brilliance, it becomes a great fragrance even when prepared with a mild fire. (275)
Camphor is desired in a quantity of one and a half parts of the five-fold pair;
half of the camphor and madana is desired for the leaf-paste and so forth.
Even when cooked and strained, it should be properly ground while still warm.

That leaf-paste which is given for the purpose of increasing the fragrance is called *patrakalka*. By using those aforementioned purificatory processes for the fragrances here again with double the quantity, this becomes the most excellent oil known as *lakṣmīvilāsa*.

The first [consecration] is performed with water from five leaves; the second with scented water; the third also with that same [water], or else by means of cooked [water] or perfumed water. (279) Adhikāra 23.
One should treat superficial vāta-śoṇita (blood disorders) with external applications such as plasters, massages, and affusions, or by means of oral intake;
one should treat deep-seated cases with purgation, non-unctuous enemas, and the drinking of unctuous substances.
One should let the blood from both types flow out using a horn, a needle, a gourd, or leeches.
One should drain [the blood] from the body by means of venesection or by scarification, moving it toward a specific region.
However, one should not drain [the blood] when there is exhaustion of the limbs, nor when the condition is dry or dominated by Vāta.
A digestive preparation (pācana) is perfected with three karṣas each of Amṛtā, Nāgara, and Dhanyāka.

The decoction derived from *vatsādanī*, when drunk combined with *guggulu*, conquers blood-tinged *vāta* and all types of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) without exception; it thoroughly purifies the blood associated with *samīraṇa* (wind). || 4 ||
One should drink a decoction of vāsā, guḍūcī, and caturaṅgula with castor oil; by this process, even all diseases affecting the entire body will be eliminated without exception.
One conquers the disorder arising from blood and wind (vātarakta).
By licking the powder of *muṇḍitikā* combined with honey and clarified butter,
and drinking a decoction of *chinnā*, one destroys even the most difficult-to-cure vātarakta.
Alternatively, having eaten three or five *pathyā* fruits with jaggery, one should drink a decoction of *chinnaruhā*; this pacifies even aggravated *vātarakta*.
For even that which is mixed with māṣa must necessarily be [prepared] with ghee for vāta, with jaggery for obstructed [vāta],
with sugar for pitta, and with honey for kapha.
Guḍūcī mixed with ginger and *rubu* oil pacifies severe *vātāsṛj* (hemorrhagic disorders) and *āmavāta*.
One may administer the fresh juice, paste, powder, or decoction of guḍūcī.
By consuming [this] for a long time, one is liberated from vātaśoṇita (gout).
Milk boiled with daśamūlī immediately relieves pain;
likewise, a lukewarm affusion with ghee is effective when vāta predominates.
By drinking a decoction prepared with *paṭola*, *kaṭukā*, *abhīru*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *amṛtā*, a person shall conquer vāta-śoṇita accompanied by burning sensations.
[One may also take] wheat flour, goat’s milk, and ghee.
A paste of *rubu* seeds mixed with the milk of a female goat should be applied as an ointment;
for sprinkling, ghee washed a hundred times is to be used, and the milk of a sheep is likewise recommended. || 12 ||
A plaster made of ground sesame seeds similarly fried and cooled in milk,
along with a paste of kaṭukā, amṛtā, yaṣṭyāhva,
and śuṇṭhī mixed with honey and drunk with cow’s urine, conquers vātaśoṇita accompanied by kapha.
Or, in cases where phlegm (kapha) predominates, one should take a decoction of dhātrī, haridrā, and mustā.
In cases where phlegm predominates, one should drink long pepper (kṛṣṇā) with a decoction of kokilākṣa and amṛtā;
by eating wholesome food (pathyā), one is freed from vāta-śoṇita within three weeks.
Jaggery and ghee (guḍaghṛta) are remembered as being beneficial for the heart and as pacifiers of phlegm and blood;
in cases of combined disorders (saṃsarga), one should apply a mixed treatment according to the predominance of each humor.
In all such conditions, one may take harītakī with jaggery or simply a decoction of guḍūcī.
Or, being well-composed, one should practice the *pippalī-vardhamāna* regimen.
A decoction made from three parts each of triphalā, nimba, mañjiṣṭhā, vacā, kaṭukarohiṇī, vatsādanī, and dāruniśā constitutes the "nine-kārṣika" formula.

It removes vātarakta, as well as leprosy (kuṣṭha), scabies (pāmā), erythematous patches (raktamaṇḍala), and kāpālika-leprosy, simply by drinking it. This preparation of nine karṣas should be made with five raktikas per māṣa.
However, once the decoction has been prepared in this manner, the appropriate dose is administered.
Ghee boiled with the decoction and paste of guḍūcī along with milk destroys vāta and blood disorders, and conquers even difficult-to-cure leprosy (kuṣṭha).
Ghee cooked with four times its weight of the juice of śatāvarī, an equal amount of milk, and a paste of śatāvarī as an internal ingredient, destroys vātaśoṇita (gout/rheumatism).
Amṛtā, madhuka, drākṣā, triphalā, nāgara, and balā—
Vāsā, āragvadha, vṛścīra, devadāru, trikaṇṭaka, kaṭukā, asavarī, kṛṣṇā, and the fruits of kāśmarya;
along with rāsnā, kṣuraka, gandharva, vṛddhadāra, ghana, and utpala.
Having prepared these equal parts of the pastes, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee, adding an equal amount of *dhātrī* juice and three times as much water;
once it is known to be properly prepared, it is recommended for both food and drink. (24–25)
Vata, associated with many doshas and combined with blood, whether superficial or deep-seated, causes pain in the sacrum, calves, thighs, and knees;
it also occurs in kroṣṭuśīrṣa, mahāśūla, and the most dreadful āmavāta.
It quickly destroys the extremely difficult-to-overcome pain of one afflicted by wind-disease (vāta),
as well as dysuria, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), urinary disorders (prameha), and irregular fever—
all those arising from wind, bile, and phlegm.
This most excellent and unsurpassed ghee, prepared by the two Aśvins, increases complexion, longevity, and strength when used at all times. [29] 7.
Oil, four times the quantity of milk, [prepared] with the decoction and paste of balā...
This preparation, cooked ten times, conquers wind-blood disorders (vātāsṛj) and the combination of wind and bile (vātapitta).
It is auspicious, promotes virility, increases the semen of men, cures disorders of the seminal fluid and the female reproductive tract, and alleviates wind-related ailments.
Oil prepared with a decoction of *guḍūcī* and milk, or with lac juice,
or with the juices of *madhuka* and *kāśmarya*, cures *vātarakta*.
Oil processed with a decoction of *padmaka*, *uśīra*, *yaṣṭimadhu*, and *rajanī* [is likewise effective].
This oil, prepared with the pastes of *sarja*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *vīrā*, *kākoli*, *candana*, *khujjaka*, and *padmaka*, removes the disorders of *vāta* and *asṛj*.
One should cook one *tulā* of purified *nāgabalā*.
Having drained it, one should add one āḍhaka of oil here, mixed with an equal amount of goat’s milk, but not the paste of yaṣṭīmadhuka. || 34 ||
One should cook five palas each of these separately; once well-cooked,
this [medicinal oil] pacifies even aggravated vātarakta after seven nights of its administration via enema (basti).
When drunk, it renders one free from disease within ten days.
(35) For substances measured by the *tulā*, one *droṇa* of water is prescribed; for a *droṇa* of substance, one *tulā* of water is considered the standard.
(36) [One should take] equal parts of beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*), *mañjiṣṭhā*, resin (*sarjarasa*), and *sārivā*.
Pinda-taila, when used for massage, removes the pain of vatarakta (gout/vasculitis).
Oil cooked with śārivā, sarja, mañjiṣṭhā, yaṣṭīmadhu, and beeswax, along with milk— either with or without mañjiṣṭhā— cures vatarakta of the thighs.
Having cast a *prastha* of guggulu resin, which has a color resembling the eyes and belly of a choice buffalo, into a mass of water;
And one should carefully administer thirty-two palas of chinnaruhā, along with triphalā in the prescribed quantity. || 39 ||
One should cook it with care,
stirring it repeatedly with a ladle until half the water has evaporated.
Having removed what has arisen from contact with fire and strained it with a cloth, one should place it back into the vessel once again. 41
When that [mixture] had become thick,
he placed half a pala of triphalā powder upon a slab of ice.
The powder of the three pungents (trikaṭu) is six akṣas in measure;
half a pala of the powder of krimiripu (viḍaṅga), and one karṣa each of trivṛt and dantī.
Having given one pala of guḍūcī and having carefully infused it,
one should then take it with a suitable after-drink (anupāna).
One who follows a diet and lifestyle according to one's desire should always consume this medicinal broth with fragrant water. 44.
This well-known, thoroughly dried [medicinal preparation] conquers vāta and blood disorders arising from a single cause, those born of a combination of two, and even those that have been chronic.
As well as eruptions and diseases extending below the knees;
ulcers, cough, leprosy, abdominal tumors, swellings, dropsy, scrotal enlargement, and urinary disorders.
When consumed constantly, it quickly destroys weak digestion, constipation, and the carbuncles of urinary disorders (prameha). || 46 ||
Overcoming all diseases by the power of time, it destroys them and returns the form of youthfulness, transcending the defects of old age. || 47 ||
For each [of the three fruits], one *prastha* of *triphalā* and six *āḍhakas* of water [are used];
the cooking of *guggulu* is like that of jaggery (*guḍa*), but it should especially be fragrant.
[Alternatively,] one *prastha* of *guḍūcī* and half a *prastha* of *guggulu* [may be used].
One should specify that same quantity for each of the three fruits (triphalā).
Having crushed everything together, one should cook it in water until a quarter remains; having strained it, one should place it back upon the fire.
One should cook the decoction until it reaches a thick consistency;
then, having strained it, one should take half a pala of each of the following: dantī, vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, guḍūcī, pippalī, and tvak. (51)
One should prepare one karṣa of trivṛt entirely in one place.
Once it is well-cooked, the wise person should add it while it is still lukewarm;
then, having ascertained the patient's digestive strength, one should administer the appropriate dose.
It cures vātarakta, as well as leprosy (kuṣṭha), hemorrhoids, loss of digestive fire, malignant ulcers, urinary disorders (prameha), rheumatism with fever (sāmavāta),
fistula-in-ano, sinus tracts, and all types of swelling caused by wind (vāta).
Indeed, the guggulu known as Amṛta was created by the Aśvins in the past;
here, half a prastha each of the three myrobalans (triphalā) is taken,
along with two prasthas of amṛtā and one prastha of guggulu.
One *prastha* each of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and one *prastha* of *varṣābhū*—
having crushed all of this together, one should boil it in salt water until it is reduced to a quarter and reaches a thick consistency.

Take half a pala each of the roots of *dantī* and *citraka*, *kaṇā*, *viśva*, the three fruits (*phala-trika*), *guḍūcī*, bark, and *viḍaṅga*; and one *karṣa* of *trivṛt*. One should grind all these together into a powder.
Once it has been prepared and has become warm, one should add *amṛtā* and *guggulu* to it.
One who suffers from *amlapitta* should especially eat this according to the strength of his digestive fire;
it likewise cures *vātarakta*, skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), hemorrhoids, and loss of appetite.

This Guggulu, known as Amṛta, was fashioned by the two Aśvins in ancient times; it destroys malignant ulcers, urinary disorders (prameha), rheumatism with fever (sāmavāta), fistula-in-ano, sinus tracts, and edema caused by vāta, as well as all diseases.
One should have ten *pala* each of these— *śatāvarī*, *nāgabalā*, *vṛddhadāraka*,
*mūrcchā*, *punarnavā*, *amṛtā*, *kṛṣṇā*, *vājigandhā*, and *trikaṇṭaka*—
ground into a fine powder.
The wise man should thoroughly knead that powder mixed with half as much sugar;
then, having stirred it together with half an āḍhaka of honey and one prastha of ghee, he should place it in a very sturdy vessel along with three palas of the "three aromatics" (trisugandhi).
A person should eat that, which is most desired, according to their digestive strength;
it cures vātarakta, consumption, leprosy, emaciation arising from pitta and blood, as well as other diseases originating from vāta, pitta, and kapha of a similar nature. (65)
Having destroyed [the impurities], it makes a man free from wrinkles and grey hair;
this is called the nectar of the essence of yoga, which increases fortune and splendor.
One should likewise avoid sleeping during the day, exposure to fire, physical exertion, and sexual intercourse.
One should avoid pungent, hot, heavy, obstructive, salty, and sour substances.
(67) Chapter 24:
That which effects the depletion of phlegm (*śleṣman*) and does not provoke the wind (*māruta*).
All of that should always be employed as the remedy for ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs).
For this condition, oleation therapy is not to be administered, nor is enema or purgation; rather, every dry (rukṣa) procedure should be performed, beginning first with measures that destroy kapha.
Thereafter, for the destruction of Vāta, the entire course of treatment should be performed;
in cases of Ūrustambha, one should drink Śilājatu, Guggulu, Pippalī, or Nāgara with urine or with the decoction of Daśamūla. (3)
Bhallātaka, amṛtā, śuṇṭhī, dāru, pathyā, and punarnavā,
combined with the two types of pañcamūla, destroy ūrustambha; or else, a decoction of pippalī, pippalīmūla, and bhallātaka alone [is effective].
Alternatively, a paste (kalka) mixed with honey should be administered to destroy ūrustambha; one should lick a compound of triphalā, cavya, kaṭuka, and granthika with honey.
For the destruction of ūrustambha, one may drink purāṇa-ghee with urine.
Or one should lick the powder of triphalā mixed with kaṭukā and honey;
or a man should drink the ṣaḍdharaṇa powder with lukewarm water;
or he may take the pippalī-vardhamāna preparation with honey or with jaggery.
In cases of ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs), they recommend either Gaṇḍīrāriṣṭa or a preparation of Cavya,
Abhayā, Agni, and Dāru along with honey for the retention of urine. One should also apply a paste made of Karañja fruits and mustard seeds mixed abundantly with urine.
The physician should apply a firm massage combined with honey, mustard seeds, and earth from an anthill, along with an ointment, for the treatment of ūrustambha; furthermore,
he should engage the patient in physical exercises as far as possible in order to diminish the kapha.
One should step over the medicinal paste on dry ground and cross rivers against the current using two leaves; this preparation of eight parts of *pippalī* root and ginger,
along with one *prastha* of oil and an equal amount of curd, cures sciatica and stiffness of the thighs (*gṛdhrasī-ūrugraha*).
In this "eight-fold" oil preparation, mustard oil is prescribed.
One should cook mustard oil with kuṣṭha, śrīveṣṭaka, udīcya, sarala, devadāru, keśara, ajagandhā, and aśvagandhā.

Therefore, one afflicted by ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs) should drink, in the proper dose, the beneficial *saindhavādya* oil mixed with honey; likewise, *varṣābhva*, *amṛta*, and *guggulu* [are beneficial].
(Chapter 25, Verse 15)
Fasting, sudation, bitter and pungent substances that stimulate digestion,

purgation, the drinking of fats, and enemas are indicated for Āmamāruta (wind associated with undigested matter). After administering an oil enema with Saindhava and other salts, an alkaline enema (kṣārabasti) is recommended.
In cases of *āmavāta*, food and drink prepared with *pañcakola* are desired.
Likewise, dry sudation (*rukṣasveda*) should be administered using sand-pouches. [The following herbs are used:
*śaṭī*, *śuṇṭhī*, *abhayā*, *ugrā*, *devāhvā*, *ativiṣā*, and *amṛtā*.
For one suffering from āmavāta, a decoction that is parching and digestive, along with a diet of dry food,
and a paste of *śaṭī* and *viśvauṣadhi* combined with a decoction of *varṣābhū*,
should be drunk for seven nights by the person to digest the *āma* of the vāta.
A decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), amṛtā, eraṇḍa, rāsnā, nāgara, and dāru, taken with castor oil (rubūkataila), destroys heavy vāta associated with āma.
Alternatively, one should drink it with a decoction of the ten roots or with water boiled with nāgara.
In cases of pain in the abdomen, bladder, and waist, one should use oil derived from the castor plant (eraṇḍa).

One should drink [a decoction of] rāsnā, guḍūcī, eraṇḍa, devadāru, and mahauṣadha in cases of generalized vāta, as well as when it is associated with āma and has reached the joints, bones, and marrow.
One should drink a decoction of rāsnā, amṛtā, āragvadha, devadāru,
trikaṇṭaka, eraṇḍa, and punarnavā,
mixed with the powder of nāgara.
For one suffering from pain in the calves, thighs, back,
sacrum, and sides, a decoction of ginger and gokṣura, consumed every morning, acts as a digestive stimulant and destroys the pain in cases of sāma-vāta and lumbago.
In cases of āmavāta, one should drink the decoction of daśamūla combined with pippalī,
or eat abhayā and viśva, or guḍūcī with nāgara;
or a person should properly consume harītakī mixed with castor oil according to the prescribed method.

One afflicted by the pain of undigested matter (āmānila) and constantly tormented by the enlargement of the spleen (gṛdhrasī-vṛddhi) should always drink one karṣa of powdered ginger with sour gruel (kāñjika).
This is the supreme remedy for pacifying āmavāta and removing kapha and vāta.
One should drink the powder of the five pungents (pañcakola) with warm water; it destroys weak digestion, colic, abdominal tumors (gulma), anemia, phlegm disorders, and loss of appetite.
Powder made from amṛtā, nāgara, gokṣura, muṇḍitikā, and varuṇaka [is likewise effective].
This preparation, drunk with whey and *āraṇāla*, is renowned for destroying undigested matter (*āma*) and wind disorders (*anila*).
[14] Two parts of *māṇimantha* and likewise two parts of *yamānī*, three parts of *ajamodā*, and five parts of *nāgara*. [15]
Twelve auspicious *harītakī* fruits, finely powdered, when drunk with whey (*mastu*), *āranāla*, buttermilk (*takra*), clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*),
or warm water, conquer *āmavāta*, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and diseases of the heart and bladder.
It destroys the spleen, colic and other ailments, abdominal distension, and hemorrhoids; it also removes constipation and diseases of the stomach as well as those of the hands and feet.
This powder, known as Vaiśvānara, is said to facilitate the downward movement of the bodily winds (vāta). || 17-18 ||
One should prepare fine powders of ālambuṣā, gokṣuraka, guḍūcī, vṛddhadāraka, pippalī, trivṛtā, musta, varuṇa,
punarnavā, triphalā, and nāgara.

Curds, fermented rice-water (āranāla), buttermilk, milk, or meat broth quickly destroys Āmavāta and swelling located in the joints. Equal parts of Śatapuṣpā, Viḍaṅga, Saindhava salt, and Marica [should be used].
This powder, when drunk with warm water, is an excellent stimulant for the digestive fire. 21.

This powder—consisting of asafoetida, chavya, viḍa salt, ginger, black cumin, and white lotus seeds, each subsequent ingredient being one part more than the preceding—is a cure for wind-born colic when drunk. 22.
Citraka, the root of pippalī, yamānī, kāravī, as well as viḍaṅga, ajamodā, jīraka, and suradāru;
cavya, elā, saindhava, kuṣṭha, rāsnā, gokṣura, and dhānyaka.
One should prepare a fine powder of triphalā, mustaka, vyoṣa, tvak, uśīra, yavāgraja, tālīsapatra, and patra; then,
one should take an amount of guggulu equal to the total weight of these powders.
Having thoroughly mixed it with clarified butter, one should store it in a well-oiled vessel;
then, one may administer the appropriate dose even while following one's usual diet.
This formulation, known as Yogarāja, is like nectar itself.
It destroys disorders such as āmavāta and adhyavāta, as well as worms, malignant ulcers, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, abdominal distension, flatulence, and hemorrhoids;
it kindles the digestive fire and likewise increases vitality and strength.
This conquers even those diseases of the limbs that have reached the joints and the marrow.
Three palas of well-ground powder of triphalā decoction, one pala of saugandhika, and likewise one pala of kauśika [should be taken]. 29.
Taking one *kuḍava* of each of these and all the *citrataila*, a physician skilled in the art of cooking should carefully cook it in a sturdy vessel made of iron.
It destroys wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*), as well as lameness and paraplegia.
It destroys breathlessness that is very difficult to conquer, as well as the five types of cough;
it overcomes skin diseases, gout, abdominal tumors, colic, and enlargement of the abdomen, and it conquers rheumatism (āmavāta) even when neglected by physicians.
By the practice of this yoga, the destruction of old age and graying hair occurs; one should eat śāli rice with ghee, oil, and meat broth.
This is known as "Lion's Roar" (Siṃhanāda), which destroys the pride of the elephants of disease.
This, spoken by Daṇḍapāṇi, increases the digestive fire in men.
[One should take] Alambuṣā, Gokṣuraka, Triphalā, Nāgara, and Amṛtā,
with each subsequent ingredient increasing by one part, and Śyāmā powder in an amount equal to all of them combined.

One should drink it with wine, sour gruel, *kāñjika*, or warm water; when drunk, it conquers *āmavāta* along with swelling and *vātaśoṇita*, as well as [disorders] located in the three types of joints—namely the knees and thighs—and it destroys fever and loss of appetite. (36)
One following the regimen for old age should drink a portion each of *pathyā*, *akṣa*, *dhātrī*, and *triphalā*;
or else, one should drink the powder of equal parts of *pathyā*, *viśvā*, and *yamānī* with buttermilk, warm water, or sour gruel (*kāñjika*). || 37 ||
It quickly destroys āmavāta, swelling, and even weak digestion.
[The powder of] ajamodā, marica, pippalī, viḍaṅga, suradāru, citraka, and śatāhvā—
Saindhava salt and the root of pippalī should each be one pala; the nine parts [of the other ingredients] should be one pala each, and ginger should be ten palas.
One should prepare a powder by combining all these ingredients together: five palas each of the aforementioned items, and five palas of harītakī (pathyā). || 40 ||
For one who eats equal parts of jaggery and *vaṭaka* pills,

All diseases are indeed very severe:
viśvacikā, pratitūnī, tūnī, hṛdroga, and the terrible gṛdhrasī.
There is also a bursting sensation in the waist, bladder, and anus, as well as intense pain in the bones and shanks,
and swelling in the joints of the limbs.
And whatever other diseases have arisen from āmavāta,
they all go to destruction like darkness destroyed by the rays of the sun. || 43 ||
One should cook one prastha of ghee with the decoction and paste of nāgaraka, using either four times that amount of the same liquid or plain water alone.
This is supreme for pacifying vāta and kapha and for stimulating the digestive fire.
This is called Nāgara-ghṛta; it destroys pain in the waist and hips.
With the decoction and paste of Amṛtā and Mahauṣadha, one prastha of ghee should be cooked over a gentle fire; this is the supreme remedy for vātarakta (gout).

When administered, it quickly destroys disorders such as āmavāta and adhyavāta, as well as worm-infested ulcers, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors (gulma), and colic (śūla). [It consists of] hiṅgu, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), cavya, and likewise māṇimantha.

Having made pastes (kalka) of [the herbs] weighing one pala each, one should cook one prastha of ghee with one āḍhaka of Āranāla; that clarified butter cures abdominal enlargement, colic, constipation,
flatulence, āmavāta, and stiffness of the waist.

It destroys disorders of the *grahaṇī* and is a supreme stimulant for weak digestion. For the sake of nourishment, it should be prepared with milk; for the sake of stimulating the digestive fire, it is prescribed by the wise when prepared with a collection of burnt feces and urine, or with whey (*mastu*).

Clarified butter prepared with a paste of *nāgara* (ginger) and four times its quantity of *sauvīraka* (sour gruel) is excellent for stimulating the digestive fire and is a supreme remedy for *āmavāta*.
[51] One hundred *pala* of garlic and one *kuḍava* of sesame likewise...

as well as śatapuṣpā, kuṣṭha, the root of pippalī, citraka, ajamodā, yamānī, and coriander.

having added a *mānikā* of oil and half a *prastha* of fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*).
One should consume a karṣa measure [of the powder] and drink water or wine afterwards. This is for cases of āmavāta and vāta located in the whole body or a single limb,

It is recommended for those suffering from colic caused by the breaking of wind associated with insanity. 56.
One *prastha* of jaggery and garlic cooked in one *āḍhaka* of a decoction of *prasāraṇī*, with a quarter-part (*pāda*) of the powder of the five pungents (*pañcoṣaṇa*), destroys *āmavāta*. 57.
Into a jar, one should place one hundred measures of well-fermented *bahulā* liquor; then, add fifty measures of purified and finely minced garlic (*rasona*),
along with long pepper (*pippalī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), cumin (*ajājī*), costus (*kuṣṭha*), and leadwort (*citraka*).
One akṣa each of powdered nāgara, marica,
and cavya should be drunk after seven days; it destroys wind diseases,
worms, skin diseases, consumption, abdominal distension, gulma, hemorrhoids, and splenic disorders.
It stimulates the digestive fire and destroys jaundice.
(60) One prastha of well-washed, dehusked white mustard seeds should be placed in water along with one prastha of rice-scum (maṇḍa) and left for three days. (61)
Then, having powdered one *pala* each of *alambuṣā*, *gokṣuraka*, *śatapuṣpī*, *punarnavā*, *prasāraṇī*,
the bark of *varuṇa*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *madana*, one should add them to a heap of grain.
Having recognized that it is properly cooked, it is prepared by mixing it with rice;
seasoned with mustard oil and combined with asafoetida and rock salt,
when eaten with salt, it conquers severe fever caused by undigested matter (*āmaja*).

This peyā, which cures udāvarta and promotes strength, complexion, and digestive fire, is effective against wind disorders arising from a single cause, from two combined causes, from curable combinations, or from all three combined (sānnipātika), as well as those affecting the waist, thighs, knees, and the sacrum, and those characterized by flatulence. || 65 ||
19. Those [roots] such as kula and others, which are fresh, devoid of bark and so forth, and completely dried, should be reduced to a fine powder.
In winter, three hundred palas [of this oil];
with one hundred [palas] of pungent oil (kaṭutaila) mixed with vyoṣa, rāmaṭha, dhānyaka, krimighna, dīpyaka, niśā, cavikā, granthika, and ārdraka.
With the two types of cumin, vṛścīra, surasa, arjaka, and śigru;
with the ten roots (daśamūla) and ātmaguptā; and with mārkava and the three salts—all these powdered in portions of one pala each and saturated with āraṇāla—[one should proceed].
One should place it in a vessel of oil and then set it upon a heap of grain;
after seven nights have passed, having extracted it, this Sidhmala-ghṛta should be administered through drinks, snacks, and meals, especially in cases of Vāta associated with Āma.
Those afflicted by broken limbs, fever, or other ailments; those who tremble or crawl upon their haunches—
by destroying gout, burning sensations from fire, colic, abdominal tumors, and enlargement of the belly, as well as wrinkles, graying hair, and baldness, they shall possess stainless senses.
One afflicted by *āmavāta* should avoid curd, fish, jaggery, milk, *potakī*, black gram, and flour-based foods, as these are heavy and cause the obstruction of the channels (*abhiṣyandi*).
(72) Chapter 26.
Emesis, fasting, sudation, digestive stimulants, medicinal suppositories, alkalis, powders, and pills are recommended for the alleviation of colic.
For a man afflicted by colic, sudation alone brings comfort.
Milk-porridge, kṛśara, flour-based preparations, or even unctuous heaps of sugar quickly destroy colic caused by Vāta; likewise,
a soup of horse-gram (kulattha) combined with fats does so.
[This soup] contains rock salt, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and mutton, enriched with asafoetida, sauvarcala salt, and pomegranate;
[it is prepared] with balā, punarnavā, eraṇḍa, the two types of bṛhatī, and gokṣura.
Asafoetida and salt, when drunk, immediately alleviate the pain of Vāta.
One suffering from colic (śūla) and intestinal obstruction (vibandha) should drink the powder of asafoetida, ativiṣā, trikaṭu, vacā, sauvarcala salt, and abhayā with warm water.

One suffering from wind-pain (vāta-śūla), abdominal tumors (gulma), or fainting (apatantraka) should drink a mixture of *tumburu*, *abhayā*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), lotus seed (*pauṣkara*), and the three salts with barley-water. Having drunk an equal quantity of the paste of viḍaṅga, kampillaka, and aśvamūtrī combined with wine,
one shall destroy colic of a vāta-nature.
Long pepper, asafoetida, rock salt, alkali, sauvarcala salt, and chebulic myrobalan should be drunk with the scum of wine; these destroy wind-pain (vāta-śūla).
One should drink water boiled with dry ginger and the root of castor plant.
Combined with asafoetida and sauvarcala salt, it provides immediate relief from colic.
A decoction of asafoetida and puṣkaramūla, or asafoetida and sauvarcala salt,
or of viśva, eraṇḍa, and barley, provides immediate relief from colic.
Similarly, a decoction of rubu, yava, and kvātha, combined with hiṅgu and sauvarcala;
or hiṅgu, amla, kṛṣṇā, lavaṇa, yamānī, kṣāra, abhayā, and saindhava, in equal parts.
One should drink this powder mixed with the scum (*maṇḍa*) of *vāruṇī* liquor for the relief of increased pain born of *vāta*.
[This powder is made] from *sauvarcala*, *amlīkā*, *jīraka*, and black pepper, each succeeding ingredient being double the quantity of the preceding one.
A pill made by grinding [these] with the juice of *mātuluṅga* removes wind-pain (*vāta-śūla*).
A pill prepared from *hiṅgu*, *amlavetasa*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*),
*yamānī*, and the three salts, combined with the juice of *bījapūra*, likewise removes wind-pain.
One should cause [the patient] to drink one karṣa of the root of *bījapūraka* together with ghee; this conquers colic born of wind (*vāta*).
Having ground the root of *bilva*, sesame, and *eraṇḍa* with sour water and the wash-water of parched grain...
One should rotate a warm pill to destroy the pain of Vata.
Having made a pill with sesame seeds, one should rotate it over the abdomen;
this pill pacifies even the most unbearable colic.
One may conquer colic by applying a plaster of *madana* mixed with sour gruel (*kāñjika*),
or by a paste of *jīvantī* root combined with oil, which relieves pain in the flanks.
[17] Molasses, *śāli* rice, barley, milk, and the drinking of clarified butter act as purgatives.
The meat of wild animals is a medicine for those suffering from bile-induced colic (pitta-śūla).
For bile-induced colic, emesis should be induced with milk, as well as with the juices of sugarcane, paṭola, and nimba.
Cold water immersions, riverbanks with breezes, and vessels made of bell-metal and other metals submerged in water— these,
along with purgatives that remove pitta, are recommended.
The juices of the hare and the quail are recommended, as is nourishing food prepared with parched grain and honey;
these applications should be very cold and mixed with honey. (20)
In cases of vomiting, fever born of pitta,
severe colic, burning sensations, and excessive thirst, one should take a gruel of barley mixed with honey.
A person seeking comfort should drink very cold [water].
One should drink the juice of dhātrī or vidārī, or the water from a cow’s udder (goṣṭhanambu) with sugar; this immediately destroys pitta-type colic.

A person should drink the juice of śatāvarī mixed with honey in the morning for the alleviation of burning sensations and colic, as it removes all diseases caused by pitta. [23] Bṛhatī, the two types of bṛhatī, gokṣura, eraṇḍa, kuśa, kāśa, ikṣu, and ālikā—
Yellow [medicines] would instantly destroy even the most severe colic arising from bile (pitta).
One should drink water boiled with śatāvarī, yaṣṭyāhva, vāṭyāla, kuśa, and gokṣura, cooled, and mixed with jaggery, honey, and sugar.
One should cause [the patient] to drink [this] decoction prepared with triphalā, nimba, yaṣṭīmadhu, kaṭukā, and āragvadha, mixed with honey, to alleviate burning sensations and colic,
and to immediately remove fever accompanied by a burning sensation. (26)
Alternatively, castor oil produced from the *eraṇḍa* plant, combined with a decoction of *madhuka*,
destroys colic arising from *pitta* as well as *pitta*-derived *gulma*.
Likewise, a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and *āragvadha*, mixed with honey and sugar, [achieves the same].
One should administer [this] which destroys *rakta-pitta* and relieves burning sensations and pain;
one should lick the powder of *dhātrī* with honey, which destroys *pitta*-type colic.
When *kapha* is predominant, emetics and fasting are indicated.
One should employ head-purgatives (śirovireka), the drinking of honey-liquor (madhuśīdhu), honey, wheat, barley, and fermented liquors (ariṣṭa), as well as all dry and pungent substances. (30)

A gruel prepared with water from long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), chaba pepper (cavya), leadwort (citraka), and dry ginger (nāgara) serves as a digestive stimulant and a destroyer of colic.
Pañcakola, combined with the three salts and asafoetida (rāmaṭha), [is likewise beneficial].
Drunk with lukewarm water, it destroys phlegm and colic.
Furthermore, the root of *vilva*, *eraṇḍa*, *citraka*, and *viśvabheṣaja* (ginger),
combined with asafoetida and rock salt, immediately wards off colic.
One should drink Musta, Vacā, Tiktakarohiṇī,
Abhayā, and Nirdahanī in equal parts,
combined with cow’s urine, for the cure of diseases arising from Kapha.
Likewise, for the purpose of digesting the *āmadoṣa* in colic, one should drink a powder of *vacā*, *mustā*, *citraka*, *abhayā*, and *tiktā* combined with cow’s urine;
or one should drink a decoction of the *bilvādi* group mixed with alkali (*kṣāra*) to alleviate *kapha*-type colic. || 34–35 ||

Either the juice of *mātuluṅga* or another decoction of *śigru*, taken with alkali and honey, removes pain in the sides, the heart, and the bladder. In the case of *āma-śūla*, treatment that destroys *kapha*-related pain should be administered.

One should drink in the morning, with lukewarm water, a powder consisting of hiṅgu, tumburu, vyoṣa, yamānī, citraka, abhayā, along with kṣāra and salt; this removes everything that is consumed [undigested] and increases the strength of the digestive fire. || 37-38 ||
Citraka, granthika, eraṇḍa, śuṇṭhī, and dhānyaka boiled with water destroy pain in the feces, urine, and flatus; it is digestive and stimulates the digestive fire.
When combined with hiṅgu, biḍa salt, and pomegranate, it is used for colic, abdominal distension, and constipation. (39)
Dīpyaka, saindhava, pathyā, and nāgara in equal parts— this "four-in-one" (catuḥsama) formulation quickly conquers severe colic and stimulates a weak digestive fire.
One suffering from a condition characterized by both pitta and vāta should drink this with honey along with the drugs of the bṛhatyādi group.
Or one should employ a combined treatment for a colic (śūla) caused by pitta and vāta.
Whatever treatment has been described separately for that born of pitta or that born of kapha,
one should apply those treatments combined together in the case of that born of kapha and pitta.
One should drink a decoction of paṭola, triphalā, and ariṣṭa mixed with honey for the pacification of fever caused by pitta and kapha, as well as vomiting, burning sensations, and colic.
One who desires relief should drink garlic mixed with honey upon waking in the morning.
This [decoction], which kindles the digestive fire, destroys colic born of vāta and kapha;
it is prepared with the water of viśvā, urubūka, daśamūla, and yava, along with the two alkalis (dvikṣāra), hiṅgu, the three salts (lavaṇatraya), and puṣkara.

One suffering from stiffness of the heart, flanks, and waist; from pain in the stomach, colon, and shoulders; and from fever, abdominal tumors (gulma), and colic, should drink this powder with a decoction.
In the case where the powder is drunk with a decoction, the decoction is the primary element.
Therefore, in this case, the four liquids do not proceed with the expectation of powder.
[In conditions] arising from phlegm and wind, one should take equal parts of *rucaka* salt, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and great medicine (*mahauṣadha*)—namely ginger—with water. || 46 || 9 ||
It should be drunk for pain in the heart, sides, back, and abdomen, as well as for cholera; likewise, in cases of constipation due to feces,
it should be taken with barley juice or with ginger-water— thus is the application made by the wise.
Therefore, only a small amount of asafoetida (hiṅgu) is prescribed here.

One should drink a powder consisting of asafoetida, black salt (sauvarcala), yellow myrobalan (pathyā), biḍa salt, rock salt (saindhava), tumburu, and puṣkaramūla, with the decoction of daśamūla and barley.
It is recommended for pain in the sides, heart, waist, back, and shoulders; in tetanus, convulsions, swelling, excessive secretions of phlegm, and ear diseases.
[The paste of] castor, bilva, the two types of bṛhatī, and mātuluṅga—

A decoction prepared from *pāṣāṇabheda*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, and *mūlaka*, mixed with alkali, asafoetida, salt, and *rubū* oil, should be drunk for pains in the hips, thighs, penis, heart, and breasts. || 51 ||
Asafoetida, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), kuṣṭha, alkali of barley (yavakṣāra),
and rock salt— this powder, combined with the juice of mātuluṅga, removes splenic pain.
[The powder] should be burnt without emitting smoke.
Deer-horn taken with cow’s ghee removes pain arising from the heart and the hips, just as fire consumes a heap of wood. (53)
The powder of *krimiripu* (viḍaṅga) licked with the juice of *vaṅgasena* certainly destroys, without delay, the colic arising from indigestion; this is a medicinal electuary (*leha*).
Vidārī and pomegranate juice, combined with the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) and salt, [is likewise effective].
Combined with honey, it quickly conquers colic arising from the three humors (doṣas).
[55] The fruits and roots of eraṇḍa, the two types of bṛhatī, gokṣura, the parṇinīs, sahadevī, siṃhapucchī, and kṣurālikā— [56]
One should drink water boiled with these [drugs] in equal parts and combined with yavakṣāra; this destroys colic arising from individual doṣas as well as that arising from all of them.
Maṇḍūra prepared with cow’s urine and combined with the powder of triphalā [is also effective].
Licked with honey and ghee, it destroys colic born of the three doṣas.
Conch-shell powder mixed with salt, asafoetida, and the trikaṭu (vyoṣa),
when drunk with warm water, destroys colic born of the three doṣas.
The excellent powder of triphalā combined with sharp iron filings should be administered with honey and ghee; it alleviates all types of pain.
[One should also take] pure [iron] processed within cow’s urine and mixed with iron powder.
One should eat abhayā with jaggery today for the pacification of all piercing pains (śūla).
Pippalī, nāgara, bilva, kāravī, cavya, citraka, hiṅgu, dāḍima, vṛkṣāmla, vacā, kṣāra, and amlavetasa [are also used]. 62.
The preparation of *varṣābhū*, black salt, cumin seeds, and citron,

cooked with three parts curd and clarified butter, is known as *dādhika*. It destroys abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, pain in the heart and flanks, and diseases of the female reproductive tract.
The preparation with curd (dādhika) is remembered as the best for pacifying the humors (doṣas).
For one whose body is wrapped in a blanket while performing breath control (prāṇāyāma),
incense made from roasted grain flour (saktu) smeared with pungent oil is the supreme remedy for colic (śūla).
A person suffering from colic should avoid physical exertion, sexual intercourse, alcohol, salt, pungent and bitter vegetables, suppression of natural urges, grief, and anger. (66) Chapter 27.
Emesis with bitter and sweet substances, purgation,
and enemas are also recommended for pain arising from *pariṇāma* (metabolic transformation).
Viḍaṅga seeds, *vyoṣa*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, and *citraka* [are used for this purpose].

Having prepared all these, one should have them made into fine powders. Having formed a bolus with jaggery, one should eat it upon rising in the morning; one should take warm water as an after-drink, which increases the digestive fire.

One who eats a bolus made from the paste of ginger and sesame seeds prepared with milk will conquer colic born of the three doṣas and that arising from the transformation of food (pariṇāma-śūla). 2, 4.
The fierce colic resulting from indigestion caused by *śambūka* disappears instantly within three weeks if the ash of that creature is drunk with warm water.
This destroys colic born of digestive disorders, just as Viṣṇu destroyed the Asuras; one should lick a powder of Abhayā and Kṛṣṇā mixed with honey.
One should eat Śatīla, barley, and parched grain-flour with curd from which the essence has been removed.
A person is soon freed from colic by repeatedly turning over [the medicine].
[One should take] one part each of sesame, dry ginger, and pathyā, and two parts of the ash of snails; having combined these with jaggery, one should form pills (guḍī) weighing one akṣa each.
In the forenoon, one who subsists on milk should eat cold water;
having drunk meat-broth in the evening, a man shall be freed from difficult-to-conquer ailments arising from indigestion and even from chronic colic.
Having made pills of equal parts of śambūka, tryūṣaṇa, and the five salts,
one should consume them with the juice of kalambū at dawn or at the time of breakfast, according to one's strength.
A person who drinks barley meal alone with lentil broth for seven nights is suddenly liberated from colic born of the digestive transformation process.
This conquers chronic pain of transformation, let alone that which is newly arisen—
iron powder combined with *varā*, licked with honey and clarified butter. (13)
One should pacify *pariṇāma-śūla* by administering its specific impurity,
or one should consume the powder of *kṛṣṇā*, *abhayā*, and iron along with jaggery. This destroys *pakti-śūla*, abdominal enlargements, and weak digestion.
It also eliminates disorders of *āmavāta* and obesity.
A powder of *pathyā*, iron filings, and *śuṇṭhī*, taken with honey and ghee,
destroys pain arising from the transformation of food (*pariṇāmaruja*), whether it be of the nature of *vāta*, *pitta*, or *kapha*.
Sāmudra salt, saindhava salt, kṣāra, rucaka, raumaka,
viḍa salt, dantī, iron filings, iron dross, trivṛt, and śūraṇaka— these taken in equal parts and cooked over a gentle fire with curd, cow’s urine, and milk, [form a medicinal preparation].
For example, one should drink Agnibala powder with warm water.
After each meal has been digested, one should eat meat and other foods prepared with ghee.
This cures pain in the navel, pain in the liver, and that which is caused by abdominal tumors (gulma) or the spleen (plīha).
It destroys abscesses and *aṣṭhīlikā* arising from phlegm and wind; indeed, there is no medicine superior to it for all types of colic,
and it is especially considered the end-maker of that which arises from digestive transformation (*pariṇāma*).
A coconut filled with water and salt,
when properly cooked over a fire, cures colic arising from the process of digestion,
as well as disorders caused by vāta, pitta, kapha, and their combination (sānnipātika). || 21–22 ||
One should lick a powder of madhuka and triphalā mixed with an equal amount of iron filings, combined with honey and ghee; thereafter, one should properly drink cow's milk.
This cures vomiting accompanied by darkness before the eyes, colic, acid bile, fever, and exhaustion.
It destroys constipation, retention of urine, and swelling.
One should cook ghee with long pepper and jaggery in four times the amount of milk;
this cures acid bile (amlapitta) and colic born of digestive transformation (pariṇāma-śūla).
Ghee prepared with the decoction and paste of long peppers (pippalī), when combined with honey and given to one who subsists on milk and rice,
will certainly destroy [the disease].
This is known as *pariṇāma-śūla*, which has become aggravated.
[One should take] equal parts of *kola*, *granthika*, *śṛṅgavera*, *capalā*, and alkali, ground into a powder.
Having boiled iron rust (maṇḍūra) in eight times its quantity of fragrant water until it has become thick, one should eat it at the beginning, middle, and end of meals.
One who generally eats milk and boiled rice may overcome diseases caused by vāta and kapha, as well as colic and various types of pain, upon digestion. || 27 ||
With kola, granthika,
viśvauṣadha, māgadhī, yavakṣāra, and one prastha of ayorajas (iron powder);
Mixed with powdered portions of *palikā*,
and combined with eight times its weight of urine,
one should bring the entire mass to a solid state through gradual heating.
Pills the size of jujube fruits should be consumed at the beginning, middle, and end of a meal;
[these consist of] juice, ghee, broth, and milk. || 29 ||
A man eating with meat prevents the turning away of food and, at the end, cures abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, and loss of digestive fire.
One should cook eight *pala*s of iron dross in half an *āḍhaka* of cow’s urine;
when that is prepared with one *prastha* of milk, it removes digestive colic (*pakti-śūla*) in men.
One should cook eight *pala*s of iron dross in eight times as much cow’s urine.
Having powdered cavikā, nāgara, kṣāra, pippalīmūla, and pippalī—one pala of each—one should add them to that [mixture] once it has reached consistency;
from this, one should prepare pills that alleviate pain caused by digestive disorders (pakti-śūla). || 32–33 ||
One should consume purified iron rust (*maṇḍūra*) or iron filings along with jaggery; one is thereby freed from colic arising from digestive transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Having thoroughly cleansed eight *palas* of iron rust and reduced it to powder, [one should take it with jaggery].
Taking eight *palas* of the juice of *śatāvarī*, as well as four *palas* each of curd, milk,
and cow's clarified butter (*gavya-sarpis*), one should cook them all together until they attain the consistency of a solid mass.
One should consume the prepared *maṇḍūra* in the middle of a meal or even at the beginning;
this formulation undoubtedly destroys colic caused by wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and that arising from indigestion (*pariṇāma*). (37)
Take nine parts each of viḍaṅga, citraka, cavya, triphalā, and the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), equal in measure to the iron dross (lohakiṭṭa).
Having added twice as much cow’s urine and half as much molasses, [cook them together].
Having cooked it slowly with a mild fire until it is well-prepared and has attained the consistency of a bolus,
one should place it in a greased vessel and consume it in the measure of a *kola*.
It should be employed at the beginning, middle, or other times of the meal according to the sequence.
This yogic formulation quickly pacifies even the most severe colic of digestion (pakti-śūla),
as well as jaundice, anemia, edema, weak digestive fire, hemorrhoids, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī-doṣa), worms, abdominal tumors, and abdominal enlargements.
It destroys acid bile (amlapitta) and reduces obesity; one should avoid dried vegetables and those that are burning, sour, or pungent.
Indeed, this preparation known as Guḍī-maṇḍūra is an ender of colic caused by indigestion.
Out of compassion for those afflicted by colic, [this remedy] was proclaimed by Tārā:
having given half a karṣa each of vaśira, śvetavāṭyāla, madhuparṇī, mayūraka, and taṇḍulīya, both below and above [the patient].

Well-digested *maṇḍūra* (iron rust) that is fit for cooking should be kept in cow's urine for two days, then burnt while containing internal steam; having been thus processed, it should be kept for three more days.
Then, having powdered it, it should be thoroughly mixed with twice its amount of jaggery (*guḍa*).
At the beginning, middle, and end of a meal, one should consume one-third of a karṣa of this powder as food.
Buttermilk should be used as a post-drink, and sour tree-fruits should be avoided here;
yet for those with sour-bile (āmlapitta) and colic (śūla), this is as beneficial as nectar.
Take two palas of powdered pathyā,
one pala each of gandhakasāra and purified iron filings, and half a pala of purified mercury.
Having added one *prastha* each of the juice of *bhṛṅga* and *keśarāja*,
one should then rub it with a rod in an iron vessel.
The dried [substance], mixed with ghee and honey and kneaded, should be placed in a smooth vessel;
this, when used, will soon—
It destroys diseases born of phlegm and bile, as well as colic, acid dyspepsia, malabsorption syndrome, and even severe jaundice. || 51 ||
If one consumes well-refined iron powder cooked with the fresh juices of *akṣa*, *āmalaka*, and *śivā*, along with jaggery;
It immediately relieves colic born of the three humors (tridoṣa).
[Verse 52] One part of iron powder, three parts of triphalā, eight parts of jaggery, and four times as much urine as the jaggery [should be combined]. [Verse 53]

One who is skilled in the method of preparing jaggery should cook all of this together and consume it according to one's capacity, in cases of wasting, colic, and disorders arising from indigestion. [Eight parts of] āmalakī powder... 18... *Note: The text fragment "18dhātrīcūrṇasyāṣṭau" appears to be a numbering marker followed by the beginning of a subsequent instruction regarding eight parts of āmalakī powder.*
One should take four palas of iron powder and two palas of the powder of yaṣṭīmadhuka, rubbed together with a stone.
This powder should be saturated with a decoction of *amṛtā* for seven days and dried in the fierce heat of the sun.
Having ground it again, it should be placed in a new jar;
having consumed it mixed with ghee and honey, first, in the middle, and likewise at the end.
Even if one eats wholesome food three times, it destroys the appetite at the beginning of the meal due to the persistence of the humors (doṣas). || 57 ||
It instantly overcomes diseases arising from bile and wind, as well as indigestion caused by food in men; moreover, the food does not burn within. (58)
Practiced at the end of a meal, it overcomes diseases caused by food and drink;
likewise, it aids in the digestion of the food.
It destroys even the most severe colic of men; and this formulation, when properly administered, also suddenly removes chronic bile disorders.
It is beneficial for the eyes, removes gray hair,
and conquers diseases arising from phlegm and bile; it also clarifies the blood.
It overcomes paleness and jaundice.
19. Thin iron leaves, made equal in thickness to a sesame seed, having been smeared with a paste of *kaśikā* root or with mustard, [are heated].
Having dried it with the rays of the sun, one should apply a fresh coating once again.
It should be heated repeatedly in water of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and then ground into a powder and strained through a cloth.

One should consume this according to the application, with honey and ghee, in a dose of one māṣaka, or three times that, or even four times that, in accordance with the strength of the digestive fire;
if goat's milk is unavailable, one should use it as a post-consumption drink (anupāna).
This "iron-nectar" (lohāmṛta), prepared with sixty-four times the amount of cow's ghee and milk,
certainly destroys colic of digestion within one month;
it is the most excellent, having been created by Brahmā in ancient times.
Whatever is preceded by the letter 'ka', whatever is proclaimed to be sour, and meat originating from marshy regions— these should not be consumed here.
Half a *tulā* of well-steamed and pressed *kūṣmāṇḍa* should be seasoned with clarified butter.
One should cook an amount of sugar equal to half a *prastha* in the juice of *āmalaka*.

Then, while stirring with a ladle, one should add it to a *prastha* of well-boiled *kūṣmāṇḍa* juice; once that has reached the proper consistency, one should grind [the other ingredients] into a powder and throw them in.

Two palas each of *kaṇā*, *ajājī*, and *śuṇṭhī*, one pala of *marica*, and one karṣa each of *tālīsa*, *dhanyāka*, the four spices (*cāturjātaka*), and *mustaka*; along with half a prastha of honey. || 70 ||
This destroys colic pain arising from the three humors (doṣas),
as well as vomiting, nausea, jaundice, fainting, dyspnea, cough,
loss of appetite, heartburn, internal hemorrhaging, and back pain.
This is the most excellent elixir known as Khaṇḍāmalaka. In this preparation, one kuḍava of well-ground coconut should be cooked with one pala of ghee and an equal amount of sugar.

Having cooked this very [mixture] in its own juice until it reaches the measure of one *prastha*, and once it has become well-cooled like molasses (*guḍa*), one should then add portions of *dhanyāka*,
*pippalī*, *payoda* (musta), *tugākṣīrī*, and *jīraka*.

Having finely powdered the three spices along with ginger and keśara, this [preparation] destroys acidity, bile disorders, loss of appetite, consumption, internal hemorrhaging, colic, and vomiting; it is captivating and provides full manly vigor. (74)

Two parts of *kalāya* powder and one part of iron powder should be thoroughly rubbed together with the juice of *kāravella* and *palāśa*. Then, a person should consume a single pill weighing one *karṣa*.
Taken with a decoction of *maṇḍa*, it destroys even severe chronic bile (*jaratpitta*). Alternatively, one should lick the powder of the three myrobalans (*traiphala*) combined with iron powder;
or, for that disease, one should lick it mixed with the powder of *yaṣṭīmadhu* along with honey.
Having performed emesis until the end of pitta and purgation until the end of kapha, one should administer the liquid food regimen prescribed for aging pitta;
once the stomach and the large intestine are purified, the liquid food will reach a state of equilibrium.

Māṣeṇḍarī, steamed with husks and mixed with ghee, is beneficial. In that case, wheat cakes combined with ghee and jaggery, or [wheat] kneaded with cold milk and sugar, are considered beneficial. (79–80)
Or one may take lukewarm rice-scum (śālitaṇḍulamaṇḍa) free from grains,
or *vāṭya* prepared with milk, filled with ghee and mixed with sugar;
or, having eaten sugar, one should drink boiled milk.
One should eat powdered chickpeas with a soup made from *paṭola* leaves.
Since the digestive fire becomes weak when bile is aged within the liquid food,
one should therefore prepare the food and drinks in small quantities.
Chapter 28:
Barley-based food prepared with the juices of *trivṛt*, sudhā leaves, sesame, and other vegetables, as well as those from domestic, aquatic, and marshy animals.
Furthermore, one who has consumed refined oils, urine, and feces, and drinks clear wine (prasannā), molasses (guḍa), and rum (sīdhu), [is prepared for treatment].
For a disorder born of Vāta, an asthāpana enema is recommended after the patient has been lubricated and fomented.
In the case of a fecal obstruction (purīṣaja), the procedure for intestinal distension (ānāhika) should be performed;
there, the physician should administer alkaline and vaitaraṇa enemas.
[The drugs used are: śyāmā, dantī, dravantī, tvak, mahāśyāmā, snuhī, and trivṛt.
Saptalā, Śaṅkhinī, Śvetā, Rājavṛkṣa along with Tilvaka,
Kampillaka, Karañja, and Hemakṣīrī— this is the group [of drugs]. It [is used] in ghee, oil, powder, decoction, and paste, as well as in any one of these.
It destroys upward-moving wind (udāvarta), abdominal enlargement (udara), flatulence (ānāha), poison,

and abdominal tumors (gulma). Trivṛt, kṛṣṇā, and harītakī taken in two, four, and five parts respectively, made into pills with an equal amount of jaggery, remove diseases caused by the obstruction of feces and flatus.
This powder—consisting of *harītakī*, alkali of barley (*yavakṣāra*), *pīlu* seeds, and likewise *trivṛt*—should be drunk with ghee; it destroys upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*).
[7] As for *hiṅgu*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, *sarja*, and *biḍa*, each subsequent one is double the amount of the preceding.
That powder, when drunk with wine, is an excellent remedy for upward-moving wind (udāvarta).
One pala of sugar, equal amounts of trivṛtā and upakulyā, should be finely ground into a smooth powder.
Before eating, a wise person should lick honey with *biḍālapadaka* salt;
this [is for use] when the stool is hard.
This sweet powder, named Nārācaka, should be administered in cases of pitta associated with kapha; it is fit for kings. || 10 ||
One who desires [relief] should drink garlic mixed with wine in the morning;
it destroys abdominal tumors, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), and colic, and it stimulates digestion and increases strength.
Having cooked asafoetida, honey, and rock salt, one should prepare a well-made suppository.
One should apply [a suppository] smeared with ghee into the rectum; it destroys upward movement of wind (udāvarta).
A medicinal pellet (phalavarti) composed of madana, pippalī, kuṣṭha, vacā, white mustard seeds, jaggery, and alkali is highly recommended.
The wise physician should insert into the inflamed anus radish mixed with house-soot, rock salt, oil, and sour gruel, or crushed *nirguṇḍī* leaves.
In the case of a ruptured anus, one should drink wine enriched with *sauvarcala* salt along with urine.
Or he may drink cardamom with wine, or milk, or water; or likewise the juice of the duḥsparśā plant, or a decoction of the kakubha tree,
or he may drink castor seeds mixed with water and salt.
One should employ milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī) or even grape juice in every way for the treatment of dysuria and urinary calculi.
One should treat upward-moving wind (udāvarta) caused by suppressed yawning with oleation and sudation therapies.
In cases born of tears, one should induce the shedding of tears; in cases born of dreams, wine and pleasant stories [should be used].
In cases born of sneezing, one should induce sneezing by means of a leaf placed in the nose.
Likewise, for disorders above the clavicle, massage, sudation, and medicated smoking with nasal drops [are indicated].

In cases of vomiting arising from upward movement (udgāra), one should administer wholesome, vāta-alleviating food and ghee taken after meals, followed by the systematic application of unctuous medicinal smoke (snaihika-dhūma).
One should overcome vomiting caused by injury according to the specific doṣa involved, using treatments such as nasal drops (nasya) and oleation (sneha).

After eating, induced vomiting, medicated smoking, fasting, bloodletting, dry food and drink, physical exercise, and purgation are recommended here. Milk boiled with four times its quantity of water and containing a decoction that cleanses the bladder is also advised. || 21-22 ||
When the obstruction has been removed, women dear to him should delight the man who has drunk the boiled decoction to his heart's content and whose semen is flowing upwards.
In this case, oil massages, baths, wine, and peacocks are beneficial.
Śāli rice, milk, and decoctions are recommended, as is sexual intercourse.
For the alleviation of hunger, a meal that is unctuous, warm, and small in quantity is beneficial;
for the alleviation of thirst, one should drink a cooling mantha or gruel (yavāgū).
A person exhausted by fatigue and labored breathing should eat with relish once well-rested;
in cases of sleeplessness, one should drink milk, and employ sleep-inducing measures and massages.
In cases of upward-moving wind (udāvarta), constipation (ānāha), and the presence of undigested toxins (āmadoṣa), fasting and digestive treatments should be administered.
Indeed, double the quantity of each of the following— hiṅgu, vacā, kuṣṭha, and suvarcikā— along with powdered viḍaṅga,
taken with warm water, [relieves] the pain of abdominal distension and viṣūcikā.
It cures heart disease, abdominal tumors, and upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta).
[One should take] vacā, abhayā, citraka, yavaśūka, along with pippalī, ativiṣā, and kuṣṭha.
By drinking warm water, one who eats wholesome rice will quickly conquer abdominal distension, delusion, and wind disorders.
One should saturate trivṛt, harītakī, and śyāmā with the milky sap of snuhī.
These pills, when taken with urine, are excellent for breaking up abdominal distension (ānāha).
Furthermore, the fruit and root mentioned for purgation, asafoetida with arka-root, and the superior ten-roots (daśamūla) [are also used].
Snuk, citraka, and punarnavā in equal parts, along with all five salts,
should be crushed together with fats and urine.
One should cook well-ground salt in a well-smeared earthen saucer; when cooked, it is an excellent remedy for abdominal diseases, to be taken with food and drinks. (31)

A suppository (varti) the size of a thumb, prepared by cooking together vāṭha, dhūma, biḍa, vyōṣa, jaggery (guḍa), and cow’s urine, should be inserted into the rectum; it cures constipation and colic.
A suppository [prepared with] trikaṭu and saindhava—
Having cooked mustard seeds, house-smoke, kuṣṭha, and madana fruits in honey or molasses,
one should cause [the woman] to drink it from the size of a thumb. || 33 ||
This suppository, smeared with ghee and inserted slowly into the rectum, cures abdominal distension and upward movement of wind (udāvarta) when its fruit is seen.
It is a pacifier that wards off abdominal tumors (jaṭhara-gulma).
Having ground dried and fresh radish, *varṣābhū*, the five roots (*pañcamūla*), and the fruit of *ārevata*, one should cook ghee with that [mixture]. || 34 ||
When drunk, that [mixture] will undoubtedly pacify udāvarta. [Likewise,
the same applies to] the group beginning with sthira, punarnavā, sampāka, pūtīka, and karañja.
A *prastha* of ghee prepared with two *pala* portions each of these [drugs] in a decoction is effective for obstructed wind (*pratiruddhavāta*).
(36) Chapter 29.
Light food that is digestive-stimulant, unctuous, hot, carminative for the wind (vāta), and nourishing— all such food is beneficial for all those suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma).
After the patient has been treated with oleation, the physician should administer sudation (sveda) for the pacification of the tumor.
Having softened the channels and conquered the aggravated wind,
sudation applied to one who has been oleated removes a Gulma that is obstructed.
A skilled physician should employ the Kumbhī, Piṇḍa, and Iṣṭakā types of sudation.
Warm poultices (śālvaṇa) and the like should be applied, along with footwear;
bloodletting from a vein in the middle of the arm and localized irrigation are recommended, as is sudation to promote the downward movement of doshas, for all types of gulma patients.
Gruels prepared with Vata-alleviating herbs, soups of horse-gram (kulattha), and the meat-broths of wild animals,
along with sugar and the five roots (pañcamūla), are beneficial for those suffering from Gulma as food.
Juice of citron (mātuluṅga), asafoetida (hiṅgu), pomegranate, biḍa salt, and rock salt [are also beneficial].

One should drink half a pala of powdered ginger (nāgara) with one pala of husked sesame (luñcita-tila) and one pala of jaggery (guḍa), along with the scum of wine (surāmaṇḍa) and warm milk; this cures the pain of vāta-gulma.
It destroys vātagulma, udāvarta, and vaginal pain (yoniśūla).
Alternatively, one should drink castor oil mixed with the scum of vāruṇī wine;
or a person suffering from vātagulma should drink that same oil with milk.
One should prepare four palas of clean, dried garlic in eight times its quantity of milk and water; when only the milk remains, one should have the patient drink it.
This cures vātagulma, udāvarta, gṛdhrasī, and irregular fever.
That milk quickly pacifies heart disease, abscesses, and consumption.
When the milk has been prepared in this manner, even a small amount of alkali— either that produced from *sarjikā* and *kuṣṭha*, or that derived from *ketakī*— is added to it.
When drunk with oil, it pacifies gulma arising from wind (vāta).

In vāta-gulma where phlegm (kapha) has increased, emesis and the administration of powders and such are recommended. In the case of pitta-type gulma, a lubricating purgative is indicated; in the case of blood-type gulma, the evacuation of blood is required.
When a pitta-type gulma arises from unctuous and hot factors, purgation is beneficial;
however, when it has arisen from dry and hot factors, ghee is the supreme remedy.
One should treat a patient with pitta-gulma using the Kākolyādi, Mahātiktaka, and Vāsādi groups [of drugs].
After lubricating the patient, one should subsequently administer purgation and then apply the therapy of enemas (basti).
In the case of a pitta-type gulma arising from unctuous and hot factors, one should lick kampilla with honey.
Alternatively, for the purpose of purging, one may drink the juice of grapes mixed with jaggery.

One should recognize that gulma is undergoing suppuration by the presence of burning sensations, pain, agitation of the vāyu, loss of sleep, anorexia, and fever; such a case should be treated with poultices (upanāhana).
Once it has suppurated, the procedures for incision, purification, and healing should be carried out as in the case of an ulcer.
If that disorder should arise spontaneously, whether upward or downward,
one should neglect it for twelve days while protecting against other complications.
However, clarified butter mixed with honey and bitter substances is the supreme remedy for grief.
One karṣa each of rohiṇī, kaṭukā, nimba, madhuka, and the bark of triphalā,
along with one pala each of trāyamāṇā, paṭola, and trivṛt, and two palas of masūra, should be boiled in eight times the amount of water. || 20-21 ||

One should drink four *pala* of ghee, with the remainder being equal to the ghee; when these are mixed together, the bile-born (*paittika*) abdominal tumor (*gulma*) is pacified, as well as fever, thirst, colic, dizziness, fainting, and restlessness. (22)
Those men who have a strong digestive fire, large bodies, and a natural fondness for unctuous substances; those suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma), snakebite, or erysipelas (visarpa)—
they should especially drink the maximum dose of eight palas.

When fasting, scraping therapies, and sudation have been performed and the digestive fire has been well-stimulated, a patient suffering from *kapha*-type gulma should drink ghee mixed with alkaline substances and pungent herbs.
A weak digestive fire, dull pain, and heaviness or stiffness of the abdominal cavity [are the signs].
One whose stool is mixed with mucus and is unattractive has a gulma that resembles vomiting.

When the digestive fire is weak and the wind is obstructed, having ascertained that the internal receptacle (āśaya) contains phlegm, pills, powders, and decoctions should be administered for those suffering from kapha-gulma. (26–27)

The group of alkaline preparations and fermented liquors (ariṣṭas) is also prescribed for burning sensations and dryness; one suffering from a kapha-type gulma should drink water prepared with the five roots (pañcamūla), aged wine, or the juice of vāruṇī at the proper time, or even honey-wine (mādhvīka) once it has been digested.
Or, having smeared [the area] with sesame, castor, linseed, and mustard seeds,
the physician should apply fomentation using iron vessels filled with lukewarm water.
Alternatively, one may use buttermilk mixed with powdered *yamānī* and salted with *biḍa* salt.
One should drink a digestive stimulant that facilitates the downward movement of wind, urine, and feces; when the doshas are combined, the entire course of treatment should likewise be combined.
In a gulma arising from sannipāta (the combination of all three doshas), a regimen that subdues the three doshas is beneficial.
Vacā, biḍa salt, abhayā, śuṇṭhī, hiṅgu, kuṣṭha, agni, and dīpyaka— taken in the sequence of two,
three, six, four, eight, seven, and five parts respectively— their powder, when drunk with wine or other liquids, removes abdominal tumors (gulma), flatulence, and enlargement of the abdomen (udara).
Yamānī, hiṅgu, sindhūttha, kṣāra, sauvarcala, and abhayā destroy colic, hemorrhoids, dyspnea, and cough; they are excellent for stimulating the digestive fire (grahaṇī) and,
when drunk with the scum of wine (surāmaṇḍa), they alleviate abdominal tumors (gulma) and colic.
Hiṅgu, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), pāṭhā, hapuṣā, abhayā, śaṭhī, ajamodā, ajagandhā, tamarind, amlavetasa,
pomegranate, pauṣkara, coriander, cumin, citraka, and vacā.
One should powder together the two types of alkali, the two salts, and cavya.
This powder should be used without hesitation with food and drinks;
it may be taken before a meal, or drunk with wine or warm water.
In cases of pain in the sides, the heart, and the bladder; in abdominal tumors (gulma) caused by vāta and kapha;

in intestinal obstruction (ānāha), dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), and pains in the anus and vagina; in disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī) and hemorrhoids (arśas); and in splenic enlargement, jaundice, and loss of appetite. || 38 ||
In cases of chest congestion, hiccups, dyspnea, cough, and throat obstruction, this powder of *mātuluṅga* should be processed with its own juice;
one should then prepare many pills weighing one karṣa each, or even more than that. (39–40)
Having burned pūtīka leaves, gajacirbhaṭī,
cavya, vahnī, and the three pungents (vyoṣa) arranged on a bed with salt as an underlayer, one should grind them into a powder and administer it mixed with whey (dadhimanda).
In cases of the arising of gulma, abdominal enlargement, edema, and jaundice,
[one should use] asafoetida, puṣkaramūla, tumburu, harītakī, śyāmā, biḍa salt, rock salt, yavakṣāra, and mahauṣadha.
One should cause him to drink this, fried in ghee and mixed with barley decoction; by that, his gulma—along with its pain and its spreading—is broken up.
[Also: Vacā, harītakī, hiṅgu, rock salt, and amlavetasa.
One should drink barley-alkali and *yamānī* with warm water.
For this, within seven nights, breaks up even a mass of abdominal tumors (*gulma*) accompanied by pain and complications, and it also produces an increase in the digestive fire.
Surā liquor, when drunk combined with pippalī, pippalīmūla, citraka, ajājī, and saindhava, quickly destroys even the most difficult-to-cure gulma.
[Likewise, it may be prepared with] nādeyī, kuṭaja, arka, śigru, and bṛhatī—
Snug, bilva, bhallātaka, vyāghrī, kiṃśuka, pāribhadraka, jaṭāmāṃsī,
apāmārga, nīpa, and agni.
Having burnt vāsā, muṣkaka, and pāṭalā along with salt, it should be cooked in water;
this is declared to be [the preparation] with the addition of the hiṅgvādi group as a post-throw.
In cases of gulma, abdominal enlargement, and aśmari (stone-like growths),
[one should use] hiṅgu, ugragandhā, biḍa salt, śuṇṭhī, ajājī, harītakī, puṣkaramūla, and kuṣṭha.
This powder, increased by one part at each stage, is desired for abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, indigestion, and cholera.
[5.48] Triphalā, kāñcanakṣīrī, saptalā, nīlinī, and vacā;

One who is afflicted by all types of gulma, abdominal enlargement, splenic disorders, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, and swelling should drink a powder of trāyantī, hapuṣā, tiktā, trivṛt, saindhava, and pippalī, mixed with urine, warm water, meat broth, or similar liquids. || 49-50 ||
One should collect one *pala* each of *śaṭhī*, *puṣkaramūla*, *dantī*, *citraka*, *āḍhakī*, *śṛṅgavera*, and *vacā*. Furthermore, one should take one *pala* of *trivṛtā* and three [palas] of *hiṅgu*.
Two palas of barley-alkali and two palas of amlavetasa;
one karṣa each of yamānī, ajājī, marica, and dhānyaka; and likewise one-eighth part each of upakuñcikā and ajamodā. || 52–53 ||
The physician should prepare pills with the juice of *mātuluṅga* itself;
one, two, or even three of these should be drunk with warm water, or with sour liquids, wines, soups, clarified butter, or milk. (54)
This pill, spoken by Kāṅkāyana, destroys abdominal tumors (gulma),
pacifies hemorrhoids and heart disease, and eradicates worms;
when combined with cow’s urine, it subdues even long-standing kapha-type gulma.
One should treat a pitta-type gulma with milk, and a vāta-type gulma with sour liquors;
a sānnipātika type should be suppressed with the juices of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and urines.
In the case of a blood-gulma (raktagulma) in women, one should administer camel’s milk.
One should cook ghee with hapuṣā, vyōṣa, pṛthvīkā, cavya, citraka, saindhava, ajājī, pippalīmūla, and dīpyaka,
along with the juices of kola and mūlaka, as well as milk, curd, and pomegranate.

That supreme ghee destroys vāta-gulma (abdominal tumors caused by wind), and it relieves colic, distension, and constipation. It also eliminates disorders of the female reproductive tract, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī-doṣa), dyspnea, cough, anorexia, fever, and pain in the flanks, heart, and bladder. || 59-60 ||
One *picu* (24g) of long pepper, half of that (12g) of pomegranate, two *palas* (96g) of coriander, one *pala* (48g) of ghee, one *karṣa* (12g) of dry ginger, and four times as much milk—
this ghee, when prepared with these, immediately treats *vātagulma*.

Clarified butter prepared with the pastes of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the three myrobalans (triphalā), coriander (dhānya), vidanga, chavya, and chitraka, along with milk, cures pain in the female reproductive organs, headache, hemorrhoids, and irregular fevers; it also destroys Vata-type abdominal tumors (vātagulma).

One should prepare [the decoction] by boiling four *palas* of *trāyamāṇā* in ten times as much water until it is reduced to one-fifth; then, having strained it, one should add one *karṣa* each of the following pastes:
*rohiṇī*, *kaṭukā*, *mustā*, *trāyamāṇā*, and *durālabhā*.
With the pastes of tāmalakī, vīrā, jīvantī, candana, and utpala;
having added eight palas each of the juice of āmalakī, milk, and ghee, one should cook it thoroughly. || 65–66 ||
This excellent ghee destroys pitta-gulma, rakta-gulma, erysipelas (visarpa), pitta-type fever, heart disease, jaundice (kāmalā), and skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
When the measurement is given in terms of palas or lekhās, doubling is not intended here.
With that [quantity of herbs], there should be forty palas of water, which becomes ten times [the weight of the herbs].
One should cook one pala each of grapes, madhuka, dates, vidārī, śatāvarī, parūṣakas, and the three myrobalans (triphalā). || 68–69 ||
One should prepare ghee by boiling one *āḍhaka* of *āmalaka* juice with one-fourth part remaining, along with sugar-cane juice and milk, and a paste of *abhayā* equal to one-fourth [of the ghee];
once the ghee is cooked, one should add sugar and honey, each equal to one-fourth [of the ghee].
One should administer this, which destroys pitta-type gulma and removes all disorders of pitta.
(71) Here, due to their constant association, the decoction is considered equivalent to the ghee and other ingredients taken separately.
