or, a plaster made from sandalwood, madhuka, padma, uśīra, and blue lotus ground with milk should be applied to alleviate burning sensations, swelling, and pain.
An ointment made from the paste of the five barks mixed with ghee should be applied.
In all cases arising from pitta, measures that alleviate pitta should be employed; in cases arising from blood, bloodletting is required.
However, in cases of increased kapha, one should apply an ointment made of substances with hot potency ground with urine.
One should drink a decoction of *pītadāru* combined with urine;
however, for a swelling arising from fat (*medas*), one should apply a plaster of the *surasādi* group after fomentation,
or else apply drugs used for head-purgation (*śirovirecana*) that are lukewarm and mixed with urine.
Having fomented it, one should wrap the [wound] arising from urine with a cloth bandage.
One should indeed pierce it with a *vrīhimukha* instrument below the seam on its side; leaving the suture at the edge of the ear above the conch-shell [of the ear], one should cauterize it.

Alternatively, one should pierce the veins in reverse order to cure intestinal hernia; having incised the skin at the middle of the thumb, one should cauterize it when the limbs are affected in the opposite manner.
[This oil] is prepared with *rāsnā*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *amṛtā*, *eraṇḍa*, *balā*, and *gokṣura*.
A decoction mixed with *rubu* oil quickly destroys inguinal hernia (*antravṛddhi*).
By drinking castor oil combined with milk processed with *balā*,
a person overcomes inguinal hernia accompanied by flatulence and colic.
One should consume Harītakī every morning, prepared with cow's urine, mixed with oil and salt, which removes diseases caused by Kapha and Vāta.
[It should be] prepared with cow's urine and fried in castor oil.
A person who eats Harītakī combined with Saindhava salt, followed by a drink of lukewarm water, destroys even long-standing and greatly increased hemorrhoids. 13.
One who is vigilant should drink a decoction of triphalā mixed with cow’s urine in the morning;
this destroys swelling arising from kapha and vāta that has originated in the testicles.
[Likewise, one should use] saralā, aguru, kuṣṭha, devadāru, and mahauṣadha.
Combined with cow’s urine and *āraṇāla*, it destroys swelling and subdues *kapha* and *vāta*.
(15) A paste made from *pathyā* fried in castor oil, combined with black pepper and rock salt, is an excellent remedy for the disease of *vṛddhi*. (16)
Clarified butter from three cows, mixed with rock salt and carefully placed in a conch-shell vessel,
should be heated by the rays of the sun for seven days.
It destroys even excessively increased *kūraṇḍa*.
Powder made from the root of *aindrī*, rubbed with *rubu* oil and drunk for three days with cow’s milk, prevents all types of enlargement (*vṛddhi*). || 17-18 ||
An increase, even one long-standing, is undoubtedly pacified when smeared with the root of *rudrajaṭā* and bound with the skin of a spotted deer (*karaṭavyaṅka*).
The bark of the root of *rūpikā*, ground with *māraṇāla*, [is likewise effective].
An ointment destroys an enlargement (vṛddhi), even one that is firmly rooted and deep-seated.
An ointment made from a paste of *vacā* and mustard seeds destroys enlargement;
an ointment made from *lajjā* and *gṛdhramala* is an excellent remedy for removing enlargement.
The roots of *bilva*, *kapittha*, *aralu*, *agni*, the two types of *bṛhatī*,
*śyāmā*, *pūtikarañja*, and *śigru*; along with *viśvauṣadha*, *āruṣkara*, *kṛṣṇā*, *granthika*, *cavya*, the five salts (*pañcalavaṇa*), alkali (*kṣāra*), and *ajamodā*.
Yellow *kāñjika* or warm water, stirred and reduced to a powder, cures scrotal enlargement (*bradhna*).
Alternatively, a lukewarm plaster made from the paste of wheat or *kunduruka* mixed with sheep’s milk is an excellent remedy for removing the pain of scrotal enlargement.
Immediately upon the crow's death, when it has been dissected, the wise man should insert the penis for a moment; at that very instant, he shall become free from disease.
Ajājī, hapuṣā, kuṣṭha, wheat, and jujubes— [these are the ingredients].
Having ground these together with sour gruel (kāñjika), one should apply them as a plaster over the sunken area.
[25] Saindhava salt, madana, kuṣṭha, śatāhvā, nicula, vacā, hrīvera, madhuka, bhārgī, devadāru, and nāgara— [26]
Having ground together kaṭphala, pauṣkara, medā, cavika, citraka, śaṭhī, viḍaṅga, ativiṣā,
śyāmā, reṇukā, nalinī, sthirā, bilva,
ajamodā, kṛṣṇā, dantī, and rāsnā; || 27 ||
Castor oil, when properly prepared, cures disorders of Vāta;

through its use as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana), it destroys hernia, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids, splenic enlargement, urinary disorders, excessive Vāta, flatulence, and even urinary stones.
Ghee prepared with *saurāṣṭrā* should be administered to alleviate enlargement of the spleen (*bradhnavṛddhi*).
[Adhikāra 40] Barley,
mung beans, and *paṭola*, along with pungent and dry food, [are recommended].
One should employ [this] for vomiting and the discharge of blood in cases of goiter (galagaṇḍa).
A goiter is cured when it is smeared with the root of hastikarṇapalāśa ground with rice-water. || 1-2 ||
One should grind mustard seeds, *añśu* seeds, hemp seeds, flax seeds, barley, and radish seeds with sour buttermilk;
[this cures] swellings, glandular tumors, and even most severe goiters. || 3 ||
By means of this application as a paste, [the ailments] are pacified and go to dissolution before long.
The juice of ripe karkāruka, combined with viḍa salt and saindhava salt, destroys even a recent goiter when used as a nasal medication; of this there is no doubt.
One should drink the burnt ashes of *jalakumbhīka*, processed by boiling and strained through cow’s urine, while eating a meal of *kodrava* grain, for the pacification of goiter (*galagaṇḍa*).
For the application of a poultice (*upanāhana*) on a goiter, [one should use] *sūryāvarta* and garlic.

By means of the discharge of pustules, the goiter (galagaṇḍa) is pacified; of this there is no doubt. Water that has been kept for seven days in a ripe bitter gourd (*alābu*) fruit, or river water, destroys the goiter when drunk by one who follows a wholesome diet.
Kaṭphala powder held within the throat for a year destroys goiter,
just as if it were drunk mixed with ghee.
The root of the white mountain-karṇikā plant,
mixed with buffalo urine and placed in a jar containing iron rust for one month.
One should lick [this] burnt with internal smoke mixed with honey for goiter (galagaṇḍa).
Twelve veins are declared to be on the sides and below the tongue.
Of those [veins], one should gradually cut the two *sthūlaśiras* veins from below.
Having grasped them with a hook, the wise physician, using a blade of *kuśa* grass,
should apply jaggery and fresh ginger to that wound once the blood has flowed out.
Food that does not cause secretions and soup made from *kulattha* beans are recommended;
furthermore, one should apply [pressure] to the area situated on the external junction between the two ears and the middle of the neck.
In a case of *galagaṇḍa*, one should incise three veins, one above the other.
One should cook mustard oil with viḍaṅga, kṣāra, sindhu, ugra, rāsnā, agni, vyoṣa, dāru,
and the juice of the fruit of kaṭutumbī;
by using this as a nasal drop (nasya), one may eliminate even long-standing galagaṇḍa.
One should drink oil prepared with amṛtavallī, nimba, hiṃsrā, vṛkṣaka, pippalī,
the two types of balā, and devadāru.
It is always beneficial for one suffering from goiter.
A decoction made from the roots of *varuṇa*, rich in honey, when drunk even once,
quickly destroys *gaṇḍamālā* (scrofula) that has persisted for a long time.
The auspicious bark of the *kāñcanāra* tree, ground with the water of the month of Jyeṣṭha and combined with *viśvabheṣaja*, should be drunk; it is a supreme remedy for removing *gaṇḍamālā*.
Likewise, the root of *āragvadha* should be quickly ground with rice-water.

One should eradicate *gaṇḍamālā* through the correct application of nasal drops (*nasya*) and medicinal pastes (*pralepa*). For those afflicted by the disease of *gaṇḍamālā*, one should properly employ the root of *nirguṇḍī* ground with water for the administration of nasal therapy.
One should administer nasal drops (nasya) with the fresh juice of *koṣātakī*,
or with that of *tumbī* mixed with long pepper (*pippalī*), or with oil produced from *vāriṣṭa*.
The two upakulyās together with honey [cure it].
Or, the root of aindrī or girikarṇī, taken with cow’s urine when drunk, removes even long-standing gaṇḍamālā.
One should drink two palas of the fresh juice extracted from *alambuṣā* leaves;
it is a destroyer of *apacī*, *gaṇḍamālā*, and *kāmalā*,
and it shall eliminate goiters (*galagaṇḍa*), *gaṇḍamālā*, and *kūraṇḍa*.
The root of *brāhmaṇayaṣṭikā*, ground with *jyeṣṭhā* water,
destroys severe *gaṇḍamālā* among men through an external application;
likewise, an excellent oil cooked with *chucchundarī* certainly [effects the same] in an instant.
Oil prepared with the bark of *śākhoṭaka*, as well as that cooked with *bimba*, *aśvamāra*, and *nirguṇḍī*, cures goiter; it is also effective when used as nasal drops (*nāvana*).
Furthermore, [oil] prepared with the fresh juice of *nirguṇḍī* and the paste of the root of *lāṅgalī* [is likewise beneficial].
Oil used as a nasal drop quickly destroys even the most severe gaṇḍamālā.
One should eat cakes made by cooking the root of vanakārpāsikā together with rice to destroy apacī.
Śobhāñjana and devadāru ground with sour gruel (kāñjika) and applied as a lukewarm paste will destroy even the most difficult apacī.
Having burned mustard seeds, ariṣṭa leaves, and bhallātakas together—
Ground with goat's urine, this is an ointment that destroys apacī.
One should burn the wood of the aśvattha tree, nicula, and cow's teeth;
the ash, when combined with boar's marrow, cures the severe ulcers of apacī.
Having measured twelve finger-breadths toward the heel and avoiding the indrabasti, the physician should properly incise [the area] which resembles fish-eggs.
Having drawn out the contents of the cysts, one should apply fire [cauterization].
Alternatively, the physician should properly make three lines above the wrist, separated by the width of a finger, for the complete pacification of apacīs.
A root grown from a blue lotus (utpala) tied with the Puṣya asterism cures apacī;
or one should cut the Apāmārga plant when it reaches the surface of the tongue.
[One should also use] vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, madhuka, saindhava, and devadāru.
Oil boiled with these [ingredients], when used as a nasal drop (nasya), will conquer even a difficult case of apacī.
(35) Sandalwood, abhayā, lac, vacā, and kaṭukarohiṇī—oil boiled with these, when drunk, will conquer apacī along with its very roots. (36)
Oil prepared ten times with cow’s urine along with *guñjā*, *hayāri*, *śyāmāka*, and mustard seeds, when combined with a powder of *kaṇā*, the five salts, and black pepper,
conquers [the disease] in all its stages.
Through massage, one may cure severe apacī, as well as valmīka, piles, tumors, and ulcers.
In cases of unripe (āma) glandular swellings, the physician should apply treatments for edema;
once they have ripened, he should incise them, purify the area, and heal the wound with medicinal ointments.
Hiṃsrā, sarohiṇī, amṛtā, bhārgī,
śyāmāka, bilva, aguru, kṛṣṇagandhā, and tālaparṇī, ground together with cow bile, [are used as a collyrium].
In the case of a swelling caused by Vāta, an application (pralepa) should be applied to the glandular mass;
however, for one caused by Pitta, water-based substances are beneficial,
as is sprinkling with milk and water.
One should drink cool decoctions of *kākolī* and *varga*, mixed with sugar,
or with grape juice or sugarcane juice. (41)
Or one should drink a powder of *harītakī*, and one should apply medicinal plasters made from the barks of *madhūka*, *jambu*, *arjuna*, and *vetasa*. (42)
When the complications have arisen in due order,
the physician should perform scarification on a swelling caused by phlegm after it has been fomented.
And with the dust from the big toe, stones, and sprouts;
and with the roots of the vikaṅkata, āragvadha, kākaṇantī, kākādanī, and tāpasavṛkṣa trees.
The wise physician should apply an ointment made of *alābu*, *bhārgī*, *karañja*, *kālā*, and *madana*; likewise,
[an ointment] consisting of the root-bark of *dantī* and *citraka*, *sudhā*, the milk of *arka*, and jaggery.
A plaster of *bhallātaka* seeds and iron sulfate (*kāsīsa*) would split even stone (55).
A plaster derived from the insect known as *mātṛvāhaka* cures glandular swellings, tumors, and the like;
likewise, an alkaline solution of *sarjikā* root combined with powdered conch shell [is effective].
A sharp medicinal paste (pralepa) has been prescribed; it destroys tumors, swellings (arbuda), and other such growths.
Or, having extracted unripened tumors arising from vital points (marmas), the physician should apply fire (cauterization).
One should indeed cauterize them with an alkali after repeatedly scarifying them according to the instruction;
for there is no distinction between a *granthi* and an *arbuda*.

Therefore, a physician who knows the prescribed procedures should treat abdominal tumors (arbuda) by means of the treatment for glandular swellings (granthi), according to the location, cause, shape, defects, and the affected tissues. 48.
In the case of a tumor caused by Vāta,
the skilled physician should apply poultices made of unctuous meats or *vesavāra*, and then administer fomentation (*sveda*) using a tube.
One should repeatedly extract the blood with a horn;
furthermore, mild fomentation and poultices,
as well as purgatives for the body, are beneficial in the case of a pitta-type tumor (pittārbuda).
Having rubbed [the area], one should smear it profusely with finely ground leaves of *udumbara*, *śāka*, and *gojī* mixed with honey,
along with *sarjarasa* and *priyaṅgu*. || 50 ||
An ointment made with pataṅga, lodhra, arjuna, yaṣṭikāhva, conch powder, and the ashes of radish roots should be applied;
it removes kaphaja tumors (arbuda) and is especially effective for glandular swellings (granthi) and similar conditions. || 51-52 ||
One should apply a plaster made from the paste of *niṣpāva*, oil-cake, and *kulattha* beans,
enriched with meat and kneaded with curd, so that worms may emerge from it.
Or they release their offspring like flies;
when only a small portion remains and it has been devoured by worms, one should then scrape it and subsequently apply fire.
When the root is small, one should wrap it with tin, copper, lead, or crow feathers,
and then apply caustic, fire, or surgical instruments.
Constantly observing his vital breath,
he should treat the humors as they arise spontaneously, bringing them to maturity through the process of ripening according to the prescribed method. || 55 ||
Upodika roots, smeared with juices and wrapped in their own leaves,
cause the various types of pustules and tumors of men to perish quickly. Upodika ground with sour gruel and buttermilk [is likewise effective].
The application of a poultice mixed with salt is seen by some to be for the pacification of tumors (arbuda), whether occurring daily or in those born from the three vital points (marmas). || 57 ||

An ointment made from the ashes and husks of *rambhāmocaka* (a type of bamboo) that conquers tumors, combined with the powder of conch shell, or else with lizard blood, ginger, sulfur, barley, *viḍaṅga*, and dry ginger;
or the sweat of *snuhī* and *gaṇḍīrī*— these destroy arbudas (tumors).
Alternatively, with lead, salts, or *piṇḍāraka* fruit;

or a plaster consisting of turmeric, *lodhra*, *pattuṅga*, soot from a house, and realgar, thickened with honey—this is a supreme remedy for removing fatty tumors (*medas*) and arbuda swellings. || 59-60 ||
One should perform this entire procedure for a *śarkarārbuda* (gravel-like tumor) as well.
[Adhikāra 41] By means of fasting (*laṅghana*), plasters (*lepana*), sudation (*sveda*), purgation (*recana*), and bloodletting (*raktamokṣaṇa*), [the treatment is completed].
One should generally treat elephantiasis (ślīpada) with hot applications that alleviate phlegm (kapha).
A plaster made from dhattūra, eraṇḍa, nirguṇḍī, varṣābhū, śigru,
and sarṣapa destroys even long-standing and extremely severe elephantiasis.
The bark of the *rūpikā* root, ground with *māranāla*,
destroys elephantiasis (*ślīpada*)— even when it is deeply rooted and firmly established— by means of an external application. [Likewise] that which originates from the *piṇḍāraka* tree...
The *bandākaśiphā*, when drunk with clarified butter or tied firmly with a thread around the shank, certainly conquers even severe elephantiasis. 4.
For anointing, *citraka* or *devadāru* is always beneficial,
or a paste of *siddhārtha* and *śigru* ground with urine and made lukewarm.
In cases of *ślīpada* caused by Vāta, the physician should apply oleation, sudation, and poultices.
Having positioned [the patient], one should pierce the vein four finger-breadths above the ankle;

for a case of *ślīpada* caused by pitta, one should pierce the vein below the ankle and perform pitta-alleviating treatments, as in the case of a pitta-type tumor (*arbuda*) or erysipelas (*visarpa*).
Having ground together mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, rāsnā, sahiṃsrā, and punarnavā with *araṇāla*, this ointment is for the pacification of *pitta*-type elephantiasis (ślīpada).
In the case of kapha-type elephantiasis, one should carefully pierce a vein at the thumb.
A person should frequently drink astringent decoctions mixed with honey.
For the cure of elephantiasis (ślīpada), one should drink mustard oil,
or else the juice derived from the leaves of the pūtīkarañja tree according to one's strength.
By this very same procedure, one should drink the juice of *putrajīvaka* with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), or the powder of *vṛddhadāraka* with [cow's] urine.
A person should drink *rajanī* (turmeric) combined with jaggery with cow's urine.
It destroys elephantiasis arising from chronic fever, and especially ringworm and skin diseases.
He who drinks Harītakī fried in Gandharva oil with cow's urine becomes free from the constriction of elephantiasis within seven nights.

Fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) combined with oil destroys kapha and vāta; it is digestive, cures disorders of undigested matter (āmadoṣa), and eliminates elephantiasis (ślīpada). A person should eat black gram cakes (māṣeṇḍarī) together with the root of the *godhāvatī* plant.
One will surely conquer fever arising from the provocation of *ślīpada* immediately; there is no doubt.
The *ślīpadaghna-rasa*, prepared with *guḍūcī* and combined with oil, when used regularly, [overcomes it].
[The ingredients are] *trikaṭu*, *triphalā*, *cavya*, *dārvī*, *varuṇa*, and *gokṣura*.
One should powder Alambuṣā and Guḍūcī in equal parts;
having taken the powder of all these, one should add an amount of Vṛddhadāra equal to that. It should be drunk with sour gruel (kāñjika) in a dose of one Akṣa.
When digested, this food may be consumed without restriction and satisfies all desires.
It destroys elephantiasis, obesity, and severe āmavāta; it removes abdominal tumors, skin diseases, and disorders of wind, and it alleviates fevers caused by wind and phlegm.
Take two palas each of pippalī, triphalā, dārunāgara, and punarnavā; to these, add an equal amount of vṛddhadāraka.
One should drink one karṣa of this powder, measured according to the standard, with kāñjika.
When digested, this food may be consumed without restriction and fulfills all desires.
It destroys elephantiasis, diseases of the wind (vāta), and splenic disorders;
it kindles a formidable digestive fire and subdues the condition of "burning ash" (bhasmaka).

One karṣa each of kṛṣṇā, citraka, and dantī, half a pala of harītakī (twenty fruits), and two palas of jaggery—this bolus should be eaten with honey; it destroys even difficult-to-cure elephantiasis. (23)
Surasā, devadāru, the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā),
all types of salt, viḍaṅga, citraka, cavikā,
pippalīmūla, guggulu, hapuṣā, and vacā. || 24 ||
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *karṣa* each of the pastes of *yavāgraja*, *pāṭhā*, *śaṭī*, *elā*, and *vṛddhadāruka*,
along with a decoction of *daśamūlī* and a liquid of *dhānyayūṣa*.
One should drink three karṣas of the cooked, palatable ghee from the paste, having prepared it separately in portions of one prastha each combined with whey (dadhimaṇḍa).
This cures elephantiasis (ślīpada) caused by kapha and vāta, as well as that which has taken refuge in the flesh and blood.
It certainly destroys pitta-originated swellings located in the fat; of this there is no doubt.
It destroys scrofula (apacī), cervical lymphadenitis (gaṇḍamālā), intestinal hernia (antravṛddhi), as well as tumors (arbuda), disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa), edema, and hemorrhoids.
This ghee named Saurēśvara is highly digestive, beneficial for the heart, and destroys worms in the abdomen; when consumed, it cures elephantiasis (ślīpada).
Indeed, this destroyer of hosts of diseases was prepared by Jīvaka.
Alternatively, for the cure of elephantiasis (ślīpada), one may drink oil cooked with viḍaṅga, marica, arka, nāgara, citraka, bhadradāru, elā, and all types of salts. || 31 ||
Adhikāra 42:
The application of leeches is recommended for every type of abscess (vidradhi), except for those dominated by pitta; mild purgation, light food, and sudation are also advised.
In the case of a Vata-type abscess (vātavidradhi), a thick, lukewarm plaster made from the paste of Vata-alleviating roots, saturated with muscle fat (vasā), oil, and ghee, should be applied.
Fomentations and poultices (upanāha) combined with the roots of the Shigru tree should also be administered.
One should apply a plaster made of barley, wheat, and mung beans, ground into a paste and cooked;
thus, even an unripened abscess (vidradhi) dissolves in an instant.
Furthermore, [it may be treated] with water boiled with *punarnavā*, *dāru*, *viśva*, and the ten roots (*daśamūla*), along with *abhayā*.
In a Vata-type abscess, one should drink either guggulu or rubu oil;
in a Pitta-type abscess, one should apply a plaster made of sugar, parched rice, and madhuka,
combined with śārivā, or alternatively, a plaster of payasyā, uśīra, and candana ground with milk.
Or one should drink a decoction of triphalā combined with one akṣa of the paste of trivṛt.
An ointment should be applied using the paste of the five barks mixed with ghee, along with liquorice, śārivā, dūrvā, the roots of nala, and sandalwood.
An ointment made from brick-dust, sand, iron filings, cow dung, chaff, and soil, ground with milk, should be applied for the pacification of a pitta-type abscess (pittavidradhi).
Furthermore, one should constantly apply fomentation to a kapha-type abscess (śleṣmavidradhi) using these same substances ground with urine.
One should sprinkle a swelling or an ulcer accompanied by pain with a lukewarm decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) mixed with oil or with meat broth.
One should drink a decoction of triphalā, śigru, varuṇa, and the ten roots.
In the case of an abscess arising from phlegm (kapha), one should administer guggulu mixed with urine; otherwise,
an expert should perform all the treatments for a pitta-type abscess without exception for both blood-born and exogenous abscesses.
A decoction of *śobhāñjanaka* combined with asafoetida and rock salt,
when consumed every morning, quickly destroys abscesses (*vidradhi*).
One should wash the root of the *śigru* tree in water and boil it after grinding it into a fine paste.
Having drunk its juice with honey, a person destroys internal abscesses;
likewise, the root of *varṣābhū* and the root of *varuṇaka*,
boiled with water and drunk, conquer unripened abscesses.
For the pacification of an internal abscess that has not yet suppurated, one should indeed drink a decoction of the *varuṇādi* group with an addition (*pratīvāpa*) of the *uṣakādi* group;
the root of *pāṭhā* brings about such pacification.
Taken internally with honey and rice-water, it quickly eradicates an internal abscess in a person. || 16 ||
This [treatment] is prescribed for the unripe stage; however, when it has ripened, the procedure is like that for a wound.
Even after the discharge, whether upwards or downwards, one should drink the *varuṇaka* group of drugs with *maireya*, sour liquids, *surā*, or *āsava*, or else the juice of *madhuśigru*.
Priyaṅgu, dhātakī, lodhra, kaṭphala, and the bark of tila—
oil cooked with these is the supreme healer for healing an abscess (vidradhi).
(Chapter 43)
First, one should perform debridement; second, irrigation; third, application of a poultice; fourth, the act of incision;
fifth, purification; and sixth, healing is prescribed.
These stages of the ulcer have been described; the seventh is that which removes deformity.
2. Mātuluṅga, agnimantha, bhadradāru, mahauṣadha, ahiṃsrā, and rāsnā constitute a plaster that destroys swelling caused by Vāta. 3.
A paste made from the bark of the śākhoṭaka tree ground with sour gruel (kāñjika) is unctuous and destroys red swellings, just as Suparṇa destroys serpents.
Likewise, dūrvā grass, the root of nala, madhuka, and sandalwood [are used].
All cool medicinal groups constitute a paste that destroys swelling caused by pitta.
A paste made from the bark of nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, and vetasa, mixed with ghee, is known to alleviate swelling.
This same course of treatment applies to exogenous swellings arising from blood;
furthermore, a paste of *ajagandhā*, *aśvagandhā*, *kālā*, along with *saralā*,
*ekeśikā*, and *ajaśṛṅgī*, destroys phlegmatic swelling.

For swelling caused by kapha and vāta, a lukewarm paste composed of punarnavā, śigru, dāru, daśamūla, and mahauṣadha is prescribed. One should not apply a plaster at night, nor should one allow an applied plaster to fall off.
One should not apply a medicinal paste that has been kept overnight; nor should one insist on applying it while it is drying, but rather overlook it as it dries during the process of pressing.
Furthermore, one should not smear the face with it, for by doing so, the impurity is released.
Having anointed stable swellings with little pain with unctuous substances that alleviate Vāta and Kapha,
and having fomented them, one should then gently massage them with a bamboo tube,
or with the palm or the thumb, for the purpose of causing them to soften.
A wise physician should perform bloodletting at the very outset in the case of a wound that is large, confluent, painful, and swollen,
provided it does not subside through the application of plasters, fomentations, affusions, and depleting therapies.

That swelling also quickly goes to destruction through the letting out of blood. On one side are all other treatments, and on the other side is bloodletting; for if that [blood] does not become putrid, there is no pain. (14–15)
If the swelling, thus treated, does not subside, then for that which has ripened, incision is said to be beneficial after applying poultices;
[the incision should be made] with either oil or clarified butter, or with a ball of flour mixed with both of them.
A lukewarm poultice (upanāha) is recommended for the purpose of ripening an inflammatory swelling (śotha).
A bolus made of sesame seeds, linseed, sour curd, and parched grain flour,
combined with yeast, kuṣṭha, and salt, is praised for use as a poultice.
For children, the elderly, the weak, the emaciated, the timid, and even for women;

and when [the disease] has arisen upon a vital spot (marman), or when there is a ripened swelling or a severe inflammation, one should apply a paste of cow's tooth (go-danta) rubbed in water to the size of a jujube fruit. || 19 ||
Even in the case of an extremely hard swelling, it is treated with applications of snake-skin ashes mixed with pungent oil for the purpose of ripening and breaking it open;
thus the accumulation of the goitre subsides and its inflammation quickly bursts.
Cirabilva, agnika, dantī, citraka, and hayamāraka;
the excrement of pigeons, herons, and vultures is also a means of causing rupture.
Whatever substances are alkalis, or indeed alkali itself, is the supreme agent for causing rupture.
For substances that are slimy, one should apply the bark and roots [of medicinal plants], massage, and, in brief, the powders of barley, wheat, and black gram (māṣa).
Then follows a wash with a decoction made from the leaves of *paṭola* and neem (*nimba*).
In cases of both impure and pure [disorders], the bark of the *nyagrodha* group and others is used.
The two groups of five roots (*pañcamūla*) are for wind disorders (*vāta*), while the *nyagrodha* group is for bile disorders (*pitta*).
The *āragvadha* group should be employed in all procedures for phlegm disorders (*kapha*).
A paste of sesame seeds with salt, the two types of *haridrā*, *trivṛt*, ghee, *madhuka*, and *nimba* leaves constitutes an ointment that purifies wounds.
*Nimba* leaves, sesame seeds, *dantī*, *trivṛt*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and honey [constitute another].
This ointment is a subduer of malignant ulcers and a lion among purifiers.
Alternatively, the root of *śārivā* alone is a purifier of all ulcers;
as are *paṭola*, sesame, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, and *niśā*. (27–28)
An ointment made of nimba leaves with salt purifies wounds. Triphalā, khadira, dārvī, nyagrodha, and the rest, along with balā and kuśa [roots], [are used for healing].
A decoction of nimba and kola leaves is beneficial for purification.
With this, a healing paste (kalka) made of sesame seeds combined with madhuka should be applied to the site where putrid flesh has failed to grow;
however, when combined with nimba leaves and honey, it is known as a purifying (saṃśodhana) agent. || 30–31 ||
The paste of nimba leaves and sesame seeds, combined with honey, cleanses wounds; when combined with ghee, it promotes healing. This same procedure applies to a paste of barley as well. (32)
A suppository made from neem leaves, ghee, honey, barberry (*dārvī*), and licorice (*madhuka*),
or a paste of sesame seeds, causes the wound to swell and then heals it.
A paste of the milk of the *saptapala* tree [achieves the same].
The *śarapuṅkhā*, when applied as a medicinal paste mixed with honey, pacifies malignant ulcers; it is declared to be a healer of all wounds. (34)
One should smear a human skull or its bone with urine;
this is a healing agent for wounds.
One should cleanse with a suppository (varti) those ulcers that are incurable even by hundreds of other methods— ulcers that are narrow-mouthed or located in vital spots (marma) and joints—
with Abhayā, Trivṛtā, Dantī, Lāṅgalī, honey, and Saindhava salt. || 35–36 ||
Suṣavī, patra, pattūra, karṇamoṭa, and kuṭheraka— these, applied individually as a paste, heal deep wounds;
or alternatively, with the powders of the five barks combined with the powder of oyster shells.
Or with the powder of dhātakī and lodhra, those wounds heal likewise. Those wounds which are accompanied by burning and pain, and in which wind (māruta) predominates—
for them, one should use sesame seeds and māṃsa, fried and then cooled in milk.
Having ground [the ingredients] with that very milk, the physician should apply it as an ointment;
he should also fumigate those [afflictions] caused by wind (vāta) and other [humors], or by spirits (bhūta), which are accompanied by discharge and severe pain,
using barley, ghee, *bhūrja* bark, *madana*, *śrīveṣṭaka*, and *surāhvaya*.
Fumigated with *śrīvāsa*, guggulu, agallochum, and the resin of the *śāla* tree,
the ulcers become hardened and the intense pains vanish.
Sesame seeds, milk, sugar, honey, oil, *madhuka*, and sandalwood— [The above constitutes the first part of the verse.]
By means of this plaster, one should pacify swelling, pain, burning, and bleeding in wounds.
A physician should properly apply this plaster and other treatments for the pacification of pitta-type abscesses (vidradhi) and erysipelas (visarpa), as well as for burns caused by fire.
An application of Mahārāṣṭra hair mixed with burnt flour and the powder of grass from an old house is considered beneficial for burns.
Following this, an ointment of Jīvaka paste [should be applied].
Ghee mixed with lac and resin, when applied as an ointment, removes the pain caused by fire burns in half a moment. || 46 ||
A hatchet that has been burnt out destroys a burn by means of an ointment;
likewise, a powder made from the dried bark of the *aśvattha* tree destroys it by being sprinkled over it;
and oil prepared with earthworms destroys it entirely through massage.
Having ground *śālmalī* cotton and sand with water,
the physician should sprinkle a fresh wound accompanied by pain with this paste and with slightly warm clarified butter mixed with a paste of *yaṣṭīmadhuka*. || 47-48 ||
Having diagnosed an exogenous wound, the physician should administer ghee mixed with honey and employ cooling treatments that destroy the heat of pitta and rakta.
One part of smooth kāntakramuka (nutmeg) should be ground with cow’s ghee.

It certainly pacifies a wound caused by external trauma when applied as a plaster; of this there is no doubt. Or, by means of the juice extracted from Apāmārga leaves, the blood flowing from fresh wounds is immediately arrested.
A wound inflicted by a weapon in men, when bound with camphor, clarified butter,
and *śarapuṅkhā*, *kākajaṅghā*, and the excrement of a pregnant buffalo, heals immediately, free from pain and inflammation. (52)
Lajjā is indeed a separate remedy for healing fresh wounds. A powder made from the tongue of a dog causes immediate healing of cuts.
Cakra-taila is considered the supreme healer for wounds and pierced injuries.
Having consumed barley-alkali, one should apply a medicinal bolus over the ulcer;
by means of the root of *śṛṅgālakolī*, the lost stone will emerge.
Alternatively, it may be brought out by an application of the root of *lāṅgalī* or likewise the root of *gavākṣī*.
For the purpose of suppressing the heat generated by the injury and for blood that has spread at that time,
applications such as plasters that are astringent, cold, sweet, and unctuous are beneficial.
When the blood is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), emesis is said to be the appropriate treatment.
When [the blood] is located in the colon (pakvāśaya), a purgative should undoubtedly be administered;
a decoction made of bamboo bark (vaṃśatvak), castor plant (eraṇḍa), cow’s thorn (śvadaṃṣṭrā), and pāṣāṇabheda,
drunk with asafoetida (hiṅgu) and rock salt (saindhava), will cause the blood situated in the abdominal cavity (koṣṭha) to flow out.
One should eat food with the unsalted broth of barley, jujube, and horse-gram, or drink gruel mixed with rock salt.
This is generally prescribed where one observes that blood is flowing excessively. || 59–60 ||

Then, when the blood has been depleted and the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated causing excessive pain, one should administer the drinking of fats (sneha-pāna), affusion (pariṣeka), unguents and poultices (lepa-upanāhana),
and an oily enema (sneha-basti) prepared with drugs that subdue vāta. || 61 ||
Thus has been declared the seven-day regimen which is beneficial for wounds immediately.
After seven days, one should perform treatment as for a bodily wound;
the juice of karañja, ariṣṭa, and nirguṇḍī destroys worms in the wound.
A leaf of *kalāyavidalī* and the stone of a *koṣāmrā* fruit, used as a filling, [should be applied];
or there should be irrigation with the juices of the *surasādi* group, or an ointment made from their own expressed juice.
[The trees] *nimba*, *sampāka*, *jāti*, *arka*, *saptaparṇa*, and *aśvamāraka* [are also used].

Worm-destroying [substances] combined with urine should be used for sprinkling, as ointments, and for washing. Alternatively, after cleansing the wounds, one may eliminate the worms by applying a paste of meat or a paste of garlic (*laśuna*) which destroys worms. (65–66)
Those large wounds that are characterized by moisture, suppuration, discharge, and foul odor, and which are painful and swollen,
subside when treated with [medicines] mixed with guggulu.
With yellow [ghee], it brings about pacification; with the juice of triphalā, it does the same.
Guggulu mixed with triphalā powder and formed into pills (vaṭaka) acts as a free-flowing remedy that destroys constipation and cleanses and heals ulcers.
Amṛtā-guggulu is recommended, as is Vajraka oil;
one should eat a powder of viḍaṅga, triphalā, and vyoṣa in equal parts with guggulu, made into boluses with clarified butter, while following a wholesome diet. (69)
It cures malignant ulcers, apacī, urinary disorders, leprosy, and sinus ulcers.
[This is] from amṛtā, paṭola root, triphalā, trikaṭu, and krimighna.
The powder of the equal parts [of the herbs] should have a portion of *guggulu* equal to the whole; one dose should be taken every day. || 71 ||
One should consume it for the duration of a meal to conquer diseases such as wounds, wind-blood disorders, gulma, abdominal enlargements, and swellings. || 72 ||

Ghee prepared with equal parts of *jātī*, nimba, paṭola leaves, kaṭukā, dārvī, niśā, sārivā, mañjiṣṭhā, abhayā, tuttha, siktha, madhuka, and the seeds of naktāhvā— by this, [the disease] located in the vital points (*marman*) is reduced to a fine opening.

Deep-seated wounds that discharge pus and are accompanied by pain heal and grow only after they have subsided; likewise, those that are white, yellow, madder-colored, containing *māṃsī*, or honey-colored [heal]. (73) 12. Gaurī, haridrā, mañjiṣṭhā, māṃsī, and madhuka as well.
Prapauṇḍarīka, hrībera, bhadramusta, and candana;
jātī, nimba, paṭola, karañja, and kaṭurohiṇī; madhūcchiṣṭa, madhuka, and likewise mahāmedā. || 74–75 ||

One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with the water of the five barks (*pañcavalkala*). This "Gaura" [ghee] is of great potency and purifies all types of wounds—whether they are accidental, congenital, or those that have been long-standing. (76)
One should also quickly purify even an uneven channel.
Thus, oils such as Gaurādya and Jātikādya are prepared for use in cases of deep wounds with narrow openings that have become corrupted.
The leaves of *naktamāla*, the fruits of *varuṇa*, the leaves of *sumanā*, as well as those of *paṭola* and *ariṣṭa*;
the two types of *haridrā*, beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*), *madhuka*, and *tiktarohiṇī*.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *karṣa* each of the following ingredients: mañjiṣṭhā, candana, uśīra, utpala, śārivā, and trivṛt.
This [medicinal ghee] pacifies malignant ulcers and likewise purifies sinus tracks.
And for fresh wounds, a preparation of *karañja* and other such herbs is recommended here.
Ghee boiled with *prapauṇḍarīka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *madhuka*, *uśīra*, *padmaka*, and *haridrā*, along with milk, promotes the healing of wounds.
One should cook wound-healing ghee with *tikta*, *āsiktha*, *niśā*, *yaṣṭī*, *naktāhvā*, fruits and sprouts, as well as the leaves of *paṭola*, *mālatī*, and *nimba*.
[Verse 83] [One should cook ghee with] *sindūra*, *kuṣṭha*, poison, *hiṅgu*, *rasona*, and *citraka*... [Verse 84]
Oil cooked with the paste of *bāṇāṅghri* and *lāṅgalikā*, its foam driven away by blowing while reciting the *prāsāda-mantra*,
is a "Viparītamalla" (the wrestler who overcomes the contrary) that pacifies malignant ulcers.
This preparation named *Viparītaka-malla* destroys sword-wounds, severe scrotal swellings, major secondary infections (*upadaṃśa*), sinus ulcers, common sores, eczema, leprosy, and skin rashes.
For one who desires oil for use with beds, seats, and food as much as desired:
one should prepare one hundred palas of *kuṭhāraka* in water from a pond; when reduced to one-fourth, one should cook one *prastha* of oil with that decoction.
An ointment made from the pastes of *kuṭhāra*, *apāmārga*, *proṣṭhikā*, and *makṣikā* [is used for healing].
Oil prepared with equal parts of these, along with *prapauṇḍarīka*, *madhuka*, the two types of *kākoli*, and *candana*, is the supreme healer of wounds.
Alternatively, oil prepared with the fresh juice of *dūrvā* grass, with *kampillaka*,
and with a paste of *dārvī* bark is the primary remedy for healing wounds.
One should prepare clarified butter (*ghṛta*) by the very same procedure used for the oil.
Having recognized that blood-bile (raktapitta) is predominant, one should cook clarified butter alone.
Having ground mañjiṣṭhā, candana, and mūrvā, one should cook the clarified butter;
this is desired as a healing agent for all those burned by fire.
21. A pungent oil prepared from the decoction and paste of *pāṭalī* destroys pain, discharge, burning sensations, and eruptions in burnt wounds.
22. Sandalwood, the bud of *ghaṭa*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and likewise *madhuka*...
Prapauṇḍarīka, mūrvā, pataṅga, and likewise dhātakī—
with these, oil should be cooked together with ghee and milk; this is highly recommended for burns from fire, as an excellent ointment and for pouring over the wound.
Realgar, orpiment, madder, lac, and the two types of turmeric,
applied as a paste with ghee and honey, is an excellent means for purifying the skin.
Iron powder, green vitriol, and the flowers of the three myrobalans [are also used].
Every kind of ointment produces blackness on all fresh skin.
An ointment made from the best juices of kālīyaka, latā, tāmra, asthi, and hema,
combined with cow-dung juice, is the supreme means for restoring the natural complexion.
Indeed, by smearing the ground with the skin, hair, hooves, horns, bones, and ashes of four-footed animals and then pulverizing it, the ground becomes hairy again;
or else, the physician should conquer a wound-nodule (vraṇagranthi) with an alkali (kṣāra), just as one treats a nodule. || 98 ||

Having investigated the course of the channels and incised them with a surgical instrument, the expert in the scriptures should apply the entire regimen for wounds, beginning with purification, healing, and so forth. (44.1)
The physician should apply a plaster of ground sesame seeds mixed with the fruit of *pratyakpuṣpī* to a sinus caused by Vāta that has been properly incised;
for one caused by Pitta, he should apply a plaster of sesame, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *nāgadantī*, and the two types of *niśā*.
One should apply a paste of sesame, liquorice, *nīlakaṇṭha* (or *kumbha*), *ariṣṭa*, and rock salt for a phlegmatic ulcer;
for one born from a foreign body, one should apply a paste of sesame, honey, and ghee after excising and purifying it.
A powder of *āragvadha*, turmeric, and *kāla* (black pepper), combined with ghee and honey, [is also used].
A plug made of urine should be applied to the ulcer; it is purifying and destroys the sinus tract.
The bark of the ghoṇṭā fruit, madana fruits, the nutmeg (pūga) shell, and the primary salt [should be used].
This paste, made into a wick together with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*,
destroys the sinus (*nāḍī*) before long.
[The same] wick, when combined with honey, [achieves the same].
The best salt, which destroys the channels, or the oil prescribed for malignant ulcers— when used, it quickly destroys the [disease's] course.
A suppository made from *jātī*, *arka*, and *sampāka*, along with *dantī*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *sauvarcala* salt, and *yāvaśūka*,
destroys fistula-in-ano (*nāḍī*) in a short time.
Ground with the milk of a she-goat and mixed with honey, combined with buffalo curd and *kōdrava* grain,
it removes even long-standing [jaundice].
The powder of the root of *kaṅgunikā* has been consumed for a most severe fistula;
and for those who are emaciated, weak, or fearful, there is the treatment for a fistula located in a vital spot (*marman*).
One should cut it with an alkaline thread and never with a surgical instrument.
Having sought out the path with a probe following the alkaline thread,
one should insert a needle at the end and, having raised [the stone], quickly extract it.

Having brought the thread to the end, the wise physician should apply a firm tie; then, observing that its strength has diminished, he should insert another thread soaked in caustic (kṣāra) so that the track is not severed. || 11 ||

This same procedure should also be performed by a knowledgeable physician in cases of fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇdara). Furthermore, in cases such as tumors (arbuda) and the like, one should draw up [the swelling] and insert a thread at its base,
having covered it all around with a network of needles shaped like barley grains.
One should bind the root with a thread, and when it is severed, one should treat the wound.
Guggulu combined with Triphalā, Vyoṣa, and an equal amount of meat, mixed with clarified butter, destroys sinus tracts,
malignant ulcers, colic, and fistula-in-ano.
Oil extracted from the seeds of sarjikā, sindhu, dantī, agni, rūpikā, anala, nīlikā, and svaramañjarī, cooked in cow’s urine,
pacifies malignant ulcers and removes ulcers caused by kapha and sinus tracts. 15
Having prepared a decoction from the unripe fruits of the *kumbhīka*, *kharjūra*, *karīra*, and *bilva* trees— these being among the forest trees— one should cook the oil.
Having obtained māyā, musta, sarala, and priyaṅgu;
and having indeed added saugandhika, mocarasa, ahipuṣpa, lodhra, and dhātakī; || 16 ||
By this means, a sinus tract originating from a splinter shall indeed heal, and the wound-mouth shall close quickly;
[this is achieved] with bhallātaka, arka, marica, and the best salt.

This prepared oil, made with viḍaṅga, the two types of rajanī, and citraka, along with the juice of mārkava, destroys sinus tracts caused by kapha and vāta, as well as apacī swellings and ulcers. || 18 ||
Having crushed *nirguṇḍī* along with its roots and leaves, one should prepare an equal amount of oil with that juice; this cures fistulas and malignant ulcers.
It is beneficial for scabies and scrofula when used as a drink, an ointment, or an errhine.
For various types of sphoṭas as well as for all kinds of ulcers,
one should cook oil with haṃsapādā, ariṣṭapatra, and jātī leaves along with their juices and pastes; this oil promotes the healing of sinus ulcers (nāḍīvraṇa).
Chapter 45:
Having recognized swelling of the anus, one should dry it and then purify it; bloodletting should be performed so that suppuration does not occur. 1.

A well-ground paste of *vaṭa* leaves, brick-dust, ginger, *guḍūcī*, and *punarnavā* is recommended as an application at the onset of the carbuncles (*pīḍakā*) in cases of fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṇdara*).
For these carbuncles while they are still unripe, treatment preceded by fasting (*apatarpaṇa*) is advised.
One should perform treatment until the end of purgation; for those [wounds] that have burst open, the procedure will now be described.

Having carried out the sequence of scraping with a probe, incision, cauterization with alkali or fire, and so forth, one should treat them like ulcers, according to the specific humor and in the proper order.
Trivṛt, tila, nāgadantī, and mañjiṣṭhā, combined with ghee, rock salt, and honey, shall serve as an ointment for scarifying.
Rasāñjana, the two types of haridrā, mañjiṣṭhā, and nimba leaves [are also used].
A paste of *trivṛt*, *tejovatī*, and *dantī* cures sinus ulcers (*nāḍīvraṇa*).
Kuṣṭha, *trivṛt*, *tilā*, *dantī*, *māgadhī*, rock salt, honey, turmeric, *triphalā*, and *tuttha* are beneficial for purifying wounds.
Having prepared a wick with the milky sap of *snuhi* and *arka*, along with *dārvī*, the wise physician, having ascertained the course of the fistula-in-ano, should diligently fill it.
This [wick] undoubtedly destroys any sinus located anywhere in the body.
Sesame, *abhayā*, *lodhra*, *ariṣṭa* leaves, *niśā*, *vacā*, *lodhra*, and soot are used for fistula-in-ano,
sinus tracts, and venereal sores.
This [ointment] purifies and heals malignant ulcers.
(10) A plaster of the powder of *khara*, *asra*, *pakva*, and *bhūroga* destroys fistula-in-ano; likewise, a plaster of *dantī*, *agni*, and *ativiṣā*, or even dog’s bone, does so. (11)

An ointment made from cat bone combined with the juice of triphalā quickly destroys fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇdara) and is supreme for healing malignant ulcers. [12] A formulation consisting of three, five, and one parts of triphalā, puru, and kṛṣṇā [respectively]...
This pill is beneficial for those suffering from swelling, abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano. [The ingredients are:
trikaṭu, triphalā, musta, viḍaṅga, amṛta, citraka, śaṭī, elā, pippalīmūla, hapuṣā, and devadāru. (13–14)
Tumburu, puṣkara, cavya, viśālā, the two types of rajanī, biḍa, sauvarcala, the two kṣāras, saindhava, and gajapippalī—
of as much quantity as these powders, there should be twice that amount of guggulu.
One should consume a pill the size of a jujube fruit with honey. It cures cough and asthma, as well as swelling, hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano,
pain in the heart, pain in the flanks, and afflictions in the abdomen, bladder, and anus.
[It cures] urinary calculi, dysuria, scrotal enlargement, and worms;
for those afflicted by chronic fever and those whose minds are impaired by wasting (kṣaya),
as well as abdominal distension, insanity, skin diseases, and abdominal enlargements.
This twenty-seven-ingredient [preparation] indeed destroys all diseases, including all types of sinus ulcers, urinary disorders (prameha), and elephantiasis (ślīpada).
One should also eat the meat of a jackal as a side dish or in other culinary forms.
One who avoids indigestion is freed from fistula-in-ano within a month.
The *pañcatikta* ghee is recommended, as is *pañcatikta* guggulu; furthermore, the *nyagrodhādi* group of drugs is beneficial for purification and healing.
Oil or clarified butter cooked with these destroys fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇdara):
citraka, arka, trivṛt, pāṭhā, malapū, hayamāraka, sudhā, vacā, lāṅgalikī, haritāla, and suvarcikā.
A wise physician should cook oil with jyotiṣmatī;
this oil, named Viṣyandana, should be administered for fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara),
as it is both purifying and healing, and likewise restores the natural skin color.
One should cook oil with *karavīra*, *niśā*, *dantī*, *lāṅgalī*, salt, and *agni*, along with *mātuluṅga*, *arka*, and *vatsāhva*, for the treatment of fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*).
*Niśā*, *arka*, milk, rock salt, *agni*, *purāśvahan*, and *vatsaka*— [these are used for the preparation].
Oil for massage, when prepared with these, is effective in curing fistula-in-ano.
A man whose wound has healed should avoid sexual intercourse, fighting, riding on the back of animals, and heavy foods for one year.
For one whose body has been lubricated and fomented, venesection in the middle of the penis,
or the application of leeches, as well as purification through the upper and lower tracts, should be performed.
The digestive fire must be protected with great effort, for it causes the wasting away of the penis;
one should drink a decoction of *paṭola*, *nimba*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *ḍugūcī*, or a decoction of *khadira* and *aśana*.
The application of guggulu combined with triphalā is a practice that removes all types of secondary infections (upadaṃśa).
[2] Prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, rāsnā, kuṣṭha, and punarnavā—
In cases of Vātika [fever], one should apply plasters and affusions using Śarala,
Aguru, and Bhadra; for Paittika [fever], one should thoroughly plaster with Gairika, Añjana, Mañjiṣṭhā, Madhuka, Uśīra, Padmaka, Candana, and Utpala, mixed with unctuous substances.
One should prepare washes, ointments, and medicated ghees from nimba, arjuna, aśvattha, kadamba, śāla, jambū, vaṭa, udumbara, and vetasa.
Powders [should be used] for upadaṃśa arising from pitta and blood.
One should perform the washing of the ulcer with a decoction of triphalā or with the juice of bhṛṅgarāja for the pacification of upadaṃśa.
One should burn equal parts of the three myrobalans (triphalā) mixed with honey in an iron cauldron; this ointment, when applied, immediately heals the ulcer in cases of upadaṃśa.
Alternatively, one may use rasāñjana combined with śirīṣa or pathyā.
Or, as a plaster mixed with honey, it removes all diseases of the penis;
likewise, dusting with the powder of *babbūla* leaves,
or with the powder of pomegranate bark or human bone, is the supreme remedy for *upadaṃśa*.
One should apply an ointment made from betel nut or the root of *aśvamāra*; likewise, one should always consume a diet of barley and drink only well-water.
One should also [treat the horse] separately with the leaves of *jayā*, *jātyaśvamāra*, *arka*, and *sampāka*.
Once washed, one should apply a decoction of bhūnimba,
nimba, triphalā, paṭola, karañja, jātī, khadira, and aśana for the treatment of inflammation of the penis (meḍhrapāka). || 11 || 3 ||
Ghee cooked quickly with the pastes of these [herbs] along with water is declared to be a remover of all types of upadaṃśa (venereal sores).
[The paste consists of: karañja, nimba, arjuna, śāla, jambū—
Ghee prepared with the paste and decoction of *vaṭa* and other such plants cures the disorder of *upadaṃśa*, along with its burning sensation, suppuration, discharge, and redness. (13)
One should cook oil with house-soot, turmeric, wine, and iron dross— these three in increasing proportions— to cure itching, swelling, and pain;
it is both purifying and healing, and likewise restores the natural complexion.

For hemorrhoids that have been excised or cauterized, the treatment should be performed as in the case of *upadaṃśa* (syphilis). Furthermore, the drinking of ghee and purgation are beneficial and wholesome.
Bloodletting is beneficial, as is a light diet.
One should scarify the *sarṣapī* ulcer and dust it with fine astringent powders; with those same ingredients, one should prepare an ointment oil for the healing of the wound.
This same procedure applies to Adhimantha as well; likewise, blood should be drained from both [types].
In the case of Aṣṭhīlā, once the blood has been removed, one should treat it like a Kapha-granthi (Kapha-nodule).
In Kumbhikā, one should remove the blood; when it is suppurated, the ulcer should be cleansed.

An ointment made from *tinduka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *lodhra*, along with oil, serves for healing. This same therapeutic procedure is to be followed for *alajī* after blood has been removed.
A wise physician should apply fomentation (*sveda*) using a tube (*nāḍī-sveda*) to a *grathita* swelling that has been treated with oleation (*snigdha*).
One should apply poultices that are lukewarm and unctuous.
However, having incised and extracted with a hook the pustule known as *uttamā*,
one should treat it with pastes, powders, and decoctions mixed with honey.
The procedure prescribed for *pitta*-visarpa is beneficial for *puṣkarī* and *mūḍha* swellings.

In cases of *tvakpāka* (skin suppuration) and loss of sensation (*sparśahāni*), one should repeatedly sprinkle the affected area with lukewarm *balā*-oil and apply poultices (*upanāha*) made of drugs belonging to the *madhura* group.
Rasakriyā should be administered once the *śatāvarī* has been applied;
immediately thereafter, oil prepared with *pṛśniparṇī* and other herbs should be given.
Furthermore, the treatment for a blood-born tumor (*arbuda*) is the same as that for a bile-born abscess (*pittavidradhi*).
Having carefully examined each case, one should apply decoctions, pastes, medicated ghees, oils, powders, and medicinal extracts for both cleansing and healing wounds,
as well as for tumors, carbuncles, abscesses, fistulas, and moles.
Having rejected [other treatments], the physician should perform their remedial therapy. First, having diagnosed the fracture, one should sprinkle it with cold water.
One should apply a plaster of mud and perform a bandage using *kuśa* grass;
having observed what has been stated by Suśruta regarding fractures, one should carry out the bandaging and other treatments accordingly.
That which is depressed should be raised, and that which is elevated should be lowered.
One should apply [the paste] to the area that has been excised, displaced, or has sunk down, and then turn it upward.
For the purpose of anointing, a plaster consisting of *mañjiṣṭhā* and *madhuka* ground with sour liquids, mixed with *śatadhauta* ghee and rice flour, should be applied. 2–3.
Every seven nights during the cool seasons, a release [of the animal] should be performed by one who knows; likewise, during the hot seasons, one should release it every three nights.
And at the appropriate time, when the heat is mild, one should release it every five nights.
And for sprinkling, one should use a cooled decoction of *nyagrodha* and other such trees;

or, in the case of pain, one should administer milk boiled with the five roots (*pañcamūlī*), or the wise physician should apply *cakrataila* after it has been brought to a comfortably warm temperature.
Meat, meat broth, clarified butter, milk, and soup made with sesame seeds, as well as nourishing food and drink, should be administered by one who understands the treatment of fractures.
Milk from a cow that has calved for the first time, mixed with clarified butter and prepared with sweet medicinal herbs, [should also be given].

A person who has suffered a fracture should drink it cooled and mixed with grapes in the morning. For a fracture involving a joint, a man should drink asthisamhāra, lac, wheat, and arjuna, along with ghee and milk.
For those who consume a paste of garlic, honey, lac, ghee, and sugar in equal parts,
the joining together of bones that are severed, shattered, or fallen out will occur before long.
Alternatively, one may take two or three *guñjā* measures of powdered yellow cowrie shells.
Unripe milk, when drunk, promotes the healing of fractured bones.
Milk mixed with lac, madhuka, and ghee, along with the jīvanīya group of drugs, is both life-sustaining and brings comfort.
One with a broken bone should drink the bark-milk of the arjuna tree,
or else wheat flour with ghee;
likewise, lac, asthisamhṛt, kakubha, and ashvagandhā—
Powdered *nāgabalā* mixed with *saṃbhagna* destroys the pain of bone fractures and makes the limbs as firm as a thunderbolt. || 13 ||
In this case, since it has been observed elsewhere as well, guggulu is equal [in measure] to the powder.
Guggulu, equal in measure to all these combined—namely, bhārṅgī, triphalā, and vyoṣa—should be administered; it heals broken joints.
In the case of a fracture with an ulcer, however, one should rub the ulcer with the finest ghee and honey,
treat it with decoctions, and manage the remainder according to the procedures for fractures.
The physician should strive in such a way that the fracture does not undergo suppuration.
One should employ here the unctuous substances (snehas) prescribed for Vātavyādhi.
One should soak black sesame seeds in stagnant water every night,
and having dried them thus day after day, one should saturate them with milk.
For a third week, one should cultivate [the plant] with honey-water;
then, after it has been watered with milk again and is well-dried, the physician should powder it along with kākolyādi,
śvadaṃṣṭrā, mañjiṣṭhā, and śārivā.
One should grind together kuṣṭha, sarjarasa, māṃsī, devadāru, candana, and śatapuṣpā, and mix them with sesame powder; furthermore,
milk boiled with all these fragrant substances should be prepared for the purpose of pressing.
One should cook that oil again with four times as much milk,
along with cardamom, aṃśumatī, patra, cumin,
tagara, lodhra, prapauṇḍarīka, and kālānuśārivā.
Having ground śaileyaka, kṣīraśuklā, anantā, samadhūlikā,
śṛṅgāṭaka, and the previously mentioned medicinal herbs, one who is learned in the scriptures should cook that oil with these over a gentle fire.
This oil is always wholesome for those with fractures in all therapeutic procedures, as well as for convulsions, hemiplegia, wasting of the limbs,
and facial paralysis; it is also beneficial for stiffness of the neck, diseases of the head, earache, and lockjaw.
In cases of deafness, blindness, and those who have suffered loss through women, one should employ this as a drink, for anointing, nasal drops, and enemas;
by this very means, the growth of the neck, shoulders, and chest is produced. || 26-27 ||
The face becomes like a lotus, and its breath carries its own natural fragrance;
this scented oil, known by this name, cures all disorders of the wind (vāta).
This, which is worthy of kings, should be prepared only by wise physicians for kings.
The powder is desired to be mixed with one-fourth part of sesame powder.
One who has suffered a fracture should avoid salt, pungent substances, alkaline matter, sour things, sexual intercourse, exposure to the sun, physical exercise, and even dry food.
Chapter 49:

In skin diseases (kuṣṭha) where vāta is predominant, ghee [is indicated]; where kapha is predominant, emesis; and where pitta is predominant, bloodletting and purgation are the foremost treatments. 1.
In mild cases of kuṣ� venereal skin disease, scarification is recommended; in severe cases, bloodletting is advised.
A patient suffering from kuṣṭha with an abundance of morbid humors (doṣas) should be thoroughly purified repeatedly, while carefully protecting his life-force.
[One should employ] the roots of vacā, vāsā, paṭola, nimba, and the bark of phalinī.
A decoction (kaṣāya) drunk with honey and combined with madana induces vomiting;
however, a purgative (virecana) should be administered using trivṛt, dantī, and the three fruits (phalatrika). As for the ointments (lepa) for skin diseases (kuṣṭha)...
They are applied to those from whom the faults of the impurities have departed and whose internal dispositions have been purified;
for them, success occurs immediately.
Realgar, red ochre, black pepper, sesame oil,
castor oil, milk, karañja seeds, and iḍagaja— this application, together with kuṣṭha, destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
An excellent external application is one ground with cow's urine.
Having ground the leaves of *Caturaṅgula* and the leaves of *Kākamācī* with buttermilk, [one should apply them].

For a man whose body has been anointed with oil, one should rub away the skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) using the leaves of the *aśvahan* tree. [Likewise,] *āragvadha*, *aiḍagaja*, and *karañja* [are used].
Vāsā, guḍūcī, madana, the two types of haridrā, śryāhva, surāhva, khadira, dhava, nimba, viḍaṅga, and karavīraka. || 8 ||
And the granthi, bhūrja, garlic, śirīṣa, salomaśa, guggulu, kṛṣṇagandhā, phaṇijjaka, vatsaka, and saptaparṇī—
Pīlu, kuṣṭha, the sprouts of sumana, vacā, hareṇu, trivṛt, kumbhī,
bhallātaka, gairika, and añjana.
Realgar, orpiment, soot from a house, cardamom, green vitriol, lodhra, arjuna, musta, and sarja—
these six are prepared in half-measurements. || 10 ||
Furthermore, these same powders, soaked in cow-bile and ground again, should be prepared by the physician and applied as dusting powders or plasters mixed with mustard oil. || 11 ||
It cures skin diseases, difficult urination, fresh leucoderma,
alopecia (surendralupta), kiṭibha, and sadadru, as well as fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, scrofula, and scabies.
When applied, these quickly destroy [the worms] of men:
realgar, cinnamon bark, *kuṭaja*, along with *kuṣṭha*,
*salomaśa*, *aiḍagaja*, and *karañja*.
A knot of birch bark and the root of karavīra,
these powders should be prepared with *tuṣodaka* or with the juice from the burning of *palāśa*.
They prescribe a paste of *dārvī* (daruharidrā) measured by one *āḍhaka* for every *karṣa* [of the other ingredients]; this application is said to be supreme for the destruction of *kuṣṭha*. || 14 ||
Kuṣṭha, the two types of haridrā, sarasa, paṭola, nimba, aśvagandhā, devadāru, śigru,
along with mustard seeds, tumburu, dhānya, and vanya—

One should prepare *caṇḍā* and *dūrvā* in equal proportions. With these, mixed with buttermilk, one should first endeavor to rub the body— which has been anointed with oil— in order to perform anointment (*udvartana*).
Likewise, his itching, pustules, wheals,
skin diseases, and swellings come to an end.
[The compound] *dhātryakṣapathyākrimiśatruvahni-*...
An ointment made from bhallātaka, āvalguja, iron, and bhṛṅga— increased in parts by one for each successive ingredient and mixed with sesame oil—
destroys all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha). || 17 ||
A plaster made from *viḍaṅga*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *śivā*, *śaśirekhā*, mustard, *karañja*, and *rajanī*, ground with cow’s urine, destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) like the sun.
[18] [Also prepared] from *viḍaṅga*, *aiḍagaja*, *kuṣṭha*, *niśā*, rock salt, and mustard...
This plaster, made from grains soaked in sour gruel (dhānyāmla) and ground together, removes the pain of ringworm and skin diseases (dadrū-kuṣṭha).
Dūrvā grass, abhayā, rock salt, cakramarda, and kuṭheraka, ground with sour gruel (kāñjika) and buttermilk (takra), [are similarly applied].
By three applications of this ointment, they ward off ringworm and leprosy that have taken deep root.
The juice of the *sāla* tree is equal [in measure] to chaff.
Even for one afflicted by ringworm, a plaster made from *abhayā* mixed with water and flour, ground together with water and applied at that time,
is a lion to the elephant-king of *dadru*. (21)
The seeds of *prapunnāḍa*, *dhātrī*, resin of *sarja*, and *snuhī*, ground with *sauvīra* [alkali], is an excellent ointment for ringworm (*dadrū*).
Equal parts of the seeds of *cakramarda* and *karañja* [are also used].
A small amount of the root of *sudarśana* destroys ringworm and leprosy (23).
Both by application as an ointment and by ingestion, *tṛṇaka* likewise destroys ringworm.
And the root of *yūthī* and *punnāga*, ground with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), [cures it] when applied as an ointment (24).
The root of *kāsamarda* ground with *sauvīra* (sour gruel) conquers *dadru*, *kiṭibha*, and *kuṣṭha* through the application of this as an ointment.
(25) *Mūlaka* seed well-ground with the juice of *śikhari* [sorrel] [cures] *sidhma* through the application of an ointment.
Or one destroys it with the alkali of the plantain mixed with turmeric (26).
Ground with the powder of sulphur and barley-alkali, or with pungent oil, it quickly goes to the destruction of sidhma. (27)
The seeds of *kāsamarda* and likewise those of radishes,
mixed with sulphur (*gandhapāṣāṇa*), are the supreme medicine for *sidhma*.
The juice of *dhātrī*, resin of *sarja*, and *sapākya* [are also used].
Likewise, when combined with ground *sauvīra* (antimony),
it acts as an exfoliant (*udvartana*) such that the *sidhma* spots do not recur. || 29 ||
Kuṣṭha, radish seeds, priyaṅgu, mustard seeds, and turmeric— this "hair-destroying" (keśara) kuṣṭha preparation destroys even long-standing sidhma.
Having repeatedly smeared the body with the expressed juice of blue kuruṇṭaka leaves...
An ointment made from the roots and seeds of *limpa* with buttermilk (*takra*) indeed destroys *sidhma*.
A plaster of *cakrāhvaya*, saturated with the milky sap of *snuhī* and mixed with urine,
heated slightly by the sun, removes *kiṭibha* when applied.
One should grind the leaves of *āragvadha* with sour gruel (*āranāla*); this destroys ringworm, *kiṭibha*, leprosy, and even *sidhma*.
Alternatively, one may use the seeds of radish or mustard.
Having ground lac, the two types of *prapuṇāḍa* seeds, *śrīveṣṭaka*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *viḍaṅga*, and *kuṣṭha* with urine, it should be used as an ointment. || 34 ||
It destroys ringworm, vitiligo, kiṭibha, scabies, kapāla-leprosy, and irregular skin diseases,
This ointment destroys worms, skin spots, ringworm, and leprosy.
(36) A paste of mustard seeds cooked over a smoldering fire applied to the stem of the *snuk* plant cures eczema (*vicarcikā*), just as a surge of passion overcomes shame. (37)
Having burnt bamboo stalks in a hollow space, along with soot from a house, rock salt, *antardhūma*, and oil, an ointment applied [to the skin] destroys *vicarcikā*.
[Likewise, a paste of] *eḍagaja*, sesame seeds, mustard, *kuṣṭha*, *māgadhikā*, and the three salts, mixed with whey...

This, having been fermented for three days, destroys scabies, ringworm, and leprosy. 39. Castor oil should be cooked with the seeds of *unmattaka* and alkaline water from *māṇaka*; it quickly destroys elephantiasis (*vipādikā*). 40.
Rice placed in coconut water becomes putrid; [likewise], through this application, it destroys chronic elephantiasis (vipādikā) that has persisted for a long time. Sarjarasa and Sindhusambhava...
This proven preparation— consisting of jaggery, honey, mahiṣākṣa, red ochre, ghee, and beeswax— when cooked together, cures the cracking of the feet.
Avalguja, kāsamarda, and cakramarda combined with niśā,
taken in equal parts with māṇimantha and ground with whey and sour gruel (kāñjika)—
this proven king of formulations conquers even severe scabies and itching. (43)
A tender lion-face petal,
ground with fragrant water along with rock salt,
certainly [acts] within three days. || 44 ||
Two palas of cow’s urine mixed with a paste of turmeric destroys itch when applied as an ointment;
if a man who acts according to his desire drinks it, it destroys both itch and scabies. (45)

Haritaki (Pathyā), prepared with cow’s urine, cures edema and anemia, removes abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, and phlegm, and indeed destroys scabies and skin rashes. One who drinks the powder of Gaṇḍapāṣāṇa along with mustard oil [attains similar results].

One who is afflicted by leprosy, having been thoroughly heated by the rays of the sun for half a *pala* [of time], then sprinkled with milk for three days, and subsisting on a diet of milk, quickly becomes endowed with the luster of gold and possessed of desire. (47)
With the leaves of *niśā*, *sudhā*, *āragvadha*, and *kākamācī*, along with *darvī* and the seeds of *prapuṇāṭa*,
ground together with buttermilk and mixed with mustard oil;
This is prescribed as a medicinal paste for ringworm and similar skin ailments.
Powdered vermilion and black pepper, combined with buffalo butter and applied repeatedly as an ointment, destroys ringworm; or alternatively, oil processed with oleander (karavīra) may be used.
The group of drugs consisting of māṃsī, candana, sampāka, karañja, ariṣṭa, sarṣapa,
śaṭī, kuṭaja, dārvī, and abda destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha). [Also] bhallātaka, dvīpi, sudhā, and the root of arka...
Having cooked together guñjā fruit, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), conch powder, blue vitriol (tuttha), kuṣṭha, the five salts, the two alkalis (kṣāra), and lāṅgalikā; || 51 ||
One should prepare a thick paste from the milky sap of *snuhā* and *arka* placed in an iron vessel,
and apply it with a probe as an ointment for leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), vitiligo (*kilāsa*), and freckles (*tilakālaka*).
For all manner of malignant growths (*durnāman*) and *carmakīla*,
[one should use] poison, *varuṇa*, turmeric, *citraka*, soot, fire, black pepper, and *dūrvā* grass, along with the milk of *arka* and *snuhī*.
The crescent moon, together with the heartwood of the viḍaṅga, burns away all types of leprosy as soon as it is applied, like a thunderbolt released from the hand of Indra in his wrath. (53) 10.
The crescent moon, together with the heartwood of the viḍaṅga...
Taken as a linctus with long pepper, the roots of *hutāśa*, sour gruel, *āmalaka* fruit, and oil, it destroys all types of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). (54)
One whose body is afflicted by severe leprosy should eat *somarājī* according to the prescribed rule for one year, accompanied by black sesame seeds.
That [Vāgujī] surpasses Somarājī in its beauty.
One who consumes warm water while following a regimen of hot [medicines],
and drinks Vāgujī while subsisting on milk, shall be freed from the disease of leprosy after three weeks.
One part of sesame and two parts of *somarājī*—
this, when consumed in the morning, destroys secret skin diseases (*guhyadadru*).
Having drunk one *karṣa* of *avalguja* seeds with lukewarm water, [the same result follows].
Food prepared with clarified butter (sarpiṣ) should be consumed, as it destroys all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
This decoction, consisting of triphalā, paṭola, rajanī, mañjiṣṭhā, rohiṇī, vacā, and nimba, when practiced regularly, destroys skin diseases born of kapha and pitta.
Or else, the natural juice of the *chinna* plant may be consumed according to one's strength;
once it has been digested, one should eat a small amount with ghee, or with vegetable broth or water.
Even a person whose body is extremely foul-smelling shall become possessed of a divine form. (60)
A patient suffering from skin diseases (kuṣṭha) who observes a bitter diet should drink a decoction made from paṭola, khadira, ariṣṭa, triphalā, and black vetra; this removes the skin disease.
[One should also take] sesame, ghee, triphalā, honey, vyōṣa, bhallātaka, and sugar.
These seven are aphrodisiacs; they are equal [in potency], purifying, and destroyers of skin diseases for those who act according to their desires.
(62) The powder of viḍaṅga, triphalā, and kṛṣṇā, licked with honey, destroys skin diseases, worms, urinary disorders, sinus ulcers, and fistulas. (63)
Having taken the "Indra-stone" (vajra) extracted on an auspicious day, one should lick its powder with honey and ghee while subsisting on milk and ghee.
Having destroyed all forms of leprosy, one shall live for two hundred years. (64–65)
Whoever should eat *abhayāriṣṭa* or black pepper and *āmalaka* shall conquer all forms of leprosy after one month; of this there is no doubt.
The juice of *khadira* wood, extracted from the root, should be placed in a pot that is being heated over a fire.
This elixir, consisting of ghee, dhātrī juice, and honey, destroys leprosy (kuṣṭha).
A pill prepared from vayasthā, iḍagaja, kuṣṭha, and kṛṣṇā, ground with goat’s urine, destroys vitiligo (śvitra) when applied as an ointment.
The tender leaves of *pūtīka*, *arka*, *snuh*, *narendradruma*, and *saumanasa*, ground with urine and applied as a paste,
destroy vitiligo and ringworm sores.
It cures leprosy, hemorrhoids, fractures, and sinus ulcers (69).
By anointing with the soot from the skins of elephants, leopards, and tigers,
or by anointing with *pūtikīṭa* insects, vitiligo shall go to destruction (70).

One *kuḍava* of *avalguja* seeds mixed with a fourth part of yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), ground with cow’s urine, is a supreme remedy for making the skin uniform in color in cases of vitiligo (*śvitra*).
Having drunk a decoction of *dhātrī* and *khadira* combined with *avalguja*, [one attains the same result].
It undoubtedly and swiftly destroys vitiligo as white as a conch shell or the moon.
When elephant dung has been burnt and much elephant urine has been poured over it, [it is applied]. || 72 ||
Having added one-tenth part of *droṇa* measure [of oil], one should cook the seed of *avalguja*;
when this reaches a state of黏稠ness (viscosity), [it is ready].
Then one should employ the well-perfected pill;
having smeared the universe with it, whatever is rubbed by that [pill] then quickly attains the state of being the same color. (74)
The root of white jayantī ground and drunk with cow’s milk certainly destroys vitiligo on Sundays; this is the command of Vaidyanātha.
During the flowering season, one should take its flowers, and during the fruiting season, its fruits.
Having crushed the bark, roots, and leaves of *picumarda*,
one should collect two parts of each and prepare them as single portions.
[Then add] *triphalā*, the three acridities (*tryūṣaṇa*), *brāhmī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *aruṣkara*, and *agnika*.
Take equal parts of viḍaṅga essence, vārāhī, iron powder, and amṛtā, along with the two types of haridrā, avalguja, and vyādhighāta, together with sugar,
kuṣṭha, indrayava, and pāṭhā; having prepared these well-mixed powders, [administer them].
One should saturate the five-nimb preparation seven times with a thick decoction of khadira, asana, and nimba, and then with the fresh juice of mārkaava;

One should drink one *pala* [of the powder] with honey, or with bitter clarified butter (*tiktahavis*), or with water boiled from *khadira* wood, or as a linctus with warm water; this dose should be increased by one *kola* daily.

Eczema, fig-like sores, white lotus-like eruptions,
skull-like lesions, ringworm, scabies, itching, and the like; [as well as] hundred-petalled sores, boils, erysipelas, and scabies.
The three types of kilāsa caused by the provocation of kapha, fistula-in-ano, elephantiasis, vātarakta,
congenital blindness, sinus ulcers, and diseases of the head.
It destroys all types of prameha, all forms of pradara, the venom of fangs, and root-poison.
One who has a large belly becomes one with a belly as lean as a lion's.

Those who bite, such as serpents and the like, go to their swift destruction through the consumption of honey, even when it is applied in small quantities, provided the joints [of the wound] are well-knit. || 85 ||
May he live long, free from disease and old age, delighting in auspicious things and possessing a luster equal to the moon.
[One should take] citraka, triphalā, vyoṣa, ajājī, kāravī, and vacā.
Saindhava salt, ativiṣā, kuṣṭha, cavya, elā,
yāvaśūka, viḍaṅga, ajamodā, mustā, and amaradāru— taking all these ingredients in equal parts, one should add an amount of guggulu equal to the total weight of them all.
