one should consume them according to one's strength at the time of the morning meal.
This destroys the eighteen types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), as well as worms and malignant ulcers.
It quickly subdues disorders of the digestive tract, hemorrhoids, diseases of the mouth, throat obstructions, sciatica, fractures,
and abdominal tumors; it conquers other diseases located in the internal organs just as Viṣṇu conquers the Asuras.
Having cut five *bhallātaka* fruits, one should prepare a decoction according to the prescribed method;
one should drink that when cold, with the lips and palate smeared with ghee.
One should drink it, increasing by five [fruits] each time until reaching seventy, and thereafter decrease [the dose].
When digested, one should eat cold boiled rice accompanied by ghee and milk.
This is a rejuvenative tonic that promotes intelligence, destroys wrinkles and graying hair,
cures skin diseases, hemorrhoids, worms, and humors, and eliminates defects of the semen.
One should drink the oil of *bhallātaka* for a month according to one's strength;
freed from all afflictions, one shall live firmly for a hundred years.
[This applies] in the acts of anointing, rubbing the body, bathing, drinking, and eating.
Water boiled with *khadira* destroys all skin diseases.
[One should take] *nimba*, *paṭola*, *dārvī*, *durālabhā*, *tiktakarohiṇī*, and *triphalā*.
One should take half-pala portions of parpaṭaka and trāyamāṇā.
When the decoction of these, boiled in one āḍhaka of water, has been reduced to one-eighth part,
one should strain it and add sandalwood, kirātatiktaka, māgadhikā, and trāyamāṇā.
Mustā and the seeds of vatsaka should be made into a paste in portions of half a karṣa each; this, along with six palas of fresh ghee, should be prepared as a medicated ghṛta to be drunk.
It cures skin diseases (kuṣṭha), fever, abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya), and edema (śvayathu).
It cures scabies, erysipelas, pustules, itching, and dermatitis when prepared with [the aforementioned ingredients].
One should take ten palas each of nimba, paṭola, vyāghrī, guḍūcī, and vāsaka, and grind them well. 100–101.
One *droṇa* of water should be boiled down until one-fourth remains;
with that, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee, adding the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) as an internal ingredient.
This is known as Pañcatikta ghee, which destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
By drinking it, one casts away eighty diseases born of wind, forty born of bile, and twenty born of phlegm;
it also destroys malignant ulcers, worms, hemorrhoids, and the five types of cough. (103-104)
Having boiled triphalā, dvinisā, vāsā, yāsa, pārpaṭaka, kūlaka, trāyantī, kaṭukā, and nimba— each measured at two palas—
in one droṇa of water, until one-fourth remains; with that decoction, [one should proceed].

One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with the pastes of *pippalī*, *ghanasārā*, *candana*, *trāyantī*, *śakra*, and *bhūnimba*. When drunk, this Tikta-ghṛta destroys skin diseases, fever, hemorrhoids, swelling, and disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*).
This is also recommended for jaundice, erysipelas, and even for those who are impotent.
[One should take] *saptacchada*, *prativiṣā*, *sampāka*, *tiktarohiṇī*, *pāṭhā*, *musta*, *uśīra*, *triphalā*, *paṭola*, *picumarda*, and *parpaṭaka*.
Dhanvayāsa with sandalwood, upakulyā, padmaka, the two types of rañjanī, ṣaḍgranthā along with viśālā, both types of śatāvarī and śāriva;
vatsaka seeds, vāsā, mūrvā, amṛtā, and kirātatikta. || 109 ||
The wise physician should prepare a paste (kalka) of *yaṣṭyāhva* and *trāyamāṇā*.
The paste constitutes one-fourth part,
water eight parts, and the juice of *amṛtaphala* [is added].
Twice the amount of ghee should be added; this prepared clarified butter should be administered to cure skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta). || 111 ||
It cures powerful hemorrhoids, blood-discharging diseases, erysipelas, acid dyspepsia (amlapitta), and anemia caused by wind and blood (vātāsṛkpāṇḍuroga). || 112 ||
Eruptions with scabies, insanity, jaundice, fever, anemia,
heart disease, abdominal tumors, and carbuncles—
This ghee, when drunk at the proper time according to one's strength, immediately destroys excessive menstrual discharge (masṛgdara) and scrofula (gaṇḍamālā).
From the hundredfold yogas, [one may obtain] the Mahāvikāra and the Mahātiktaka, which are difficult to conquer;
[therein are] five *tulās* of *khadira*, and one *tula* each of *śiṃśapā* and *asan*.
All these—karañja, ariṣṭa, and vetasa—are each half a tulā;
likewise parpaṭa and kuṭaja, which are aphrodisiacs and destroyers of worms, as well as the two types of haridrā, kṛtamāla, guḍūcī, triphalā, and trivṛt. || 115–116 ||
One should crush seven-leafed *saptaparṇa* in ten *droṇas* of water and strain the decoction until one-eighth remains. Then,
one should cook it with an equal portion of *dhātrī* juice and one *āḍhaka* of clarified butter.
With the pastes of great bitter herbs as previously described, measured at one pala each,
it destroys all types of skin diseases through drinking, massage, and application;
this is known as Mahākhadira, the supreme destroyer of kuṣṭha.
One should boil ten palas each of nimba, amṛtā, vṛṣa, paṭola, and nidigdhikā separately in a pot of water; then,
with the water reduced to one-eighth and well-strained, [one should proceed].
One should cook one *prastha* of clarified butter with a paste consisting of one *picu* each of *pāṭhā*,
*viḍaṅga*, *suradāru*, *gajapippalī*,
the two types of alkali (*dvikṣāra*), *nāgara*, *niśā*, *miśi*, *cavya*, and *kuṣṭha*.
With *tejovatī*, black pepper, *vatsaka*, *dīpyaka*, *agnirohiṇī*, *uruṣkara*, *vacā*, and the root of *kaṇa*,
along with *mañjiṣṭhā*, *ativiṣā*, *yavānī*, and *yamānī*... [121]
Even with five pure pieces of guggulu resin, when consumed, it subdues extremely powerful wind disorders— even those residing in the joints, bones, and marrow— as well as leprosy of this kind. (122)
It cures sinus ulcers, tumors, fistula-in-ano, cervical lymphadenitis,
and all types of abdominal tumors located above the clavicle; it also treats hemorrhoids, urinary disorders,
consumption, anorexia, asthma, chronic catarrh, cough, and wasting.
Heart disease, anemia, throat abscesses,
and gout [are cured by] vāsā, guḍūcī, triphalā, paṭola, karañja, nimba, aśana, and kṛṣṇavetra.

Ghee cooked with the decoction and paste of those [drugs] is declared to be "Vajraka," which cures leprosy; it heals even those whose ears, fingers, hands, and feet are shattered. || 124 || viśīrṇakarṇāṅgulihastapādaḥ || 124 ||
Even a mortal whose throat is torn by worms and who suffers from leprosy shall regain his ancient luster and live for a hundred years without hindrance. 125
One who knows the proper procedure should cook oil with āragvadha, dhava, kuṣṭha, yellow orpiment, realgar, and the two types of turmeric;
by anointing with this, the person afflicted with vitiligo will find that the white spots quickly disappear.
Oil prepared with mañjiṣṭhā, aruṇa, niśā, cakramarda, and the tender leaves of āragvadha, along with the fresh juice of tṛṇaka, is pungent and destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
[127] Haridrā, triphalā, dāru, hayamāraka, and citraka... [128]
Saptacchada, nimba bark, karañja, bālaka, nakho, kuṣṭha, seeds of meḍagaja, lāṅgalī, gaṇikārikā,
jātī leaf, dārvī, haritāla, and manaḥśilā. || 129 ||
Kaliṅga, atīsa leaf, arka milk, and guggulu;
jaggery, cinnamon bark, black pepper, saffron, granthiparṇaka, sarja, parṇāśa, khadira, viḍaṅga, long pepper, and vacā. (130–131)
Ghana, reṇu, amṛtā, yaṣṭikā, keśara, dhyāmaka, viṣa, viśva, kaṭphala, mañjiṣṭhā, bola, the fruit of tumbī,
as well as the leaves of snuhī and sampāka, and the seeds of vāgujī and māṃsī; || 132 ||
The root of elā-jyotiṣmatī, śirīṣa, and the juice of cow dung;
candana, kuṣṭha, nirguṇḍī, viśālā, the two types of mallikā, vāsā, aśvagandhā, brāhmī, śryāhva, campaka, and kaṭphala. (133–134)
One should cook oil with these pastes along with the liquid juice of *tṛṇaka*; this is known as Mahātṛṇaka, which removes all skin diseases.
[It is prepared from] the [oils] derived from *saptaparṇa*, *karañja*, *arka*, *mālatī*, and *karavīra*.
The roots of snuhā and śirīṣa, as well as those of citraka and āsphota;
karañja seeds, triphalā, the three pungents (trikaṭu), the two types of turmeric (rajanīdvaya), siddhārthaka, viḍaṅga, along with prapunnāḍa and sesame—these [should be used]. || 136–137 ||
One should cook oil with these ingredients ground with urine; this oil, named Vajraka, destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha) when used as an ointment and removes sinus tracts and malignant ulcers.
[138] 27. Black pepper, realgar, *arka* milk, *aśvārijaṭā*, and *trivṛt*...

One should cook one *prastha* of *kaṭutaila* (mustard oil) with cow-dung juice, *viśālā*, *āruṣkara*, the two types of *niśā* (turmeric and *dāru-haridrā*), *dāru* (deodar), and *candana*, along with two *akṣa* measures each of [the aforementioned herbs] and one *pala* of *viṣa*.
When used as an ointment (*abhyaṅga*), it destroys *dadru* and *śvitra*.
This oil is recommended for all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
[The ingredients are: black pepper, trivṛt, dantī, milk, the latex of *arka*, the juice of cow dung, devadāru, the two types of haridrā, māṃsī, kuṣṭha, and sandalwood. (140–141)
Viśālā, karavīra, haritāla, manaḥśilā, citraka, lāṅgalākhya, viḍaṅga,
cakramardaka, śirīṣa, kuṭaja, nimba, saptaparṇa, snuhī, and amṛtā. || 142 ||
Sampāka, naktamāla, abda, khadira, pippalī, vacā, and jyotiṣmatī—one pala each; two palas of poison;
one āḍhaka of mustard oil (kaṭutaila); and four times that amount of cow urine. || 143–144 ||
One should cook this excellent oil slowly over a mild fire in either an earthen or an iron vessel; having cooked it, one should apply it to ulcers arising from internal heat,
as well as to scabies, eczema, ringworm, itching, and eruptive boils.
Wrinkles, graying hair, dark spots, and discoloration are likewise eliminated by massage, and a state of youthful delicacy is produced.
This [oil] should be administered as a nasal drop to women in their first stage of life.
Even upon reaching extreme old age, the breasts do not lose their firmness.
Whether it be an ox, a horse, or an elephant, when afflicted by wind, its strength will become intense through these ointments. 147–148.
Naktamāla, the two types of Haridrā, Arka, Tagara, Karavīra, Vacā, Kuṣṭha, Āsphotā, Raktacandana,
Mālatī, Saptaparṇa, Mañjiṣṭhā, and Sindhuvārikā. || 149 ||
Taking half-pala portions of these and one pala of poison,
one should cook one prastha of oil in four times as much cow urine.
This cures vitiligo, eruptive boils, kiṭibha, insect bites, spider venom, and eczema.

This oil, known by the name Viṣataila, purifies all wounds, including those afflicted by the disorders of itching and scabies, as well as those corrupted by poison. [The ingredients are: the juice of white Karavīra, cow’s urine, Citraka, and Viḍaṅga.
(152) 30. [The juice of] white Karavīra, cow’s urine, Citraka, and Viḍaṅga.

This proven application of oil for skin diseases (kuṣṭha) is approved by physicians. Oil prepared with the root of white oleander (śvetakaravīra), one part of which is combined with poison (viṣa), and boiled in cow’s urine, cures leucoderma (carmadala), scabies (pāmā), vitiligo (sidhma), eruptions (visphoṭaka), worms, and thickened patches (kiṭibha).

Having ground half a *pala* of vermilion (*sindūra*) and likewise one *pala* of cumin (*jīraka*), one should cook them in mustard oil; this is a supreme remedy that instantly removes scabies (*pāmā*). One should collect priyaṅgu, padmaka, kuṣṭha, mañjiṣṭhā, khadira, vacā, jāti, arka, trivṛtā, nimba, karañja, viṣa, kṛṣṇavetra, kalodhra, and prapunnāḍa. (156–157)
One should grind all these ingredients finely and administer them with the appropriate quantity of oil; when used as an ointment for massage, it destroys all types of *kuṣṭha*,
as well as *pāmā*, *vicarcikā*, itching, *visarpa*, and other such ailments.
It destroys many such diseases arising from blood and bile (raktapitta). 159.
Oil cooked with the sun (ādityapāka) using powdered mañjiṣṭhā, triphalā, lākṣā, niśā, śilājatu, and gandhaka is supreme for removing skin diseases (pāmā). 160.
One should cook oil four times the quantity of *dūrvā* juice with its own natural essence;
by mere anointing, it destroys scabies, eczema, and ringworm.
Castor oil cooked with the juice of *arka* leaves and combined with *niśā* [turmeric] [achieves the same].
Or even combined with realgar (manaḥśilā), it destroys scabies, itch, and similar ailments.
[162] With gaṇḍīrikā, citraka, mārkava, arka, kuṣṭha, drumatvak, and salts, along with urine—
One should cook this oil, which removes ringworm, dandruff, leprosy, malignant ulcers, pain, and kiṭibha skin disease. [163] Then, from the roots of citraka, nirguṇḍī, and hayamāra—
One *pala* each of *nāḍī*, *bījādviṣa*, and ground *kāñjika*;
eight *palas* of *karañja* oil and one *pala* of *kāñjika* are mixed together and heated by the sun; this oil cures leprosy, ulcers, and hemorrhaging. (164–165)

One should cook mustard oil with *somarājī*, the two types of *haridrā*, mustard seeds, *āragvadha*, *gada*, the seeds of *karañja* and *eḍagaja*, and [the fruit] pulp; this removes sinus tracks and malignant ulcers. (166)
By this, the eighteen types of leprosy (kuṣṭha) are quickly pacified, as well as blue-black spots (nīlikā), pustules (piḍaka), facial blemishes (vyaṅga), deep-seated vāta-śoṇita, itching (kaṇḍū),
and the alleviation of difficult cases of scabies (kacchu) and skin eruptions (pāmā). || 167–168 ||
Every fortnight one should resort to emetics;
every month, one should also take purgatives;
and every three days, one should apply nasal drops.
One should let blood be drawn every six months for six months.

For those suffering from leprosy, the avoidance of women, meat, and wine, as well as aged *śāli* rice, mung beans, barley and other grains, bitter vegetables, and the meat of wild animals, is beneficial.
Chapter 50:

1. In cases of urticaria (udarda), one should first perform an oil massage with pungent oil (kaṭutaila) followed by a sprinkling with warm water; thereafter, emesis should be induced using a decoction of paṭola and ariṣṭa.
In this condition, purgation with Triphalā, Pura, and Kṛṣṇā is recommended;
or one should drink nine karṣas of Triphalā mixed with honey.
The physician should also employ the Amṛtādi formulation mentioned in the treatment of Visarpa here as well.
If a man who eats wholesome food should consume white sugar mixed with Madhuka, or jaggery with Āmalakas, or Dīpyaka with jaggery,
his urticaria arising throughout the entire body will vanish within seven days.
A massage with a paste of *siddhārtha*, turmeric, *prapunnāṭa*, and sesame seeds,
mixed with mustard oil, is beneficial.
An ointment combined with *dūrvā* grass and turmeric destroys scabies and skin rashes.
The root of Agnimantha, ground and drunk with clarified butter, is an excellent remedy for worms and parasites, as well as for cold-pitta (śītapitta).
It destroys cold-pitta, urticaria (udarda), and skin eruptions (koṭha) within seven days alone.

One should also follow the regimen prescribed for skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and that which pacifies acid dyspepsia (amlapitta). Furthermore, in the case of Koṭharoga, one should briefly perform the treatment mentioned for Udarda;
after drinking Mahātikta ghee, bloodletting should be carried out.
One should always consume the leaves of the nimba tree mixed with ghee and āmalakī; this cures eruptive boils, carbuncles, wounds, and śītapitta.
One should cause the bile associated with itching to be expelled suddenly.
One should apply an oil massage to the body using alkaline substances, rock salt, and oils;
furthermore, one should take ripe Gambhārikā fruit, dry it, and then steam it again.

When consumed with milk by one following a wholesome diet, it destroys cold-pitta (śītapitta); furthermore, the elādika group [of drugs] should be applied in conjunction with an oil massage and an ointment. It may also be taken with a soup of dried radish or with the broth of horse-gram (kulattha).
Food should always be prepared from the meat of the common quail (*lāva*) or the partridge (*tittiri*).
Having ascertained the movement of the *doṣas*, the physician should administer either cold food and drinks or hot ones at the appropriate time in cases of *śītapitta*.
In the case of amlapitta, after inducing emesis, one should administer a mild purgation;

A non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) should be administered when the disease has been long-standing, taking into account the humors (doṣas) and other factors; for once the body is purified by such treatment, pacifying therapy (śamana) should be applied according to the nature of the residual complications (anubandha).
When a disease arises from a combination of humors, a therapeutic regimen consisting of both medicine and diet must be devised.

The wise physician should eliminate upward-moving [doshas] with emetics and downward-moving ones with purgatives; he should also prescribe food or drink that is predominantly bitter. He should provide preparations of barley and wheat, free from sharp processing.
One should drink parched grain flour mixed with sugar and honey according to one's own constitution;
or, a decoction of dehusked barley, vṛṣa, and dhātrī, combined with the three aromatics and honey, when drunk, [cures these ailments].
It removes acid bile (amlapitta) if one eats it with mung bean soup;
it destroys phlegm, bile, vomiting, itching, fever, eruptions, and burning sensations.
A decoction of *śṛṅgavera* (ginger) and *paṭola* is digestive and appetizing.
Having boiled *paṭola*, *nāgara* (ginger), and *dhānya* (coriander) in water, one should drink it; it destroys itching, skin diseases, pain, and colic, and overcomes phlegm, bile, and weak digestion.
One should drink water prepared with *paṭola*, *viśva*, *amṛtā*, and *rohiṇī* in cases of an excess of *pitta* and *kapha*, as well as for colic, vertigo, loss of appetite, and weak digestion.
That [decoction] prevents burning fever and vomiting.
One should drink a decoction of barley, long pepper, and paṭola mixed with honey;
it destroys acid bile (amlapitta), as well as loss of appetite and vomiting.

A decoction made from vāsā, amṛtā, parpaṭaka, nimba, bhūnimba, mārkava, and the three myrobalans (triphalā) along with kulaka, mixed with honey, destroys acidity. A decoction of the three fruits (phalatrika), paṭola, and tiktā, combined with sugar [is also effective].
Yellow [ghee], when mixed with *klītaka* and honey, conquers fever, vomiting, and acid dyspepsia (*amlapitta*).
Powdered *pathyā* and *bhṛṅgarāja*, combined with aged jaggery, overcomes vomiting caused by acid dyspepsia and the burning sensation (*vidāha*) following food intake.
Combined with the consumption of *vāsā*, *nimba*, *paṭola*, *triphalā*, and *āsanaya*, this conquers excessive phlegm (*kapha*) and acid bile (*amlapitta*).
Guggulu should be administered gradually.
Alternatively, one may drink water boiled with Chinnā, Khadira, Yaṣṭyāhva, and Dārvī, mixed with honey;
or one should eat Abhayā together with grapes, honey, and jaggery.
A white electuary of *kaṭukā*, as well as *paṭola* and *viśva* combined with honey, are recommended;
or, in cases of hemorrhage, *khaṇḍakūṣmāṇḍaka* is excellent when used appropriately.
[Likewise, a preparation] with *paṭola*, *dhanyāka*, *mahauṣadha*, and *abda*...
A prepared decoction quickly destroys weak digestion and diseases caused by pitta, balāsa, burning sensations, vomiting, fever, undigested matter (āmā), wind (anila), and colic pain. || 16 ||
Three *pala* of well-decocted and well-cooled leaves of *chinnodbhava*, *nimba*, and *paṭola*,
combined with honey, [cures] bile of many forms.
Indeed, it destroys even the most severe *amlapitta*.

One should drink a decoction of *paṭola*, *triphalā*, and *nimba* mixed with honey for the alleviation of fever caused by *pitta* and *kapha*, as well as vomiting, burning sensations, and colic. 17–18.
By drinking a decoction of *siṃhāsya*, *amṛtā*, and *bhaṇḍākī* mixed with honey,
a person may conquer acid dyspepsia (*amlapitta*), cough, dyspnea, fever, and vomiting.
[One should also use] *vāsā*-ghṛta, *tikta*-ghṛta, and *pippalī*-ghṛta.
Likewise, jaggery and pumpkin (guḍakūṣmāṇḍaka) should be employed in cases of amlapitta.
Formulations that cure colic of the digestive tract (paktiśūla), as well as sugar and āmalakī combined with long pepper and honey, are destroyers of amlapitta.
The fresh juice of the jambīra fruit, drunk in the evening, destroys acid bile (amlapittaka).
A bolus (modaka) made from equal parts of jaggery, long pepper (pippalī),
and harītakī (pathyā) is said to remove bile and phlegm (pitta-śleṣman) and kindle a sluggish digestive fire.
Asafoetida, kataka fruits,
tamarind bark, and ghee roasted in a closed vessel (puṭapāka) pacify that [condition of] acid bile (amlapitta).
If the dose for each subsequent ruler of the earth (mamlabhuj) is doubled,
then the paste of *varā* soaked overnight and combined with sugar and honey, through the practice of regular application, is known to remove phlegm and bile.
One part of the five *nimba* fruits, double that amount of *vṛddhadāraka*,
and ten times as much sugar should be given, sweetened with sugar;
when drunk with cold water, it cures colic arising from *pitta* and *kapha*.
This powder, taken with honey, destroys even the most severe acid bile (amlapitta).
Then, abhraka (mica) ground with fresh rice-water and kept there for a time [is used];
likewise, [the juice] of kanda, māṇa, asthi-saṃhāra, khaṇḍa, and karṇa [is employed].

The physician should perform grinding, saturation, and roasting many times using *taṇḍulīya*, *śāli*, and the juice of *kālamāriṣa*, as well as those produced from *vṛścīra*, *bṛhatī*, *bhṛṅga*, *lakṣmaṇā*, and *keśarāja*. || 29–30 ||

Until it becomes free of any luster like that of the moon, such is the purification of the sky (the crucible). Then, gold, pyrite, and rice, having been smelted and quenched in water, as well as iron, magnetite, and so forth, should likewise be powdered in a decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā). || 31 ||

With the juices derived from *bṛhatpattra*, *karīka*, *karṇa*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *vṛddhadāra*; with those produced from *māṇakanda*, *asthi*, *saṃhāra*, and *śṛṅgavera*; and with those originating from *daśamūlī*, *muṇḍitikā*, and *tālamūlī*.
Having wrapped it with great care and effort, it will thus attain purity;
one should place vaśira, white vāṭyāla, madhuparṇī, mayūraka, taṇḍulīya,
and varṣābhū both below and above [the mercury].
One should cook iron rust (lohakiṭṭa) with old maṇḍūra and cow’s urine for three days;
having kept it inside [the vessel] without burning it while emitting steam, it should likewise be left for another three days.
Once pulverized, this is shown to be the purification of iron rust.
By means of the juice of *jayantī*, *vardhamāna*, and *ārdraka*,
and likewise following the sequence with *vāyasī*, this rubbing is the purification of the mercury.
Sulfur known as *navanīta* should be crushed in an iron vessel.
Dried three times in the fierce heat of the sun and saturated with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*,
it is then quickly melted in fire and strained through cloth;
when carefully cast back into the *bhṛṅgarāja* juice and dried again, it becomes purified.
Take two palas of powder from the sky (space), one pala of iron, and half a pala of iron dross; place all these together in one spot.
Then, [process them] with the juices of *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *vaśira*, and *tālamūlī*.

Then, one should take one *karṣa* each of mercury and sulphur, having powdered them together with *varī*, *bhṛṅga*, *kesara*, *rājaka*, *māriṣa*, *triphalā*, and *bhadramusta*, prepared from a pot-cooked (*sthālīpāka*) mixture. (41–42)
By rubbing that [substance] diligently in a stone mortar until it is reduced to a paste (kajjalī),
one should add vacā, cavya, yamānī, jīvaka, keśara, puṣpikā, vyoṣa, musta, viḍaṅga, granthika, and kharamañjarī. || 43 ||
Trivṛt, citraka, dantī, sūryāvarta, asita, bhṛṅga,
māṇakakanda, khaṇḍakarṇaka, daṇḍotpalā, keśarāja, kālāvaka, and kaḍaka as well. || 44-45 ||
Half a *pala* of each of these, finely powdered and rubbed on a cloth, as well as half a *pala* and one full *pala* respectively of each of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), should be taken.
Having thoroughly mixed all of this, one should then saturate it in an iron vessel.
In the sunlight, [the physician] should rub it with the juice of fresh ginger three times.
Having ground it with that same juice on a stone, the physician should form it into pills resembling the size of a jujube stone; once dried, he should store them in a well-protected place.
Three pills should be consumed at the beginning of the morning meal, followed by a drink of sour water that is free from sweet substances; this is beneficial.
Milk and coconut water, in particular, must be avoided.
Food as desired and pleasant, along with water, boiled rice, and sour gruel (amlakāñjika),
indeed cure various types of acid dyspepsia (amlapitta), colic born of digestion (pariṇāma-śūla), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), abdominal tumors (gulma), edema, ascites, and diseases of the anus. || 50–51 ||

This celebrated "Hunger-inducing Pill" (Kṣudhāvatī-guḍī) destroys consumption, the five types of cough, weak digestion, loss of appetite, splenic enlargement, asthma, flatulence, and most formidable rheumatism (āmavāta). (52)
Having ground ajājī together with dhanyāka, one should cook it with one prastha of ghee;
this removes kapha, pitta, and anorexia, and conquers weak digestion and vomiting.
[53] With the pastes of paṭola and śuṇṭhī, or with kulaka alone—
One prastha of ghee should be cooked [with these ingredients]; it is an excellent remedy for eliminating kapha and pitta.
Having risen in the morning, one should drink that ghee prepared with a decoction and paste of pippalī and saturated with honey to alleviate amlapitta.
With grapes, amṛtā, śakrapaṭola leaves, uśīra, dhātrī, ghanasāracaṃdana, trāyantikā, padmaka, kirāta, and dhānya;
One should cook ghee with these as pastes;
the physician should administer the proper dose along with the meal, and it may also be prescribed for drinking in all seasons.
This ghee quickly destroys increased *balāsa* (phlegm) and *pitta*, chronic dysentery (*grahaṇī*), cough, loss of digestive fire, fever, and acid gastritis (*amlapitta*).

For when properly prepared, it is indeed like nectar. (57) One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with an equal amount of milk and a paste of the root of *śatāvarī*, using a gentle fire, after adding four times as much milk. (58)
It destroys acid bile (amlapitta) and diseases arising from wind and bile (vātapitta),
as well as internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), thirst, fainting, dyspnea, and even high fever.
(59) Chapter 52.

One should treat the various types of visarpa according to the specific doṣa involved by means of purgation, emesis, ointments, affusions, and bloodletting, using drugs that do not cause a burning sensation.
[One may use] paṭola, picumarda, pippalī, and madana.
In cases of visarpa (erysipelas), emesis is recommended, as is the use of indrayava seeds.
Ghee combined with the juice of triphalā and trivṛt should be administered for the purpose of purgation to pacify visarpa and fever.

Or one should administer the juice of āmalaka mixed with ghee; the four groups of the five roots (pañcamūla-catuṣṭaya) should be employed, excluding grass, along with plasters, affusions, and medicated ghees, in cases of visarpa caused by vāta.
Kuṣṭha, śatāhvā, suradāru, mustā, vārāhī, kustumburu, kṛṣṇagandhā,
vātārkī, vaṃśā, and ārtagalā should be employed.
In cases of sprinkling, ointments, and likewise with ghee,
one should apply a plaster made of prapauṇḍarīka, mañjiṣṭhā, padmaka, uśīra, candana, yaṣṭīmadhu, and indīvara, ground with milk, for the treatment of pitta.
Kaśeru, śṛṅgāṭaka, padma, gundrā, along with śaivala, utpala, and mud,
filtered through a cloth, [are used] for visarpa caused by pitta.
Pastes (lepāḥ) mixed with ghee and made very cold should be applied;
affusions (pariṣekāḥ) and plasters made from the five barks (pañcavalkalaiḥ),
or from padmaka, uśīra, madhuka, and candana, are likewise recommended.
In the case of pitta, however, one should apply lotus-mud ground with conch-shell and *śaivala*,
or the root of *gundrā*, or oyster-shell, or red ochre (*gairika*), combined with clarified butter.
[Also] the roots of *nyagrodha*, *gundrā*, and the core of the plantain tree.
An ointment made from *viṣagranthi* should be saturated with clarified butter that has been washed a hundred times.
*Hareṇu*, *masūra*, and *mudga* beans, as well as *śāli* rice, may each be used individually as a poultice, or all together with clarified butter. || 10–11 ||
For visarpa (erysipelas), purification is beneficial when performed with grapes, āragvadha, kāśmarya, triphalā, eraṇḍa, pīlu, trivṛt, and harītakī. [Furthermore,
it is beneficial] with gāyatrī, saptaparṇa, arka, vāsā, āragvadha, and dāru.
An ointment made from *kuṭannaṭa* should be applied in cases of *visarpa* (erysipelas) arising from *śleṣman* (phlegm). Alternatively,
one may use *ajā*, *aśvagandhā*, *śaralā*, *kālā*,
*saikeśikā*, or *ajaśṛṅgī*.

A plaster prepared by grinding these with cow’s urine, when applied, very quickly destroys erysipelas born of kapha. [Madana, madhuka, nimba, and the fruits of vatsaka. 14. Madana, madhuka, nimba, and the fruits of vatsaka.
Emesis should also be administered in cases of visarpa arising from kapha.
A paste composed of triphalā, padmaka, uśīra, samaṅgā, karavīraka, the fruit and root [of harītakī], and anantā destroys kaphaja visarpa.
The leaves of *āragvadha* and the bark of *śleṣmātaka*, as well as *śirīṣa* flowers and *kāmācī*, are beneficial when used as a paste or for dusting [the skin].
A decoction of *mustā*, *ariṣṭa*, and *paṭola* cures all types of *visarpa*.
Alternatively, [a preparation] of *dhātrī*, *paṭola*, and *mudga* saturated with ghee;
or *amṛtā*, *viṣa*, and *paṭola* combined with the paste of *nimba*;
or an equal mixture of *triphalā*, the heartwood of *khadira*, and *vyādhighāta*.
This entire decoction, combined with a portion of guggulu, conquers poisons, erysipelas, and the eighteen types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
[It consists of] amṛtavṛṣa, paṭola, mustaka, and saptaparṇa.
Khadira, black vetra, nimba leaves, and the two types of haridrā remove various poisons, erysipelas, leprosy, eruptive boils, and itching; they also eliminate measles, chills, and fever. || 20 ||
A decoction made from *paṭola*, *amṛta*, *bhūnimba*, *vāsaka*, *ariṣṭa*, *parpaṭa*, *khadira*, and *abdayuta* (musta) removes the pain of eruptive boils (*visphoṭa*) and fever.
[21] A decoction made from *paṭola*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *ariṣṭa*, *guḍūcī*, *musta*, and *candana*...
One should administer this decoction consisting of *samūrvā*, *rohiṇī*, *pāṭhā*, *rajanī*, and *durālabhā*; it removes fever caused by *kapha* and *pitta*,
and destroys itching, skin diseases, eruptions, poison, and erysipelas (*vīsarpa*).
A decoction prepared with bhūnimba, vāsā, kaṭukā, paṭola,
the three fruits (triphalā), candana, and nimba cures erysipelas, burning sensations, fever, and the wasting away of the body.
When there is eruption, thirst, vomiting, and astringency,
one should administer Triphalā with honey when pitta is associated with kapha. Likewise, one should employ Duralabhā, Parpaṭaka, Paṭola, and Kaṭukā.
One should drink warm guggulu mixed with [the decoction of] khadira-aṣṭaka;
or water infused with kuṇḍalī and picumarda, or water infused with khadira and indrayava.
This quickly destroys eruptive boils (visphoṭa), just as the wind disperses clouds.
Sandalwood, nāgapuṣpa, taṇḍulīyaka, śārivā, and the bark of śirīṣa— this application of jasmine (jātī) is a destroyer of burning sensations.
Śuka-tree, natamāṃsī, rajanī, and padmā should be taken in equal parts.
A paste made by grinding these with cold water should be applied in cases of all types of eruptive boils (visphoṭa).
For eruptive boils, gargles consisting of the root of śirīṣa, mañjiṣṭhā, cavya, āmalaka, yaṣṭikā, and the sprouts of jātī mixed with honey are recommended.
Śirīṣa and udumbara are beneficial for irrigation and as plasters;
likewise, the bark of śleṣmātaka is beneficial as a plaster or for use in nasal drops (cyotana). [One may also use] śirīṣa, yaṣṭī, nata, candana, and elā...

An ointment consisting of these ten ingredients— māṃsī, the two types of haridrā, kuṣṭha, and bāla— combined with ghee, is prescribed as a remedy that removes erysipelas, itching, fever, and swelling. (32)
By applying a plaster made of śirīṣa, uśīra, nāgāhvā, and hiṃsrā, erysipelas, poisons, and eruptions are swiftly pacified; of this there is no doubt.
[33] With vṛṣa, khadira, paṭola leaves, and nimba—
Fresh ghee, quickly cooked with the decoction and paste of the bark of Amṛtā and Āmalakī, swiftly conquers the diseases of visarpa, along with kuṣṭha and gulma. || 34 ||
This *pañcatikta* ghee, cooked with *paṭola*, *saptacchada*, *nimba*, *vāsā*, the three fruits (*phalatrika*), and *chinnaruhā*, quickly destroys [fever].
[It cures] the three doṣas, eruptive boils, erysipelas, and itching.
|| 35 || Padmaka, madhuka, lodhra, the filaments of nāgapuṣpa, the two types of haridrā, viḍaṅga, sūkṣmailā, and likewise tagara; || 36 ||
One should stir together kuṣṭha, lākṣā, patraka, sikthaka, tuttha,
bahuvāra, śirīṣa, and kapittha fruit with water,
and then cook one prastha of ghee with that entire mixture.
O great sage, learn now those diseases which it indeed destroys:
those caused by the bites of snakes, insects, and rats; those produced by spiders and urine; various types of boils; as well as leprosy and erysipelas. (38–39)
In cases of glandular swellings (gaṇḍamālā), especially when they have burst,
the auspicious Padmaka Mahāghṛta prepared by Agastya is recommended.
As for the disease known as Snāyuka, its treatment is like that of Visarpa.
Having drunk cow’s ghee for three days, one should drink the fresh juice of *nirguṇḍī* for three days; this certainly destroys even the most virulent *snāyuka* worm—of this there is no doubt.
[One may also use] the roots and leaves of the *śobhāñjana*.
An ointment made from flour mixed with sour gruel and salt destroys diseases of the tendons; alternatively, an ointment made from the bark of the *mocaka* tree [achieves the same]. || 42 ||
Chapter 53: For all [types of poisoning], emesis is beneficial, induced by decoctions of *paṭola*, *ariṣṭa*, and *vāsaka*,
along with pastes of *vacā*, *vatsaka*, and *yaṣṭyāhvaphala*.
One should cause the patient to drink the juice of *brāhmī* with honey, or the juice of *hailamocikā*.
Once the patient has vomited, a purgative should be administered; however, for a weak man, a palliative treatment (*śamana*) should be given.
[One may also use] the exudate of *suṣavī* leaves combined with the powder of *haridrā*.
One should drink [this] for the pacification of horripilation, fever, eruptions, and smallpox.
For one whose humors have been removed by both [methods], the *masūrikā* eruptions dry up; they become free from complications, contain little pus, suppurate with little pain, and heal.
The root of Kaṇṭakumbha boiled according to the prescribed method,
taken with one māṣa of asafoetida and the seed of Jayā mixed with ghee, conquers the effects of poison when consumed by one who has fasted.
A yellow foot-powder made from sand,
or from the roots of *māghā* and *mūla*, or from the fibers of *damanaka* flowers mixed with pungent substances or even putrid matter.

Or, when the disease has first appeared, these formulations should be administered; having scooped out a handful and covered it, the medicine that is thus employed [is called a *yoga*]. 5. [A dose] which is administered after being taken up in a handful and covered is [known as such].
Those devoted to the practice of medicinal boluses call this the "fist-bolus" (muṣṭiyoga).
Alternatively, the root of uṣṭrakaṇṭaka or the root of anantā,
taken according to the prescribed rite and drunk with the water of the month of Jyeṣṭha, destroys smallpox.

Likewise, the root of *śṛgālakaṇṭaka* with water that has stood overnight destroys *masūrī*; and half a part of sulfur combined with mercury [destroys it]. Similarly, when the leaves of *niśā* and *ciñcā* are drunk with cold water, [the same result follows].
With as many Śelu leaves as there are syllables in the patient’s name,
when they are cut [into pieces], the fever subsides and does not increase; water that has been soaked [in them] and drunk with honey removes burning sensations and fever.
Or, for the purpose of drying the body, one may apply a cooling water-sprinkling made with *śelu* bark;
or [use] pungent substances, clarified butter, bamboo, indigo, barley, *vṛṣaka*, cotton, bone, and *brahmī*.
Incense made from their own juices, mayūra, and *kalākṣā* removes itching and similar conditions.
In the case of a disorder arising from Vāta, one should first administer a satiation (tarpaṇa) with parched grain flour mixed with sugar.
The meal should consist of bitter soups or the broth of gallinaceous birds.
[The decoction for this consists of] the two Pañcamūlas, Rāsnā, Dāru, Uśīra, and Durālabhā. || 12–13 ||
Sāmṛta, dhānyaka, and musta overcome [fevers] arising from vāta.
Guḍūcī, madhuka, rāsnā, the five roots (pañcamūla), and the smallest [root], candana, kāśmarya fruit, the root of balā, and vikaṅkata— [these are used for pitta-type fevers].
At the time of ripening, one should employ [this] for vāta-type masūrikā;
for pitta-type, [one should use] grapes, kāśmarya, dates, paṭola, ariṣṭa, vāsaka, parched grain, āmalaka, and dūsparśa, combined with sugar. || 15–16 ||
An ointment made from the bark of śirīṣa, udumbara, aśvattha, śelu, and nyagrodha, mixed with ghee, quickly destroys wounds, eruptions, and burning sensations.
[One should also use] durālabhā, parpaṭaka, bhūnimba, and kaṭurohiṇī.
In cases of [fever] born of kapha or born of pitta, one should administer it as a drink after decocting nimba,
parpaṭaka, pāṭhā, paṭola, kaṭurohiṇī, vāsā, durālabhā, dhātrī, uśīra, and the two types of candana.
This well-known decoction of nimba and other ingredients, when drunk with sugar, destroys the three doṣas and the asūrikā eruptions arising from fever and visarpa.
As for an eruption that has arisen and is about to enter [the body], one should lead it back outwards again. (20–21)
Water boiled with paṭola, kuṇḍalī, musta, vṛṣa, dhanvayavāsaka, bhūnimba, nimba, kaṭukā,
and parpaṭa pacifies masūrī in its undigested (āma) stage and dries it up once it has ripened.
There is nothing superior to this for the pacification of visphoṭa fever.
One should drink the root of paṭola and red taṇḍulīyaka combined with a paste of haridrā and āmalaka.
That very [juice] pacifies the burning sensation caused by eruptions and boils; it also removes fever accompanied by horripilation. Paṭola root and red taṇḍulīyaka—
In the same way, one should drink water well-decocted with *dhātrī* and *khadira*, once it has become perfectly cooled;
this is a supreme destroyer of the disease *masūrikā*. || 25 ||

A decoction made from *khadira*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *ariṣṭa*, *paṭola*, *amṛta*, and *vāsaka*— known as the "Eight-Limbed" (*aṣṭāṅga*)— conquers measles, smallpox, leprosy, erysipelas, eruptive boils, itching, and other such ailments. (26)
A decoction of amṛtā and other herbs conquers disorders consisting of pitta and kapha;
furthermore, the filaments of mātuluṅga ground with sauvīra vinegar,
when applied as a paste, quickly causes [the growth] to fall off and swiftly alleviates burning sensations.
A carbuncle arising on the foot causes a burning sensation in the feet.
For that condition, they highly recommend frequent irrigation with rice-water;
however, at the time of suppuration, the wind dries up all of them.

Therefore, nourishing treatment should be administered, and not a diet that is wholesome yet depleting. At the time of cooking, one should add the medicinal ingredients— guḍūcī, madhuka, drākṣā, moraṭa, and dāḍima— along with jaggery (guḍa).
By this means, [the doshas] quickly reach digestion and the wind (vāyu) does not become aggravated.
Alternatively, one should lick jujube powder with jaggery for the purpose of digestion; by this, those [doshas] consisting of vāta, pitta, and kapha are quickly digested.
For one afflicted by colic and flatulence, and trembling due to the wind (*vāyu*),
the juices of desert meat (*dhanvamāṃsa-rasa*) mixed with a little rock salt (*saindhava*) are recommended.
Soups (*yūṣa*) combined with the sour juices of pomegranate (*dāḍima*) are beneficial for those suffering from loss of appetite (*aruci*).
One should drink water that has been heated and then cooled, having been infused with *khadira* and *aśana*.
For purification, one should employ water produced by reciting the *Gāyatrī* many times over it, along with *jātī* leaves, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *dārvī*, betel nut, and *śamī*.
A decoction of *dhātrī* fruit and *madhuka*, mixed with honey,
is recommended for use as a gargle in diseases of the mouth and throat. They praise the irrigation of the eyes with water boiled from *gavedhu* and *madhuka*.
Madhuka, the three myrobalans (triphalā), mūrvā, the bark of dārvī, blue lotus (nīlotpala),
uśīra, lodhra, and mañjiṣṭhā— these are beneficial as a paste for eye-drops (cyotana). By this,
cataracts (masūrya) that have arisen in the vision are destroyed, and they do not progress further.
One should sprinkle the moistened [wound] with the powder of the five barks (*pañcavalkala*); some authorities desire it to be done with ashes, while others prefer the dust of cow dung.
Furthermore, out of fear of the falling of maggots, one should fumigate it with *śaralā* and other such substances.

For the purpose of pacifying the burning sensation of fever and for the purification of discharges, one should administer a decoction of *varā* with *guggulu*, or the eight drugs beginning with *khara*.
For the purification of the throat, one should lick the powder of *kṛṣṇā* and *abhayā* with honey. || 40–41 ||
Then one should employ the eight-ingredient electuary (aṣ᾽āṅgāvaleha) or a morsel of food prepared with ginger and other ingredients;
one should also administer the "five bitter" (pañcatikta) formulation through drinks, massages, and meals.
One should follow the regimen for treating ulcers and avoid oils and similar substances for a long time.
One should repeatedly apply [medicines] prepared with poison-destroying mantras;
likewise, some [afflictions] associated with blood should be treated by means of bloodletting.
[One should also use] turmeric, the two types of *uśīra*, *śirīṣa*, and *mustaka*.
An external application (pradeha) consisting of lodhra, bhadraśrī, and nāgakeśara removes perspiration, eruptive boils, erysipelas, skin diseases, foul odors, and hair loss. || 44 ||

A decoction prepared overnight with the sprouts of *bimbi*, *atimuktaka*, *aśoka*, *plakṣa*, and *vetasa* destroys the fear of smallpox (*masūrī*). On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, one should go to a house of *snuhī* accompanied by a red flag.
Placed upon a white-painted jar, it wards off the diseases of sin from afar. 46.
Adhikāra 54.
There, one should treat an *ajagallikā* that is still in its undigested (*āmā*) stage with leeches.
One should repeatedly apply a paste of oyster shell, saurāṣṭrī, and alkali.
One should liquefy a hard ajagallikā with applications of alkaline substances.
The physician should conquer anuśayī with a paste of śleṣmavidradhi.
One should conquer *vivṛtā*, *indravṛddhā*, *gardabhī*, *jālagardabha*,
*irivellikā*, and *gandhanāmā* in the same manner as one treats *pittavisarpa*.
One should heal the ulcers with clarified butter prepared with sweet medicinal herbs.
One should conquer Vidārikā with many bloodlettings, sudations,
and depletions, as well as with plasters made from Śigru and Devadāru.
A physician should treat Panasyikā and Kacchapikā according to this same procedure.
One should treat other hard swellings arising from the *doṣas*,
as well as *antrālajī*, *kacchapikā*, and *pāṣāṇagardabha*.
Having applied fomentation with *suradāru*, *śilā*, and *kuṣṭha*, one should apply an ointment.

An ointment [made of] manaḥśilā, alambuṣā, bhallātaka, sūkṣmailā, aguru, and candana destroys kapha, vāta, and swelling in the case of pāṣāṇagardabha. Having excised a valmīka with a surgical instrument, one should treat it with alkali and fire. 7–8.
One should cook neem oil with the paste of *jātī* leaf-buds;
this indeed destroys anthills that have many holes and many sounds. In cases of cracking feet (*pādadārī*), one should pierce the vein that cleanses the soles.
Once the feet have been prepared with oleation and sudation,
one should repeatedly apply an ointment made from a mixture of beeswax, fat, marrow, ghee, and alkali;
this should be combined with the powder of the resin known as *sarja* and rock salt (*saindhava*), saturated with honey and ghee.
Rubbing the feet with mustard oil produced by churning [the seeds] is beneficial;
or one may use water in which the ashes of upodakā, mustard, nimba, moca, karkāruka, and ervāruka have been dissolved.
Oil cooked with a portion of salt, when applied as an ointment, destroys *pādadārī* (cracking of the feet).
In the case of *alasa*, one should apply an ointment after the feet have been sprinkled with acidic liquids for a long time.
Repeatedly [apply a paste] of paṭola, ariṣṭa, kāśīsa, and triphalā. This ointment—
consisting of karañja seeds, rajanī, kāśīsa, madhuka, honey, rocanā, and haritāla— is beneficial for those suffering from alasa (loss of appetite).
An application of a paste made from lac and the juice of *abhayā* should be performed, or bloodletting should be carried out;
furthermore, the physician should give a crushed *jātī* leaf in cases of *alasa*.
Having anointed [the area] with oil prepared with the juice of *bṛhatī*, the wise [physician] should proceed.
Or one should rub [the area] with the powders of śilā, rocanā, and kāśīsa.
One should extract the kadara [fungus] and cauterize it with oil or fire.
Having fomented the cippa [disease] with warm water, one should excise it, anoint that wound, and [treat it]. 16–17.
Having applied powdered resin of the *sarja* tree and bound it, one should treat it like a wound.
Having ground *abhayā* in a black iron vessel with the fresh juice of turmeric,
one should repeatedly smear the ear-flap (*cippa*) with the resulting paste.
An ointment made from the roots of *cipiṭa*, *saṭaṅkaṇa*, and *āsphotā* bestows beautiful nails.
For *padminī-kaṇṭaka*, emesis induced with neem water is beneficial;
likewise, ghee prepared with neem water and mixed with honey is recommended for drinking.
An alkaline solution prepared from lotus stalks destroys the *padminī* [skin disease] when applied as an ointment;
alternatively, frequent rubbing with a paste of *nimba* and *āragvadha* is beneficial.
An ointment made from *nilī* and the root of *paṭola*, combined with clarified butter, is also beneficial.
In the case of *jālagardabha* disease, it immediately destroys the pain.
In *ahipūtanaka*, one should first purify the breast milk of the wet-nurse;
the washing of the ulcers should always be performed with decoctions of *triphalā* and *khadira*.
Ghee prepared with karañja, triphalā, and bitter herbs is beneficial for the child; especially rasāñjana is beneficial both for internal consumption and as an external application.
In the case of prolapse of the rectum, one should quickly lubricate the anus with unctuous substances and push it back inside.
Once it has entered, one should also apply intense pressure with a "cow-horn" (goṣphaṇā) bandage.
It is determined and declared that for one who eats tender lotus leaves mixed with sugar, there shall be no exit from the anus.

One suffering from prolapse of the anus should habitually consume vṛkṣāmla, anala, cāṅgerī, bilva, pāṭhā, and yavāgraja with buttermilk; this kindles the digestive fire. Furthermore, one should confidently smear the anus with cow's urine.
Protrusion of the rectum (gudabhraṃśa) is difficult to treat, yet it enters [back inside] quickly; of this there is no doubt.
Alternatively, one should apply a proper ointment to the rectum with the fat of mice, or one should foment the rectum with the flesh of a steamed mouse. || 28–29 ||
Ghee boiled with cāṅgerī, kola, curd, sour [gruel], ginger, and alkali should be drunk; it removes the pain of prolapse of the rectum.
Here, ginger and alkali are used as a paste, while the remainder is intended to be liquid.
Having boiled a large quantity of the five roots (*pañcamūla*)— excluding *mūṣikā*— in milk,
one should cook oil in that [decoction] along with drugs that subdue Vāta.
This oil cures prolapse of the rectum (*gudabhraṃśa*) through drinking and external massage.

In the case of *parikartikā*, having applied fomentation (*svedana*) and poultice (*upanāha*), and having anointed [the area] with ghee, one should then slowly introduce the skin [flap] as instructed.
One should apply a poultice of warm, fresh meat;
likewise, one should treat Avapāṭikā with oleation and sudation.
In the case of Niruddhaprakaśa, one should insert a double-ended tube made of gold or other metals.
Having inserted and left [the tube], one should sprinkle it with a small amount of oil or fat,
or with oil prepared from the fragrant substances of *vaca*, *dāru*, and *gandha* for three days. Again, a thicker tube should be applied to increase the flow of the channels.
Having avoided the *sevanī* (perineal raphe) with the surgical instrument, one should incise it and treat it like a common wound.
This same therapeutic procedure applies even when the anus is constricted;
it also applies to skin tags (*carmakīla*), moles (*jatumaṇi*), freckles (*masaka*), and birthmarks (*tilakālaka*).
Having extracted [the worm] with a surgical instrument, one should burn it completely with alkali or fire; by rubbing with the powder of *rubu* stalks, the destroyer of *masaka* [worms] prevails.
Alternatively, through rubbing with the ashes of a snake’s slough, the *masa* [worm] shall always attain pacification.

One should conquer facial eruptions (piḍakā), freckles (accha), dark spots (nīlikā), scars (vyaṅga), and sugar-like skin lesions (śarkarā) even in the young by means of venesection, medicinal pastes, and likewise by ointments;
a paste of lodhra, dhānya, and vacā removes the eruptions of youth.

Similarly, black pepper combined with *gorocanā* applied as a pleasant ointment, or an application of white mustard, *vacā*, *lodhra*, and rock salt, quickly destroys the pustules arising from youth; emesis also swiftly destroys them. (41)
For the minor limbs, an ointment consisting of *arjuna* bark with honey, or *mañjiṣṭhā* with honey, or white clay mixed with butter, or soot produced from the hoof of a white horse;
or red sandalwood, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *lodhra*, *kuṣṭha*, and *priyaṅgu*. (42–43)
The sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree and lentils (*masūra*) destroy facial blemishes and bestow radiance upon the face; an ointment for blemishes made with the blood of a rabbit is also recommended.
An application made to the face with lentils ground with ghee and mixed with milk [is likewise beneficial].
Within seven days, it will truly become radiant like the petal of a white lotus.
An ointment made from citron-root, clarified butter, realgar,
and the liquid from cow dung produces facial luster and conquers pimples, moles, and dark spots.
An ointment made of fresh butter, jaggery, honey, and the marrow of *kola* fruit cures facial freckles (*vyaṅga*).
Alternatively, the bark of *varuṇa* ground with goat’s milk serves the same purpose.
An application of the paste of *jātīphala* destroys blue moles, freckles, and similar blemishes.
In the evening, an anointing with pungent oil (kaṭutaila) clarifies the face.
[This is done] with kālīyaka, blue lotus, curd-whey, jujube stones, and madhuphali.
And the face becomes anointed with moon-like luster within seven nights [by using] smooth barley free from husks— || 49 || [The following line appears to be a fragment: tuṣarahitamasṛṇayava-
By applying a paste of powdered yaṣṭīmadhu and lodhra, the face attains a beautiful splendor that surpasses refined gold. || 50 ||
The face, when smeared with milk prepared from the two *rakṣoghna* herbs along with *śarvarī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *gairika*, [attains beauty].
It shines like the orb of the rising moon,
with [ointments made of] matured curds, reed-leaf arrows,
blue-lily petals, kuṣṭha, sandalwood, and uśīra.
The frown, acting as a tilaka-mark upon the beauty of the lotus-face, triumphs.
[52] With the two types of turmeric, licorice, kālīyaka, and kuca-sandalwood—
One should apply a paste made from *prapauṇḍarīka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *padma*, *padmaka*, saffron,
and the leaves of *kapittha*, *tinduka*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa*, mixed with milk; or one may perform an anointing with oil prepared from these same ingredients.
One who uses this constantly will quickly conquer moles, dark spots, freckles, and blemishes that disfigure the face, and shall make the face beautiful.
One should cook one *kuḍava* of oil with a decoction of *madhuka*.
With the pastes of *priyaṅgu*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *candana*, *utpala*, and *keśara*,
that oil named Kanaka is produced; it is supreme for bestowing beauty upon the face, and it is highly esteemed for cleansing *abhīru*, *nīlikā*, and *vyaṅga* [skin blemishes].
Take one karṣa each of mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, lākṣā, mātuluṅga, and yaṣṭīmadhu; with these,
prepare one kuḍava of oil along with twice that amount of goat’s milk, cooking it slowly over a mild fire.
By mere anointing, one shall destroy dark spots, pustules, and facial blemishes.
Through application for seven nights, the face becomes bright and full, free from wrinkles and graying hair, and comes to resemble gold.
Saffron, sandalwood, lac, madder, liquorice, kālīyaka, usīra, padmaka, and blue lotus;
the roots of the nyagrodha, the shoots of the plakṣa, and the filaments of the lotus.
One should boil one *pala* each of the decoctions of the two groups of five roots (*pañcamūla*) separately;
once reduced to one-quarter, it should be removed from the fire.
Then, [one should add] *mañjiṣṭhā*, *madhuka*, *lākṣā*, *pattaṅga*, and *madhuyaṣṭikā*.
With these [ingredients] measuring one karṣa each, one kuḍava of oil and twice that amount of goat’s milk should be cooked slowly over a mild fire.
When properly cooked, this is indeed excellent for clarifying the complexion of the face.
One shall destroy dark spots, pustules, and facial blemishes simply by means of anointment.
Through application for seven nights, the skin becomes like gold;
this *kuṅkumādya* oil was prepared in ancient times by the two Aśvins.
Saffron, *kiṃśuka*, lac, *mañjiṣṭhā*, red sandalwood, *kālīyaka*, *padmaka*, the filaments of the citron,
safflower, licorice, *phalinī*, and *madayantikā*.
The physician should cook one *prastha* of oil with two *niśās*, *rocanā*, *padma*, *utpala*, and *manaḥśilā*,
combined with the drugs of the *kākolyādi* group in quantities equal to one *akṣa* each, along with lac-resin and milk. || 68–69 ||

This oil, beginning with saffron and other ingredients, when used as an ointment, instantly makes the face resemble gold; it bestows nourishment, grace, and luster, generates good fortune and prosperity, and is an excellent means of subjugation. (70)
The physician should cook ghee with a paste made of madhuka, candana, kaṅgu, sarṣapa, padmaka, kālīyaka, haridrā, and lodhra; once cooked, he should strain it through a cloth.
Having added one-quarter part of saffron and beeswax, one should cook it over a gentle fire. When that is prepared, one should pour it into cold water and then extract it;
this is the ghee known as *varṇaka*, which clarifies the complexion.
Indeed, by this practice, even a face that has become wrinkled will gradually become like the spotless orb of the moon, possessed of beauty, once it is anointed with [the remedy].
When blood has been sprinkled in the case of herpes (arūṃṣikā), [it should be treated as follows].

Then, after venesection or by means of leeches, an ointment made from the fat of a horse, varuṇa, and rock salt should be applied to the head, which has been sprinkled with water infused with nimba. || 75 ||
An ointment made of old oil-cake (piṇyāka), cow dung, or chicken excrement ground with urine will quickly destroy arūṃṣikā.
Powdered fried kuṣṭha combined with oil is a destroyer of arūṃṣi.
This oil, prepared with the two types of haridrā, bhūnimba, triphalā, ariṣṭa, and candana, is beneficial when used as an ointment for the healing of aruṃṣi (scars).
However, for their excision, one should perform venesection on a vein located on the forehead after the area has been lubricated and fomented.
One should apply nasal compressions (avapīḍa), head-poultices (śirobasti), and massages (abhyaṅga).
For the purpose of loosening, one should use a decoction of grass-alkali from *kodrava* grains for washing the head, and an application mixed with honey should be made as a paste upon the scalp.
Māṣa beans, kept for three weeks in sour gruel (kāñjika) mixed with priyaṅgu seeds, madhuka, kuṣṭha, and rock salt, remove the condition known as dāraṇaka;
likewise, [beans treated] with blue lotus filaments and yaṣṭīmadhu [achieve the same].
Myrobalan fruit, even if long-standing, when combined with licorice and sesame seeds, brings relief to the disease of cracking of the scalp. || 81 ||

One should cook oil with triphalā, rajas, māṃsī, mārkava, utpala, śārivā, and rock salt; by massaging with this, one conquers ukthikā. [Likewise, oil may be prepared with] citraka, the root of danti, and koṣātakī.
Having ground the paste, one should cook oil that destroys hair loss and ringworm (83).
Oil boiled with guñjā fruits and the juice of bhṛṅgarāja, however, destroys itching, tearing [of the skin], heart disease, leprosy, and diseases of the skull (84).
Cook this oil with *bhṛṅgarāja*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), blue lotus (*utpala*), *śārī*, and iron dross;
it is a destroyer of cracks.
It makes the hair thick, firm, and curled.
[One should prepare] one *kuḍava* of oil with one *karṣa* each of *prapauṇḍarīka*, *madhuka*, *pippalī*, *candana*, and *utpala*, along with twice that amount of *āmalaka* juice.
This proven remedy, which includes *pratimarśa* (nasal drops), removes all diseases of the head.
Oil prepared with *mālatī*, *karavīra*, *agni*,
and *naktamāla* is highly recommended for massage as a supreme cure for *indralupta* (alopecia).
For this [application] quickly destroys [the disease], being certainly tearing for men.
(88) From an ointment of the marrow of *dhātrī* and mango, there arises firmness of the thighs and glossy hair;
in cases of *indralupta* (alopecia), having pierced the veins with [the application of] *śilājatu*, *kāsīsa*, and *tuttha*, [hair grows]. (89)
One should apply pastes all around; oil made from *kuṭannaṭa*, *śikhī*, *jātī*, *karañja*, and *karavīra* is beneficial for massage.
Furthermore, after repeatedly scarifying the area where the foot has deeply penetrated, [one should apply these remedies].
One should smear the scalp all over with *guñjā* fruits for a long time.
Having prepared ink from elephant tusks together with the finest *rasāñjana*, hair will grow even on the palms of men's hands by means of this.
An ointment made from any one of these— bhallātaka, the fruit of bṛhatī, or the root and fruit of guñjā— combined with honey, brings relief to one afflicted by *aindralupta* (alopecia).
Likewise, the root of the guñjā fruit ground with the juice of the bṛhatī fruit [is a remedy] for *aindralupta*.
Gold that has been rubbed and scraped must always be given [to the artisan].
For "Indralupta" (alopecia), one should apply a rubbing with rough leaves;
for the body afflicted by Indralupta, a powder of ground black pepper serves as a remedy.
Those smeared with the collyrium from goat's milk and the soot of an elephant tusk burnt in a closed crucible become [effective] within seven nights.
Indeed, even on the forehead,
the hair becomes curled by an application of honey, blue lotus, mūrvā, sesame, ghee, cow’s milk, and *bhṛṅgarāja*. || 96 ||
In a short time, they become possessed of thick hair, firm jaws, and straight bodies.
[The ingredients are] the milky sap of *snuhī*, the milk of the *arka* plant, *mārkava*, *lāṅgalī*, and poison. 97.20.
Goat's urine with cow's urine, *raktikā*, *indravāruṇī*, white mustard,
and sharp oil— having added these as an internal ingredient and cooked them over a gentle fire, this prepared oil destroys baldness.
Even if it is as hard as the back of a tortoise, it becomes painful, hair-removing, and smeared with this [ointment], becoming hairy like the body of a bear.
[One should apply] the powder of *vaṭāvaroha* and *keśinī*, cooked in the sun.
Oil processed with the fresh juice of *guḍūcī*, when used as an ointment, causes the regrowth of hair.

(101) *Sandalwood*, *madhuka*, *mūrvā*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *kāntā*, the aerial root of the banyan tree (*vaṭāvaroha*), *guḍūcī*, and *viśa* [are the ingredients]. (102)
One should cook oil with iron powder, as well as the two types of Keśī and Śāvira, along with the fresh juice of Mārkava, over a gentle fire.
When applied to the head, hair that has fallen out grows back thick and curly.
This excellent oil— firm-rooted, unctuous, and resembling the color of a bumblebee—
destroys premature graying when used as a nasal drop (nasya).
Oil boiled with yaṣṭīmadhuka, milk, and āmalaka fruits [is likewise effective].
When administered as a nasal drop (nasya), it produces hair and even facial hair.
Triphalā, the leaves of nīlinī, iron, and bhṛṅgaraja in equal parts,
combined with goat’s urine, is an excellent means for blackening the hair.
One should place iron powder mixed with the powder of the three myrobalans (triphalā) inside a slightly ripened coconut filled with the juice of bhṛṅgarāja;
after leaving it there for one month, it should be properly extracted from the interior.
Then, having shaved the head, the excellent physician should apply an ointment;
after wrapping it with plantain leaves, he should remove them on the seventh day.
One who subsists on milk and meat broth should wash the area with decoctions of triphalā.
This is the coloring of the skull, an excellent method for blackening;
one should place the blue lotus together with milk in the ground for a month.
This is prescribed as a means for blackening the hair and making it glossy.
Bhr̥ṅgapuṣpa and javāpuṣpa, ground with the milk of a ewe,
should be stirred with that same [milk] and placed in an iron vessel, buried beneath the earth.
After seven days, it should then be extracted and mixed with the juice of bhr̥ṅgarāja.
Having stirred [the ingredients], applied them to the head, and wrapped it with a cloth, one should remain there for the night;
in the morning, washing must be performed. In this way, the coloring of the hair is achieved;
the same procedure applies to vermilion, bālāmba, conch-shell, and the juice of the *bhṛṅga* plant.
Having rubbed lead with the powder of a newly burnt conch shell sprinkled with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), [one should apply it] as a paste to the hair,
which becomes like the leaf of the *arka* plant.
A man who always bathes with the paste of iron rust and *āmalaka* along with *japā* flowers makes white clothes turn a deep blue.

One who bathes in the Gaṅgā does not see the hells here, just as one does not see the grey hairs [of old age] when neem seeds have been infused [with its potency]. 115. For indeed, the seeds of the neem tree [are transformed].
Likewise, oil from *bhṛṅga* and *toya-aśana* destroys gray hair by means of nasal administration (*nasya*), even for one who eats milk and rice, uprooting it completely. (116)
If the oil of the nimba tree, left in its natural state,
is administered as nasal drops according to the proper procedure for one month, while the person subsists on cow's milk;
It destroys gray hair that has reached its peak. 117.
One *prastha* each of milk, the excellent juice of *mārka*, and *madhuka*, along with one *pala* of *taila*, cooked together; when used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), it removes gray hair. 118.
The roots of the *ādityavallī* plant, the leaves of the black *śairīyaka*, the *surasā*, and the fruit of the black *aśana*; as well as *mārkava*, *kākamācī*, *madhuka*, and *devadāru*.
Ten palas each of long pepper, the three myrobalans,
collyrium, prapauṇḍarīka, mañjiṣṭhā, lodhra, black agallochum, blue lotus, the pulp of mango stones, black earth, lotus stalks, and red sandalwood. || 120–121 ||
The seeds of *nīlī* and *bhallātaka*, *kāsīsa*, *madayantikā*, *somarājī*, *aśana*, *śastra*, black [pigment], *piṇḍīta*, and *citraka*;
the flowers of *arjuna* and *kāśmarya*, and the fruits of *āmra* and *jambū*. || 122 ||
One should cook one āḍhaka of bibhītaka oil with four times its quantity of āmalaka juice and five separate parts of well-ground [herbs] weighing five palas each;
this should be prepared using the "sun-cooking" method until the juice has evaporated.
Then, one should employ this purified and thoroughly cleansed [oil] in a metal vessel for drinking, for nasal administration (nasya), and likewise for anointing the head;
it is beneficial for the eyes, promotes longevity, and cures all diseases of the head. (125)
Known as Mahānīla, it is the unsurpassed destroyer of graying hair.
Ghee cooked in the juice of Bhṛṅgarāja and prepared with a paste of peacock bile, when used as a nasal drop for seven days, destroys gray hair.
When the oil from the marrow of śelu seeds ground with sour gruel falls into a perforated iron vessel due to the heat of the sun,
its application as nasal drops and ointment makes the hair instantly glossy and dark like a swarm of bees. (128)
This [application] destroys diseases of the eyes, ears, neck, and internal organs.

A plaster made of green vitriol (kāsīsa), equal parts yellow pigment (rocanā), yellow orpiment (haritāla), and antimony (rasāñjana), ground with sour liquids, cures elephantiasis, skin diseases, and poison from snakes.
Ghee cooked with *paṭola* leaves, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *rasāñjana*, when drunk, quickly destroys even severe *ahipūtanā*.
Equal parts of *rajanī* and the root of *mārkava*, ground with cold water, [should be applied].
It cures the terrible *visarpa* known as "boar's tusk" through application as a paste.
Alternatively, the powder of *nāgakeśara* should be ground with clarified butter washed a hundred times and applied as a paste for burning and tingling sensations in the feet. (132–133)
In Chapter 55:
For inflammation of the lips caused by Vāta, one should apply a poultice (upanāhana) with *śālvaṇa*;
likewise, oil boiled with Vāta-alleviating drugs should be used as an enema (mastiṣka) and as nasal drops (nasya).
Fomentation, oil massage, internal administration of fats, and rejuvenative therapy (rasāyana) are desired here.
One should apply a rubbing paste consisting of śrīveṣṭaka, resin of the sarja tree, guggulu, devadāru, and the powder of yaṣṭimadhuka. || 1-2 ||
Venesection of the vessels, emesis, purgation, drinking bitter decoctions, a diet of meat broth,
cold plasters, and affusion.
One should apply [treatment] to the lower parts when they are afflicted by pitta;
one should treat those arising from pitta, blood, or injury with leeches, and should also perform the entire therapeutic procedure as for a pitta-type abscess (pittavidradhi).

Head-purgation (śirovirecana), medicated smoking (dhūma), sudation (sveda), and the holding of gargles (kavaladhāraṇa) should be employed once the blood has been removed in cases of lip inflammation (oṣṭhakopa) caused by kapha.
Trikaṭu, alkali of sarjikā, and alkali derived from barley-ash [should be used].
This should be applied as a rubbing paste mixed with honey.
In the case of a carbuncle caused by fat (medoja), once it has been fomented, incised, and cleansed, the application of fire (cauterization) is beneficial.
A rubbing paste consisting of priyaṅgu, triphalā, and lodhra, combined with honey, should also be used.
The powder of triphalā mixed with honey is beneficial as an ointment; likewise,
[an ointment] composed of sarjarasa, nakha, gairika,
dhanyāka, ghee, oil, and sindhu [salt].
Beeswax, when proven effective and sweetened with honey, removes a wound that has burst open.
In the case of *śītāda*, once the blood has been removed, one should [apply] ginger and mustard seeds in water.
One should also prepare a decoction of triphalā and hold it as a gargle (gaṇḍūṣa).
Priyaṅgu, yava, mustā, and triphalā should be used as a paste (pralepana).
Likewise, kuṣṭha, dārvī, abda, lodhra, and samaṅgā [should be used].
A powder made from pāṭhā, tiktā, tejanī, and pītikā is recommended for rubbing onto the teeth;
it stops bleeding, itching, and pain. || 11 ||
Chewing *bakula* flowers stabilizes loose teeth;
a gargle of the decoction of *ārtagala* leaves removes the shaking of teeth.
For the shaking of teeth, chewing sesame seeds and *ugrā* is always beneficial and excellent.
In the case of *dantapuppuṭaka*, bloodletting should be performed while the condition is still mild.
A caustic (*kṣāra*) mixed with the five salts and honey is used as a rubbing agent (*pratisāraṇa*).
Furthermore, gargles (*kavala*) that subdue Vāta are beneficial for the piercing pain and hypersensitivity of the teeth.
In the case of loose teeth, a gargle made from the bark of the *bakula* tree is beneficial;
one should hold in the mouth honey mixed with long pepper (*pippalī*) and clarified butter (*sarpis*).
This is declared to be the foremost medicine for removing toothache. (15)
Once the gums have been drained, one should rub the wound with powders of *lodhra*, *pattaṅga*, *madhuka*, and *lākṣā*, with honey as the predominant ingredient. For gargles,
milky trees should be used along with honey, ghee, and sugar.

In the cold season (śiśira), when blood has been removed, an application of lodhra, musta, and rasāñjana mixed with honey is recommended; for gargles, trees of the milk-exuding class (kṣīrin) are beneficial. A wise physician should perform the treatment prescribed for śītāda in cases of paridara.
Then, having cleansed both [the ear and the head],
the physician should treat the *upakuśa* [disease] by draining it with the leaves of *kākodumbarikā* and *gojī*,
and rub it with salts mixed with honey and *vyoṣa*.
One should collect long pepper (pippalī), white mustard (sarṣapa), white ginger (śvetā-nāgara), and the fruit of naicula, and apply them as a gargle with lukewarm water.
In the case of dental abscesses (danta-vidarbha) treated with surgery, one should cleanse the roots of the teeth.
Then one should apply alkali and all cooling treatments.
Having extracted the supernumerary tooth, one should then apply fire;
in this case, the procedure should be performed by the wise practitioner as in the case of *krimidantaka*.
Having excised the excess flesh, one should treat it with these powders mixed with honey:
*pāṭhā*, *vacā*, *tejovatī*, *sarjikā*, and *yavaśūka*.
Pippalī with honey as the second ingredient is also prescribed here as a gargle.
In this case, a decoction of paṭola, nimba, and triphalā should be used for washing,
and head-purgation (śirovireka) as well as purgative fumigation (vairecanadhūma) are beneficial.
One should perform the treatment for sinus ulcers (nāḍīvraṇa) on the dental sinuses (dantanāḍī).
If a sinus should develop upon a tooth, one should extract that tooth. Having cut away the excess flesh with a surgical instrument— if it is not a tooth growing on top—
one should cleanse the area and cauterize it with either alkali or fire.
If neglected, the jawbone destroys the teeth; therefore, one should extract the broken tooth along with its root and the bone as well.
However, when the upper tooth is extracted, blood flows profusely.
Furthermore, due to excessive application of bloodletting, the aforementioned terrible diseases may arise.
Therefore, the physician should not extract even a loose upper tooth; [he should instead treat it] with a decoction of jasmine, madanaka, kaṭuka, sweet, and thorny plants.
The oil prepared with *lodhra*, *khadira*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *yaṣṭyāhva* is indeed a purifying agent that destroys diseases located in the teeth.
Having first prepared a decoction, one should then grind the paste of *lodhra* and the other ingredients.
Kaṇṭakī, madana, svādukaṇṭa, and vikaṅkata should be employed [as gargles]. Lukewarm boluses of oil or of trivṛta ghee,
as well as decoctions of wind-alleviating herbs, destroy tooth hypersensitivity.
Oil-based medicated smoke and oil-based nasal drops are beneficial;
then, without injuring the roots of the teeth, the physician should extract the *śarkarā* (dental calculus).
Thereafter, he should rub it away with powdered lac mixed with honey.
One should also completely eliminate the action of excessive tearing.
Even in cases of *kapālikā*, which are difficult to cure, this same procedure is prescribed. One should conquer *acala* and *krimidantaka* by means of sudation and drainage.

Likewise, for worms in the teeth, a wise physician should administer hot asafoetida along with head-poultices (avapīḍa) that subdue vāta, holding oil-gargles (sneha-gaṇḍūṣa), plasters of bhadradārvādi and varṣābhū, and unctuous foods. (37)
A gargle consisting of *bṛhatī*, *bhūmikadambaka*,
*pañcāṅguli*, and *kaṇṭakārikā* mixed with oil.
It is a pacifier of the pain of worms and toothaches. (38) Now, each of the roots of nīlī, vāyasajaṅghā, snuh, and dugdhī [is effective].
They say that by chewing it thoroughly while held between the teeth, it destroys dental worms;
or, having extracted a loose tooth, one should cauterize the socket.
Then, one should employ oil prepared with vidārī, yaṣṭyāhva, śṛṅgāṭaka, and kaśeru, along with ten times the amount of milk, for use as a nasal drop (nasya).
In cases of jaw dislocation (hanumokṣa), the treatment prescribed for facial paralysis (ardita) should be applied.
One suffering from dental disease should avoid sour fruits, cold water, dry food, and brushing the teeth;
likewise, one should avoid very hard foods.
Filling the tooth sockets with a mixture of *saptacchada* and the milky sap of the *arka* plant destroys dental worms.
Filling the cavities of the worms with life-giving milk,
or likewise with the milky sap of the *arka* plant— this single formulation is praised by the virtuous.
[43] The juice of *droṇapuṣpī*, combined with foam, honey, and oil, [is also recommended].
For the destruction of worms and decayed teeth, one should perform the filling of the ear.

A paste made from the powders of *paṭola*, *kaṭukā*, *vyoṣa*, *pāṭhā*, *saindhava*, and *bhārgī*, mixed with honey, should be applied as a plaster; likewise, a gargle (*kavala*) should be prepared with honey and oil.
This medicinal procedure should be performed for diseases of the tongue.
Oil prepared with mustā, madhuka, nirguṇḍī, khadira, uśīra, dāru, mañjiṣṭhā, and viḍaṅga removes worms.
The treatment previously described for inflammation of the lips caused by Vāta should indeed be administered by the physician in cases of *kaṇṭaka* (herpes) arising from Vāta.
In those caused by Pitta, once they have been rubbed and the vitiated blood has been drained, [the following should be done].
Sweet gargles, mouthfuls of liquid, and nasal drops are beneficial. When the thorns [of the throat] have arisen from phlegm and have been scraped, and there is a loss of blood,
a paste of the pippalyādi group mixed with honey should be used for rubbing.
One should also take morsels of food with white mustard and rock salt,
and one should feed the patient with soups made from *paṭola*, *nimba*, and eggplant, along with alkaline preparations.
This cures chronic numbness of the tongue.
Rubbing with a mixture of manaḥśilā, bhasma,
and salt, or chewing sour substances such as jambīra fruit slightly moistened with the milk of snuhī, also destroys it. || 51 ||
The sound of teeth grinding is cured by anointing with ghee cooked with the juice of *karkaṭāṅghri*, or by applying a paste of *karkaṭāṅghri* to the teeth.
Having scraped the *upajihvā* (under-tongue), one should rub it with an alkaline solution.
One should treat this condition with head-purgatives (śirovireka), gargles (gaṇḍūṣa), and medicinal smokes (dhūma).

This powder of the three pungents (vyoṣa), alkali (kṣāra), abhayā, and agni should be used for rubbing (pragharṣaṇa) to pacify the sublingual swelling (upajihvā); one should also cook oil with these same ingredients.
One should rub the excised *galashuṇṭhī* with *vyoṣa*, *ugrā*, honey, and rock salt;
or likewise with *kuṣṭha*, *uṣaṇa*, *vacā*, rock salt, *kaṇā*, *pāṭhā*, and *plava*.
The physician should perform the rubbing of *galashuṇṭhī* with these ingredients mixed with honey.
Puncturing the nasal septum (upanāsāvyadha) destroys galashunthī completely.
Likewise, chewing the root of shephālī removes galashunthī;
as do vacā, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, rāsnā, and kaṭukarohiṇī.
One should prepare a decoction of *picumarda* and apply it as a gargle (57).
Soups made from *mudga* beans processed with alkali (*kṣāra*) are also beneficial for food in cases of *tuṇḍikerī*, *adhruṣa*, *kūrma*, *saṃghāta*, and *tālupuppuṭa* (58).
This same procedure should be performed; however, in the case of surgical intervention, the specific treatment for inflammation of the palate (tālupāka) is that which destroys pitta.
In cases of dryness of the palate, oleation and sudation should be applied, along with a regimen that subdues vāta.
For the Rohiṇī types of Sādhya diseases, bloodletting is beneficial.
Emesis, inhalation of medicinal smoke, gargling, and nasal therapy (nasya) should also be employed.
Once the blood has been removed from Ghātikī, one should rub the area with salts.
One should also frequently hold lukewarm oil-gargles (tailakavala);
for the Pitta-type [disease], one should rub it with the powder of pataṅga and sugar.
A decoction of drākṣā and parūṣaka is beneficial as a gargle.
One should clear away phlegm-born [disorders] with household smoke and pungent substances.

Oil prepared with white flowered leadwort (śvetā), embelia (villanga), and turpeth (dantī), along with rock salt (saindhava), should be administered as nasal therapy (nasya) and as a gargle (kavala) in cases of excessive phlegm. || 63–64 ||
The physician should treat Rohiṇī arising from blood in the same manner as Pittaja-vatsā;
having drained Kaṇṭhaśālūka, one should treat it like Tuṇḍikerī.
One should eat barley-food once a day, in small quantities, and with unctuous substances.
One should treat adhijihvikā in the same manner as upajihvikā.
Having lifted the tongue and drawn out the adhijihvikā with a hook,
one should excise it with a scalpel (maṇḍalāgra), using sharp, hot measures such as rubbing and so forth.
Having drained a single mass, one should perform the purificatory procedure;
furthermore, that disease which is like a stone (a tumor) should be treated with a surgical instrument.
One should incise a galavidradhi (throat abscess) when it is located away from vital spots (marmans) and has fully ripened.
In cases of throat diseases, bloodletting and the administration of sharp nasal drops (nasya) and other procedures should be performed.
One should drink a decoction made from the bark of *dārvī*, *nimba*, *tārkṣya*, and *kaliṅga*,
or a decoction of *harītakī* mixed with honey.
