Kaṭukā, ativiṣā, dāru, pāṭhā, mustaka, and kaliṅgaka, boiled in cow’s urine and drunk as a potion, destroy diseases of the throat. House-soot, yavakṣāra, pāṭhā, vyoṣa, and rasāñjana— [these should be used].

Tejohvā, triphalā, iron, and citraka—these, powdered together with honey, should be held in the mouth; this destroys diseases of the throat. This powder, named Kālaka, removes diseases of the teeth, tongue, and mouth.

This powder, consisting of equal parts of pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, nāgara, and sarjikākṣāra, cures diseases of the throat. [74] Manahśilā, yavakṣāra, haritāla, and saindhava— [these are used together].
This powder, including dārvītvak, combined with honey and mixed with the scum of clarified butter (ghṛtamaṇḍa), should be held in the mouth for throat diseases;
it is celebrated as the excellent formulation known as Pītaka for oral diseases. || 75-76 ||
One should prepare pills with honey from *yavāgraja*, *tejavatī*, *pāṭhā*, *rasāñjana*, *dāru*, *niśā*, and *kṛṣṇā*,
and apply them to the mouth.
One should administer that [decoction] for all diseases of the throat.
One should drink warm broth made from the ten roots (daśamūla), or from radish and horse gram (kulattha), along with milk, sugarcane juice, cow's urine, curd-whey, sour gruel, or sour kāñjika.
Having examined the specific humor (doṣa), one should administer boluses with oil or ghee,
as well as powders of the five spices (pañcakolaka), tālīsa, patra, elā, marica, and tvac, along with the alkalis of palāśa and muṣkaka, and yava-kṣāra.
When old jaggery has been boiled down to twice its original volume, pills the size of a *karkandhu* fruit should be made. Kept for seven days in the ashes of the *muṣkaka* tree,
they become like nectar when applied to all diseases of the throat.
One should habitually apply a paste of *śivā* (emetic nut) steamed in cow's urine, mixed in equal parts with sweet flag (*madhuka*), costus (*kuṣṭha*), and realgar (*tālaka*);
by doing so, one may conquer diseases of the mouth as well as a bad taste.
In cases of generalized suppuration caused by *vāta*, one should rub the area with powders of the salts.

Oil prepared with drugs that subdue Vāta is beneficial for gargling and nasal administration. In cases of Pitta-type [diseases], once the body of the person has been purified, all therapeutic measures that alleviate Pitta— sweet and cooling in nature— should be employed using all types of meat broths.

In all types of saras caused by kapha, one should apply a regimen that eliminates kapha, including cleansing with powders (pratisāraṇa), gargles (gaṇḍūṣa), medicated smoke (dhūma), and purificatory treatments. In cases of oral ulceration (mukhapāka), venesection (śirāvedha) and purgation of the head and body (śiraḥkāyavirecana) should be performed.
Furthermore, the constant chewing of *jātī* leaves is always beneficial for the treatment.
A decoction made from *jātī* leaves, *amṛtā*, grapes, *yāsa*, *dārvī*, and the three fruits (*phalatrika*),
mixed with honey and used as a cold gargle, cures inflammation of the mouth.
From the powder of black cumin, costus, and indrayava, taken for three days, the inflammation of the mouth, ulcerous discharge, and foul odor are pacified.
[Likewise] rasāñjana, lodhra, and abhaya— || 88 ||
Realgar, nagara, red ochre, pāṭhā, turmeric, and gajapippalī— when held in the mouth together with honey, this serves as a treatment for the face. (89)
The decoction made from the fresh sprouts of *paṭola*, *nimba*, *jambu*, *āmra*, and *mālatī*—
known as the "five sprouts" (*pañcapallava*)— is excellent for cleansing the mouth.
Alternatively, a decoction of the "five barks" (*pañcavalka*) or a decoction of *triphalā* may be used.
In cases of facial inflammations (mukhapāka), this [decoction] mixed with honey should be used for rinsing the mouth.
A concentrated extract (rasakriyā) made from the boiled juice of *dārvī* (daruharidrā),
mixed with honey, cures diseases of the mouth, blood disorders, sinus tracts, and ulcers.
With saptacchada, uśīra, paṭola, musta, harītakī, tiktakarohiṇī,
yaṣṭyāhva, rājadruma, and candana;
One should drink a decoction of paṭola,
śuṇṭhī, triphalā, viśālā, trāyantī, tiktā, dviniśā, and amṛtā, which removes inflammation of the mouth. || 93 ||
A yellow decoction, when held in the mouth with honey, destroys all diseases of the mouth without exception.
Triphalā, pāṭhā, raisins, and jasmine buds, when boiled together, [achieve the same].
Triphalā, when consumed or used as a gargle, cures inflammation of the mouth.
Sesame seeds, blue lotus, ghee, sugar, and milk, mixed with honey,
used as a gargle for one whose face has been burned, alleviate burning and suppuration.

A gargle with oil or sour gruel (kāñjika) removes the burning sensation caused by powders. A mouthful (kavala) consisting of costus (kuṣṭha), cardamom (elā), coriander (dhānyaka), licorice (yaṣṭīmadhu),
and valerian (elavāluka) removes excessive foul odor from the mouth, as well as the smell of liquor and garlic.
Likewise, one should properly boil one *tulā* of blue *kuraṇṭaka* in a *droṇa* of water; having strained it, one should add oil to the decoction when it has been reduced to one-fourth.
One should cook [the oil] with the pastes of *anantā*, *khadira*, *arimeda*, *jambu*, *āmra*, *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, and *utpala*, each weighing half a *pala*. || 98 ||
That oil, when held in the mouth for even a moment, immediately bestows stability upon the teeth.
[99] Fifteen: One hundred palas of *irimeda* bark...
Having cut fresh linen into pieces and boiled it with four āḍhakas of water, [one should use] the decoction when reduced to one-fourth. || 100 ||
With that decoction, a wise person should slowly cook half an āḍhaka of oil with medicinal pastes in portions of one akṣa each.
Of madder, lodhra, and licorice;
of *irimeḍa*, khadira, kaṭphala, lac, nyagrodha, musta, and small cardamom.
Of camphor, agallochum, padmaka, cloves, kaṅkola, and nutmeg;
and of pataṅga, red ochre, varāṅga, flowers, and dhātakī. || 102 ||
The physician should administer this proven remedy for diseases arising in the mouth:
namely, in cases of loose teeth, abscesses, śaiśira, śītāda, and danta-harṣa; and in cases of dental caries, loosened or putrefied gums, and the sloughing away of diseased tissue.
This oil should be used for foul breath and for the aforementioned diseases.
One *prastha* each of lac juice and milk should be cooked together with four times as much decoction of *ariṣṭaka*, along with [other] liquids measuring one *pala* each. 104–105.
Oil prepared with *lodhra*, *kaṭphala*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, the filaments of *padma*, *padmaka*, sandalwood, blue lotus, and *yaṣṭyāhva* should be used for gargling;
it cures toothache, loosening of the teeth, lockjaw, and *kapālikā*.

It destroys sitalada, putrid mouth, loss of appetite, and a bad taste in the mouth; it cures these diseases of the mouth and makes the teeth firm. [107] Bakula fruit, lodhra, vajravalli, and kuruṇṭaka—
The consumption of *caturaṅgula*, *vavvola*, *vājikarṇī*, and *eranda*—
oil cooked with the decoction and paste of these, when held in the mouth and used for brushing the teeth, brings stability to loose teeth. (108–109)
Having placed equal parts of cardamom, bamboo shoots, the fruit of the *vanikā* plant, *śītakoṣa*, and the two types of *kola*, along with *khadira* wood, into a decoction measuring ten parts;
Having cooked it like a medicinal poultice within the opening petals of a blooming *kaitaka* flower,
one should then grind that entire mass— along with a portion of moon-like [white] powder equal in measure— with fresh mango juice, using both hands.
Having smeared it, one should prepare a pill as desired,
which serves as a kinsman to the fragrance of the mouths of both women and men.
One should properly boil one *tulā* of khadira wood in one *droṇa* of water.
When the remaining eighth part remains, one should cause the addition of ingredients to be made right there:
nutmeg, camphor, betel nuts, and kakkola fruits.
This pill should be prepared, which increases the beauty of the mouth.
In cases of diseases of the teeth, lips, and mouth, as well as ailments of the tongue and palate,
one should take two and a half *tulās* of the bark of the *ariṣṭa* tree— equal in essence to the *Gāyatrī*— along with four jars of water.
Having boiled it down until one-quarter remains, and having strained it through a fine cloth,
one should then cook it slowly over a mild fire. When that [liquid] has reached a thick consistency, one should add the powder of these [ingredients].
And one should gently administer gargles for those who partake in mouthfuls [of medicine], consisting of cardamom,
lotus stalks, white sandalwood, red sandalwood water,
*śyāmā*, *tamāla*, *vikaṣā*, and thick iron-staff [decoctions]. 115.
Of the three fruits of *lajjā*, *rasāñjana*, *dhātakī*,
*bhaśrīpuṣpa*, *gairika*, *kaṭaṅkaṭa*, *kaṭphala*, *padmāhvā*, *lodhra*, *vaṭaroha*, and *yavāsaka*.
One should prepare a powder consisting of one *pala* each of *māṃsī*, *niśā*, fragrant bark (*surabhivalkala*),
*kakkola*, nutmeg (*jātiphala*), mace (*koṣa*),
and cloves (*lavaṅgaka*).
Having removed it from the cold and added four palas of camphor, one should form pills the size of peas;
when dried and placed in the mouth, they ward off [fever]. (117)
Produced from the limbs of the plant, the teeth, the lips, the tongue, the twice-born (teeth), and the palate, these [medicines] create fragrance, sharpness, and relish in the mouth;
they provide supreme stability to the teeth and lightness to the tongue. (118)
For the alleviation of earache, one should fill the ear with the auspicious, pleasantly warm juices of *kapittha*, *mātuluṅga*, sour [fruit], and *śṛṅgavera*. (56.1)
Fresh ginger, honey, rock salt, and oil—
this pungent and hot mixture should be applied to the ears to alleviate pain. [Or] garlic, fresh ginger, śigru, suraṅgī, and radish...
The fresh juice of the plantain (kadali) is excellent; when slightly warm, it should be used for filling the ear, or one may dust it with the powder of sea-foam (samudraphena).
[Likewise,] ginger (ārdraka) and sunflower (sūryāvartaka)—
The fresh juices of the root of śobhāñjana and of mūlaka,
each separately combined with honey, oil, and rock salt and applied warm, remove earache.
The resin of *Śobhāñjanaka* mixed with sesame oil,
applied warm and clearly heated as a filling in the ear, brings relief from earache. [This may be done] with any one of the eight types of urine.
One should fill the ears with lukewarm [oil] for the alleviation of earache. Alternatively, having prepared a trough made of *aśvattha* leaves with many leaves,
one should place it over the ear, smeared with oil and filled with glowing coals.
The oil that drips from a khallāda seed heated over charcoal, upon reaching the auditory canal, immediately causes intense pain.
The juice produced from the leaves of snuhī, burnt on a cloth made of arka leaves, [is likewise used].
Slightly warm, this very filling [of the ear] is a remedy for earache.
Then, having wrapped eight-finger-length sections of the great *pañcamūla* in linen cloth and soaked them in oil, one should set them on fire.
The oil that drips from these [medicinal woods] should be applied while lukewarm;
it should be known as *dīpikā-taila*, which immediately seizes the pain.
One should proceed in this same manner with *bhadrakāṣṭha*, *kuṣṭha*, and *sāra-kāṣṭha*.
The oil from the *matimāndī* plant is a remedy for earache.
A leaf of the *arka* tree, yellowed by ripening, smeared with clarified butter, and heated over a fire—
Water squeezed from a cloth and poured into the ear destroys pain and even intense agony;
[this applies] when the ear is afflicted with sharp pain, accompanied by ringing, and discharging a foul secretion.
One should add goat's urine that is lukewarm and sprinkled with rock salt (saindhava).
The physician should cook oil in the urine of a horse or a sheep combined with bamboo scrapings; with this, one should fill the ear of a patient suffering from earache.
Sesame oil or mustard oil prepared with asafoetida, *tumburu*, and ginger is said to be the primary and beneficial filling for earache.
[Likewise,] the alkali of young radish roots, ginger, asafoetida, and *nāgara*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the content available.]
Śatapuṣpā, vacā, kuṣṭha, dāru, śigru, rasāñjana, sauvarcala, yavakṣāra, sarjika, udbhida,
saindhava, bhūrjagranthi, viḍa, musta, honey, and four times as much fermented gruel (śukta). || 17–18 ||
Oil should be cooked with the juice of *mātuluṅga* and the juice of *kadalī*; this is a supreme remedy for earache,
as well as for deafness, tinnitus, and severe purulent discharge from the ear.

By filling the ear with this oil, worms residing in the ear quickly meet their destruction, according to the instruction of Kṛṣṇātreya. This excellent alkaline oil (kṣārataila) removes diseases of the mouth and teeth.
Furthermore, there is *madhuśukta*, which is sour gruel (*śukta*) in which honey is the primary ingredient; likewise,
one should place the juice of *jambīra* fruit combined with the root of *pippalī* into a honey jar and store it within a heap of grain.
That which has acquired its essence over a month is called *madhuśukta*.

For ringing in the ears (*karṇanāda*) and buzzing in the ears (*karṇakṣveḍa*), one should perform filling with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*); for deafness caused by such sounds, one should apply the medicinal remedies prescribed for earache.
Sesame oil prepared with a paste made from the alkaline water of *apāmārga* removes ringing in the ears.
And deafness [is cured] by filling [the ears].
25.5. Dry *sarjikā* root, asafoetida, black pepper, ginger, and *śatapuṣpā*: oil cooked with these, using four times as much vinegar (*śukta*), [is effective].
It quickly removes ringing in the ears, pain from ear-ache, deafness, and discharge.
One should cook one *prastha* of oil with a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūlī*), adding this paste; this is the supreme medicine for deafness. (26–27)
Having ground the fruit of the *vilva* with urine, one should cook oil with goat’s milk; indeed, filling the ears with this will remove deafness.
This same procedure should be performed for *praṇāda*, preceded by nasal therapy (*nasya*).
An errhine (nasya) made from jaggery and ginger mixed with water is beneficial for both [types of ear disease].
For ear discharge (karṇasrāva), they recommend filling the ear with a powder of the five astringents (pañcakaṣāya) combined with the juice of wood-apple (kapittha) and honey.
The pair of ears afflicted by the disease of putrefaction (pūti-roga) is filled with either the juice of *mālatī* leaves mixed with honey or with cow urine; otherwise, it must be abandoned from afar.
Haritāla mixed with cow urine, when used as a filling, conquers putrid ear-disease.
The juice extracted from the fruit of the *kārpāsī* plant, combined with the powder of *sarja* bark and mixed with honey, is highly recommended for ear discharge (*karṇasrāva*).
[Verse 32] Young leaves of the *jambu* and *āmra* trees, taken in equal parts—
Experts declare that the juice of fresh kapittha and cotton seeds, when crushed together and mixed with honey, cures discharges from the body.
Oil of *nimba* and *karañja*, boiled with these and with mustard seeds, is prescribed as a cure for discharges (*srāva*).
A tumor (*goṇḍaka*) arising from the dung of an elephant that has been steamed according to the procedure for *puṭapāka* [is likewise used].
A medicinal preparation (rasa) made with oil and rock salt is an excellent remedy for ear discharge.
One should cook mustard oil with the meat of a jackal;
by the mere filling of the ear with it, an ear canal (karṇanāḍī) is pacified.
Eight palas of *kaṭutaila* cooked with one pala of *niśāgandha* and the juice of *dhustūra* leaves is excellent for curing ear canal obstructions.
Now, in cases of ear blockage (*karṇapratīnāha*), one should employ oleation and sudation therapies.
Then, once the head has been purged, one should perform the treatment appropriate for the condition.
For an abscess of the ear (karṇapāka), one should apply the same remedies as for a wound-type erysipelas (kṣatavisarpa),
as well as tubular fomentation (nāḍīsveda), emesis, medicated smoking, and head-purgation (ūrdhvavirecana).
Every procedure that subdues *kapha* removes ear-itching;
however, after moistening [the area] with oil and liquefying it with fomentation,
the physician should properly clear the ear-wax (*karṇagūtha*) using a probe.
The juice of *nirguṇḍī*, oil, the powder of *sindhudhūma*, and jaggery,
combined with honey, cure chronic ear infections when used as an ear-drop.
Oil cooked with the juice of *jātī* leaves likewise conquers chronic ear infections.
Oil prepared with the tender leaves of *varuṇa*, *arka*, *kapittha*, *āmra*, and *jambū*,
or with the juice of *jātī* leaves, cures *pūtikarṇa*. Likewise, the fresh juice of *sūryāvartaka* and the juice of *sindhuvāra* [are effective].
One should fill the ear infested with worms with a decoction of *lāṅgalī* root mixed with powdered *tryūṣaṇa*; this is a supreme destroyer of parasites.
For the purpose of eliminating ear-worms, one should employ this worm-destroying procedure.
The smoke of eggplant (*vārtāku*) and mustard oil are also beneficial; when the ear is thoroughly filled with the expressed juice of *halī*, *sūryāvarta*, and *vyoṣa*,
all species of worms fall out suddenly.
Blue lotus, rice-water, oil, rock salt, and sour gruel, combined and made lukewarm,
cause the total expulsion of worms when used for filling the ear.
For ear malodor, fumigation with guggulu is said to be the best remedy.

One should perform the washing of the ear with water from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree or similar plants, or with water containing *surasā* and other herbs; the filling [of the ear] should be done with these powders.
Ghee, *rasāñjana*, and honey mixed with a woman’s milk [should be used].
This is commended even for chronic cases of purulent otitis with discharge.
Oil prepared with kuṣṭha, hiṅgu, vacā, dāru, śatāhvā, viśva, and saindhava, along with goat's urine, cures putrid ear disease.
In cases of abscesses as well, one should indeed administer the treatment prescribed for abscesses;
moreover, oil cooked with śatāvarī, vājigandhā, payasyā,
and eraṇḍa seeds, along with milk, is an excellent means for nourishing the earlobes.
When fresh butter has risen from buffalo milk mixed with powdered *guñjā* seeds,
its application as an ointment increases the growth of the earlobes.
[Similarly,] bitter *tumbī* oil containing poison, cooked eight times over a donkey’s fire— 53–54.
That [oil], cooked in urine, increases the earlobe when used as an ointment;
likewise, oil prepared with the paste of the *jīvanīya* group of drugs in milk,
along with a decoction of the meat of marshy animals, nourishes and enlarges the earlobe.
The powder of the *navamūsalī* root, combined with buffalo butter and kept for seven days within a heap of grain,
brings about healing for the earlobes.
When the ear is difficult to pierce, there may arise agitation and pain.
In that case, for the purpose of making the difficult-to-heal wound firm, the physician should apply a plaster all around with madhūka, barley, mañjiṣṭhā, and rubu roots combined with honey and ghee;
thus the severed ear-joint is healed.
One should apply the treatment according to how the patient is afflicted.
If it is corrupted by Vāta, one should perform an irrigation with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) and warm water;
if by Raktapitta, with milk; and if by Kapha, with warm water. || 59-60 ||

Then, having sewn it, one should stabilize the joint with a bandage; thereafter, having anointed it with honey and clarified butter, one should wrap the joint with a cotton pad and dust it with powdered skull-bone or with *pathyā*. (61)

Milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī), citraka, and harītakī; ghee-jaggery confection (sarpirguḍa); and the six-ingredient soup (ṣaḍaṅgayūṣa) are for the alleviation of chronic catarrh (pīnasa). 1.57.1–2.
This powder, consisting of equal parts of the three pungents (vyoṣa), citraka, tālīsa, tamarind, sour vetasa, and chavya,
along with cardamom, cinnamon, and cinnamon leaves each added in one-quarter part, should be combined with aged jaggery. This is the Vyoṣādika powder.
It destroys chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, and cough, and is excellent for promoting relish and the voice.
Oil properly prepared with pāṭhā, virajantī, mūrvā, pippalī, jasmine buds, and dantī, when used as a nasal drop (nasya), is effective in cases of chronic rhinitis.
Oil cooked with vyāghrī, dantī, vacā, śigru, surasa, vyoṣa, and saindhava, when used as nasal drops (nāvana), conquers the disease of putrid nose (pūtināsā).
[Likewise, oil prepared] with trikaṭu, viḍaṅga, saindhava, bṛhatī-phala, śigru, surasa, and dantī...

Oil prepared with cow's urine should be used as a nasal medication (nasya) for putrid nose (pūtinasya). An expressed oil (avapīḍa) made from kaliṅga, asafoetida, black pepper, lac, surasa, kaṭphala, kuṣṭha, ugrā, śigru, and jantughna is highly recommended.
One should cook pungent oil (kaṭutaila) with those same [substances] combined with urine;
this is proclaimed as the supreme pacifier for chronic rhinitis (apīnasa) and fetid rhinitis (pūtinasya). For inflammation of the nose (nāsāpāka), the Pitta-alleviating regimen [should be applied].
One should remove all external and internal blood; the bark of milk-exuding trees should be used for irrigation, and poultices mixed with ghee should be applied.
Astringent decoctions that destroy pus, serous discharge, blood, and bile, as well as nasal drops (nāvana),
and oil or clarified butter prepared with a paste and decoction of ginger, kuṣṭha, long pepper, bilva, and grapes, when used as a nasal medication, remove sneezing and pain.
In the case of a burning fever characterized by pitta,
one should employ all sweet and cooling treatments; in nasal obstruction, the primary treatment is the internal administration of oleaginous substances.
In the case of vātika coryza, one should regularly consume unctuous medicated smokes and enemas to the head;
furthermore, one should drink ghee prepared with the five salts and the first group [of drugs] according to the prescribed sequence.
One should observe the entire procedure for nasal therapy (nasya) and other treatments as described by Ātreya;
for those conditions arising from pitta and blood, ghee processed with drugs of the sweet group should be drunk,
and one should also apply cooling affusions and plasters.
In the case of a kaphaja [type of vomiting], one should first administer an unctuous enema with ghee,
or induce emesis with gruel (yavāgu) cooked with sesame and māṣa beans; thereafter, one should follow the therapeutic regimen for subduing kapha using dārvī, iṅgudī, nikumbha, kiṇihī, and surasa.

In this case, wicks (varti) should be prepared and applied for smoking according to the prescribed method; alternatively, the physician should administer smoke to those suffering from acute coryza by placing roasted barley flour mixed with ghee inside a hollowed-out mallikā flower. 17.
He who, suffering from catarrh, drinks very cold water on the ground while lying down in bed at the time of sleep, is liberated from that disease.
A leaf of *jayā* cooked in a closed vessel (*puṭapāka*) combined with sea-salt oil [is likewise effective].

In all types of catarrh, the habitual use of pungent substances combined with jaggery is the supreme medicine. A diet consisting of unctuous curd and sour foods specifically cures acute catarrh and promotes the digestion of kapha.
In cases of acute coryza, soup made from the leaves of the tamarind (*ciñcā*) is recommended;

thereafter, once the *kapha* is known to have matured, one should eliminate it with head-purgatives (*śīrṣavirecana*), as well as by means of head-anointing, fomentation, and the consumption of pungent and sour foods. (21)
One should treat those [diseases] with emetics and the drinking of ghee, according to their respective requirements. Immediately after eating,
one consumes salted, well-steamed, and very hot black gram (māṣa).
It conquers all types of chronic catarrh that has been long-standing.
(23) Long pepper, drumstick seeds, *viḍaṅga*, and black pepper—

This *avapīḍa* (nasal squeeze) is praised as a remedy for preventing coryza. A wise person should employ the aforementioned treatments for worms, as well as anthelmintic medicines, for the purpose of nasal administration (*nāvana*).
For the remaining disorders, however, the treatment should be according to their respective [specific] natures.
(25) Oil prepared with red karavīra flowers, jasmine, aśanaka, and mallikā is excellent for destroying hemorrhoids of the nose. (26)
Oil prepared with house-soot, *kaṇā*, wood-ash, *naktāhva*, rock salt, and the seeds of *śikhari* is beneficial for hemorrhoids of the nose.
[Also] *citraka*, *cavika*, *dīpyaka*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the portion supplied.]
Oil prepared with *nidigdhikā*, seeds of *karañja*, salt, and *arka*, combined with cow’s urine, is prescribed for hemorrhoids of the nose. (28)
Having added one hundred palas each of the juices of citraka, āmalakī, guḍūcī, and daśamūla, along with one āḍhaka of powdered pathyā and one hundred palas of jaggery,
one should cook it until it becomes thick; then, when it has reached consistency, one should add twelve palas [of the remaining ingredients].

On the following day, having added half a pala each of the three spices (vyoṣa) and the three aromatics (trijātaka), as well as half a prastha of honey to the alkali, one should consume it according to one's digestive fire without restriction;
this leads to the increase of the digestive fire and cures wasting, cough, difficult nasal catarrh, and worms.
This elixir destroys gulma, udāvarta, hemorrhoids, and dyspnea.
(Chapter 58) [One should treat] by means of fasting, external applications, sudation, venesection, and purgation.
One should treat [the patient] with ointments, eye-drops, nasal drops, and so forth that cause moistening.
When the ocular disease is not clearly manifested, one should apply a powder made of *śrīvāsa*, *ativiṣā*, *lodhra*, and a small amount of *saindhava* salt externally over the area.
Diseases arising in the eyes and abdomen, as well as catarrh, ulcers, and fever—
these five subside within five nights through fasting (*laṅghana*). For four days, one should employ sudation, medicinal pastes, bitter food, and affusion.
Fasting is recommended for eye diseases, while the six digestive remedies are for undigested matter (āma).
Collyrium, filling the eyes, and drinking decoctions are advised when āma is present. The expressed juice of *dhātrī* fruit destroys a recent onset of eye disease when used as a filling.
Or, an irrigation with the juice of *śigru* leaves mixed with honey and rock salt [is beneficial]. Alternatively,
filling [the eye] with *dārvī* juice and *rasāñjana* combined with breast milk quickly destroys the burning, tearing, and pain arising from *syanda*.
The pair of eyes becomes firmly filled with abundant water arising from the cutting of the tender sprouts of the *karavīra* tree.
Suddenly, at that very moment, [the eye] becomes inflamed. 7.

But sour gruel (*mastu*), mixed with a little rock salt (*saindhava*) and rubbed on the base of the eyelid (*śikhari-mūla*) in a copper vessel (*tāmra-kabhājana*), removes the fresh swelling of the eye through its application. 8.
A paste made from ground saindhava salt, dāruharidrā, gairika, pathyā, and rasāñjana, when applied externally as a plaster, removes all eye diseases without exception.
Likewise, śāravaka and lodhra fried in ghee constitute a biḍālaka application.
Likewise, a *biḍālaka* (a medicinal paste) prepared with *harītakī* and fried in ghee should be used;
this *biḍālaka* is prescribed as an external application for the eyes in the science of *śālākya*.
An external application composed of equal parts of mountain-clay (*girimṛd*), sandalwood (*candana*), ginger (*nāgara*), and chalk (*khaṭikā*) is also employed.
When mixed with water, it undoubtedly acts as an eye-salve.
Ground *āmalakī* from the earth, combined with rock salt and house-water, and applied as a thick paste upon copper, conquers the pain of the eyes through external application. (12–13)
For an eye disease born of Vāta, eye-drops (āścyotana) and a lukewarm decoction of the Bilvādi group are beneficial;
likewise, a lukewarm decoction of Eraṇḍa, Bṛhatī, Tarkārī, and Madhuśigru is helpful.
Goat's milk boiled with the leaves, roots, and bark of Eraṇḍa is also recommended.
For eye diseases that have reached full maturity, irrigation with lukewarm water of Kaṇṭakārī roots is beneficial;
furthermore, the application of collyrium and similar treatments is prescribed,
resulting in the restoration of a healthy path for the eyes and the subsiding of congestion and lacrimation.
Mild pain, itching, and the symptoms of a matured eye ulcer (pakvākṣigada) shall be described in detail later, along with the procedures for collyrium and other treatments.
[17] Bṛhatī, the root-bark of eraṇḍa, and the root of śigru, together with rock salt—
A medicinal wick (varti) ground with goat’s milk cures wind-related eye diseases.
One should grind the two types of turmeric, madhuka, pathyā, and devadāru with goat’s milk; this is an excellent collyrium (añjana) for abhiṣyanda.

Red ochre, rock salt, long pepper, and ginger, ground with water in increasing proportions by two parts each, are prescribed as a pill-ointment (guḍikāñjana). [Alternatively, an ointment may be prepared] from prapauṇḍarīka, licorice, turmeric, āmalaka, and padmaka.
An irrigation with cold water mixed with honey and sugar cures pitta-type eye diseases.
Milk boiled with grapes, madhuka, mañjiṣṭhā, and the jīvanīya group of drugs is beneficial when used as an eye-drop in the morning for those suffering from swelling and pain in the eyes.
Having coated lodhra with the leaves of nimba, one should apply it as a powder or a paste using the heat of fomentation; this,
combined with human milk, serves as an eye-drop (āścyotana).
It is declared to be the foremost remedy for the afflictions of pitta, rakta, and vāta.

In cases arising from kapha, one should administer fasting, sudation, nasal medication (nasya), and the consumption of bitter food; furthermore, one should perform sharp blowing of the nose (pradhamana) and sharp poultices (upanāhana).
One should administer sudation or apply a medicinal paste made from phaṇijjaka, āsphota, kapītana, bilva, pattūra, pīlu, surasa, arjaka, and bhaṅgā.
A medicinal paste made of *barhiṣṭha*, ginger, *suradāru*, and *kuṣṭha*;
or a paste of ginger and *nimba* leaves mixed with a little rock salt, should be applied lukewarm to the eye. By means of this application, it removes swelling, itching, and pain.
The bark of the *pārijāta* tree, along with oil, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), and rock salt,
destroys eye pain arising from the *kapa* [disease], as does the "tree-destroying thunderbolt" (*tarughna-kuliśa*). Likewise,
*lodhra* mixed with rock salt and fried in clarified butter [is effective].
One should apply an eye-drop made from ground sauvīra bound in a white cloth; it will destroy itching, burning, and pain in the eye. || 28 ||
Those arising from Vāta are pacified by unctuous and hot [remedies]; those born of Pitta by soft and cold;
and those of Kapha nature by sharp, dry, hot, and clear [remedies].
A Sānnipātika [disease] is cured by the alternating application of sharp, hot, soft, and cold [remedies].
An irrigation with a paste made of *tirīṭa*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *yaṣṭī*, sugar, and *bhadramustaka*,
mixed with cold water, destroys *raktābhiṣyanda*. Likewise, a powder of *kaśeru* and *madhuka* combined with a cloth [for irrigation] serves the same purpose.
When these have been placed in water and allowed to infuse, it becomes an āścyotana (eye-drop).
One should boil dārvī, paṭola, madhuka, nimba, padmaka, utpala, and prapauṇḍarīka in four times as much water.
Having boiled it down until one-quarter remains, one should cook that again until it measures one *kuḍava*.
When it has cooled, one should then add honey amounting to one-quarter of that.
This *rasakriyā* cures burning sensations, lacrimation, diseases, and pain caused by blood disorders.
The drinking of bitter ghee and frequent purgation,
as well as the application of leeches all around the eyes, and the therapeutic regimen prescribed for the pacification of pitta-abhishyanda should be employed.

The resin of the *śigru* leaf, well-ground and fumigated with ghee inside a copper vessel, destroys swelling, itching, lacrimation, and pain. [36] With the leaves of the *nimba* tree, ground until they are exceedingly pure...
Mixed with *rjāti* and *sindhūttha*,
containing within its interior a very potent pill,
it is fried in *lodhra* powder.
Enveloped on all sides with cotton wool moistened with Sauvīra juice— extremely soft—
it brought about for a long time the pacification of eye-irritation for those looking upward.
Being rotated, it acts [as a purgative]. 37.
The juice of bilva leaves, purified and combined with rock salt and clarified butter, rubbed upon a copper plate and fumigated over a fire of cow-dung [is used for this purpose]. 38.
When stirred with milk and used to fill the eyes, it relieves swelling and pain; it is recommended for ophthalmia (abhiṣyanda), glaucoma (adhimantha), lacrimation, and blood disorders.
Sour gruel (kāñjika) mixed with salt and pungent oil [should be kept] in a bronze vessel.
When ground, rubbed with a stone, fumigated over a fire of cow-dung,
sprinkled with goat's milk, and applied while the wind and phlegm are provoked, it conquers eye pain, discharge, swelling, and redness. (40)
The juice of *āmalaka* (Emblica officinalis) from trees growing on riverbanks cures all eye diseases;
likewise, aged clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) removes all ailments of the eyes in every way. This entire procedure is also recommended for the preparation of *mantha* and other such preparations.
If there is no subsiding, one should apply cauterization in every way above the eyebrows.
In Netrapāka, the application of leeches is recommended, as is purgation;
or one should perform venesection, along with eye-washes and ointments, as in the case of Śukra.
A decoction made from vibhītaka, śivā, dhātrī, paṭola, ariṣṭa, and vāsaka, when drunk with guggulu, destroys swelling, pain, and ophthalmia (akṣipāka).
It also cures pilu, ulcers, leucoderma (śukra), and discolorations of the eyes (rāga).

Ghee cooked with these [herbs] also dispels those very diseases. A preparation consisting of *āṭarūṣa*, *abhayā*, *nimba*, *dhātrī*, *mustā*, *akṣa*, and *kūlaka* destroys bleeding and phlegm; the *vāsakādi* group is beneficial for the eyes.
Vāsā, ghanā, nimba, paṭola leaves,
tiktā, amṛtā, candana, vatsaka bark, kaliṅga, dārvī, citraka, and śuṇṭhī—
On the preceding day, one should drink this decoction consisting of eight parts of a boiled mixture of bhūnimba, dhātrī, abhayā, and vibhītaka.
It destroys cataracts, itching, films, tumors, and the *śukra* discharge; it heals both ulcerated and non-ulcerated wounds, as well as *pīlu*, *kāca*, and *mahāraja*.
This Vāsādi formulation, renowned for its efficacy, destroys night-blindness, redness, swelling, and pain, as well as all diseases of the eyes. (49)
Three pathyās, six bibhītakas, and twelve dhātrīs should be boiled in half a prastha of water until reduced to one-eighth.
Having drunk this, one conquers abhiṣyanda, discharge, redness, and timira.
When the eyes are injured, one should apply cold treatments such as eye-drops (āścyotana) and the like, which destroy agitation, redness, pain, and tearing, and clarify the vision;
one should quickly perform the procedure that produces clarity of sight.

The physician should treat her in the same manner even when she is afflicted by the application of unctuous, cold, and sweet substances, as well as by the distress caused by sweating, fire, smoke, fear, grief, pain, and heat. || 53 ||
Having observed the presence of an exogenous disorder (āgantudoṣa), one should first apply a fomentation using the heat from the mouth; then,
an immediate eye-drop (āścyotana) with breast milk should be administered.
And that which also removes disorders arising from bile and blood [is effective] for one whose vision is impaired by gazing at the sun during an eclipse, fire, lightning, and so forth. || 54 ||

Nourishing therapy with unctuous and cooling substances should be employed, and the administration of Triphalā should be practiced in the evening. [One should take] Niśā, Abda, Triphalā, Dārvī, sugar, and Madhuka combined.
Filling [the eyes] with cow's milk cures injury and pain in the eyes;
likewise, filling the eyes with the fresh juice (svarasa) of *itkuṭa* sprouts is effective.
Goat's ghee, a vessel of milk, *madhuka*, and blue lotuses [are also used]. || 56-57 ||
One should also cook ghee with jīvaka and ṛṣabhaka ground together;
this ghee is recommended for all injuries to the eyes.
Saindhava salt, devadāru, śuṇṭhī, the juice of mātuluṅgī, and ghee [are also used].

That collyrium should be prepared with breast milk and water for the condition known as *śuṣkapāka*. Furthermore, as in the case of *vātābhiṣyanda*, other treatments for *vāta* should be applied; in cases of *mārutaparyaya*, ghee is beneficial when taken before a meal, and milk is beneficial during the meal.
One should also drink ghee prepared with milk and the juice of *karkaṭa*, along with *vṛkṣādanī*, *kapittha*, the five roots (*pañcamūla*), and *mahat* (gudūcī),
for the treatment of *abhiṣyanda*, *adhimantha*, or *arjuna* arising from blood.

One should bring about the pacification of diseases of the head, such as *śirotpāta* (head-splitting pain), *śirāharṣa* (throbbing of the vessels), and other ailments arising in the eyes, by means of clarified butter (*ājya*) boiled with *kaumbha* (the *kuṃbhī* plant). For the purpose of alleviating the condition caused by exposure to sour substances, one should apply very cold medicinal pastes.

Ghee prepared with *tainduka* or the three myrobalans (*traiphala*), or even aged ghee alone, is beneficial; a treatment that alleviates *pittasrāva* (pitta-discharge) should be administered without venesection.
Ghee mixed with honey should serve as the medicinal remedy for *śirotpāta*.
Similarly, rock salt and green vitriol ground with breast milk is highly recommended.
In the case of irritation of the vessels (sirāharṣa), one should apply a collyrium (añjana) consisting of treacle mixed with honey,
or antimony combined with honey, or green vitriol mixed with honey.
To pacify ulcerated semen (vraṇaśukra), one should drink six-part guggulu along with the fruit of *kataka*, conch shell, *tinduka*, and silver.
Ground in a bronze vessel with breast milk, this conquers the pain and discoloration caused by wounded semen.
A suppository made of sandalwood, red ochre, lac, and jasmine buds is equal [in efficacy];
it removes wounds and semen and clarifies the blood.
Alternatively, one may extract blood from the eye using a needle or leeches.
Collyrium made from the marrow of an elephant applied in the evening with breast milk destroys semen;
likewise, a single white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) sprinkled with goat’s milk cures passion, tears, and pain, as well as injuries, suppuration, and complications. (70)
Tutthaka mixed with water destroys semen when used to fill the eyes.
A wick made from sea-foam, the skin of a cock's egg, rock salt, honey, and the seeds of *śigru*, along with *śigru* water, destroys semen.
A decoction of *dhātrī* fruit, *nimba* and *paṭola* leaves, *yaṣṭyāhvā*, *lodhra*, *khadira*, and sesame seeds,
when well-cooled and applied as an eye-drop, [is beneficial].
It destroys semen in every way. Sprinkling with water infused with crushed *punnāga* leaves, or with water boiled from *śyāmāka* grain, removes [the appearance of] flowers.
This collyrium formulation, consisting of equal parts of *dakṣāṇḍatvak*, stone, conch-shell, glass, sandalwood, and red ochre, scrapes away *puṣpārma* and other such conditions;
it may also be prepared with *śirīṣa* seeds, black pepper, long pepper, and rock salt.
In the case of seminal discharge, friction [of the penis] should be performed with either sugar or rock salt (saindhava). Alternatively,
a substance repeatedly saturated with the fresh juice of *palāśa* flowers conquers [the condition] before long.
A wick made from *naktāhva* seeds destroys even long-standing accumulations of impurities in the eyes;
likewise, [the use of] rock salt, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), black pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), *kaṭukā*, and conch-shell (*śaṅkhanābhi*) [achieves the same].
A wick made from ground copper filings destroys semen.

This powder— consisting of sandalwood, rock salt, harītakī, and the blood of the palāśa tree, each increasing in quantity by one part in sequence— is for scraping away *śukrārma* and other such lesions.

A tooth-stick made from the teeth of an elephant, boar, camel, cow, horse, goat, or donkey, combined with conch shell, pearl, sea-foam, and one-quarter part of black pepper, will cure even the disease of seminal injury (kṣataśukra). || 80 ||
Four parts of conch shell, half of that amount of realgar, half of the realgar of black pepper, and half of the black pepper of rock salt—

Piccaṭa should be combined with honey, and likewise arbuda with whey;
