A patient with *pillī* (pterygium) who has been treated with oleation should first undergo emesis; once the blood has flowed out, venesection should be performed.

One should improve the vision with *śilājatu*, *rasāñjana*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and cow’s bile. Tagara ground with *haritāla*, *vacā*, *dāru*, and *urasāra*, or ground with the juice of *abhayā*, destroys eye-secretions (*pillana*).

A wise person should fumigate one afflicted by pillar-disease (pilliaroga) with devadāru wood that has been soaked in goat's urine and mixed with oil, along with a single fruit of kākamācī combined with ghee;
the worms will fall away before long.
Rasāñjana, sarjarasa, jasmine flowers,
realgar, sea-foam, salt, red ochre, and black pepper— these, taken in equal parts and ground with honey, [are used] for moistened eyelids (praklinnavartman).
Collyrium made from the pulp of the *mastakāsthi* (the seed of the *citraka*) mixed with *tuṣodaka* (fermented grain-water) and salt cures moisture and itching and promotes the growth of eyelashes;
when rubbed in a copper vessel, this collyrium is used for *pilla* and *praklinna-vartman*.
Roots of *guhā* (mūṣikaparṇī), rock salt (*sindhūttha*), and black pepper, ground together with *āranāla* in a copper vessel,
constitute a collyrium that destroys *pillaka*.
Likewise, the two types of turmeric (*haridrā*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *lodhra*, *madhuka*, and red sandalwood (*raktacandana*) [prepared similarly serve the same purpose].
Having ground [the ingredients] in the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* and rubbed them in an iron vessel, as well as in copper, for seven days, one should prepare either a wick or a powder.
This cures *picciṭī*, *dhūmadarśī*, and vision impaired by *timira*.
One should regularly apply [this] in the morning and evening; it removes all eye diseases.
Mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, utpala, the froth of the ocean, tvak, sevya, and gorocanā—
This collyrium consists of all these ingredients— māṃsī, candana, śaṅkha, patra, girimṛt, tālīsa, puṣpa, and añjana— in equal parts.
This is always recommended for the eyes; it removes itching, moisture, impurities, tears, blood, pain, pilla, arma, and śukra.
One *pala* of tutthaka (copper sulfate) and twenty white pepper seeds, ground with thirty *palas* of fermented rice-water (*kāñjika*), should be placed in a copper vessel;
it renders cataracts (*pillāna*) and non-cataracts (*apillāna*) curable, even those arising many years ago.

By sprinkling that [medicine], one should destroy the discharge, tears, itching, swelling, and inflammation. However, *pakṣmoparodha* (eyelash obstruction) is palliable through the extraction of eyelashes and scraping.
That which has accumulated on the eyelid (*vartman*) should be scraped; blood that is provoked should be drained.

The wise physician should slowly extract the excessively grown eyelashes from a patient who can endure it; he should remove the lashes on the upper lid with forceps and those on the lower lid with a probe,
while protecting the eye by cauterizing the lash with a heated gold needle.
Furthermore, in the disease of the eyelashes (pakṣmara), the growth of new hair never occurs again.
[The following are types of] *utsaṅginī*, *bahulakardamavartmanī*, the dark (*śyāva*), and that which is torn (*paṭita*)— these are known here as *baddhavartman*.
The *kliṣṭa*, the *pothakī*, the *vartman* (in this context), the *kumbhīkinī* along with the *śarkarā*,
and the two types of *śleṣmopanāha* should be scraped; the *bisa* should be incised.
Regarding the glandular swelling caused by worms (*krimikṛta-granthi*) and the condition called *añjananāmikā*:

one should repeatedly scarify a case of phlegm-induced distension (*kaphānāha*) with a round-tipped instrument (*maṇḍalāgra*) smeared with powdered rock salt (*saindhava*) and ghee, or else perform scarification all around it.
The procedure of pouring medicinal drops (āścyotana) with decoctions of *paṭola* and *āmalaka* is beneficial; likewise, the juices of *phaṇijjaka* and *rasuna* destroy *pothakī*.
One should cauterize an obstructed carbuncle (*ānāha-piḍakā*) with fire after it has been fomented and incised obliquely.
Likewise, for the conditions known as arśas, vartma, śuṣkārśas, and arbuda,

the physician should gradually excise them at the base with a sharp maṇḍalāgra instrument, using a paste of rock salt, pippalī, kuṣṭha, parṇinī, and the juices of the three myrobalans (triphalā). || 240-241 ||

A wick (varti) made with the scum of wine (*surāmaṇḍa*) destroys excessive *kapha* (*śleṣmābhiṣyanda*), as well as *pothakī*, obstruction of the eyelids (*vartmoparodha*), worms, glandular swellings (*krimigranthi*), and *tūṇaka*. (242) Section 59.

In cases of head diseases caused by vāta, one should administer oleation, sudation, nasal drops (nasya), as well as drinks, food, and medicinal offerings that alleviate vāta disorders. For skin diseases (kuṣṭha), castor oil ground with kāñjika should be applied as a paste.
It quickly destroys headache, as does the flower of the *mucukunda* tree.
(2) One should administer milk boiled with the five roots (*pañcamūlī*) as a nasal drop (*nasya*) for diseases of the head.
Having stretched out a hide from the head upwards and raised it eight finger-breadths high, (3) [one should apply it].
Having wrapped it with that [cloth], one should smear the area below the head with a paste of black gram (māṣa);
while the patient remains seated and motionless, one should fill [the cavity] with warm oils.
One should maintain this for a watch (yāma) or even half a watch, until the pain subsides.

This head-poultice (śirobasti) conquers diseases of the head arising from wind (vāta), as well as pain in the jaw, temples, eyes, and ears, facial paralysis (ardita), and tremors of the head. Having filled the head with oil for five hundred mātrās, [it provides relief].
In cases of phlegm (kapha), one should remain for eight [nāḍīs]; in bile (pitta), for eight; and in wind (vāta) or diseases of the head, for ten.
This same procedure should be followed for filling the ears and eyes.
In the case of pitta, ghee, milk, sprinklings, cold plasters, and nasal drops (nasya) are indicated.
Life-prolonging medicated ghees, as well as food and drink that pacify pitta, [are beneficial].
In cases of head disease caused by pitta, one should properly administer an unctuous purgative using the juices of grapes, triphalā, and sugarcane, as well as milk and ghee.
Anointing with *ghṛta* purified a hundred times, exposure to cool breezes and the like, and the constant application of cooling sensations should be practiced for the relief of burning pain.
[One should apply] sandalwood, *uśīra*, *yaṣṭyāhvā*, *balā*, *vyāghrī*, *nakha*, and blue lotus.
An external application (pradeha) made from milk and ground [herbs] should be used, or a pouring of decoctions (pariṣecana) should be administered.
One should apply a head-poultice (śiro-dhi) with smooth and cool lotus stalks, lotus roots, lotus tubers, sandalwood, blue lotuses, and saffron; likewise, one may use āmalaka and blue lotuses.
Ghee prepared with yaṣṭyāhva, candana, anantā, and milk is beneficial;
or, for a pitta-born [nasal disease], nasal drops (nāvana) made from sugar, drākṣā, and madhuka are likewise helpful.
A paste of tvak, patra, and sugar, mixed with rice-water, may also be used as a nasal drop.
Milk, ghee, or wholesome meat-broths from wild animals are beneficial as nasal drops (nasya).
In cases arising from blood (raktaja), all treatments— diet, ointments, and sprinklings— should be like those for pitta,
with the specific distinction being the alternating application of cold and heat and bloodletting.
In cases arising from *kapha*, fasting, sudation with dry and hot substances that promote digestion,
sharp nasal drops (*avapīḍa*), medicinal smokes (*dhūma*), and sharp gargles (*kavala*) are beneficial. One should also administer clear, aged ghee and subsequently apply sudation.
One should foment the head with the essence of *madhūka* and administer a head-purgative (*virecana*).
An application of paste made from *kṛṣṇā*, *abda*, *śuṇṭhī*, *madhuka*, *śatāhvā*, *utpala*, and *pākala*, ground with water, provides immediate relief from headache.

A plaster made of *devadāru*, *nata*, *kuṣṭha*, *nalada*, and *viśvabheṣaja*, ground with *kāñjika* and mixed with oil, removes headache. In cases arising from *sannipāta*, a treatment that pacifies the three *doṣas* should be administered.
Indeed, they prescribe the drinking of ghee, especially that which is aged;
[along with] trikaṭu, puṣkara, rajanī, rāsnā, suradāru, and turagagandhā.
The decoction, when drunk through the nose, wards off the multitude of headaches.
Milk mixed with the paste of *nāgara* (ginger), when administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*) to men, [achieves the same].
Blue lotus combined with sandalwood and kuṣṭha, applied as a plaster with ghee, destroys even the most intense headache arising from various causes. (22)
A plaster consisting of prapauṇḍarīka, suradāru, kuṣṭha, yaṣṭimadhu, elā, kamala, and utpala,
mixed with ghee, [is used] for headache.
Oil boiled with *lohairaka*, *padmaka*, *coraka*, *śatāhvā*, the root of *eraṇḍa*, *grāva*, and the fruits of *vyāghrī*,
used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), removes wind-disorders, phlegm, cataracts, and diseases of the upper body. (23–24)
Oil cooked with milk and *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *drākṣā*, sugar, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *balā*, and *utpala* should be used as a nasal drop (*nasya*) for diseases of the head caused by *vāta* and *pitta*.
*Jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *drākṣā*, *madhūka*, *madhuka*, and *balā* [are also used for this purpose].

One should slowly cook one *prastha* of oil with blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), sandalwood (*candana*), *vidārī*, and sugar; likewise, with six times as much milk and the broth of half a *tulā* of the meat of wild animals. || 26–27 ||
This oil for nasal administration (nasya) is proven to cure hemicrania (ardhāvabhedaka),
deafness, earache, blurred vision, and tonsillitis;
it pacifies all diseases of the head caused by Vāta and Pitta.
It draws out loose teeth, headache, and facial paralysis. (29) Eranda root, tagara, śatāhvā,
jīvantī, rāsnā, along with rock salt—
Bhr̥ṅga, viḍaṅga, madhuyaṣṭikā,
and viśvauṣadha, along with oil of black sesame and goat’s milk mixed with oil.
Six drops of this [oil] cooked in four times the amount of *bhṛṅgara* juice should be administered through the nose; they quickly destroy disorders of the head. || 31 ||
It makes fallen hair grow back and loose teeth firm; it strengthens roots that are poorly established and makes the eyes resemble the gaze of Suparṇa.
It bestows superior strength upon the arms.
In the case of wasting (kṣayaja), one should employ nourishing (br̥ṃhaṇa) measures once the stage of wasting has been reached;
ghee processed with vāta-alleviating and sweet [drugs] should be used for drinking and as nasal drops.

For worm-induced [diseases], nasal drops (nāvana) consisting of *vyoṣa*, *naktāhva*, and the seeds of *śigru*, combined with goat's urine, are an excellent vermifuge; this nasal treatment (*nasya*) is supreme for overcoming worms. [One should also use] the fruits of *apāmārga*, *vyoṣa*, *niśā*, alkali, and *karāmaṭha*.
Oil boiled with *viḍaṅga* and cow’s urine, used as nasal drops (*nasya*), overcomes worms.
In all diseases such as arm-stiffness (*bhujastambha*) and other upward-moving disorders, one should administer ginger with jaggery, or *viśva* (śuṇṭhī) with long pepper and rock salt.
In the case of Sūryāvarta, medicinal treatments such as nasal therapy (nasya) should be administered;
one should cause [the patient] to drink ghee mixed with jaggery and eat ghee-filled cakes (ghṛtapūra).
In Sūryāvarta, bloodletting of the head and nasal drops of milk and ghee should be employed.
The habitual consumption of milk and ghee is beneficial, as is purgation with those two;
fomentation with sesame seeds ground in milk and with *jīvanīya* herbs is recommended.
Saffron mixed with sugar and fried in ghee [is also beneficial].

Nasal therapy (nasya) should be administered for pain in the eyebrows, temples, ears, eyes, and head arising from wind (vāta) and blood (asṛj), as well as for diseases that increase with the passage of days. || 39 ||
Fresh butter prepared with the juice of *kṛtamāla* sprouts and the paste of *kharamañjarī*,
when used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), certainly conquers [the disease].
The decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī), combined with ghee and rock salt,
used as a nasal drop (nasya) destroys hemicrania (ardhāvabhedaka) and relieves the headache of sūryāvarta, which is otherwise very difficult to restrain.
One should administer an *avapīḍa* (nasal drop) prepared with the roots and fruits of the *śirīṣa*;
or an *avapīḍa* boiled with *vacā* and *pippalī* would be beneficial. Furthermore, one should prepare a poultice (*upanāhana*) using the meat of wild animals.
By this, his most dreadful Sūryāvarta disease is pacified;
this entire procedure should also be performed for Ardhabhedaka.
Śārivā, utpala, kuṣṭha, and madhuka, ground with sour liquids, [should be applied].
An ointment of ghee and oil is used for *sūryāvarta* and *ardhabheda*.
One should drink milk with sugar, or coconut water,
or very cold water, or ghee as nasal drops (*nastaḥ*) for these two conditions.
In the case of *anantavāta*, the procedure beneficial for *sūryāvarta* should be performed,
and venesection must be carried out for the pacification of *anantavāta*. Furthermore, a diet that destroys wind and bile (*vātapitta*) should be prescribed.

The same regimen applied with honey, mastuka, saṃyāva, and oblations of clarified butter is beneficial for Sūryāvarta; however, for Śaṅkhaka, it should be administered without fomentation (sveda). For Śaṅkhaka, they praise the administration of milk and ghee through nasal drops and internal potions.
One should properly apply a medicinal paste consisting of śatāvarī, black sesame seeds, madhuka, blue lotus (nīlotpala), mūrvā, and punarnavā; likewise,
one should employ sprinklings of cold water and cool milk-baths.
An ointment should be applied using the pastes of milky trees and conch-shell. Furthermore,
for that [wound] which has been treated with the juices of the krauñca, kādamba, haṃsa, śarārī, and tortoise, the [discharges] arising from the joints of the conch-shell [occur].

A wise physician should pierce only the three vessels above; he must not strike the head itself. In cases of tremors of the head (śiraḥkampa), treatments that are anti-wind (vātaghna)—such as oleation, sudation, and the use of amṛtā, rāsnā, balā, fats, and fragrant substances—as well as the application of a head-pouch (śirobasti), are recommended.

Ghee prepared with liquorice (*yaṣṭīmadhu*), *balā*, *rāsnā*, and water decocted from the ten roots (*daśamūla*), along with the drugs of the sweet group (*madhura*), cures diseases above the clavicle.
[53] [This ghee is prepared] together with three *palas* each of the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *balā*, *rāsnā*, and *madhuka*.

Having boiled a peacock— excluding its feathers, bile, intestines, excrement, feet, and beak— in water, one should cook a *prastha* of ghee with an equal amount of milk and the paste (*kalka*) of sweet drugs (weighing one *karṣa* each);
this cures diseases of the head and facial paralysis.
This preparation, beginning with peacock [meat], is renowned for destroying diseases of the ears, nose, eyes, tongue, mouth, and throat; it removes ailments above the clavicle.
Furthermore, a wise person [should prepare it] with mice, chickens, swans, and hares as well.
One should cook ghee with this paste; it removes diseases that move upward.
Here, a peacock equal in size to the *daśamūla* and other ingredients is taken;
others, however, understand the inclusion of the peacock by its physical appearance alone.

Oil prepared with prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, pippalī, candana, and utpala in the juice of dhātrī, when used as a nasal drop or for massage, destroys all diseases of the upper body and, when practiced regularly, removes gray hair. (59)
One should boil one hundred palas of peacock meat along with ten roots (*daśamūla*) and one *tulā* of *balā* in one *droṇa* of water until it is reduced to one-quarter; then,
having added one *droṇa* of milk, one should cook it there with one *āḍhaka* of ghee.

This peacock-based [preparation], prepared with the drugs mentioned in the group beginning with *prapauṇḍarīka* and those that are vitalizing (*jīvanīya*), promotes intelligence, intellect, and memory; it cures diseases of the supraclavicular region and is a supreme remedy for all wind disorders.
It destroys pain of the neck, ears, head, and eyes, as well as epilepsy; it cures poison, diseases caused by wind (vāta), asthma, irregular fevers, and cough.
(63) Chapter 60.
A woman afflicted by vāta-āsṛgdara (menorrhagia or metrorrhagia) should drink a mixture of sauvarcala salt, ajājī, madhuka, and blue utpala with curd and honey.
She should also drink the blood of a deer combined with sugar and honey.
In cases of Pitta-type disorders, one should take the fresh juice of Vāsaka or the juice of Guḍūcī.
In cases of Pāṇḍu and Asṛgdara (menorrhagia), one should drink the paste of Rohītaka roots with water,
or the paste of Āmalaka seeds with sugar and honey.
One should drink either an akṣa-measure of dhātakī, or āmalakī mixed with honey,
or the root of kākajaṅghā, or the root of kārpāsa,
with rice-water for the sake of pacifying pāṇḍu-pradara.
One should drink milk boiled with a decoction of *aśoka* bark, well-cooled, in a dose according to one's strength in the morning; this destroys severe menorrhagia (*asṛgdara*).
[Also effective are: *dārvī*, *rasāñjana*, *vṛṣa*, *abda*, *kirāta*, and *bilva*.
A decoction prepared with *bhallātaka* fruits and drunk with honey overcomes even severe *pradara* (menorrhagia), whether it be accompanied by pain and characterized by yellow,
black, reddish, crimson, blue, or white discharge.
Rasāñjana and the root of taṇḍulīya,
taken with honey and drunk with rice-water,
destroy menorrhagia of all origins.
One should also take śvāsa, bhārgī, and nāgara together.
Having extracted daśamūla, one should grind it with rice-water;
by drinking this, a woman is freed from pradara after three days.
One should drink the juice of the fruit of *udumbara* mixed with honey for the destruction of *asṛgdara*, while consuming food with milk and sugar.
The root of *balā* drunk with milk and mixed with honey destroys *pradara*.

The root of *kuśa*, *vāṭyālaka*, and *raktākhya* with rice-water pacifies the effects of drinking liquor; both of these [roots] are known as *rakta* and *śukla*. Likewise, the powder of *badarī* with jaggery, or raw *moca* with milk [pacifies it].
Yellow lac combined with ghee, used separately, destroys pradara;
one should also treat cases of pradara according to the procedures for raktapitta, and specifically employ the Kuṭajāṣṭaka formulation in cases of asṛgdara.
The bark of the jambū and āmra trees, śilābheda, rasāñjana, ambaṣṭhakī, mocarasa, samaṅgā,
padmakeśara, bāhlīka, ativiṣā, musta, bilva, lodhra, and gairika— these are pure for recitation. (14)
Kaṭphala, marica, śuṇṭhī, mṛdvīkā, and red sandalwood;
kaṭvaṅga, vatsaka, anantā, dhātakī, madhuka, and arjuna—having extracted these on the day of Puṣya, one should prepare them as equal parts of fine powder. || 15–16 ||
One should mix these with honey and have them drunk with rice-water in cases of menorrhagia, diarrhea, and the discharge of blood that is passed;
it also destroys those ailments of children caused by the bodily humors (doṣas) or by external factors (āgantu).
One should forcibly eliminate the defects of the womb, the defects of the menstrual flow, and [discharges] that are white, blue, yellow, or dark-red and coppery;
this beneficial powder named Puṣyānuga, honored by Ātreya, should be used. (18–19)
Ghee prepared with a decoction of mudga and māṣa beans, along with rāsnā, citraka, nāgara, pippalī, and bilva, is excellent for treating asṛgdara (menorrhagia).
Kumuda, padmaka, uśīra, wheat, and red śāli rice [are beneficial].
Mudgaparṇī, payasyā, kāśmarī, and madhuyaṣṭikā;
the roots of balā and atibalā, utpala, tālamastaka, vidārī, śatamūlī, śālaparṇī, and jīvaka. || 21–22 ||
Take fresh seeds of the three fruits (triphalā) and plantain fruit;
of these, take portions of half a pala each, along with four times as much cow’s milk and twice as much water,
and cook them with one prastha of ghee.
In cases of menorrhagia, internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), blood-tumors (raktagulma), and jaundice (halīmaka);
in that pitta which manifests in many forms, as well as in jaundice (kāmalā), gout (vātaśoṇita), loss of appetite, chronic fever, anemia (pāṇḍuroga), intoxication, and vertigo; || 24–25 ||
For a young woman who has few menses and does not conceive,
this elixir called Śītakalyāṇaka, which increases pleasure for women day by day, is highly recommended. (26)
The physician should crush one prastha of śatāvarī juice and squeeze it out, then add one prastha of ghee and twice as much milk (two prasthas).
To this, he should add these medicinal pastes (kalkas), each equal in size to a large jujube fruit (udumbara).
The eight life-sustaining (jīvanīya) drugs are: yaṣṭī, padmaka, and candana; śvadaṃṣṭrā, ātmaguptā, balā, and likewise nāgabalā;
as well as śālaparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, vidārī, and the two types of śārivā.
Sugar and *kāśmarya* fruits should be added in equal measure; once it is known to be properly prepared, one should remove that ghee from the fire.
It is used for disorders of *rakta-pitta* and those caused by *vāta* and *pitta*.
It cures vātarakta, consumption, dyspnea, hiccups, and difficult-to-overcome cough;
burning sensations in the limbs and the head arising from raktapitta,
menorrhagia of all types, and most severe dysuria.
These diseases he pacifies, just as the sun dispels darkness. (32) Chapter 61: In disorders of the female reproductive tract, treatment that conquers Vata is most highly recommended.

Enemas, massage, affusion, and external applications, as well as the application of cotton swabs [soaked in oil], should be employed. [The ingredients are] vacā, upakuñcikā, jātī, kṛṣṇā, vṛṣaka, saindhava salt,
ajamodā, yavakṣāra, and citraka, combined with sugar.

Having ground [the powder] and stirred it with *prasannā* wine, one should eat it fried in ghee for the alleviation of pain in the vagina and flanks, heart disease, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and hemorrhoids.
One should also perform sprinkling with decoctions of *guḍūcī*, *triphalā*, and *dantī*.

A tampon (picu) prepared from oil processed with nata, vārtākinī, kuṣṭha, saindhava, and amaradāru should be applied to the vagina to alleviate pain. For yonis that are dominated by pitta, however, treatments such as pouring liquids (sekā), massage (abhyaṅga), and the application of tampons (picu-kriyā) are indicated.

Cold applications that alleviate *pitta* should be employed, as well as unctuous substances (*sneha*) such as ghee; however, for a vagina corrupted by *balāsa*, all medicines that are dry and hot should be used.
[These include] long pepper (*pippalī*), black pepper (*marica*), black gram (*māṣa*), dill seed (*śatāhvā*), costus (*kuṣṭha*), and rock salt (*saindhava*).
A wick-like tampon, equal in size to the index finger, should be held [in place] for the purification of the vagina.
One suffering from Vāta should apply a lukewarm paste of Hiṃsrā and hold it;
one suffering from Pitta should use the paste of the five barks (pañcavalka); and one with a predominance of Kapha should use that of Śyāmā and other such plants.

Oil mixed with mouse meat and processed by exposure to the sun, when used for massage, destroys hemorrhoids of the female genital tract; likewise, fomentation with that same meat and rock salt [is effective]. Linen cloth soaked three times seven times in cow-bile or fish-bile [should be applied].
One should administer either honey or yeast powder (kiṇva-cūrṇa), which removes the inability to walk;
it cleanses the channels and removes swelling, itching, and discharge. Furthermore, a sudation procedure should be performed for a woman with a foul-smelling vagina.

Then the sequential treatment should be performed; thereafter, saturation with medicated cotton swabs (*picu*) should take place using the barks of *śallakī*, *jiṅginī*, *jambu*, *dhava*, and the five types of bark (*pañcavalkala*).
Oil prepared with the decoctions of these should be used as a cotton swab application to remove *viplutā*.

In cases of *karṇinī*, a wick (*vartikā*) made from kuṣṭha, pippalī, the tips of arka flowers, and rock salt, prepared with goat's urine, should be inserted; furthermore, all remedies that alleviate phlegm are beneficial.
In conditions of upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*) and pain caused by wind, the three-fold unctuous substance (*traivṛta*) serves as an emollient, and sudation (*sveda*) should be applied.
And that very [act] is prescribed when the Great Yoni has been displaced;
the flesh of a rat, having been immediately cut into many small pieces,
should be fried in oil until it certainly melts thoroughly.
Constantly wearing a garment soaked in that oil on the region of the vulva destroys the shameful consequences of the female organ; there is no doubt about this.
Likewise, [it is cured] by the application of *śatapuṣpā* oil or that produced from *badarī* leaves.
By applying a paste made from the root of *peṭikā*, a prolapsed vagina is pacified.

By applying a paste made from the root of *suṣavī*, a vagina that has entered internally becomes external; through anointing with the juice of *mūṣa*, even one that has receded back inside shall enter [the body] again.
An ointment of *lodhra* and *tumbī* fruit makes the vagina firm, as does washing with a decoction of the roots of the reed (*vetasa*). Similarly,
anointing with the fat of a female rat (*mūṣikā*) or a female mongoose (*vāguli*) grants firmness to the vagina.
Vacā, blue lotus, kuṣṭha, and likewise black pepper,
along with aśvagandhā and turmeric, constitute an excellent means for firming [the body].
When filled with madana fruit, liquorice, and camphor, it becomes [an aphrodisiac] for women who desire love.
For one whose youth has faded, the most excellent part [the penis] is exceedingly delicate;
[therefore], an ointment made from *pañcapallava*, *yaṣṭī*, *āhvā*, and *mālatī* flowers— either cooked with the sun’s heat or otherwise— destroys vaginal odor.
A wick made from *ikṣvāku*, *bīja*, *dantī*, *capalā*, jaggery, *madana*, *kiṇva*, and *yaṣṭyāhva*,
along with the milky sap of *snuhī*, inserted into the vagina, brings about the production of menses. Likewise,
*javā* flowers with sour gruel and fried leaves of *jyotiṣmatī* [achieve the same].
By consuming the flour of dūrvā grass, a woman shall obtain her menses.
The powder of dhātrī, añjana, and abhayā, when drunk with water, removes the menstrual flow;
likewise, eating it ground together with the leaves of the śelu plant serves the same purpose.
The root of *lakṣaṇā* (puṣpoddhṛta), ground by a girl whose feet bear the mark of a wheel (*cakrāṅgā*), when drunk with milk and ghee during her fertile period (*ṛtu*), bestows a son.
Milk prepared with the decoction of *hayagandhā* along with ghee [is likewise effective].
A young woman who has bathed after her menses, having drunk this, will conceive; of this there is no doubt.
Long pepper, ginger, black pepper, and likewise saffron should be drunk with ghee; even a barren woman obtains a son.
When the powder of gold, silver,
and copper, mixed with clarified butter,
is drunk in a pure field, [the result is] pure.
From the application of medicine, conception may occur.
Having performed purification and bathing, and having fasted for a day, one should then [take it] in the morning.
Having bathed and likewise worshipped with devotion the Lord of the World (Lokanātheśa) and the white *balā*, *aṅghrika*, and *yaṣṭī* [medicinal herbs] for the sake of the twice-born; || 30 ||
Having ground one *karṣa* at a time of sugar, [one should prepare it] with the milk of a cow whose calf is of the same color and still living. || 31 ||
When this has been drunk with an abundance of ghee,
no other food should be given on that day; however, for one who is hungry, food with milk may be given.
She,
being courageous and leaning toward the right side, should offer [the oblation] on an even day with an auspicious conjunction, until the presence of a man [is achieved]. || 32 ||
For a man whose attachment to other women has been abandoned, whose mind is filled with joy, and whose humors are greatly increased, even a mere encounter—
From that, one certainly obtains a son.

Furthermore, two māsas and two white mustard seeds combined with curd [should be offered] at a *vaṭaka* tree grown in a cow-pen, on a branch of the kind previously mentioned, provided it is auspicious.
These two, when colored with flowers and applied to a woman who has quickly conceived, bring about the birth of a son.
One should meditate upon these male figures— whether made of gold, silver, or iron— as being the color of fire, and [submerge them] in milk, curd, or water.
Having cast [these] into his cupped hands during the Puṣya asterism, one should drink them to ensure the conception of a son; [the ingredients are]:
mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, kuṣṭha, triphalā, sugar, balā, medā, payasyā, kākolī, and the root of aśvagandhā. (35–36)

One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *karṣa* each of the following ingredients: *ajamodā*, the two types of *haridrā*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *kaṭurohiṇī*, blue lotus (*utpala*), white water lily (*kumuda*), grapes (*drākṣā*), the two types of *kākolī*, and the two types of sandalwood (*candana*). || 37 ||
One should add four times as much milk and the juice of śatāvarī as there is ghee.
By drinking this ghee regularly, a man becomes like a bull among women,
and a woman gives birth to sons who are endowed with intelligence and are pleasing to behold.
This is recommended for those who have a stagnant fetus, or who gives birth to one that dies, or one of short life, or for her who gives birth to a female child;
it is also prescribed for defects of the womb, defects of the menses, and for excessive discharge. || 40 ||

This is indeed proclaimed by the Aśvins as "Phalaghṛta," which increases progeny, promotes longevity, and wards off all malevolent planets. Physicians add the root of Lakṣmaṇā here, even though it was not explicitly mentioned.
In this case, the ghee of a cow that has a single-colored calf is highly recommended;
furthermore, the sacrificial fire is kindled with wild cow dung.
[One should take] the two *sahacara* plants, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *guḍūcī*, and *punarnavā*.
Having made a paste of śukanāsā, the two types of haridrā, rāsnā, medā, and śatāvarī, one should cook one prastha of ghee with four times as much milk;
a woman afflicted by pain in the vagina should drink that once it is prepared.
Those that are compacted, those that have moved, those that have emerged, and those that are opened; those born from a mass, those that are dissolved, and those known as the neuter birth—
all these enter their place and repeatedly take up conception in the womb.
This is known as Etatphala-ghṛta (Ghee from these fruits), which is supreme for removing disorders of the female reproductive tract.
Siddhārthaka, vacā, brāhmī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, punarnavā, payasyā, amaya, yaṣṭyāhva, kaṭukā, elā, and the three myrobalans (triphalā)—[these are the ingredients]. 48.

The wise man, having properly cooked one prastha of ghee with śārivā, rajanī, pāṭhā, bhṛṅga, dāru, suvarcalā, mañjiṣṭhā, triphalā, śyāmā, vṛṣapuṣpa, and gairika, consecrated it with the appropriate mantras. || 49 ||
A woman pregnant for two months should not employ [this treatment] for six months;
it produces a son with all limbs complete, who is heroic and considers himself wise,
and it removes from him dullness, stammering, and muteness simply by drinking it.
By practicing this for seven nights, a person becomes a possessor of the Veda;
neither fire burns his house, nor does the thunderbolt strike it, nor do malevolent planets harm it. No child dies where he dwells, accompanied by Soma.
Even a barren woman obtains a son who is free from all diseases; and those women whose wombs are impaired, as well as those men whose seed is impaired, [attain their desire].
By the power of this [mantra], even one residing in the womb speaks with clear speech.
Grapes, *parūṣaka*, and *āśmarya* are declared to be the "three fruits.
[Mantra: "Oṃ, salutation to Mahāvināyaka!
Protect my nectar and grant me the accomplishment of the fruit."
"Give [it], by the word of Rudra, svāhā!"—
thus consecrated seven times with *dūrvā* grass.
Blue lotus, *uśīra*, *madhūka*, and *yaṣṭī*...
Ghee cooked with grapes, vidārī, kuśa, the five roots (pañcamūla), and the life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs, mixed with the juice of śatāvarī and milk, [is beneficial]. || 56 ||
This, combined with sugar and the like, is highly recommended for menorrhagia, disorders of wind and blood,
loss of strength, and the total depletion of semen.
In cases of difficult labor, hemorrhaging, and abdominal tumors (gulma):
one should crush four *tulās* of the root of *śatāvarī* and boil it with an equal amount of milk; with that decoction, one should cook one *āḍhaka* of ghee.

The physician should [prepare a paste] with one akṣa each of the life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs, śatāvarī, mṛdvīkā, parūṣaka, and priyāla, along with two parts of yaṣṭīmadhuka; once this has been cooked and cooled, he should add eight palas of honey and pippalī.
Having given ten palas of sugar mixed with that [mixture],
one should first have the Brahmins taste it, and then lick a palmful of it oneself;
for that destroys defects of the uterine blood and semen, is aphrodisiac, and promotes the birth of male offspring.

It conquers wasting due to injury, hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta), cough, dyspnea, chlorosis (halīmaka), jaundice, gout (vātarakta), erysipelas (visarpa), stiffness of the heart and head, insanity and other such conditions, and epilepsy caused by vāta and pitta. || 62 ||
Having burnt a conch shell, one should throw it into the juice of the *rambhā* plant;
that [conch] ground together with an equal amount of *ala* destroys hair growth on the private parts and other areas when applied as an ointment.
Oil of mustard seeds mixed with red collyrium and the powder of a cow's tail [achieves the same].

Having remained [applied] for seven days, it undoubtedly destroys the body hair from the roots; or, anointing with safflower oil once the hair has been plucked out brings about its end. Two palas of the root of *āragvadha* and two karṣas of conch-shell powder—
One *prastha* of yellow orpiment is cooked with donkey urine and pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*).
This oil, when powdered with conch shell and yellow orpiment and applied as an ointment, eradicates body hair; there is no possibility of their regrowth.
Camphor, bhallātaka, powdered conch-shell,
barley-alkali, realgar,
and oil cooked with yellow orpiment— [this mixture is used].
It eradicates body hair in an instant.
(67) Having burnt the long-stalked *samuṣkaka* plant along with pearl-oysters, snails, and conch shells, one should collect the resulting ash and dissolve it in donkey urine. (68)
A wise man should cook this mustard oil with half a measure of alkali;
this oil, honored by Ātreya, should be administered within the inner apartments.
Wherever a single drop falls, there hair shall grow anew.
This [oil], prepared by the two Aśvins, should be applied to wounds caused by passion (madana) and the like.
This excellent Kṣāra-taila is supreme for hemorrhoids, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), scabies (pāmā), ringworm (dadru), and eczema (vicarcikā); it is the best remover of all moist discharges.
Chapter 62:
Madhuka, śākabīja, and suradāru with milk; aśmantaka, black sesame, tāmravallī, and śatāvarī.
Vṛkṣādanī, payasyā, as well as utpala and śārivā,
anantā, śārivā, rāsnā, padmā, and madhuka;
the two types of bṛhatī, kāśmarya, milky sprouts, bark, and ghee.
Pṛthakparṇī, balā, śigru, śvadaṃṣṭrā,
madhuyaṣṭikā, śṛṅgāṭaka, bisa, drākṣā, kaśeru, madhuka, and sitā—
these shall be seven formulations for the [seven] months; indeed, there are seven half-verses for the seven [months].
In cases of miscarriage, these should be administered in their proper order combined with milk:
wood-apple, bilva, bṛhatī, paṭola, sugarcane, and digdhikā.
On the eighth day, the physician should cause the roots, boiled in milk, to be given.
In the ninth month, one should drink a decoction of madhuka, anantā, payasyā, and śārivā.
In the tenth month, milk boiled with ginger and then cooled is recommended;
alternatively, ginger, madhuka, and devadāru taken with milk are beneficial.
In this way, the fetus is nourished and severe pain is pacified;
milk boiled with the roots of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *uruvūka*, and *gokṣuraka*, combined with sugar, is an excellent remedy for the colic of a pregnant woman. 8.
Milk prepared with kaśeru, śṛṅgāṭaka, the jīvanīya group, padma, utpala, eraṇḍa, and śatāvarī, mixed with sugar, [is beneficial].
One should stabilize the fetus that is accompanied by intense labor pains [by administering] a preparation of *kaśeru*,
*śṛṅgāṭaka*, *padmaka*, *utpala*,
*samudgaparṇī*, and *madhuka*, together with sugar.

A woman suffering from the pain of difficult labor with colic should drink milk mixed with water; one who has eaten rice with milk should also drink it. When the fetus is dried up by wind, or when infants are wasting away, [this should be administered].
Milk boiled with white lotus (*sitā*), licorice (*madhuka*), and *kāśmarya* is beneficial for inducing labor.
In cases of fetal wasting (*garbha-śoṣa*), raw meat and predatory animals (*prasaha*) are always beneficial.
By applying a paste of *nābhi*, *basti*, and *bhaga* [to the woman's body], a woman gives birth easily;
likewise, a paste of *parūṣaka* and the roots of *sthirā* applied separately [to those same parts] produces the same result.
Similarly, by binding the root of *vāsā* around the waist, she will certainly give birth quickly.
If a woman applies the root of pāṭhā to her womb at the time of childbirth,
she will give birth with ease;
one should smear [the area] with the root ground with cold water.
By this [application], a pregnant woman quickly gives birth to feet with a cleft;
a plaster made from the root of *āṭarūṣaka* should be applied to the navel, the bladder, and the vulva. When the root of the *tāla* tree is worn as a loincloth by men, [it prevents seminal emission].
Drinking house-smoke with water from the home causes the extraction of the fetus.
(17) The roots of mātuluṅga together with madhuka, mixed with honey and drunk with ghee, cause a woman to give birth easily. (18)
Anointed with the smooth soot from the skin of a snake burnt in a closed vessel, together with the juice of the *kusuma-sāra* flower, the eye becomes instantly free of the arrow-head [or pain].
A woman who is pregnant, even one with a dead fetus,
[is cured] by drinking asafoetida and rock salt with house-water for the extraction of the fetus;
O beautiful lady, here [are] Amṛta, Soma, and Citrabhānu.
And let the horse Uccaiḥśravas dwell in your palace.
Let this woman release this nectar extracted from the waters, which indeed has the essence of the ocean within it.
May those [deities]—Fire, Wind, Sun, and Indra, together with the oceans of salt water—grant peace.
The nooses have been released and are now free; the rays have been released by the Sun.
"Released from all fear, O embryo, come, come, Māricī, svāhā!
(22) Having drunk water consecrated seven times with this mantra for delivery, a woman gives birth.
And having seen both the thirty-second [day],
as well as the fifteenth days of both fortnights, a woman brings about an easy delivery,
provided she is in her fertile period (*ṛtu*) together with the eight Vasus, and on the fifteenth, tenth, eighth, and eighteenth days of the lunar fortnight.
This wonder consists of two sets of thirty, accompanied by twelve, one, four, and five;
and by eight, three, four, one, five, nine, six, seven, and four, respectively.
All of this, [amounting to] fifteen, two, and thirty, is contained within nine compartments.
An incense made of bitter gourd, snake-skin, kṛtavedhana, and mustard seeds,
combined with pungent oil, causes the amarā to fall from the womb.
When rubbed on the throat with a finger wrapped in a cloth, the amarā falls easily.
[The mantra: "O forest of eraṇḍa! A crow has come to the bank of the Gaṅgā;
from here he drinks water, and the pregnant woman shall be free of her thorns (viśalyā).
Having consecrated water seven times with this [mantra], it should be given as the *viśalyaka* [remedy]. 28–29.
When the hands and feet have been smeared with the root of *lāṅgalikī*,
one should drink wine mixed with the powder of *pippalyādi* to bring about the downfall of the immortals (gods).
[One should also take] the root of *garīmadana-dahana*, even if it is old.
It causes the fetus to fall, whether it be dead or alive.

|| 31 || Alternatively, one should drink a dose the size of a rice-root or an akṣa, combined with urine or sour gruel, along with upakuñcikā and pippalī, and as much liquor as can be obtained. || 32 ||
Combined with sauvarcala salt, this [mixture] wards off pain in the womb;
for a woman who has recently given birth, it cures pain in the heart, head, and bladder, as well as the obstruction of makkalla.
In that case, one should drink yavakṣāra with ghee or warm water.
Or one should drink a decoction of the Pippalyādi group mixed with salt.
The dung of a pigeon drunk with rice-water (śālitaṇḍulavāri) prevents hemorrhage arising from a miscarriage that has occurred during pregnancy.
An ointment and a massage with Varuṇa leaves ground with water and mixed with ghee,
when applied after rubbing with cow dung, remove the disease known as Kikkīśa.
[36] Hrībera, lotus stalk, red sandalwood, and Balā...
A pregnant woman should drink a decoction of dhanyāka, vatsādanī, mustā, uśīra, yavāsa, parpaṭa, and viṣā.
This formulation was proclaimed by the sages of old for the disease of diarrhea accompanied by various morbid humors, as well as for hemorrhaging or fever.
It is recommended for the condition known as *sūtyāmayā* (fever following childbirth),
prepared by boiling it with *amṛtā*, *nāgara*, *sahacara*,
*bhadrotkaṭa*, the five roots (*pañcamūla*), and *jalada*.
The root of sahacara, puṣkara, and vetasa, combined with honey, wards off fever and the affliction of puerperal disorders. (38)
Wood from the *vaikaṅkata* tree, boiled in water with *kulattha* pulse, rock salt, and asafoetida, immediately removes the terrible pains of childbed fever. (39)
A decoction prepared from the ten roots (daśamūlī) immediately removes the pain of childbirth.
[Likewise, one should take] long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), chaba pepper (cavya), dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), and yamānī;
two types of jīvaka, two types of turmeric (haridrā), as well as viḍa salt and sauvarcala salt.
Āraṇāla prepared by boiling these same medicinal herbs ground together is a destroyer of āmavāta, an aphrodisiac, a subduer of kapha, and an stimulator of the digestive fire;
this kāñjika known as Vajraka increases the digestive fire in women.

The supreme remedy for pacifying colic caused by phlegm (makkanda) is the thorough churning with milk; one may also prepare sour gruel (kāñjika) according to the procedure for cooking medicinal milks. [Furthermore, the following are used:
cumin, hāpuṣā, coriander, dill, and devadāru.
Yamānī, tryaṣṭaka, hiṅgupatrikā, kāsamardaka, pippalī,
pippalīmūla, ajamodā, vāpyikā, and citraka— each one pala in weight— and another four palas [of the remaining ingredients]. || 44–45 ||
One should take kaśeruka, ginger, kuṣṭha, and dīpyaka,
along with a hundred palas of jaggery and one prastha of ghee;
these, combined with two prasthas of milk, should be cooked slowly over a mild fire.
This group known as Pañcajīraka (the five aromatics) is recommended for women who have recently given birth,
for women desiring conception, and for those requiring nourishment; it cures disorders of the wind (vāta), twenty types of vaginal diseases, cough, dyspnea, fever, and consumption.

By its constant use, women with full and elevated breasts and eyes as broad as lotus petals become free from misfortune and impurity; it destroys jaundice, anemia, foul odors, and excessive urination. (49)
One should drink the root of *vanakārpāsika* and *ikṣu* with sour gruel (*sauvīraka*), or the tuber of *vidārī* with wine; this increases breast milk.
Drinking powdered *śāli* rice with milk also causes it to increase.
There is no doubt that breast milk [is purified] within seven days for a woman who consumes milk.
For the purification of breast milk, she should drink either the *haridrādi* group or the *vacādi* group [of drugs].
In the case of breast milk characterized by *vāta*, she should drink water boiled with *daśamūlī*.
When the *pitta* is vitiated, one should drink a decoction of *amṛtā*, *abhīru*, *paṭola*, *nimba*, *candana*, *dhātrī*, *kumāra*,
and *sārivā*. Or, when *kapha* is predominant, [one should drink a decoction of] *triphalā*, *mustā*, *bhūnimba*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*.
For the sake of purifying the breast milk, the wet-nurse should consume mung bean soup and broth.
She should drink the decoction of bhārgī, vacā, dāru, pāṭhā, and ativiṣā boiled together.
Chewing the root of kukkurāmañjukā and holding it in the mouth overcomes [the affliction].

Within seven days, it causes a nipple-thorn and ensures the complete cessation of breast milk. Upon observing swelling arising from the breast, the physician should administer the same medicinal treatment prescribed here for an abscess (vidradhi).
While the abscess is still unripe, and likewise once it has reached suppuration,
one should constantly express her breasts. Furthermore, an ointment made from the root of *viśālā* destroys the pain arising from the breast.
An ointment made from *niśā*, gold, and *phala* also removes pain in the breasts.
By means of anointing and massaging with the fat of a mouse combined with the powder of the flesh of a boar, an elephant, and a buffalo, the breasts become firm and full. (58–59)

Vyādhibalā and likewise Nāgabalā, ground together with the butter from the breasts of a buffalo, produce full and firm breasts through the application of massage. Oil produced from sesame seeds is prepared by means of the juice and paste of Śrīparṇī.
One should apply that oil with *tūnaka* over the breasts;
thus, the fallen breasts of women will become uplifted.
[The powder of] *kāsīsa*, *turagagandhā*,...
By means of oil cooked with śārivā, gajapippalī, and other ingredients, the breasts, ears, female genitals, and penis attain growth. 62.
During the first menstrual period, one should administer rice-water as a nasal drop; this, combined with the ghee of a cow and a buffalo, makes the breasts firm.
Oil prepared with *śyāmā*, *kṛtāñjali*,
and *vaca*, along with the three pungents (*trikaṭu*) and *niśā*, used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), is the supreme remedy for raising up the breasts.
The root of the *mādhavī* creeper, drunk with churned milk, makes the waist slender;
though previously loose, it becomes firm. (64)
The vulva, having been joined with the application of ointment and oil from the *suragopa* plant,
becomes firmly bound by the cord-like thick hair of the arrow, due to being struck by the lover. 65.

A woman's innate hatred for her husband, or that which is produced by [magical] means, is destroyed by uprooting the root of the *sitabalā* plant during the Puṣya asterism and giving it to a Brahmin along with milk-rice; when ground by a maiden and given as food, it removes his lack of desire.
One should administer this linctus, composed of kuṣṭha, vacā, abhayā, brāhmī, and kamala with honey and ghee, to a child to produce a fine complexion, longevity, and luster. (63.1)
In the absence of breast milk, one should drink goat’s or cow’s milk possessing those same qualities.
Having quenched a heated medicinal pill in mustard oil,
that oil, when drunk, destroys the protruding navel of infants.
Alternatively, a paste of *vyoṣa*, *śivā*, *ugrā*, and *rajanī* drunk with milk completely removes the *ulba* and brings about extreme sharpness of the fetus.
[One should apply] a lump of clay heated by fire, sprinkled with milk, and still warm.
One should apply fomentation to the protruding umbilicus; by this, the swelling subsides.

In the case of suppuration of the umbilicus, oil boiled with harītakī, lodhra, priyaṅgu, and madhuka is recommended for massage, or alternatively, an application of a powder made from these same ingredients is advised.
If, during the consumption of wine, the root of the *tkekri* plant is extracted according to the prescribed rite and bound upon the hips or the neck, [the desired effect follows].
One certainly destroys the *ahiṇḍikā* [disease] by drinking seven-petaled flower, black pepper, and *gorocanā* ground together;
likewise, one may consume a paste made from burnt rice-gruel and flour.
The nose of a jackal, the tongue of a crow, the navel of a boar,
bell-metal, mercury, poison, the bone from the left shank of a frog of the rainy season— these,
when combined in equal parts and applied to the neck and waist region, [bring about the desired effect].
Anointing with oil is a remedy for the pacification of *ahiṇḍikā*, though it is not strictly a wholesome regimen.
In the case of *anāmaka*, one should eat a mixture of *ghurghurikā*, *bukka*, *marica*, *rocanā*, and fresh butter; this destroys the disease.
Having administered the milk of *saptapala*, *arka*, and *snuhī* mixed with oil applied to the head and palate,
and having given the powder of *rajanī*, the disease known as *anāmaka* shall perish.
One should also have the child lick fresh butter (*navanīta*) smeared over by a dog.
Indeed, an ointment made from the juice of ripe *sphuṭaka* leaves is beneficial for that [condition].
One part of oil,
two parts of urine, and [two parts] of the juice of *śimbi* leaf-pulp [should be used].
Having thus added four times as much cow's milk, one should cook the oil;
constant massage with it removes the disease known as Anāmaka. || 13 ||
Having taken cotton from the *arka* plant and sheep’s wool, and having made a wick by placing them in a cloth smeared with the fresh juice of *keśarāja* and soaked in oil (14),
the boy, though adorned, had his pair of eyes anointed with the collyrium produced therefrom.
It destroys the disease known as *kaṣṭamanāma* as well as afflictions caused by spirits and the like.
Having soaked a cloth placed on the bottom of a washing-tub with cow's urine,
one should perform a bath with the alkaline water of washermen using *okodaśālikā*.
A necklace filled with pearls,
coins, and mercury, smeared with ghee, is placed around the neck, and a bed of lotus petals is provided.
The medicine previously specified for men suffering from fever and other ailments— which destroys the disease known as *sukaṣṭamanāma*—
is to be given to children as well, though in a smaller dose. (17–18)
For a newborn infant in the first month, a medicinal dose of one *raktikā* should be administered as a linctus with honey, milk, sugar, and clarified butter.
One should increase the dose by one *raktikā* each month until the child reaches one year of age.
Thereafter, the monthly interest shall accrue until they reach sixteen years of age.
A decoction prepared with two types of turmeric, licorice, *siṃhī*,
and *śakrayava* cures fever and diarrhea in a child, and it overcomes their bodily humors.
The powder of ghanā, kṛṣṇā, aruṇā, and śṛṅgī, combined with honey,
cures fever and diarrhea in children, and removes cough, dyspnea, and vomiting.
(22) [A preparation] made from dhātakī, bilva, dhanyāka, lodhra, indrayava, and bālaka...
A linctus made with honey conquers fever, diarrhea, and vomiting in children.
(23) Haridrā, devadāru, sarala, śreyasī, the two types of bṛhatī, pṛśniparṇī, and śatāhvā, when licked with honey and ghee, [conquer these ailments]. (24)

It stimulates the digestive fire (grahaṇī), destroys the affliction of wind (māruta-ārti) along with jaundice (kāmalā), cures fever, diarrhea, and anemia (pāṇḍu), and removes all swellings in children. [The formulation consists of] priyaṅgu, black collyrium (kṛṣṇāñjana), parched grain (lāja), karkaṭaśṛṅgī, and black pepper (marica), combined with honey.
A linctus should be prepared for the child to remove vomiting, cough, and fever;
having powdered karkaṭaśṛṅgī, mustā, and ativiṣā,
one should administer it as a linctus with honey for infants.
For those afflicted by cough, fever, and vomiting,
one should give ativiṣā alone mixed with honey; furthermore, if a woman's breast milk is vomited whenever it is drunk, she should drink it with honey and ghee.
One should have the patient lick the juice of two vārtākī fruits along with pañcakola.
A linctus made from mango stone, parched grain (lāja), and rock salt, mixed with honey, cures vomiting.
Likewise, a powder of long pepper (pippalī) and black pepper (marica), combined with honey and sugar, [is effective].
The juice of *mātuluṅga* (citron) prevents hiccup and vomiting.
A paste made from the root of *peṭīpāṭhā*, *jambū*, and the bark of *sahakāra* [is used for this].
Thus, by holding the bolus individually at the heart, the navel, the palate, and so forth,
one checks the impulse arising from vomiting and diarrhea.
It certainly brings about that very same powerful result.
Bilva fruit, flowers of the dhātakī,
water with lodhra, and gajapippalī— [these together achieve the desired effect].
A decoction and an electuary mixed with honey should be administered to children suffering from diarrhea.
Water boiled with samaṅgā, dhātakī, lodhra, and sārivā [is also beneficial].
Even in cases of difficult-to-manage diarrhea in a child, one should give [a preparation] with honey;
[or] one should have the child drink in the morning a decoction prepared from ginger, ativiṣā, musta, vālaka, and indrayava, which destroys all types of diarrhea. (33–34)
A gruel prepared from *samaṅgā*, *dhātakī*, lotus, *vayasyā*, and *kacchurā*, ground together, destroys all types of diarrhea. Likewise,
parched rice with sugar taken with a decoction of *bilva* root [is beneficial].
Having stirred it, one should have the child drink it; it destroys vomiting and diarrhea.
A paste made of priyaṅgu, the kernel of kola seeds, musta, and rasāñjana, when licked with honey, removes vomiting, thirst, and diarrhea in children. (36–37)
A gruel made from *mocarasa*, *samaṅgā*, *dhātakī*, and the filaments of the lotus (*padmakeśara*),
when ground together, destroys bloody diarrhea.
A linctus consisting of a paste of sesame, *yaṣṭyāhvaka* (liquorice), along with oil, sugar, and honey, [is likewise effective].
It certainly stops the flow of blood and dysentery in a child.
Poppy seeds, licorice, sugar, and honey,
when sprinkled with rice-water, quickly destroy dysentery.
Alternatively, the root of *aṅkoṭa* or the root of *vaṭa* drunk with rice-water cures diarrhea.
[This cures] the very difficult-to-restrain disease of *grahaṇī*.
White cumin and *sarja* powder, mixed with water from *bilva* leaves, when drunk [cures it].
Or white *sarja* resin taken with jaggery destroys *āmavāta*, blood disorders, and colic; likewise, black pepper, *mahauṣadha*, and *kuṭaja*.
This, doubled successively in each subsequent step and combined with jaggery and buttermilk,
quickly destroys the disease of *grahaṇī*. || 43 ||

Goat's milk boiled for one year with *bilva*, *śakrāmbu*, and *moca* cures a child’s *grahaṇī* accompanied by blood within three nights when drunk. Likewise, juice extracted from *jambū* bark mixed with equal parts of goat's milk has the same effect.
In cases of internal suppuration (gudapāka), one should administer Pitta-alleviating treatments for children.
Rasāñjana is especially beneficial when used both as a drink and as an ointment.
[A preparation] made with kaṇā, paṇa, sugar, kṣaudra, sūkṣmailā, and saindhava...
This excellent linctus should be administered to children suffering from urinary retention.
By licking a powder of *saindhava* salt, *viśva*, *elā*, *hiṅgu*, and *bhārgī* with ghee,
or with water, a child may conquer flatulence and Vata-type colic.
By drinking a paste of *harītakī*, *vacā*, and *kuṣṭha* mixed with honey along with breast milk, a child is freed from the falling of the palate (*tālupāta*).
In the case of mouth ulcers (*mukhapāka*) in children, [one should apply] the essence of mango (*āmrasāra*) and iron filings (*mayoraja*).
Gairika combined with honey and rasāñjana is a medicinal preparation;
for inflammation of the mouth (mukhapāka), an ointment made from the bark and leaves of the aśvattha tree mixed with honey is applied,
as is another ointment made from dārvī, yaṣṭīmadhu, abhayā, and jātī leaves mixed with honey.

Rubbing with the juice of *jambīra* and the juice of *snuhī* leaves, performed immediately, quickly destroys inflammation of the mouth in a child. Powdered roasted meat of the common quail (*lāva*) and partridge (*tittiri*), combined with flower-nectar, [is likewise effective].
It quickly makes the mouths of children resemble a forest of lotus filaments.
Regarding diseases arising from the eruption of teeth, one should not excessively restrain the child; those ailments subside of their own accord once the teeth have grown.

O twice-born ones, if the teeth that are above the upper lip are crooked, how can there be peace for him? Even for such a child, one should give a gift with sacrificial fees; one should not worship such a child.
One afflicted by hiccups should drink milk boiled with the decoction of the five roots (*pañcamūlī*), mixed with ghee and ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), along with jaggery (*guḍa*).
Alternatively, one may take the powder of golden ochre (*suvarṇagairika*) together with honey.
Having licked this, a child afflicted by hiccups quickly attains comfort.
One should likewise take the powder of citraka, śṛṅgavera, dantī, and gavākṣī, and drink it with pleasantly warm water.
It destroys dyspnea, cough, and hiccups in children.
Powdered grapes, yāsa, abhayā, and kṛṣṇā, licked with honey and ghee, quickly subdues dyspnea as well as cough and tamaka-pāṇḍuroga.
The powder of puṣkara, ativiṣā, śṛṅgī, māgadhī, and dhanvayāsaka, when licked with honey, cures the five types of cough in children. [Also] the seeds of pomegranate, jīraka, and nāgakeśara.
This powder, licked with sugar and honey, destroys thirst.
Ashes of peacock feathers,
soaked overnight in water and then infused with that same water, should be drunk.
Water mixed with the ash of eight *vaṭa* seeds, when held in the mouth, destroys thirst and cures dryness of the mouth.
[Furthermore, a paste] made from *dārvī*, *mustaka*, and *gairika*, ground together with goat's milk, [should be applied].
An external ointment is recommended for a child to remove eye diseases.
Manahshila, conch-shell navel, long pepper, and rasanjana—this wick, combined with honey, cures all eye diseases in children. (63–64)
Lac (alaktaka), processed with mother’s milk, bitter oil, and sour gruel, conquers eye diseases when heated over the flame of a lamp.
A *puṭapāka* preparation consisting of a paste of ginger, *bhṛṅgarāja*, turmeric, and rock salt [is likewise effective].
In cases of eye diseases caused by *kukūla* (smoke), *bhadramusta* is beneficial as an eye-drop (*āścyotana*).
For children suffering from *pothakī* (pustules) and *kukūla*-induced conditions, a powdered collyrium (*cūrṇāñjana*) made of anti-worm drugs, realgar, *dārvī*, lac, and golden ochre should be used.

An ointment made from the powder of the root of *sudarśanā* should be applied in a *kukūlaka* (a heated bed of chaff). A plaster made of house-soot, turmeric, *kuṣṭha*, *vājigandhā*, and *indrayava*, mixed with buttermilk, quickly destroys ringworm (*sidhma*), scabies (*pāmā*), and eczema (*vicarcikā*) in a child.
One should cook ghee with a paste of *aśvagandhā* weighing one-thirteenth part and ten times as much milk; this should be drunk by children to promote nourishment and increase strength.
One should also cook ghee with the fresh juice of *cāṅgerī* and an equal amount of goat’s milk.
A preparation prepared with wood-apple (kapittha), the three pungents (vyoṣa), rock salt (sindhūttha), samaṅgā, blue water-lily (utpala), bālaka, bilva, dhātakī,
and mocarasa cures all types of diarrhea and especially destroys difficult-to-overcome malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) in children. || 71-72 ||
15. Śaṅkhapuṣpī, vacā, brāhmī, kuṣṭha, along with triphalā;
drākṣā with sugar, śuṇṭhī, jīvantī, jīraka, and balā; 73.
śaṭhī, durālabhā, bilva, dāḍima, surasa, and sthirā.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with one karṣa each of musta, puṣkaramūla, sūkṣmailā, and gajapippalī,
along with a decoction of kaṇṭakārī and four times that amount of milk.

This auspicious *kumāra-ghṛta-ratna* bestows happiness, produces strength and complexion, is meritorious, and increases nourishment, digestive fire, and power; it removes the effects of shadows, all malevolent planets, misfortune, worms, dental ailments, and diseases.
It removes all childhood ailments, especially the eruption of teeth.
Vacā, kuṣṭha, as well as brāhmī, siddhārthaka, śārivā, saindhava, and pippalī—with ghee as the eighth ingredient—[form this remedy]. (77–78)
This consecrated ghee, being pure, should be drunk day after day;
thus the boy shall become firm in memory, quick-witted, and intelligent.
Neither Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas, nor Bhūtas, nor Mātṛs [shall harm him].

This oil, prepared with four times as much whey (mastu) as lac-juice, along with rāsnā, candana, kuṣṭha, abda, vājigandhā, and the two types of niśā, is effective for children who drink it as an auspicious tonic. (80–81)
An oil massage with *śatāhvā*, *dāru*, *yaṣṭyāhvā*, *mūrvā*, *tiktā*,
and *hareṇu* destroys fever and demons in children and promotes strength and complexion.
A bath with a decoction of *sahā*, *muṇḍitikā*, and *udīcya* wards off malevolent spirits (*graha*).
An ointment should be made with *saptacchada*, *niśā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *candana*.
[Also used are] snake-skin, garlic, *mūrvā*, mustard seeds, sprouts of *ariṣṭa*, cat-hair, excrement, wool, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *vacā*, and honey. (83–84)
This incense destroys the fever of children and eliminates all planetary influences (grahas).
For the pacification of the planets, rites of offering (bali), propitiation (śānti), and sacrifice (iṣṭa) should be performed.
Furthermore, this mantra, which fulfills all desires, should be employed at the beginning of those rites.
19. “Oṃ namo bhagavate garuḍāya tryambakāya sadyastavastutaḥ svāhā | Oṃ kaṃ paṃ ṭaṃ śaṃ vainateyāya namaḥ | Oṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ kṣaḥ. [Visualize him] with the body-measure of a child.

Holding a flower garland in every direction, an offering of rice mixed with honey should be presented for the sake of pacification (*śāntika*). “Oṃkārī svarṇapakṣī, protect, protect the child, svāhā!”—this is the offering for Garuḍa. Oṃ, to Nārāyaṇa.
Homage!
On the first day of the month or the year, the mother-spirit named Nandanā seizes [the child]. As soon as it has been seized by her, first—

Fever arises; he emits an unpleasant sound, utters cries of distress, and does not take the breast-milk. I shall describe an offering for him by which well-being is attained: [earth] from both banks of a river—
Having taken earth and fashioned a doll, one should offer white rice,
white flowers, seven white banners, seven lamps, seven svastikas,
seven vaṭakas, seven śaṣkulīs, and jambūlikās.

One should offer an oblation (*bali*) consisting of seven handfuls of incense, flowers, betel, fish, meat, liquor, and the first portion of food at midday at a crossroads in the eastern direction. Then, having placed an *aśvattha* leaf into the water-pot (*kumbha*), one should—

One should bathe [the child] with water containing *rasona* (garlic), *siddhārthaka* (white mustard), *meṣaśṛṅga*, *nimba* leaves, and the remains of offerings to Śiva (*śivanirmālya*). One should fumigate the child with these: "Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa! Destroy, destroy the disease of [Name]!"
"Muñca muñca hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having thus offered the bali for three days, one should feed a Brāhmaṇa on the fourth day; thereafter, auspiciousness is attained. || 88 ||
On the second day, month, or year, the mother-spirit named Sunandā seizes [the child]. As soon as it has been seized by her, first there is fever; she opens the eyes and makes the body tremble.
The child does not thrive, does not sleep, cries, does not take the breast, and makes a gasping sound.
I shall describe the offering for him by which well-being is attained: one handful of rice, curd, and jaggery.
One *śarāva* measure of ghee mixed with fragrant betel and yellow flowers,
seven yellow banners, seven lamps, ten svastikas,
and fish, meat, liquor, and sesame flour— [these are placed] in the western direction.
An offering (bali) should be given at a crossroads for three days during the twilight;

thereafter, one should bathe [the image] with water of pacification (śāntyudaka). One should offer incense made from the remains of Śiva’s offerings (śivanirmālya), white mustard seeds, cat hair, uśīra root, and fresh ghee.
“Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya amukasya vyādhiṃ hana dana muñca muñca hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā. On the fourth day, one should feed a Brāhmaṇa; then it becomes successful.
Auspicious!
On the third day, month, or year, the mother-spirit named Pūtanā seizes [the child]. As soon as it has been seized by her, first—

Fever arises; it agitates the body, the infant does not take the breast, clenches its fists, cries out, and gazes upward. I shall describe the offering for this [demon], by which well-being is attained: earth from both banks of a river...
Having taken the *ṭṭikā* and fashioned a doll, one should offer fragrant flowers,
betel, red sandalwood, red flowers, seven red banners,
seven lamps, seven svastikas, bird meat, liquor, and the first portion of food.
In the western direction, at a crossroads, an offering (bali) should be given in the afternoon.

For three days, one should fumigate [the area] with the remains of Śiva’s offerings (nirmālya), guggulu resin, mustard seeds, nimba leaves, and ram’s horns, while reciting: “Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, for the child...”
"Destroy, destroy the disease! Release, release it! Diminish, diminish it! Svāhā! On the fourth day, one should feed a Brāhmaṇa; thereafter, auspiciousness is attained. || 90 ||

On the fourth day, month, or year, the mother-spirit named Mukhamuṇḍikā seizes [the child]. As soon as one is seized by her, first there occurs a fever; she causes the neck to bend and the eyes [to roll].
He opens his eyes, does not take the breast, cries, sleeps, and clenches his fist; I shall describe the offering for him by which prosperity is attained:
having taken earth from both banks of a river, one should fashion an image.
Having prepared blue lotus flowers, fragrant betel, ten banners, four lamps, thirteen svastikas, fish, meat, wine,
and first-portion food, [one should offer these] in the northern direction during the afternoon.
One should offer a bali-oblation on the path. The incense for the first month is: "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya hana hana muñca muñca svāhā.
On the fourth day, one should feed a Brāhmaṇa; thereafter, it becomes successful.
Auspicious!
On the fifth day, or in the fifth year, the mother-spirit named Kaṭapūtana seizes [the child]; as soon as it is seized by her, first—

Fever arises; it agitates the body, he does not take the breast-milk, and he clenches his fists. I shall describe the offering for him, by which well-being is attained: [one should take] clay from a potter’s wheel.

Having taken a doll and fashioned it, one should offer an oblation in the northeastern direction consisting of fragrant substances, betel, white rice, white flowers, five banners, five lamps, and five *vaṭaka* cakes,
using water consecrated for peace (*śāntyudaka*).

One should bathe [the image] with the remains of offerings made to Śiva (*śivanirmālya*), sloughed-off snake skins (*sarpnirmoka*), *guggulu* resin, neem leaves (*nimba-patra*), *bālaka*, and ghee, and offer incense. One should recite: “Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa!
Powder, powder the disease of [so-and-so]! Strike, strike! Svāhā!”
On the fourth day, one should feed a Brāhmaṇa; from that, auspiciousness is attained.
On the sixth day, month, or year, Śakuni seizes [the victim].

*Nikā* is the name of a *mātṛkā*. Merely by being seized by her, first there occurs fever; it causes a breaking pain in the limbs, and there is rising up day and night, and looking upward. For her, an offering—
I shall explain that by which auspiciousness is attained: having fashioned a small image from flour,
one should offer white flowers, red flowers, yellow flowers,
incense, betel, ten lamps, ten banners, and ten svastikas.

Ten handfuls, ten *vaṭaka* cakes, milk, rose-apple (*jambu*) fruits, fish, meat, and liquor—one should cause the *bali* offering to be given in the southeastern direction at midday when [the deity] has gone forth.
One should bathe [the image] with water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*). [One should offer] the *śivanirmālya*...

One should offer incense made of *lyāraṣona*, *guggulu*, snake slough, and *nimba* leaves mixed with clarified butter. Reciting the mantra: “Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya cūrṇaya cūrṇaya hana hana svāhā,” one should feed a Brāhmaṇa on the fourth day.
From that, auspiciousness is attained.
On the seventh day, month, or year,
when the mother-goddess named Śuṣkarevatī seizes [the child], by the mere fact of being seized by her—

First there occurs a fever; it agitates the limbs, causes one to clench the fists, and makes one weep. I shall describe the offering for him, by which prosperity is attained: red flowers, white flowers, perfumes, and betel.

In the western direction, at the village boundary, one should offer a bali in the afternoon near a tree, consisting of red rice, *kṛśara*, thirteen *svastika* cakes, fish, meat, wine, thirteen banners, and five lamps.

One should blow [on it]. A bath with water for pacification (śāntyudaka) should be performed; one should fumigate [the image] with guggulu, meṣaśṛṅgī, mustard seeds, uśīra, bālaka, and ghee. [The mantra is]: “Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya dīptatejase hana hana muñca muñca svāhā. This is the fourth [chapter].
On that day, one should feed a Brahmin; from that, auspiciousness is attained.
On the eighth day, month, or year, if the mother-spirit named Aryakā seizes [the child], by her being seized—

First, a fever arises; a vulture-like stench and a putrid odor are produced, and one does not take food, while the limbs become agitated. I shall describe the offering for him, by which he becomes successful.

Auspiciousness! Red and yellow banners; sandalwood as the flower; *śaṣkulī* cakes, *parpaṭikā* wafers, fish, meat, and *surājambuḍikā*; an offering should be presented at dawn in the wilderness. The mantra is: "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya."
"Oṃ hana hana muñca muñca for the sake of liberation from the four directions, hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā. On the fourth day, one should feed a Brāhmaṇa; thereafter, auspiciousness is attained. || 95 ||

On the ninth day, month, or year, the mother-spirit named Bhūsūtikā seizes [the child]. As soon as one is seized by her, fever first arises; there is constant vomiting and a breaking pain in the limbs.

He shows [the gesture] and forms a fist. I shall describe the offering for him by which auspiciousness is attained: having taken earth from both banks of a river and fashioned a small image, one should wrap it in a white cloth.
Klapuṣpa flowers, fragrant betel, thirteen white banners,
thirteen lamps, thirteen svastikas,
thirteen figurines, thirteen fish-figurines, fish, meat, and liquor— [these are] in the north.
One should offer a bali-oblation in the direction of the village exit.
One should bathe with water for pacification and offer incense made of guggulu, nimba leaves, cow horn, white mustard seeds, and ghee. The mantra is: “Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya...”
"O Nātha, O Four-Armed One, slay, slay! Release, release! Svāhā!
On the fourth day, one should feed a Brāhmaṇa; thereafter, auspiciousness is attained. || 96 ||
On the tenth day, month, or year, the mother-spirit named Nirṛti seizes [the child]. As soon as one is seized by her, fever first arises; she makes the body tremble and causes the sound "ātkāra."
He weeps, and urine and feces are discharged.
I shall describe an offering for him by which prosperity is attained:
having taken earth from both the near and far banks [of a river] and fashioned a small image, [one should offer] perfumes and betel.

One should offer a bali in the northwestern direction consisting of red flowers, red sandalwood, five-colored banners, five lamps, five svastikas, five small figurines, fish, meat, and liquor; as well as crow droppings and cow meat.
One should fumigate with rice-gruel, horn-shavings, garlic, cat-hair, nimba leaves, and ghee, while reciting:
“Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya cūrṇitahastāya muñca muñca svāhā. Then, on the fourth day, one should feed a Brahmin.
The child becomes healthy.
On the eleventh day, month, or year, if the mother-spirit named Pilipicchikā seizes him, by her—
Immediately upon being seized, fever first arises; one does not take food, the gaze becomes upward-turned, and there is a breaking pain in the limbs.
I shall now describe the offering for him, by which prosperity and well-being are attained.

Having fashioned a doll out of flour paste, one should sprinkle its face, which has been colored with red sandalwood, with milk. There should be yellow flowers, fragrant betel, seven yellow banners, seven lamps, and eight *vaṭaka* cakes.
Eight *śaṣkulī* cakes, eight *pūrikā* cakes, fish, meat, and liquor—

this offering (*bali*) should be presented in the eastern direction. One should bathe with water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*), [using] the remains of Śiva’s offerings (*śivanirmālya*), *guggulu*, cow-horn, snake-skin, and clarified butter.
One should offer incense, reciting: “Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya muñca muñca svāhā. On the fourth day, one should feed a Brahmin; thereafter, the child becomes healthy. || 98 ||
If on the twelfth day, month, or year,
the mother-spirit named Kāmukā seizes [the child], then as soon as it has been seized, first there is a fever; she laughs and plays with the hand.
He threatens, seizes, steps upon [the victim], and sighs repeatedly;
he does not take food. I shall prescribe an offering for him by which prosperity is attained: having fashioned an image out of milk, [one should offer] perfume...
One should offer the bali for all rites with betel, white flowers, seven white banners, seven lamps, seven cakes, and curd-rice held in the hand;
one should bathe [the deity] with water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*). [The offering of] Śiva’s remains (*śivanirmālya*)...

One should fumigate with guggulu, mustard seeds, and clarified butter, reciting: "Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, release, release, slay, slay, svāhā! On the fourth day, one should feed a Brāhmaṇa; thereafter the child becomes healthy. || 99 ||
Chapter 64:
The killing of the *ariṣṭa* [serpent], the mantra, the application for removing poison,
the bite of a biting snake, or even that of one with mild venom.
He who drinks the root of the *pratyaṅgirā* plant, ground with rice-water,
on a day of the *bhadra-yoga*, becomes pure.
How can he have fear of snakes, when it is only out of pride that a serpent, possessed by delusion, bites him at the root?
In that situation, he will certainly go to the very mouth of Yama before long.
When the sun has entered Aries, one should eat lentils with nimba leaves.

For one year, there shall be no fear of poison from him; of this there is no doubt. By drinking white *punarnavā* with its roots and rice-water under the asterism of Puṣya, men ward off the affliction of snake venom for an entire year.

One who has been bitten by a snake should drink house-soot, the two types of turmeric, and *taṇḍulīyaka* with its roots, mixed with curd and saturated with ghee; even one bitten by a fatal snake lives if an enema is administered using the root of *kūlikā*.
An application made with phlegm and earwax using the left ring finger destroys even terrible poison, as does sprinkling with human urine.
White mustard seeds, saturated with the juice of *śirīṣa* flowers [are likewise effective].
For those bitten by snakes, nasal drops, oral potions, and collyrium are beneficial for up to seven days.
Two palas each of nata and kuṣṭha, along with four palas of ghee and honey—
this potion brings relief even to those bitten by Takṣaka.

The root of *vandhyākarkoṭaka*, processed with goat’s urine and combined with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), used as a nasal drop (*nasya*) for one whose mind is afflicted by poison; likewise, *trivṛt*, *viśālā*, *madhuka*, and the two types of *haridrā*.
The group of madder dyes, all types of salt, and the three pungents (kaṭutrika), having been finely powdered and mixed with honey, should be placed inside a horn.
This medicine, when employed through the application of drinking,
collyrium, ointment, or nasal drops,
destroys the force of poison with irresistible power.

The great remedy named Mahāgada possesses great power. When the poison is in the stomach, emesis should be induced; when it resides in the skin, very cold applications such as plasters and affusions are required.
One should lick the pulp of *kapittha* with sugar and honey when the poison has reached the throat;
when it has reached the stomach (*āmāśaya*), one should take a pala of the powder of *natā* along with those two;
and when the poison has reached the large intestine (*pakvāśaya*), [one should take] *pippalī* and the two types of *rajanī*.
A person should drink equal parts of mañjiṣṭhā ground with cow bile.

A person who quickly administers this conquers the poison of scorpions.

By the method of applying a paste made from *vṛścikaviṣahṛt* and *kucapaṭu* ground together with incense from the city (*puradhūpa*)—like a solar leaf (*arkacchada*)—and applied as an ointment, [the poison is removed] by the delusion of the sting. 20–21.

One pala each of gold-leaf, liquid ghee, jaggery, and milk is a poison to dogs.

The root of *aṅkoṭa* combined with *kuṣṭha*, when eaten for three days, removes poison.
