Ghee, oil, muscle fat, and marrow are considered the best among unctuous substances;
among these, ghee is the most excellent because it conforms to the requirements of processing.
Ghee alone is used for disorders of pitta, while for vāta it should be combined with salt.

It should also be administered when phlegm is excessive, combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and alkali. Likewise, ghee is recommended for those desiring intelligence, memory, intellect, and digestive fire,
as well as for those suffering from glandular swellings, sinus tracts, worms, phlegm, obesity, and diseases of wind.

Oil should be administered to those with a hard bowel (krūrakoṣṭha) for the sake of lightness and firmness, and to those whose bodily constituents (dhātu) have been depleted by wind, exposure to the sun, travel on foot, carrying loads, sexual intercourse, or physical exercise; as well as to those who are dry, afflicted by distress, suffering from emaciation, having excessive digestive fire, or whose channels are obstructed by wind.

The remaining two [medicinal preparations] should be used in the spring for disorders of the junctions (sandhi), bones, vital spots (marman), and the visceral cavities (koṣṭha), as well as for pain from burns, wounds, dislocations, and diseases of the female genital tract, ears, and head. Oil is used in the rainy season, clarified butter at the end of the rains, while the last two [preparations] are used in the month of Mādhava (spring).
In this world, during the season for oleation, one may drink oil out of necessity.
A person with a predominance of vāta and pitta should drink it at night, even in the heat;
one with a predominance of śleṣman should drink it by day, when the sun is cool.
Those addicted to sweating therapies, purification procedures, alcohol, women, or physical exercise;

those who are anxious; the elderly; children; those with diminished strength; those who are dry; those with depleted blood and semen; and those afflicted by Vāta, rheumatism, Timira, or severe constipation [should avoid these].
Those with extremely weak digestion or excessively sharp digestion, as well as the obese and the emaciated, should not be given oleation therapy.
Nor should those afflicted by thigh-stiffness (ūrustambha), diarrhea, acute (āmaja) diseases, throat disorders, poisoning,
abdominal enlargement, fainting, vomiting, anorexia, phlegm disorders, thirst, or intoxication.

One who has recently given birth, one for whom nasal medication, enema, or purgation is appropriate, one accustomed to oleation, one who can endure hardship, one who is strong, and during cool weather—
such a person should drink the oil clear; indeed, drinking it clear is beneficial.
One who desires food should drink the unctuous substance that pacifies thirst at the time of eating.
For the sake of purification, however, a person should drink it when the evening meal has been digested;
one should wait for a full day and night, a whole day, or half a day.
Regarding the quantity of oil for digestion, there are three types: superior, middling, and inferior.

For the superior [dose], the measure is one *pala*; for the middling, it is three *akṣas*; and for the inferior, it is half a *pala*. This applies to both the oil and the medicinal herbs used in the decoction.

Warm water should be drunk after ghee, while soup is recommended after oil. After muscle fat (vasā) or marrow (majjā), however, the scum of boiled rice (maṇḍa) should be taken, or else warm water may be used for all of these.
But in the case of the oils of Bhallātaka and Tuvaraka, one should drink only cold water.
A person who has drunk medicated oil (sneha) should drink warm water when thirsty;
likewise, if the oil is not digested, one should expel it with warm water.
This applies to one whose oil does not digest due to improper conduct or because of its excessive quantity.
If it becomes obstructed and causes indigestion, one should induce vomiting with warm water.
Then, once the digestive tract has become light, one should administer the oily substance (sneha) again to the person;
if there is doubt as to whether it has been digested or not, the man should drink warm water.

By this, the belching becomes pure, and there arises a desire for food; one should eat food in moderation, and when drinking, one should drink tomorrow’s drink today— whether already drunk or yet to be drunk— fluid, warm, non-obstructive, not too unctuous, and harmless.
At least for three days, but at most for seven days,
a person who has undergone oleation (sneha) should be subjected to sudation (sveda);
beyond this, they do not prescribe further oleation.
It becomes assimilated after seven days; however,
a person with a soft bowel habit becomes oleated within three nights by the use of clear [unmedicated] oil,
whereas a person with a hard bowel habit becomes oleated within seven nights.

One who consumes the juices of fatty, liquid, hot, and desert-sourced foods should practice sudation; having remained thus for three days, one should then perform purgation and emesis. For another day, one should further excite the *kapha* by means of those [emetic] agents.

The downward movement of wind, a stimulated digestive fire, and stool that is unctuous and non-adherent [indicate proper oleation]. In one properly oleated, there is a sensation of unctuousness and exhaustion; in one who is dry, the opposite occurs.
However, in one excessively oleated, there is paleness and discharge from the nose, mouth, and anus.
For one who is dry, oleation should be administered; for one who is excessively unctuous,

drying measures should be applied using *śyāmāka*, *koradūṣa* grain, buttermilk, oil-cake, and parched grain flour— [these being indicated] for children, the elderly, and others who are unable to tolerate the avoidance of fats.
One should employ these non-shocking unctuous applications (yogas) immediately.
A gruel made with a small amount of rice, prepared in a fatty meat broth and mixed with honey, when consumed, is said to provide immediate unctuousness (snehana). || 27-28 ||
A gruel prepared with one *prasṛta* each of ghee, oil, muscle fat, marrow, and rice—
known as the "five-*prasṛta*" gruel— should be drunk by one desiring oleation. Likewise, a gruel containing ghee and many sesame seeds, but with very little rice, serves the same purpose.
When consumed while lukewarm, it is said to provide immediate oleation (snehana).
Alternatively, one should milk a cow into a jar mixed with sugar and ghee, or have the patient drink this; for this is indeed called immediate oleation.

One suffering from skin diseases (kuṣṭha), edema (śotha), or urinary disorders (prameha) should employ the meat of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals, along with jaggery, curd, milk, and sesame seeds, for oleation therapy.
One should oleate those patients with appropriate unctuous substances that have been processed and are non-aggravating.
One should first administer oil prepared with long pepper (pippalī), myrobalan (harītakī), and the three fruits (triphalā); immediately after that, sudation (sveda);
and for one who has undergone oleation and sudation, purification (saṃśodhana) follows thereafter.
In Chapter 68:
Fomentation (sveda) is desired in cases of vāta-śleṣman, or in vāta alone, or in kapha alone; it is prepared as unctuous-dry, unctuous, or dry, according to the requirements.
In the presence of disease, cold, and a strong body, the sweat is considered great; in a weak body, the sweat is weak; and in a body of medium strength, the sweat is considered moderate.
When Vāta is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), [the sweat is great]; when Kapha is situated in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), [the sweat is moderate].
Sudation preceded by oleation and likewise preceded by protection [of vulnerable areas] should be applied;
one should apply sudation gently— or not at all— to the testicles, heart, and eyes,
moderately to the groins, and as desired to the remaining parts of the body.

One should not apply sudation to those who are excessively obese, dry, weak, or fainting; nor to those requiring astringent therapy, those suffering from chest wounds, consumption, poison, or disorders of alcohol;
nor to those afflicted with cataracts, abdominal diseases, erysipelas, leprosy, wasting, or obesity.
Those who have undergone purgation with yellow substances, milk, curd, fats, or honey;
those suffering from hemorrhoids, burns, exhaustion, anger, grief, or fear;
and those afflicted by hunger, thirst, jaundice, anemia, urinary disorders, or pitta-related ailments.

For a pregnant woman, one who has menstruated, or one who has recently given birth, sudation is beneficial for mild and urgent diseases. When vāta is enveloped by medas and kapha, non-thermal sudation is recommended, as well as staying in a windless room, avoiding exertion, wearing heavy clothing, and inducing fear.
Resentment, anger, rage, excessive drinking, hunger, and heat—

these ten cause a person to perspire even in the absence of the quality of fire (heat). [In cases of] the subsiding of cold and pain, stiffness, heaviness, and suppression [of urges], [the application of heat is indicated].
When softness and perspiration have arisen, one should cease from the sudation. From it [excessive sudation], there arises the eruption of blisters, provocation of pitta and blood,
intoxication, fainting, giddiness, burning sensations, and exhaustion.
In cases of excessive sweating, pain in the joints, and thirst, one who knows the procedure should apply cooling treatments.
However, all types of sudation should be administered during agni-vāta (fever with digestive fire agitation) and when food has been digested.
For those embodied beings for whom nasal medication (nasya) and enema (basti) are to be administered,
those who require purification (śodhana) should first be subjected to sudation (sveda);
thereafter, after the foreign body has been removed, those suffering from complications of retained placenta (mūḍhagarbha) should be sweated.
When the wound has healed properly at the right time, it should subsequently be treated with sudation by one who understands;
likewise for fistula-in-ano and hemorrhoids, sudation should be applied both before and after [the surgical procedure].
Sudation may be performed using heated sand, the palms of the hands, bell-metal vessels, or cloths, or else with burning coals.
Or, through massage with Vata-alleviating substances combined with sour, salty, and oily agents, it becomes comfortable when applied lukewarm;

likewise, by means of sprinkling with heated milk or water, or with decoctions and other applications that pacify Vata, and gradually with the application of hot water-sprays and the abundant steam arising from stones and other materials. || 15 ||
Sudation therapies (sveda) preceded by heat, poultices, liquids, and fomentation are [indicated]; among these, the last and the first are for kapha,
while the second is for both vāyu and kapha.
The third [type of treatment] is prescribed when [the patient] is afflicted by pitta. 16.
Chapter 69:
One who has been properly oleated and fomented [should undergo treatment] in cases of kapha, or in a combination [of doshas], or where kapha is predominant.

For one whose *kapha* has been provoked by the prospect of vomiting on the following day, [one should administer] medicine prepared with fish, meat, sesame seeds, and so forth, according to the specific disorder,
combined with honey and rock salt; having divided the dosage according to the patient's digestive capacity, it should be consecrated with mantras.

“May Brahmā, Datta, the Aśvins, Rudra, Indra, the Earth, the Moon, the Sun, Vāyu, and Agni; the sages together with the multitude of medicinal herbs, and the hosts of spirits—may they all protect you!
Like an elixir for the rishis, like the nectar of the gods...”
"May this be your medicine, like excellent wine for the best of serpents.
(4) One should cause it to be drunk in the forenoon while standing on a seat reaching the knees;
then, with the mind fixed on that [medicine] and having developed nausea and salivation, one should vomit. (5)
Alternatively, one should drink a decoction of liquorice mixed with a paste of *vaśā*, *indrayava*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), and *vacā*, using a soft tube not pressed by the fingers; by this means,
one vomits thoroughly and effectively.
One who drinks rice-water ground with *phalinī* bark and vomits it in the forenoon [is cured];
warm *phalinī* bark, when licked with honey, removes poison born of bile and phlegm;
and copper dust taken as an emetic removes the defects caused by poison.
Having boiled *āṭarūṣa*, *vacā*, *nimba*, *paṭola*, and the bark of *phalinī*,
one should drink that water together with *madana* which induces vomiting.
One should set aside one *kuḍava* of the substances to be boiled in one *āḍhaka* of water.
One should administer this when one-fourth remains in the case of emetic therapies.
Combined with a decoction of nimba, along with phalinī, gada, madana, madhuka, and rock salt, and mixed with honey— this emetic is always recommended for a full stomach due to kapha.

Phala, jīmūtaka, ikṣvāku, kuṭaja, kṛtavedhana, and dhāmārgava— these should always be combined for emetic treatments. [In this process], kapha, pitta, and then vāta are [successively] expelled in order.
He by whom [the medicine] has been properly vomited is considered one who has successfully undergone the treatment,
provided that the purification of the heart, flanks, head, sense organs, and channels is observed, as well as a lightness of the body. || 13 ||
When vomiting is difficult, there is eruption of boils, urticaria, itching, impurity of all [the humors], heaviness of the limbs,
thirst, delusion, fainting, provocation of Vāta, and loss of sleep.
One should know that there is excessive loss of strength when [the medicine] has been vomited.
Therefore, in the evening or in the morning, one who is hungry should partake of peyā and other foods.
[These include] peyā, vilepī, and food both unprepared and prepared.

Having purified the body through superior, middling, or inferior purification, one who has been cleansed should consume the broth or meat juice twice, thrice, or once, respectively, in due order. || 16 ||
In emesis, four, six, eight, and ten urges are considered desirable for the inferior, moderate, and superior types respectively;
in purgation, these are doubled and tripled.

Likewise, a *prastha* [of emetic] may be two, three, or four times that amount. They say that emesis is desired until the end of bile (*pitta*), while purgation is half of that [duration], ending with phlegm (*kapha*).

Having removed two or three of the impelled urges, this [medicine] should be measured; however, in the case of emesis, it should be drunk. In both emesis and purgation, as well as in bloodletting, [the same applies].
The wise say that thirteen and a half palas constitute one prastha.
In cases where [emesis] is not properly induced, fasting should be practiced, or alternatively, purification (purgation) should be administered.
One who has vomited excessively should be anointed with ghee and immersed in cold water.

The physician should treat [the patient] with linctuses mixed with sugar and honey; however, if vomiting has become excessive, a heart-tonic purgative should be administered. One should not induce emesis in those suffering from cataracts (timira) or abdominal tumors (gulma).

Nor should one treat those afflicted by jaundice or abdominal disease, nor those who are obese, wounded, emaciated, extremely frail, or very old, nor those suffering from hemorrhoids, facial paralysis, or convulsions. || 22 ||
When there is dryness, in acute urinary disorders, during early pregnancy,
when blood is flowing copiously upward,
or when the internal organs are infested with worms, one should not approach a person.
One should not induce emesis when the feces are excessively constipated.
These individuals who are afflicted by indigestion, those suffering from poisoning, and those with excessively aggravated phlegm should also be made to vomit using water infused with madhuka.

Purgative therapy should be administered to one who has been lubricated, sweated, and vomited; for if it is applied otherwise, it is considered to cause disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī). 1.70.1

The digestive tract may be soft due to pitta, harsh due to the predominance of vāta and kapha, or moderate due to the equilibrium of the doṣas; therefore, the dosage should be administered according to these conditions.
[One should administer] sugar and honey combined with the powder of trivṛt.

For those who are delicate, one should drink a purgative consisting of one part each of cinnamon bark (*tvak*), cinnamon leaves (*patra*), and black pepper (*marica*), combined with *trivṛt* powder and sugar; this is an excellent laxative.
Having cut a stalk of sugarcane in two and smeared it with pastes...
Having wrapped and bound it with the fibers of the *strīmaṇḍī* plant, one should cook it properly using the technique of *puṭapāka*;
then, once it has become well-cooled, the sufferer of a bile disorder should eat it. 4.
One should administer a purgative for diseases of phlegm by licking a mixture of long pepper (pippalī), ginger (nāgara), alkali (kṣāra), black turpeth (śyāmā), and trivṛt together with honey.
[5] Harītakī, viḍaṅga, rock salt (saindhava), ginger (nāgara), and trivṛt—
Long pepper and all those [other ingredients] with cow’s urine constitute a purgative.
Trivṛt in the amount of three śāṇas, Triphalā in an equal amount, and Kṣāra, Kṛṣṇā, and Viḍaṅga in equal amounts— this powder [should be taken] with honey and ghee.
One should lick it with jaggery, or having made it into pills, one should employ it for gulmas caused by kapha and vāta, as well as for splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, and fistula-in-ano.
This is also a safe purgative that destroys other ailments as well.
Abhayā, pippalīmūla, marica, and likewise nāgara;
tvak, patra, pippalī, musta, viḍaṅga, and āmalaka—
one karṣa each of these, and three karṣas of dantī.
Six karṣas of white sugar and two palas of trivṛt should be taken; having ground everything into a fine powder, a bolus (modaka) is made with honey.
One should eat one every day and drink cold water afterwards.
A person continues to purge as long as they do not consume something warm.
[This remedy cures] anemia, poison, cough, pain in the calves and sides, backache, dysuria, hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano. (12–13)

This Abhayādyo Modaka, when administered by a physician who understands the proper sequence, quickly destroys urinary stones, urinary disorders, skin diseases, burning sensations, swellings, abdominal enlargements, consumption, and diseases of the eyes. (14)
Having drunk castor oil combined with double the quantity of a decoction of triphalā, or with milk, one is purged in no long time;
this results in the purification of the channels and the clarity of the sense organs.
Lightness, vigor, digestive fire, freedom from disease, and the proper movement of feces, bile, phlegm, and wind shall occur in sequence for one who has been properly purged. (16)
There may be a simultaneous aggravation of phlegm, bile, and wind, as well as loss of digestive fire, heaviness, catarrh,
drowsiness, vomiting, and anorexia.
There is no downward movement of wind (vātānulomya) when one has been excessively purged;
rather, numbness, body ache, fatigue, trembling, and other such symptoms arise from the wind produced by the depletion of phlegm, blood, and bile.
Excessive drowsiness, weakness, entry into darkness, insanity, and hiccups occur when one has been excessively purged.
One who is purged excessively has weak digestion, is not emaciated, and is not properly cleansed.
On that day, one should not have him drink gruel;
however, in the opposite case, the procedure for drinking gruel in the evening on that same day is said to be like that for one who has vomited.
Just as a tiny spark of fire, when fanned by grass, cow dung, and other fuels, gradually becomes great, stable, and capable of sustaining everything, so too [is the mind].
For one who is pure, the internal fire is stimulated by drinks and other such substances.
When pitta is present, one should administer purgation with astringent and sweet [drugs]; when kapha is present, with pungent [drugs];
and when vāyu is present, one should cause it to flow by administering unctuous, hot, and salty [substances]. || 20–21 ||
One should foment his abdomen with warm water and the heat of the palms.
On that same day when the purgation is slight, he should eat and drink again on the following day.
However, one whose digestive tract has not been sufficiently prepared by oleation should drink [the medicine] after ten days have passed.
Furthermore, having prepared the body again with oleation and sudation,
one should properly administer a suitable purgative after thoroughly mixing it while recollecting the previous sequence;
for a man who is weak, previously cleansed, possessing few morbid humors, and emaciated— [should be treated thus].
However, one whose digestive tract (koṣḍha) is not fully understood may drink only a small amount of mild medicine.

For those with a dry, fiery, or cruel digestive tract, for those who habitually practice physical exercise, and for those with a stimulated digestive fire (dīptāgni), the medicine is digested even without causing purgation.
To those [patients], one should first administer an enema (vasti), followed by an unctuous purgative (virecana).
For one who has not been unctuous, a purgative that is unctuous is recommended; for one who has been unctuous, a non-unctuous one is highly praised.
However, for one accustomed to oleation, one should first dehydrate them and then administer a purgative once again.

One should employ padmaka, uśīra, nāgāhvaya, and candana [in cases of excessive purgation]. In the case of excessive purgation (vireka), an ointment made from the bark of the mango tree ground with sauvīraka is a remedy for diarrhea, applied as a drink, an ointment, or a sprinkling.
Those who should not be purged by enema are: children, the elderly, the exhausted, the terrified, those with recent fever;

those with weak digestion, downward-moving pitta, hemorrhoids, anal ulcers, and diarrhea; those with foreign bodies, those whose bowels have been prepared for surgery, those with hard bowels, those who are excessively unctuous, and those suffering from wasting. (29)

An enema is recommended for those who are pregnant, have recently given birth, are afflicted by thirst, or suffer from indigestion; it is also desired when the *doṣas* are excessively aggravated or when *vāta* is predominant. (Adhikāra 71)
Having fed the patient with a diet reduced by one-quarter from the prescribed amount, one should administer the enema.
Oil should never be administered to one who has not eaten;
because of its subtlety, it would quickly rise upward into an empty stomach.
Six *pala* shall be the best dose for an oil enema (*anuvāsana*), five *pala* the middling, and four and a half *pala* the smallest; thus there are three measures.
At the first administration, two *pala* should be given initially, followed by an increase of half a *pala*.
In the second [year], the increase is one pala or an increase of two karṣas; in the bladder [vessel], it is an increase of eight māṣas;
this sequence is stated for the third [year]. || 4 ||
A quantity of one *māṣa* each of rock salt (*sindhujanman*) and *śatāhvā* should be added to a *pala* of oil; when combined with powdered rock salt and *śatāhvā*,
it becomes pleasantly warm and thus quickly exits through the mouth.
If one who has undergone purgation is to receive an oil enema (anuvāsana), it should be administered after seven nights have passed.
[The nozzle] may be made of gold, silver, lead, copper, tin, brass, bronze, iron, bone, wood, bamboo, or ivory.
The eyes should be fashioned from ivory, horn, or various gems,
provided with beautiful sockets, and measuring six,
twelve, or eight finger-breadths.
For those born at twenty-six or twelve years [of age], the apertures should be covered with a wick made of mung beans, jujube fruits, and *satīla* seeds.
Just as barley grains held between the thumb and the little finger at their base and tip are thick,
straight, and shaped like cow-tails.
The openings of the boluses should be smooth; there should be one *karṇikā* at the tip, occupying a fourth part,
and two fastenings for the enema-tube attached to the base.
It may be that of an old bull, or of a buffalo-eater, or of a pig, or even of a goat;
it should have a firm body and be free from obstruction in the head.
Dyed with astringent (kaṣāya), very soft, and thoroughly purified,
it should be applied to the eyes of men according to their age, well-secured with thread. || 11 ||
In the first year, the dose for a nirūha enema is one *prakuñca*;
thereafter, it should increase by one *prakuñca* every year until it reaches six *prasṛtas*.
Beyond that, one should increase the dose by one *prasṛta* annually until the patient is twelve or eighteen years old.
This measurement [of oil] is up to seventy years of age; beyond that, ten *prasṛta*s is the maximum.
A quarter of the dose used for *nirūha* (non-unctuous enema) is the measure for *anuvāsana* (unctuous enema).
The patient should have walked about and discharged feces and urine, and lie upon a comfortable bed.
Neither on a bed that is too high nor with the head raised, the patient should lie on his left side;
having drawn up the right thigh and extended the other, he should hold the enema bag in his left hand and press it with his right hand. || 15 ||
Likewise, one should insert its nozzle—smooth at the tip and lubricated—into the anus;
having inflated the mouth of the enema bag and secured it, one should hold it without shaking the hand, directing it toward the spine with a pace that is neither too fast nor too slow. (16)
One should squeeze [the nozzle] neither too forcefully nor too slowly, but only once;
one should leave a residue, for the wind remains in what is left behind.
This same procedure is prescribed even for the administration of a *nirūha* enema.
Then, once the oil has been applied, the patient should lie on his back for one hundred recitations of the mantra;
thus, as all the limbs are extended, the potency of the oil spreads throughout.
Thereafter, he should slowly contract his thighs and arms three times each.
One should strike him gently on the palms three times each;
then, one should slowly lift him by the buttocks, the hips, and the bed three times.
When the *vastu* has been thus prepared, he should then exert little effort and speak little.
One who is devoted to his conduct may sit at will upon a prepared bed;
however, another [type of patient] should be administered [purgatives] quickly once the oil has returned, for an oil that remains too long does not accomplish its purpose.
Indeed, the oil of one who passes it along with wind and feces returns [successfully].
Remaining for three watches of the night without suffering pain, he should be properly administered an oil enema (anuvāsana).
In the morning, he should drink water boiled with coriander and dry ginger in a dose equal to half the quantity of the decoction used;
if pitta is predominant, he should drink lukewarm water in that same measure as an after-drink.
By this, his digestive fire is kindled and a desire for food arises;
even if oil is administered day and night, it does not cause harm.
It produces the benefits of an enema, though once digested, its effect becomes slight.

If an unexpelled oil enema (snehabasti) causes no distress— whether it remains entirely, in small quantity, or is obstructed by dryness— it should be disregarded by one who understands [the condition]. However, if the oil does not come out after a day and night, one should remove it even if it is accompanied by complications.
When the oil enema (snehabasti) has not returned, no other irrigation (seka) is prescribed.
Furthermore, when the oil mixed with impurities does not return from one who has not been purified,
then bodily exhaustion, fatigue, pain, and dyspnea arise.
If there is heaviness in the colon (pakvāśaya), one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa). An unctuous enema (anuvāsana) prepared with sharp medicinal drugs may also be given;
however, an oil enema (snehabasti) must not be administered to a person whose body has not been purified.
In that case, the oil absorbs its potency but does not spread through the body,
even if it has been pressed by pure vāta alone.
One should administer the non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana) at all times throughout the day and night.

One should administer an unctuous enema on the third or fifth day, and repeat it again as required, depending on the digestion of the oil; this applies especially to those with aggravated Vata, who exercise daily, have a keen digestive fire, or are dry. (31-32)

Thus, when the body has been lubricated with three or four applications of unctuous substances, one should administer a purifying *nirūha* enema for the cleansing of the channels; however, if the body is not lubricated, one should employ an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) to provide oleation to the body.
If the *anuvāsana* is deficient, there will be obstruction of flatus, feces, and urine.
Excessive application of an oil enema (anuvāsana) causes burning fever and thirst.
One should not habitually employ either the oil enema or the decoction enema (nirūha) exclusively;
for from excessive oiling arises the moistening of pitta and kapha, while from excessive decoction enemas arises danger from vāta.
Those who are described as unfit for non-unctuous enemas (anāsthāpya) are considered unfit for unctuous enemas (anuvāsya) as well;

specifically, these include those suffering from anemia (pāṇḍu), jaundice (kāmalā), urinary disorders (meha), chronic catarrh (pīnasa), absence of acidity (niramla), splenic enlargement (plīha), diarrhea (viḍbheda), heaviness of the digestive tract (gurukoṣṭha), and abdominal diseases caused by kapha (kaphodara). || 36 ||
Those suffering from excessive secretions, very large worms, a distended abdomen, or aggravated Vāta;
those who have consumed poison or artificial poison (gara), those with indigestion, elephantiasis, or goiter;
as well as those who are excessively oleated, those with chest injuries, or those who are extremely emaciated—these should not be administered non-unctuous enemas (anāsthāpya). || 37–38 ||
One suffering from diarrhea, one purified by emesis, one who has received nasal medication (nāvana),

those with dyspnea, cough, excessive salivation, hemorrhoids, hiccups, flatulence, weak digestive fire, colic in the rectum, or those who have consumed food while suffering from intestinal obstruction, perforation, or abdominal dropsy— [these should not be given purgatives]. || 39 ||
One suffering from leprosy, one with diabetes, and a pregnant woman for seven months—[these should not be treated].
A wise person should not insist on [a single course] even when it is prescribed in a solitary case;
for sometimes an action, though seemingly contradictory, may be considered appropriate.
Emesis is prescribed as a well-administered treatment for those afflicted by vomiting, heart disease, and abdominal tumors;
and enema therapy is indicated for those suffering from skin diseases (kuṣṭha), once the appropriate stage has been reached.
(Chapter 72)
Having administered an unctuous enema (anuvāsana), one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) on the third day when the body has become oleated,
at midday when the meal has been somewhat digested and auspicious rites have been performed.
[The patient] should have been anointed, sweated, relieved of waste products, and not excessively hungry.
In the sequence of honey, unctuous substance, paste, decoction, and additive,
there are respectively three, six, two, ten, and three *palas* for those suffering from wind disorders;
for bile disorders, four, four, two, ten, and four *palas*.
Six, three, two, ten, and three [palas] of *nirūha* enema should be administered for *kapha*.
Having first added one *akṣa* of rock salt (*saindhava*) and two *prasṛta*s of honey,
and having stirred them together, one should then add two *prasṛta*s of oil.
Then, when the oil has become a single mass, one should add one *prasṛta* of the paste.
Once that decoction has been fully incorporated, one should add five *prasṛtas* of it; finally, one should add two *prasṛtas* of the respective adjuvant (*yathāvāpa*).
Likewise, strained through a cloth and heated by the steam from a pot of hot water, the enema prepared in this manner should consist of twelve *prasṛta* measures.
It does not wash away the medicinal drug, nor does it remain stuck after being applied.
And that well-administered Nirūha enema does not cause the parting of the hair (sīmantam).

One should administer the rectal enema (gudavasti) according to the previously mentioned procedure; once the enema has remained for thirty mātrās, the patient should then assume a squatting posture (utkaṭaka).
Wrapping [the hand] around the kneecap with the right hand,
one should remain vigorous while producing hundreds of sounds from the flicking of the eyes;
this may be done a second, a third, or a fourth time, according to the purpose.
When the signs of a successful nirūha enema have appeared, one should stop the administration of the enema.
[The signs are: the passage of feces, urine, and flatus; a relish for food; an increase in the digestive fire; and lightness of the abdominal cavity.

The subsiding of disease, restoration to the natural state, and strength—these are the well-established signs [of successful treatment]. 12. Non-application, over-application, and the application of a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) are treated like those of purgation. 13.
One [type of meat] is unctuous and hot for wind; two are equal [to wind] when combined with fat; two are sweet and cold for bile when combined with milk;
and three are pungent, slightly warm, and dry when combined with urine.
In cases of kapha, non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) should especially be administered;
for one [enema] draws vāyu back to its own path, the second draws pitta, and the third draws kapha. (15)

The wise physician should eliminate the non-decoction enema (nirūha) that remains for the duration of three finger-breadths or one muhūrta by means of purifying [drugs], using specifically non-decoction enemas combined with alkali, urine, and sour substances.
A non-decoction enema that is obstructed by deranged vāyu may remain for a long time.
It may bring about death through piercing pain, distress, fever, or abdominal distension.
However, it is the established rule that an asthāpana enema should not be administered to one who has eaten;
for it would eliminate the undigested food (āma) and provoke the humors (doṣas), leading to vomiting. || 17–18 ||
One should also consider the sequential stages when performing a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa). If the enema is pressed with excessive force, it may bypass its intended site and,
driven by the wind (vāta), emerge through the nostrils or the mouth.
It may cause vomiting, nausea, fainting, and other such symptoms, as well as a burning sensation.
In that case, one should quickly apply pressure to the throat, perform shaking (avadhūnana), administer sharp emetics and purgatives for the head and body, and apply cold affusions. || 20-21 ||
Then, once the patient has climbed onto the couch, bathed with warm water, and eaten rice with meat broth, one should administer an unctuous enema (sneha-vasti) according to the prescribed procedure.
On that day, a powerful fear of wind (vāta) is expected for him.
On that day, rice with meat broth (rasaudana) is recommended, as is an oil enema (anuvāsana).
One should administer one akṣa of śatāhvā, one akṣa of saindhava salt, and two palas each of honey and [the aforementioned oil] along with a decoction of daśamūla.
One should add one pala of oil and one fruit together;
this enema, which possesses half the quantity of the mother-liquids (milk), should be administered like a Nirūha enema.
There is neither [requirement for] oleation nor sudation, nor is there any restrictive regimen.
For this [preparation], approved by Ātreya, wards off all diseases;
it specifically destroys consumption, colic, and worms, generates semen,
and cures vātaśoṇita (gout/rheumatism).
This enema (vasti) promotes strength and complexion, is aphrodisiac, and is supreme for inducing male offspring.
It consists of oil, jaggery, meat broth, milk, sour substances,
urine, honey, and rock salt.

One should also administer these and other unmentioned substances in the application of Nirūha; furthermore, one should add the fruit of Madana. One should give one Karṣa of salt and one Pala of Madana.
In cases of Vāta, jaggery is used; in Pitta, sugar; and in Kapha, white mustard seeds (siddhārthaka) and others.
Taking one akṣa of rock salt (saindhava) and likewise one akṣa of dill seeds (śatāhvā), along with eight palas of cow’s urine and two palas of enema fluid (vastikā). || 29–30 ||
Having diligently mixed two *pala* of jaggery with all [the other ingredients],
the wise physician should administer a comfortably warm enema that has been strained through a cloth. This cures colic, constipation, flatulence, and severe dysuria.
When consumed, it instantly destroys worms, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), abdominal tumors (gulma), and other such ailments—
prepared with one pala, one śukti, one karṣa, and one kuḍava respectively, along with sour liquids, jaggery, rock salt, and cow’s urine.
This enema, combined with oil, removes colic, flatulence, and āma-vāta. This Vaitaraṇa alkaline enema (kṣāra-basti) may also be administered after a meal.
The sprouts of *badarī*, *airāvatī*, *śelu*, *śālmalī*, and *dhanvana*, boiled in milk until well-cooked, become highly effective when combined with blood and a slimy consistency.
[Likewise, meat] from boar, buffalo, ram, cat, deer, and cock [is used]. || 35 ||
In cases of slimy discharges (*picchila*), fresh blood or goat's blood should be administered as enemas.
Although thousands of enemas have been described in the works of Caraka and others, they are generally not used in practice; therefore, they have not been included here.
Enema therapy restores youth and bestows happiness, longevity, strength, digestive fire, intellect, voice, and complexion;
it accomplishes all purposes for children, the elderly, and the young alike.
It is free from adverse effects and removes all diseases.
38. Section 73: 1. *Pratimarśa*, *Avapīḍa*, *Nasya*, and likewise *Pradhamana*.
Head-purgation (śirovirecana) and nasal therapy (nastaḥ karma)— thus [nasal therapy] is fivefold.
One should know that the quantity of oil which reaches the mouth due to slight sniffing when poured into the nose is, by measure, the pratimarśa.
Pratimarśa, however, serves the purpose of nasal medication (nasya) without being harmful; one should apply an oil-smeared finger into the nose every morning and at night.
For those who are free from disease, this pratimarśa prevents snoring and promotes firmness [of the head].

This [rite] consisting of two drops should be performed at the end of the following: after eating at night or during the day; after sleeping, traveling, or physical exertion; after the discharge of semen; after anointing the head, gargling, urination, or applying collyrium; and after using a tooth-stick or laughing. (4–5)
The *avapīḍa* is considered to be of two types: purifying (*śodhana*) and astringent (*stambhana*). It is called *avapīḍa* because it is administered by being pressed down (*avapīḍya*).
It is used for the purpose of oleation in those whose heads are empty, as well as for the neck, shoulders, and chest.
Oil is administered for the purpose of strength; the term "nastaḥ" (nasal) is used here [to denote this].
Now, for an oleaginous nasal treatment (snaihika-nasya), eight drops should be administered into each nostril of men; this is the settled rule.
The *śukti* and the *pāṇiśukti* are proclaimed to be the three measures (*mātrās*).
Here, thirty-two drops are designated as a *śukti*.
Two *śuktis*, or a *pāṇiśukti*, should be given here by skillful men.

One should always administer oil through the nose (nasya) in cases of kapha and vāta, and muscle fat (vasā) in the case of pure vāta. In pitta, one should give ghee; in vāta associated with all [doshas], marrow should be used. One should employ medicinal fumigation (dhmāpana) and purgative powders (recana-cūrṇa) by means of the breath from the mouth.
Indeed, by means of a tube six finger-breadths long with two openings and containing medicinal powder, one extracts a much greater amount of the morbid humor (doṣa) because of its powdery state.
[This is done] with head-purgative substances or with oleaginous substances prepared with vāta-alleviating drugs.
The wise physician should administer head-purgation (śirovirecana) in those diseases:
heaviness of the head, headache, numbness, ophthalmia, diseases of the throat,
emaciation, facial tumors, worms, glandular swellings, leprosy, epilepsy, and chronic rhinitis.
For one whose head has been lubricated and fomented, who has performed his prior necessary duties, and who is lying on a bed in a windless place, one should again apply sudation above the clavicle.
Then, while the patient lies supine with half the body exposed and the hands and feet extended—
With the foot slightly raised and the head slightly bent,
one should close one nostril and pour the medicine— previously heated with warm water— alternately through a tube or a cotton swab.
Having given it, one should gently massage the soles of the feet, shoulders, hands, ears, and other parts; then, having snuffed it up, one should spit it out from both sides.
Thus, until the medicine is exhausted, one should administer the nasal therapy (nasya) two or three times.
One should administer unctuous substances at the conclusion of a purgative therapy, taking into account the nature of the humors and other factors.
One should perform the oleation procedure for seven days, every third day;
likewise, one should administer a head-purgative (errhine) with a single day's interval.
When [the eyes] are properly lubricated, there is easy respiration, sound sleep and awakening, and clarity of vision;
when they are dry, there is stiffness of the eyes, dryness of the nose and mouth, and a sense of emptiness in the head.
(21) When excessively lubricated, there is excessive itching, heaviness, salivation, loss of appetite, and catarrh.
When properly purged, there is lightness of the eyes, as well as clarity of the face and voice. When poorly purged, there is an increase in disease; when excessively purged, there is emaciation.
This applies to those who have drunk water, wine, poison, or oil, and to those desiring to drink again. || 22-23 ||

For those who have just eaten, those who have bathed their heads, those desiring to bathe, those with flowing blood, those afflicted by new catarrh, those suffering from childbirth, those with asthma or coughing, those who are pure,
those who have received enemas, and likewise on cloudy days or during times of distress. || 24 ||
Except in the case of a life-threatening illness, one should not administer nasal medication (nasya) for these [patients].

One should not apply nasal medication to those under seven years of age, nor to those over eighty years; likewise, inhalation therapy (dhūma) is not for those under twelve, and gargling (kavala) is not for those under five.

Neither for one whose purity [of the channels] is deficient in the tenth decade of life, nor for one who has exceeded seventy years, is *pratimarśa* recommended from birth until death; it is, however, as beneficial as an enema (*basti*).
(27) Thus ends the section on nasal therapy (*nasya*), and the section on the five medical procedures (*pañcakarma*) is completed.
Adhikāra 74:

Smoking (dhūma) is considered to be of five types: that for habitual use (prāyogika), that for oleation (snaihika), that for purgation (vairecana), that which cures cough (kāsahara), and that for inducing vomiting (vāmana). || 1 ||

A smoking tube (dhūmanetra) is recommended that is straight, produced from the three types of bamboo, measured by the size of the tip of a jujube stone (kola), and made of the same materials as a bladder-tube (bastinetra).
For the routine (prāyogika) and other types of smoking, it should be one cubit (hasta) in length, including an additional three-quarters of a part.
In the case of the two eyes and cough, [the length] is reduced by one-third; for the remaining [diseases], it is ten finger-breadths long.
Having prepared a wick from medicinal herbs, dried while still inside a reed, and having removed the core and scorched it with fire, a person should inhale the smoke.
One should exhale the smoke through the mouth alone;

or, inhaling it through the nose or the mouth, one should inhale the smoke through the mouth when the *doṣas* are located in the chest and throat, but through the nose when they reside in the head, the nostrils, or the eyes. (5)
A suppository made from fragrant substances, kuṣṭha, and tagara is considered appropriate for the *prāyogika* (habitual) type.
However, for the *snehika* (oleaginous) type, a suppository made from beeswax, fats, guggulu, and sarjaka—
substances used for head-purgation— is considered appropriate for the *vairecana* (purgative) type.

Kāsaghnī is considered to cure coughs, and Vāmanī is regarded as a means for inducing emesis; however, these two should not be administered to those suffering from pitta or blood disorders, those who have undergone purgation, nor to those with abdominal enlargements or urinary disorders (prameha).
They are also contraindicated in cases of blindness (timira), upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), flatulence (ādhmāna), Rohiṇī disease, and after the administration of enemas (basti).
In those who consume fish, alcohol, curd, milk, honey, oils, or poisons;

in cases of injury to the head; in jaundice; and when one has stayed awake at night, [the consumption of meat] causes internal hemorrhage, bilious fever, blindness, deafness, thirst, fainting, intoxication, and delusion.

If smoke is inhaled at an improper time or in excess, then a cooling regimen is beneficial. Thus, this procedure for the administration of medicinal smoke has been briefly elucidated. (11) Adhikāra 75.

In cases of Vāta, a gargle with unctuous, hot, and fatty substances is used; in Pitta, one that is sweet and cold for clarification; in Kapha, one that is pungent, sour, salty, and dry for purification;
and in the case of an ulcer, one that is astringent, sweet, and bitter for healing.
That quantity which can be easily moved about is beneficial for gargling (kavala).
However, that quantity which cannot be moved about is prescribed for the mouthful (gaṇḍūṣa). This [gargle] should be retained for as long as it takes for the morbid humor (doṣa) to be expelled.

Furthermore, another dose should also be administered with honey, ghee, and other such substances. The signs of purity in the gargle (kavala) are the subsiding of the disease, satisfaction, clarity, lightness of the mouth, and serenity of the sense organs.
Holding honey in the mouth as a gargle destroys burning sensations, thirst, and ulcers.
Sour rice-water (dhānyāmla) eliminates bad taste in the mouth, impurities, and foul odors;
it is slightly salty, cooling, and is excellent for removing dryness of the mouth.
A gargle of quick-acting alkaline and sour substances quickly breaks up the accumulation of phlegm;
for one who is healthy, holding a gargle of oil that alleviates Vata is beneficial.
(Adhikāra 76)
For all eye diseases, eye-drops (āścyotana) are beneficial at the outset; they eliminate pain, tearing, itching, friction, discharge, and redness.
They should be warm for [diseases caused by] Vāta and Kapha, and cold for blood and Pitta disorders.
Standing in a place sheltered from the wind, having opened the eye with the left hand,
one should pour ten or twelve drops [of the medicine] from the other hand— using a cotton wick— as far as two finger-breadths away onto the pupil.
Then, having wiped [the eyes] with a soft cloth, one should gently foment them with another cloth soaked in lukewarm water for the sake of alleviating phlegm and wind.
Eye irrigation that is too hot or too sharp leads to pain, redness, and loss of vision.
Excessive coldness, however, causes pricking, stiffness, and pain;
it results in roughness of the channels, friction, and difficult urination; it produces excessive discharge, yet very little urine, along with swelling and lack of drainage. || 5-6 ||

Then, collyrium (añjana) should be applied to the eyes when the impurity is located solely in the vessels of the pure body (śuddhatanu), when the signs of ripening are present, and when characterized by slight swelling, pain, itching, and sliminess;
it should be used when there is mild friction, tearing, and redness in the eye, even in the presence of thick dūṣikā (discharge).
Collyrium is of three types: scraping (lekhana), healing (ropaṇa), and clarifying the vision (dṛṣṭiprasādana).
Among these, scraping is achieved with astringent, sour, salty, and pungent substances; healing with bitter substances; and clarifying the vision with sweet and cold substances.
A probe ten fingers long in the middle, with a bud-like tip, made of copper is recommended for scraping; one made of black iron is for healing;
one made of gold or silver, ten fingers long, is for soothing.

The preparation of collyrium is of three kinds: a solid bolus (piṇḍa), a liquid extract (rasakriyā), and a powder (cūrṇa). One should apply these respectively when the humors (doṣas) are heavy, moderate, or light.
Then, without opening the eyes, one should slowly move them about within.
When the eyelids have been anointed, one should slightly move the collyrium; then, once the eye is relieved from the contact with the medicinal substance and has become tranquil,
one should wash away the residual defects of the disease with appropriate water.
Then, using the right thumb and a cloth, one should hold the left eye on its upper eyelid;
the other [eye] should be cleansed with the left [hand].
At night, this is done while sleeping; at midday, it is done by means of the rays of the hot-rayed sun.
The humors (doṣas), when increased, provoked, or driven [into the eye], cause diseases of the eyes;

therefore, for their pacification, one should always apply collyrium (añjana) in the morning and evening during clear weather. Furthermore, in cases of itching or stiffness, one should again employ sharp collyrium or medicinal smoke (dhūma).
However, when the eyes are inflamed by sharp collyrium, a counter-collyrium (pratyañjana) is beneficial immediately.

One should not apply collyrium to those who are frightened, have vomited, have undergone purgation, have eaten, or are suffering from the urge to defecate; nor to those who are angry, feverish, have wandering vision, suffer from headache, or are emaciated or sleep-deprived.
When the sun is not visible, after bathing the head, after consuming smoke or wine,

during indigestion, when heated by the sun, during daytime sleep, or when one is thirsty— these are the times for administering a nasal drop (tarpaṇa) once the head and body have been purified and there is no wind.
At the common time of morning or evening, while lying on one's back,
one should prepare a firm, even ridge of barley and mung beans outside the corners of the eyes, two finger-breadths in height, and then apply the prepared medicine according to the specific case.
When the eyes are closed with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) and heated water has been applied to dissolve it,

one should use muscle fat (*vasā*) in cases of night-blindness, wind-induced cataracts (*vātātimira*), painful obstruction, and similar ailments; then, as the patient slowly opens the eyes from the tips of the eyelashes, one should perform the procedure.
In those cases, one should calculate the measure for the eyelid, the junctions, and the white and black parts;
likewise for the eye itself in order of progression: one hundred, three hundred, five hundred, seven hundred, eight hundred, ten, and ten [morsels] for Mantha, and ten for Vāta.
One should retain [the medicine] for six [muhūrtas] in cases of pitta, for five in the state of health (svasthavṛtta), and for five in cases of balāsa;
then, having made the outer corner of the eye the exit, one should swallow the oil into a vessel.
One should then inhale medicated smoke and must not look at the form of the sky or the sun.

In this manner, one should administer [the medicine] daily when wind (vāta) is predominant, every other day when bile (pitta), and every second day when phlegm (kapha). For one in good health, one should give it every second day until satiety is reached; thus should it be applied.
Clarity of vision, adaptability to light, well-being, and clear, light eyes result from this.
In the case of satiety, there is a contrary effect; in the case of non-satiety, there are pains arising from excessive phlegm (kapha).
One should administer *puṭapāka* to the eyelashes previously mentioned.
It is considered emollient (*snehana*) when associated with wind (*vāta*), and scraping (*lekhanīya*) when associated with phlegm (*śleṣman*).
It clarifies [the humors] when there is thirst, debility, wind, bile, or blood, or when they are in a healthy state.

A bolus the size of a bilva fruit should be prepared separately from the paste of meat or medicinal herbs, using castor, banyan, or lotus leaves, respectively, for those who require unctuousness and so forth.
Having wrapped it and smeared it with clay, one should bake it over glowing embers of dhava wood, dhanvana wood, and cow dung until it has the luster of fire; once cooked,
one should squeeze out its juice and apply it to the eyes like an eye-satiation (tarpaṇa), holding it for one hundred, two, or three [units of time].
In the procedures of scraping (lekhana), oleation (snehana), and the final [purification], the first two should be lukewarm, while the latter should be cold.
At the end of those very two, there should be the removal of smoke (dhūmapa). Their applications therein are like those of saturation (tṛpti).
One should not employ tarpaṇa or puṭapāka in one who is unfit for nasal therapy (nasya).
For as many days as one practices [this], one becomes a recipient of double the benefit.
Now, one whose body is lubricated and who has been fed a meal of unctuous juices—
Facing the sun, perspiring, and seated on a high stool with the knees raised;
with the palms of his hands covered by soft cloth and his elbows resting upon his knees, he should press firmly against his temples with his fists, the thumbs placed inside.
One should perform clenching of the teeth, coughing, and puffing out the cheeks;
the man should restrain him from behind and wrap him with a cloth.
Having encircled his neck, one should insert the left index finger into the nose.

Having thus prepared [the patient] according to the prescribed method, one should pierce a vein located in the head. One should pierce a vein of the hand by having the patient sit comfortably with the arm unbent at the elbow and having him clench his fist with the thumb tucked inside.
Above the area to be pierced, a strip [of cloth] four finger-breadths wide should be placed; when the foot is well-positioned and pressed down below the knee-joint,
one should firmly grasp its ankle with both hands while the other foot is placed upon it.
Then, having bent the second [finger] slightly upward and bound it like a hand,
one should pierce the vein; in this manner, the knower of means should apply the respective instrument to those various locations even where they have not been explicitly mentioned.
Then, having placed the *vrīhimukha* instrument on the site to be incised, the physician should press it with the thumb and index finger while covering the palm [of the other hand];
having positioned the *kuṭhārī* with the left hand, [he should operate] with the other.
One should strike with the middle finger, released while pressed by the thumb.
One should insert the "rice-mouth" [needle] to the depth of a grain of rice in a fleshy part;
for bones, one should pierce the vein with the "axe-shaped" [needle] at the depth of half a barleycorn.
If the blood does not flow properly, one should cauterize the opening of the vein with a paste made of bilva, trikaṭu, turmeric, nata,
house-soot, salt, and oil; once the bleeding has proceeded correctly, the area should be treated with lukewarm oil and salt.
Even if one is strong, an impure person should not cause more than a *prastha* of blood to flow;
for if there is excessive bleeding, death may occur or severe disorders of Vāta may arise.
In that case, massage, meat broth, milk, and blood-drinking are the remedies.
Once the blood has flowed out, one should slowly remove the instrument and wash the opening of the vein with cold water.
Then, having smeared it with oil-soaked cotton, the mouth of the vessel should be bound;
if the blood is not fully purified, one should cause it to flow again in the evening, during the day, or on the following day.
If, however, the blood persists, one should quickly perform a hemostatic treatment using *lodhra*,
*priyaṅgu*, *pattaṅga*, black gram (*māṣa*), *yaṣṭyāhva* (liquorice), and red ochre (*gairika*); [as well as] clay from a potsherd, antimony, linen, soot, milky sap, bark, and sprouts.
One should powder the opening of the ulcer and drink a cold decoction of the padmaka group of drugs;
or, one should immediately after that venesection pierce that very same vein, or quickly cauterize the mouth of the vessel with a heated probe.
Even if blood remains, it should be retained; one should not cause excessive bleeding.
One should remove the remainder with a horn or the like, or bring it to a state of clarity (prasāda).
In a location free from vital points (marman) and close to the site, one should puncture the vein.

[This is not for] those who have passed their sixteenth year, nor for those seventy years old, nor for those whose blood has flowed excessively; nor for those who are ununctuous, nor for those who have sweated excessively, nor for those afflicted by wind (vāta) diseases; nor for pregnant women, women recently delivered, those with indigestion, nor for those suffering from hemorrhaging, dyspnea, or cough. || 20–21 ||
For those suffering from diarrhea, abdominal diseases, vomiting, jaundice, or emaciation of the entire body,
as well as for those who have consumed oleaginous substances or undergone the five types of purificatory procedures (karma),
one should not pierce a vein that is unrestrained, nor one that is oblique, nor one that has not been raised.
One should not stay in places that are too cold, too hot, windy, or cloudy, except in the event of a life-threatening illness.
When blood has been removed, light food and drink that stimulates digestion are beneficial, provided they are neither too hot nor too cold.
At that time, since the blood in the body is unstable,
the digestive fire must be protected with special care by a person who follows a wholesome diet and lifestyle. (24)
For a month, he may remain with strength gained from food, his complexion and senses radiant, desiring no sense objects, and possessing unimpeded force of power.
They say that a person endowed with happiness, possessed of nourishment and strength, and having pure blood, is healthy. (25) Adhikāra 78
One should rise during the *brāhma-muhūrta* for the sake of preserving one's life; then, having attended to the needs of the body and performed the rites of purification,
and having eaten in the morning food that is soft, slightly astringent, pungent, or bitter.
One should chew a tooth-stick without injuring the gums of the teeth. One should not eat [the stick] when suffering from indigestion, vomiting, dyspnea, cough, fever, or affliction;
nor when afflicted by thirst, inflammation of the mouth, or diseases of the heart, eyes, head, or ears.
One should constantly apply *sauvīra* collyrium for the benefit of the eyes.

After seven or eight nights, one should use *rasāñjana* for the purpose of inducing lacrimation; thereafter, one may partake of nasal drops (*nāvana*), gargles (*gaṇḍūṣa*), medicinal smoke (*dhūma*), and betel (*tāmbūla*).

Betel is unwholesome for those with hemorrhaging of the eyes due to injured *pitta*, for those with dry and agitated vision, for those afflicted by poison, fainting, or intoxication, and also for those suffering from consumption (*śoṣin*).
One should practice daily massage (*abhyaṅga*), which destroys old age, fatigue, and wind (*vāta*).
One should practice this especially on the head, ears, and feet.
External massage is for those afflicted by phlegm, those who have undergone purification therapies, and those with indigestion.
Any physical activity that promotes stability is a strength-increaser.
One should perform that [massage] with a measured amount, according to the capacity of one's body;
however, those afflicted by wind or bile disorders, children, the elderly, and those with indigestion should avoid it.
(8) Likewise, anointment with fragrant unguents should be performed, and thereafter one should carry out the ritual bath.
Sprinkling the lower body with warm water bestows strength;
however, sprinkling the head with that same water produces strength for the hair and eyes.
Bathing is [contraindicated] in cases of eye disease, facial disease, ear disease, and diarrhea, as well as for those who have suffered from a stroke.

It is forbidden [to eat] when one is bloated, suffering from catarrh, indigestion, or has just finished eating. One should have the hair of the body, nails, and beard clipped short; keep the openings of the body clean; be habituated to bathing; be fragrant, well-attired, and wear spotless garments.
He should constantly carry gems, perfected mantras, and great medicinal herbs.

Protected by an umbrella and sandals, he should walk looking only a yoke’s length ahead; at night, or when there is an urgent matter, he should go with a staff, observing silence, and accompanied by an assistant.
When the food is digested, one should eat wholesome and moderate amounts; one should not forcibly suppress natural urges.
One should not attend to other tasks while under the impulse of an urge, nor until an incurable disease has been conquered.
One should abandon the ten types of evil actions through body, speech, and mind.
One should speak at the proper time, what is beneficial, measured, consistent, and gentle.
One should always regard even insects and ants as one's own self;
one should not do to others what is disagreeable to oneself.
"How do my days and nights pass now, such that I am no longer a partaker of suffering? Thus, with constant mindfulness ever present,
the six seasons are traditionally reckoned in order as the two months beginning with Māgha."
In the winter, due to the suppression of cold by the wind, the digestive fire becomes powerful;
therefore, one should consume unctuous, sweet, sour, and salty tastes, as well as preparations made from wheat flour, meat, sugarcane, and milk, along with *surā* liquor. (18–19)
Fresh food, fat, oil, warm water for cleansing, sunlight used with propriety, fomentation, and footwear at all times;
[and a bed] spread with blankets, skins, silk, woven rugs, and elephant housings.
Clad in light garments of a warm nature, he should resort to a bed;
in a chamber with an inner floor warmed by the heat of embers, he should embrace his beloved, whose thighs, breasts, and hips are full, and who is anointed with aguru.
This very same regimen should be followed during the winter as well,
especially because at that time there is cold *madhvika* wine and the dryness produced by the season of eating;
for phlegm, having accumulated during the winter, is heated by the rays of the sun in the spring.
Having thus extinguished the fire, one should then apply remedies for diseases:
strong emetics, nasal drops, gargles, medicinal powders, collyriums, physical exercise, massage, medicated smoke, and lukewarm water for cleansing purposes. || 24-25 ||

Having bathed and anointed himself with camphor, sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron, and having eaten aged barley, wheat, honey, and roasted meat on a spit, he should drink āsava, ariṣṭa, sīdhu, mādhvīka, and mādhava liquors.
In spring, one should enjoy the youthfulness of women and of the forests; however, one should avoid food that is heavy, hot, unctuous, or sweet, as well as sleeping during the day.
In summer, the sun drinks up the moisture of the world with its rays.
At that time, food and drink that are sweet, cold, liquid, and unctuous are beneficial.
One who partakes in summer of cold *mantha* mixed with sugar, meat from wild animals and birds, ghee, milk, and *śāli* rice does not suffer.
One should drink wine only in small amounts, or not at all; otherwise, one may drink it with plenty of water.
At midday, with the body moistened by sandalwood paste, one should sleep in a fountain-house at night, on the roof of a palace where the wind blows and is strewn with the rays of the moon.
With his desires stilled, being fanned with fans and touched by hands smeared with sandalwood paste, he, adorned with pearls and gems, should enjoy her company;
yet during this time, he should avoid salty, sour, pungent, and hot foods, as well as physical exertion.

In the rainy season, due to the moisture of the earth, the discharge from clouds, and the acidity resulting from the ripening of water, the wind and other humors become aggravated when the strength of the digestive fire has diminished.
One should employ all moderate measures and whatever serves to stimulate the internal heat.
A non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) is indicated for one whose body is purified; likewise, aged grain, prepared meat-broths, the flesh of wild animals, soups, honey, aged *ariṣṭa* liquors,
celestial water, well-water, or boiled water should be used as food during very foul weather.
One should avoid food that is clearly sour, salty, or oily, as well as dried food, honey-like substances, and light meals;
one should also abandon river water, fermented gruel, daytime sleep, physical exertion, and exposure to the sun.
For those whose bodies have been accustomed to the cold of the rainy season, sudden exposure to the rays of the sun [is harmful].
The accumulated pitta of those who have undergone thermal therapies generally becomes aggravated in autumn.
To conquer it, one should employ bitter ghee, purgation, bloodletting, and, when hungry, consume light food that is bitter, sweet, and astringent.
In autumn, these are wholesome: sugarcane, *śāli* rice, mung beans, lake water, and boiled milk; and at nightfall, the rays of the moon.
So too are autumnal garlands and pure garments.
One should avoid snow, alkaline salts, over-satiation, curd, oil, liquids, and exposure to the sun; as well as strong liquor, sleeping during the day, and the wind and heat from the east.
One should resort to the first three tastes in the cold season and the rainy season, and the last three tastes in the spring.
In the summer, food and drink should be sweet; in autumn, sweet, bitter, and astringent;
in autumn and spring, dry; and cold during the end of the hot season and the rainy season. In brief, otherwise it should be the opposite.
One should constantly practice all [six] tastes, increasing each one in its respective season.
The first and last seven days of a season are known as the "junction of seasons" (*ṛtusandhi*); during that time, the previous regimen should be abandoned and the subsequent sequence adopted. (43–44)

Thus has been described seasonal suitability (ṛtusātmya), which consists of activities and diet; that which is beneficial due to its propriety is called domestic suitability (okasātmya). [Now follows:
That which possesses qualities contrary to those of regions and diseases by means of its own qualities...
Those who know what is wholesome (sātmya) desire both habitual conduct and the primary diet as being wholesome.
One should always employ that which maintains one's health and which prevents the arising of disorders not yet produced. (46–47)
Just as a wise man would be attentive to his duties regarding a city as if it were his own city, or like a charioteer regarding his chariot, or regarding his own body;
[so too was] the official who served as the vessel for the *rasavatī* (the royal kitchen) of the Lord of Gauḍa.
The son of Nārāyaṇa, Sunaya, born of a lineage as renowned as the Lodhra tree of Bhānu, the illustrious Cakradatta, is the one authorized here to hold the office of author. 1.
Whoever deposits here only those superior Siddhayogas that were not written in the original Siddhayoga, or extracts them alone,
by a person who knows the three Bhaṭṭas, the three paths, and the Vedas.
May a curse fall instantly upon his head!
